value:
Now Rann the Kite brings home the night
That Mang the Bat sets free--
The herds are shut in byre and hut
For loosed till dawn are we.
This is the hour of pride and power,
Talon and tush and claw.
Oh, hear the call!--Good hunting all
That keep the Jungle Law!
_Night-Song in the Jungle_

It was seven o’clock of a very warm evening in the Seeonee hills when Father Wolf woke up from his day’s rest, scratched himself, yawned, and spread out his paws one after the other to get rid of the sleepy feeling in their tips. Mother Wolf lay with her big gray nose dropped across her four tumbling, squealing cubs, and the moon shone into the mouth of the cave where they all lived. “Augrh!” said Father Wolf. “It is time to hunt again.” He was going to spring down hill when a little shadow with a bushy tail crossed the threshold and whined: “Good luck go with you, O Chief of the Wolves. And good luck and strong white teeth go with noble children that they may never forget the hungry in this world.”

It was the jackal--Tabaqui, the Dish-licker--and the wolves of India despise Tabaqui because he runs about making mischief, and telling tales, and eating rags and pieces of leather from the village rubbish-heaps. But they are afraid of him too, because Tabaqui, more than anyone else in the jungle, is apt to go mad, and then he forgets that he was ever afraid of anyone, and runs through the forest biting everything in his way. Even the tiger runs and hides when little Tabaqui goes mad, for madness is the most disgraceful thing that can overtake a wild creature. We call it hydrophobia, but they call it dewanee--the madness--and run.
“Enter, then, and look,” said Father Wolf stiffly, “but there is no food here.”

“For a wolf, no,” said Tabaqui, “but for so mean a person as myself a dry bone is a good feast. Who are we, the Gidur-log [the jackal people], to pick and choose?” He scuttled to the back of the cave, where he found the bone of a buck with some meat on it, and sat cracking the end merrily.

As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur belled
Once, twice and again!
And a wolf stole back, and a wolf stole back
To carry the word to the waiting pack,
And we sought and we found and we bayed on his track
Once, twice and again!

As the dawn was breaking the Wolf Pack yelled
Once, twice and again!
Feet in the jungle that leave no mark!

Eyes that can see in the dark--the dark!
Tongue--give tongue to it!  Hark!  O hark!
Once, twice and again!

All the talk we ever have heard
Uttered by bat or beast or bird--
Hide or fin or scale or feather--
Jabber it quickly and all together!
Excellent!  Wonderful!  Once again!

Now we are talking just like men!
Let’s pretend we are ... never mind,
_Brother, thy tail hangs down behind!_
This is the way of the Monkey-kind.

_Then join our leaping lines that scumfish through the pines,
That rocket by where, light and high, the wild grape swings.
By the rubbish in our wake, and the noble noise we make,
Be sure, be sure, we’re going to do some splendid things!_
Mowgli’s Song

THAT HE SANG AT THE COUNCIL ROCK WHEN HE
DANCED ON SHERE KHAN’S HIDE

The Song of Mowgli—I, Mowgli, am singing. Let the jungle listen to the
things I have done.
Shere Khan said he would kill—would kill! At the gates in the twilight
he would kill Mowgli, the Frog!
He ate and he drank. Drink deep, Shere Khan, for when wilt thou drink
again? Sleep and dream of the kill.
I am alone on the grazing-grounds. Gray Brother, come to me! Come to
me, Lone Wolf, for there is big game afoot!
Bring up the great bull buffaloes, the blue-skinned herd bulls with the
angry eyes. Drive them to and fro as I order.
Sleepest thou still, Shere Khan? Wake, oh, wake! Here come I, and the
bulls are behind.
Rama, the King of the Buffaloes, stamped with his foot. Waters of the
Waingunga, whither went Shere Khan?
He is not Ikki to dig holes, nor Mao, the Peacock, that he should fly.
He is not Mang the Bat, to hang in the branches. Little bamboos that
creak together, tell me where he ran?
_Ow!_ He is there. _Ahoo!_ He is there. Under the feet of Rama lies the
Lame One! Up, Shere Khan!
Up and kill! Here is meat; break the necks of the bulls!
_Hsh!_ He is asleep. We will not wake him, for his strength is very
great. The kites have come down to see it. The black ants have come up
to know it. There is a great assembly in his honor.
_Alala!_ I have no cloth to wrap me. The kites will see that I am
naked. I am ashamed to meet all these people.
Lend me thy coat, Shere Khan. Lend me thy gay striped coat that I may
go to the Council Rock.
By the Bull that bought me I made a promise—a little promise. Only thy
coat is lacking before I keep my word.
With the knife, with the knife that men use, with the knife of the
hunter, I will stoop down for my gift.
Waters of the Waingunga, Shere Khan gives me his coat for the love that
he bears me. Pull, Gray Brother! Pull, Akela! Heavy is the hide of
Shere Khan.
The Man Pack are angry. They throw stones and talk child’s talk. My
mouth is bleeding. Let me run away.
Through the night, through the hot night, run swiftly with me, my
brothers. We will leave the lights of the village and go to the low
moon.
Waters of the Waingunga, the Man-Pack have cast me out. I did them no
harm, but they were afraid of me. Why?
Wolf Pack, ye have cast me out too. The jungle is shut to me and the
village gates are shut. Why?
As Mang flies between the beasts and birds, so fly I between the
village and the jungle. Why?
I dance on the hide of Shere Khan, but my heart is very heavy. My mouth
is cut and wounded with the stones from the village, but my heart is
very light, because I have come back to the jungle. Why?
These two things fight together in me as the snakes fight in the
spring. The water comes out of my eyes; yet I laugh while it falls.
Why?
I am two Mowglis, but the hide of Shere Khan is under my feet.
All the jungle knows that I have killed Shere Khan. Look—look well, O
Wolves!
_Ahae!_ My heart is heavy with the things that I do not understand.

_The Beaches of Lukannon—the winter wheat so tall—
The dripping, crinkled lichens, and the sea-fog drenching all!
The platforms of our playground, all shining smooth and worn!
The Beaches of Lukannon—the home where we were born!_

I met my mates in the morning, a broken, scattered band. Men shoot us in the water and club us on the land; Men drive us to the Salt House like silly sheep and tame, And still we sing Lukannon—before the sealers came.

_Wheel down, wheel down to southward; oh, Gooverooska, go!
And tell the Deep-Sea Viceroys the story of our woe;
Ere, empty as the shark’s egg the tempest flings ashore,
The Beaches of Lukannon shall know their sons no more!_

Who has delivered us, who?
Tell me his nest and his name.
Rikki, the valiant, the true,
Tikki, with eyeballs of flame,
Rikk-tikki-tikki, the ivory-fanged, the hunter with eyeballs of
flame!

Give him the Thanks of the Birds,
Bowing with tail feathers spread!
Praise him with nightingale words--
Nay, I will praise him instead.
Hear!  I will sing you the praise of the bottle-tailed Rikki, with
eyeballs of red!
(_Here Rikki-tikki interrupted, and the rest of the song is lost._)

Shiv, who poured the harvest and made the winds to blow,
Sitting at the doorways of a day of long ago,
Gave to each his portion, food and toil and fate,
From the King upon the _guddee_ to the Beggar at the gate.
_All things made he--Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo!  Mahadeo!  He made all,--
Thorn for the camel, fodder for the kine,
And mother’s heart for sleepy head, O little son of mine!_

Wheat he gave to rich folk, millet to the poor,
Broken scraps for holy men that beg from door to door;
Battle to the tiger, carrion to the kite,
And rags and bones to wicked wolves without the wall at night.
Naught he found too lofty, none he saw too low--
Parbati beside him watched them come and go;
Thought to cheat her husband, turning Shiv to jest--
Stole the little grasshopper and hid it in her breast.
_So she tricked him, Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo!  Mahadeo!  Turn and see.
Tall are the camels, heavy are the kine,
But this was Least of Little Things, O little son of mine!_

When the dole was ended, laughingly she said,
“Master, of a million mouths, is not one unfed?”
Laughing, Shiv made answer, “All have had their part,
Even he, the little one, hidden ’neath thy heart.”
From her breast she plucked it, Parbati the thief,
Saw the Least of Little Things gnawed a new-grown leaf!
Saw and feared and wondered, making prayer to Shiv,
Who hath surely given meat to all that live.
_All things made he--Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo!  Mahadeo!  He made all,--
Thorn for the camel, fodder for the kine,
And mother’s heart for sleepy head, O little son of mine!_

We haven’t a camelty tune of our own
To help us trollop along,
But every neck is a hair trombone
(_Rtt-ta-ta-ta!_ is a hair trombone!)
And this our marching-song:
_Can’t!  Don’t!  Sha’n’t!  Won’t!_
Pass it along the line!
Somebody’s pack has slid from his back,
Wish it were only mine!
Somebody’s load has tipped off in the road--
Cheer for a halt and a row!
_Urrr!  Yarrh!  Grr!  Arrh!_
Somebody’s catching it now!
ALL THE BEASTS TOGETHER

Children of the Camp are we,
Serving each in his degree;
Children of the yoke and goad,
Pack and harness, pad and load.
See our line across the plain,
Like a heel-rope bent again,
Reaching, writhing, rolling far,
Sweeping all away to war!
While the men that walk beside,
Dusty, silent, heavy-eyed,
Cannot tell why we or they
March and suffer day by day.
_Children of the Camp are we,
Serving each in his degree;
Children of the yoke and goad,
Pack and harness, pad and load!_

value.da:
Nu bringer Rann Glenten natten hjem,
som Mang Flagermusen slipper fri —
hjordene er lukket inde i stalde og hytter,
mens vi er frie til daggry.
Dette er stolthedens og magtens time,
klo og hugtand og pote.
Åh, hør kaldet! — God jagt til alle,
der følger Junglens Lov!
_Natsang i Junglen_

value.en: It was seven o’clock of a very warm evening in the Seeonee hills when Father Wolf woke up from his day’s rest, scratched himself, yawned, and spread out his paws one after the other to get rid of the sleepy feeling in their tips. And good luck and strong white teeth go with noble children that they may never forget the hungry in this world.”
value.da: Klokken var syv en meget varm aften i Seeoneebjergene, da Far Ulv vågnede efter at have sovet hele dagen. Han kløede sig, gabede og strakte poterne ud én efter én for at ryste søvnen ud af tæerne. Mor Ulv lå med sin store grå snude hen over de fire hvalpe, der hvinede og væltede rundt, og månelyset faldt ind gennem åbningen til deres hule. »Augrh!« sagde Far Ulv. »Nu er det tid til at jage igen.« Han skulle lige til at springe ned ad bakken, da en lille skygge med en busket hale smuttede ind i åbningen og klynkede: »Held og lykke følge dig, du Ulvenes Høvding. Held og lykke og stærke hvide tænder følge også dine ædle børn, så de aldrig glemmer dem, der er sultne i denne verden.«

But they are afraid of him too, because Tabaqui, more than anyone else in the jungle, is apt to go mad, and then he forgets that he was ever afraid of anyone, and runs through the forest biting everything in his way. Even the tiger runs and hides when little Tabaqui goes mad, for madness is the most disgraceful thing that can overtake a wild creature. We call it hydrophobia, but they call it dewanee--the madness--and run.
value.da: Det var sjakalen — Tabaqui, Skålslikkeren. Indiens ulve ser ned på Tabaqui, fordi han render rundt og laver ballade, sladrer og spiser klude og lædertrævler fra landsbyernes affaldsbunker. Men de er også bange for ham. For Tabaqui kan, mere end nogen anden i junglen, blive gal. Så glemmer han, at han nogensinde har været bange for nogen, og løber gennem skoven og bider i alt, hvad der kommer i vejen. Selv tigeren stikker af og gemmer sig, når lille Tabaqui bliver gal, for galskab er det mest skammelige, der kan ramme et vildt dyr. Vi kalder det hundegalskab, men de kalder det dewanee — galskaben — og flygter.

value.en: “Enter, then, and look,” said Father Wolf stiffly, “but there is no food here.”
value.da: »Kom så ind og se efter,« sagde Far Ulv stift, »men her er ingen mad.«

value.en: “For a wolf, no,” said Tabaqui, “but for so mean a person as myself a dry bone is a good feast. Who are we, the Gidur-log [the jackal people], to pick and choose?” He scuttled to the back of the cave, where he found the bone of a buck with some meat on it, and sat cracking the end merrily.
value.da: »Ikke for en ulv,« sagde Tabaqui, »men for en så ydmyg en som mig er et tørt ben et fint festmåltid. Hvem er vi, Gidur-log [sjakalfolket], til at være kræsne?« Han skyndte sig om bag i hulen, hvor han fandt benet af en buk med lidt kød på, og satte sig tilfreds og knasede i enden af det.

value.en: “All thanks for this good meal,” he said, licking his lips. “How beautiful are the noble children! How large are their eyes! And so young too! Indeed, indeed, I might have remembered that the children of kings are men from the beginning.”
value.da: »Tak for dette gode måltid,« sagde han og slikkede sig om munden. »Hvor smukke de ædle børn er! Hvor er deres øjne store! Og så unge! Sandelig, sandelig, jeg burde have husket, at kongebørn er mænd fra fødslen.«

value.en: Now, Tabaqui knew as well as anyone else that there is nothing so unlucky as to compliment children to their faces. It pleased him to see Mother and Father Wolf look uncomfortable.
value.da: Tabaqui vidste lige så godt som alle andre, at intet bringer så meget uheld som at rose børn lige op i ansigtet. Det fornøjede ham at se, hvor ubehageligt det var for Mor og Far Ulv.

value.en: Tabaqui sat still, rejoicing in the mischief that he had made, and then he said spitefully:
value.da: Tabaqui sad stille og frydede sig over ulykken, han havde anrettet, og så sagde han ondskabsfuldt:

value.en: “Shere Khan, the Big One, has shifted his hunting grounds. He will hunt among these hills for the next moon, so he has told me.”
value.da: »Shere Khan, Den Store, har flyttet sine jagtmarker. Han fortalte mig, at han vil jage her i bjergene den kommende måned.«

value.en: Shere Khan was the tiger who lived near the Waingunga River, twenty miles away.
value.da: Shere Khan var tigeren, der boede tyve engelske mil væk, nede ved Waingungafloden.

value.en: “He has no right!” Father Wolf began angrily--“By the Law of the Jungle he has no right to change his quarters without due warning. He will frighten every head of game within ten miles, and I--I have to kill for two, these days.”
value.da: »Det har han ingen ret til!« brød Far Ulv vredt ud. »Efter Junglens Lov har han ikke ret til at flytte sit revir uden at give ordentligt varsel. Han vil skræmme alt vildt væk i ti engelske mil omkring, og jeg — jeg skal jo jage for to i denne tid.«

value.en: “His mother did not call him Lungri [the Lame One] for nothing,” said Mother Wolf quietly. “He has been lame in one foot from his birth. That is why he has only killed cattle. Now the villagers of the Waingunga are angry with him, and he has come here to make our villagers angry. They will scour the jungle for him when he is far away, and we and our children must run when the grass is set alight. Indeed, we are very grateful to Shere Khan!”
value.da: »Der er en grund til, at hans mor kaldte ham Lungri [Den Halte],« sagde Mor Ulv stille. »Han har været halt i den ene fod, siden han blev født. Det er derfor, han kun har dræbt kvæg. Nu er landsbyfolkene ved Waingunga vrede på ham, og så er han kommet hertil for at gøre vores landsbyfolk vrede. Længe efter at han er rejst, vil de lede efter ham i junglen, og når de sætter ild til græsset, må vi og vores børn flygte. Ja, vi skylder virkelig Shere Khan stor tak!«

value.en: “Shall I tell him of your gratitude?” said Tabaqui.
value.da: »Skal jeg fortælle ham om jeres taknemmelighed?« sagde Tabaqui.

value.en: “Out!” snapped Father Wolf. “Out and hunt with thy master. Thou hast done harm enough for one night.”
value.da: »Ud!« snerrede Far Ulv. »Ud og jag sammen med din herre. Du har skabt ballade nok for én nat.«

value.en: “I go,” said Tabaqui quietly. “Ye can hear Shere Khan below in the thickets. I might have saved myself the message.”
value.da: »Jeg går,« sagde Tabaqui sagte. »I kan høre Shere Khan nede i krattet. Jeg kunne have sparet mig ulejligheden med at bringe nyheden.«

value.en: Father Wolf listened, and below in the valley that ran down to a little river he heard the dry, angry, snarly, singsong whine of a tiger who has caught nothing and does not care if all the jungle knows it.
value.da: Far Ulv lyttede, og nede i dalen, der løb ned mod en lille flod, hørte han den tørre, vrede, snerrende, syngende klynken fra en tiger, der ikke har fanget noget og er ligeglad med, om hele junglen ved det.

value.en: “The fool!” said Father Wolf. “To begin a night’s work with that noise! Does he think that our buck are like his fat Waingunga bullocks?”
value.da: »Sikke en tåbe!« sagde Far Ulv. »At begynde natten med sådan en larm! Tror han, vores bukke er som de fede okser ved Waingunga?«

value.en: “H’sh. It is neither bullock nor buck he hunts to-night,” said Mother Wolf. “It is Man.”
value.da: »Sssh. Det er hverken tyr eller buk, han jager i nat,« sagde Mor Ulv. »Det er Menneske.«

value.en: The whine had changed to a sort of humming purr that seemed to come from every quarter of the compass. It was the noise that bewilders woodcutters and gypsies sleeping in the open, and makes them run sometimes into the very mouth of the tiger.
value.da: Klynken blev til en slags hummende spinden, der lød, som om den kom fra alle sider på én gang. Den lyd forvirrer skovhuggere og sigøjnere, der sover udendørs, så de nogle gange render lige ind i gabet på tigeren.

value.en: “Man!” said Father Wolf, showing all his white teeth. “Faugh! Are there not enough beetles and frogs in the tanks that he must eat Man, and on our ground too!”
value.da: »Menneske!« sagde Far Ulv og blottede alle sine hvide tænder. »Fy! Er der ikke biller og frøer nok i dammene, siden han skal æde Menneske — og det på vores egen grund!«

value.en: The Law of the Jungle, which never orders anything without a reason, forbids every beast to eat Man except when he is killing to show his children how to kill, and then he must hunt outside the hunting grounds of his pack or tribe. The real reason for this is that man-killing means, sooner or later, the arrival of white men on elephants, with guns, and hundreds of brown men with gongs and rockets and torches. Then everybody in the jungle suffers. The reason the beasts give among themselves is that Man is the weakest and most defenseless of all living things, and it is unsportsmanlike to touch him. They say too--and it is true--that man-eaters become mangy, and lose their teeth.
value.da: Junglens Lov befaler aldrig noget uden grund. Den forbyder ethvert dyr at æde Menneske, medmindre det dræber for at lære sine unger, hvordan man gør; og selv da skal det jage uden for sin flok eller stammes jagtmarker. Den egentlige grund er, at når man dræber et menneske, kommer der før eller siden hvide mænd på elefanter med geværer, og hundredvis af brune mænd med gonger, raketter og fakler. Så lider alle i junglen. Dyrene fortæller hinanden, at Menneske er det svageste og mest forsvarsløse af alle levende væsener, så det er ikke fair jagt at røre ham. De siger også — og det er sandt — at menneskeædere får fnat og mister tænderne.

value.en: The purr grew louder, and ended in the full-throated “Aaarh!” of the tiger’s charge.
value.da: Spinden blev højere og højere, til den brast i tigerens fulde »Aaarh!«, mens han sprang til angreb.

value.en: Then there was a howl--an untigerish howl--from Shere Khan. “He has missed,” said Mother Wolf. “What is it?”
value.da: Så udstødte Shere Khan et hyl — et hyl, der slet ikke lød som en tiger. »Han missede,« sagde Mor Ulv. »Hvad er der sket?«

value.en: Father Wolf ran out a few paces and heard Shere Khan muttering and mumbling savagely as he tumbled about in the scrub.
value.da: Far Ulv løb et par skridt ud og hørte Shere Khan mumle og brumme rasende, mens han kastede sig rundt i krattet.

value.en: “The fool has had no more sense than to jump at a woodcutter’s campfire, and has burned his feet,” said Father Wolf with a grunt. “Tabaqui is with him.”
value.da: »Tåben var så dum at springe ind i en skovhuggers bål og har svedet poterne,« sagde Far Ulv med et grynt. »Tabaqui er hos ham.«

value.en: “Something is coming uphill,” said Mother Wolf, twitching one ear. “Get ready.”
value.da: »Der kommer noget op ad bakken,« sagde Mor Ulv, mens det ene øre sitrede. »Gør dig klar.«

value.en: The bushes rustled a little in the thicket, and Father Wolf dropped with his haunches under him, ready for his leap. Then, if you had been watching, you would have seen the most wonderful thing in the world--the wolf checked in mid-spring. He made his bound before he saw what it was he was jumping at, and then he tried to stop himself. The result was that he shot up straight into the air for four or five feet, landing almost where he left ground.
value.da: Der lød en svag raslen fra buskene i krattet. Far Ulv krøb sammen og samlede bagbenene under sig, klar til at springe. Og hvis du havde været der og set på, ville du have set noget helt forunderligt — en ulv, der standser sig selv midt i springet. Han var sprunget, før han kunne se, hvad han sprang efter, og så prøvede han at stoppe. Det sendte ham lige op i luften, fire eller fem fod, og han landede næsten på samme sted, hvor han var sprunget fra.

value.en: “Man!” he snapped. “A man’s cub. Look!”
value.da: »Menneske!« gøede han. »Det er et menneskebarn. Se!«

value.en: Directly in front of him, holding on by a low branch, stood a naked brown baby who could just walk--as soft and as dimpled a little atom as ever came to a wolf’s cave at night. He looked up into Father Wolf’s face, and laughed.
value.da: Lige foran ham stod et nøgent, brunt barn, der lige var gammelt nok til at gå. Det holdt fast i en lav gren — et så blødt og buttet lille væsen, som nogensinde var kommet til en ulvehule om natten. Han kiggede op i Far Ulvs ansigt og lo.

value.en: “Is that a man’s cub?” said Mother Wolf. “I have never seen one. Bring it here.”
value.da: »Ser et menneskebarn sådan ud?« spurgte Mor Ulv. »Jeg har aldrig set et. Kom med det herover.«

value.en: A Wolf accustomed to moving his own cubs can, if necessary, mouth an egg without breaking it, and though Father Wolf’s jaws closed right on the child’s back not a tooth even scratched the skin as he laid it down among the cubs.
value.da: En ulv, der er vant til at bære sine egne hvalpe, kan om nødvendigt holde et æg i munden uden at knuse det. Far Ulv lukkede kæberne om barnets ryg, og ikke én tand ridsede huden, da han satte det ned blandt hvalpene.

value.en: “How little! How naked, and--how bold!” said Mother Wolf softly. The baby was pushing his way between the cubs to get close to the warm hide. “Ahai! He is taking his meal with the others. And so this is a man’s cub. Now, was there ever a wolf that could boast of a man’s cub among her children?”
value.da: »Hvor lille! Hvor nøgen, og — hvor modig!« sagde Mor Ulv blidt. Barnet skubbede sig ind mellem hvalpene for at komme tæt på hendes varme hud. »Ahai! Han spiser sammen med de andre. Så det her er altså et menneskebarn. Har der nogensinde været en ulvinde, der kunne prale af at have et menneskebarn blandt sine unger?«

value.en: “I have heard now and again of such a thing, but never in our Pack or in my time,” said Father Wolf. “He is altogether without hair, and I could kill him with a touch of my foot. But see, he looks up and is not afraid.”
value.da: »Jeg har af og til hørt, at det er sket, men aldrig i vores Flok og aldrig i min tid,« sagde Far Ulv. »Han har ikke et hår på kroppen, og jeg kunne dræbe ham med et enkelt tryk af poten. Men se, hvordan han kigger op uden den mindste frygt.«

value.en: The moonlight was blocked out of the mouth of the cave, for Shere Khan’s great square head and shoulders were thrust into the entrance. Tabaqui, behind him, was squeaking: “My lord, my lord, it went in here!”
value.da: Månelyset forsvandt fra hulens åbning, for Shere Khan pressede sit store firkantede hoved og sine skuldre ind i indgangen. Bag ham hvinede Tabaqui: »Herre, herre, her gik den ind!«

value.en: “Shere Khan does us great honor,” said Father Wolf, but his eyes were very angry. “What does Shere Khan need?”
value.da: »Shere Khan viser os en stor ære,« sagde Far Ulv, selv om hans øjne brændte af vrede. »Hvad ønsker Shere Khan?«

value.en: “My quarry. A man’s cub went this way,” said Shere Khan. “Its parents have run off. Give it to me.”
value.da: »Mit bytte. Et menneskebarn løb denne vej,« sagde Shere Khan. »Dets forældre er stukket af. Giv det til mig.«

value.en: Shere Khan had jumped at a woodcutter’s campfire, as Father Wolf had said, and was furious from the pain of his burned feet. But Father Wolf knew that the mouth of the cave was too narrow for a tiger to come in by. Even where he was, Shere Khan’s shoulders and forepaws were cramped for want of room, as a man’s would be if he tried to fight in a barrel.
value.da: Far Ulv havde ret: Shere Khan var sprunget ind i en skovhuggers bål, og smerten i de forbrændte poter havde gjort ham rasende. Men Far Ulv vidste også, at hulens åbning var for smal til, at en tiger kunne komme ind. Selv hvor han stod, sad Shere Khans skuldre og forpoter fast i det trange rum, ligesom en mand ville sidde fast, hvis han prøvede at slås inde i en tønde.

value.en: “The Wolves are a free people,” said Father Wolf. “They take orders from the Head of the Pack, and not from any striped cattle-killer. The man’s cub is ours--to kill if we choose.”
value.da: »Ulvene er et frit folk,« sagde Far Ulv. »De adlyder Flokkens Høvding og ikke nogen stribet kvægdræber. Menneskebarnet er vores — til at dræbe, hvis vi vælger det.«

value.en: “Ye choose and ye do not choose! What talk is this of choosing? By the bull that I killed, am I to stand nosing into your dog’s den for my fair dues? It is I, Shere Khan, who speak!”
value.da: »I vælger og I vælger ikke! Hvad er det for snak om at vælge? Ved den tyr, jeg dræbte, skal jeg stå og snuse ind i jeres hundehul efter min retmæssige andel? Det er mig, Shere Khan, der taler!«

value.en: The tiger’s roar filled the cave with thunder. Mother Wolf shook herself clear of the cubs and sprang forward, her eyes, like two green moons in the darkness, facing the blazing eyes of Shere Khan.
value.da: Tigerens brøl fyldte hulen med torden. Mor Ulv rystede sig fri af hvalpene og sprang frem, hendes øjne som to grønne måner i mørket vendt mod Shere Khans flammende øjne.

value.en: “And it is I, Raksha [The Demon], who answers. The man’s cub is mine, Lungri--mine to me! He shall not be killed. He shall live to run with the Pack and to hunt with the Pack; and in the end, look you, hunter of little naked cubs--frog-eater--fish-killer--he shall hunt thee! Now get hence, or by the Sambhur that I killed (I eat no starved cattle), back thou goest to thy mother, burned beast of the jungle, lamer than ever thou camest into the world! Go!”
value.da: »Og det er mig, Raksha [Dæmonen], der svarer. Menneskebarnet er mit, Lungri — mit og kun mit! Ingen skal dræbe ham. Han skal leve og løbe med Flokken og jage med Flokken; og til sidst, husk mine ord, du jæger af små nøgne unger — du frøæder — du fiskedræber — så skal han jage dig! Forsvind nu, ellers sender jeg dig, ved den sambarhjort, jeg dræbte (jeg æder ikke udsultet kvæg), tilbage til din mor, du svedne junglebæst, mere halt, end da du blev født! Gå!«

value.en: Father Wolf looked on amazed. He had almost forgotten the days when he won Mother Wolf in fair fight from five other wolves, when she ran in the Pack and was not called The Demon for compliment’s sake. Shere Khan might have faced Father Wolf, but he could not stand up against Mother Wolf, for he knew that where he was she had all the advantage of the ground, and would fight to the death. So he backed out of the cave mouth growling, and when he was clear he shouted:
value.da: Far Ulv så forbløffet til. Han havde næsten glemt den gang, han vandt Mor Ulv i åben kamp mod fem andre ulve, dengang hun løb med Flokken, og navnet Dæmonen ikke bare var pæne ord. Shere Khan kunne måske have holdt stand mod Far Ulv, men mod Mor Ulv kunne han ikke gøre noget. Han vidste, at hun stod stærkt, hvor hun stod, og at hun ville kæmpe til døden. Snerrende bakkede han ud af hulen, og da han var kommet udenfor, råbte han:

value.en: “Each dog barks in his own yard! We will see what the Pack will say to this fostering of man-cubs. The cub is mine, and to my teeth he will come in the end, O bush-tailed thieves!”
value.da: »Enhver hund gør højt i sin egen gård! Vi får at se, hvad Flokken siger til at opfostre menneskeunger. Ungen er min, og mine tænder får ham til sidst, I tyve med busket hale!«

value.en: Mother Wolf threw herself down panting among the cubs, and Father Wolf said to her gravely:
value.da: Mor Ulv kastede sig udmattet ned blandt hvalpene, og Far Ulv sagde alvorligt til hende:

value.en: “Shere Khan speaks this much truth. The cub must be shown to the Pack. Wilt thou still keep him, Mother?”
value.da: »Shere Khan har ret i én ting. Vi må vise ungen for Flokken. Vil du stadig beholde ham, Mor?«

value.en: “Keep him!” she gasped. “He came naked, by night, alone and very hungry; yet he was not afraid! Look, he has pushed one of my babes to one side already. And that lame butcher would have killed him and would have run off to the Waingunga while the villagers here hunted through all our lairs in revenge! Keep him? Assuredly I will keep him. Lie still, little frog. O thou Mowgli--for Mowgli the Frog I will call thee--the time will come when thou wilt hunt Shere Khan as he has hunted thee.”
value.da: »Beholde ham!« sagde hun forpustet. »Han kom her i mørket, helt alene, nøgen og frygteligt sulten, og alligevel var han ikke bange! Se, han har allerede skubbet en af mine egne unger til side. Den halte slagter ville have dræbt ham og så være løbet tilbage til Waingunga og have ladet vores landsbyfolk gennemsøge alle vores huler for at få hævn! Beholde ham? Selvfølgelig vil jeg beholde ham. Lig stille, lille frø. Åh, du Mowgli — for jeg vil kalde dig Mowgli Frøen — en dag skal du jage Shere Khan, ligesom han har jagtet dig.«

value.en: “But what will our Pack say?” said Father Wolf.
value.da: »Men hvad vil vores Flok sige?« sagde Far Ulv.

value.en: The Law of the Jungle lays down very clearly that any wolf may, when he marries, withdraw from the Pack he belongs to. But as soon as his cubs are old enough to stand on their feet he must bring them to the Pack Council, which is generally held once a month at full moon, in order that the other wolves may identify them. After that inspection the cubs are free to run where they please, and until they have killed their first buck no excuse is accepted if a grown wolf of the Pack kills one of them. The punishment is death where the murderer can be found; and if you think for a minute you will see that this must be so.
value.da: Junglens Lov siger klart, at en ulv må forlade sin Flok, når han tager en mage. Men når hans hvalpe kan stå på egne ben, skal han vise dem frem for Flokkens Råd. Det holdes som regel hver måned ved fuldmåne, så de andre ulve kan lære hvalpene at kende. Når de er set, kan hvalpene løbe, hvorhen de vil. Og indtil en hvalp har fældet sin første buk, er der ingen undskyldning for, at en voksen ulv i Flokken dræber den. Straffen er døden, hvis den skyldige kan findes. Tænk over det et øjeblik, så forstår du, at sådan må det være.

value.en: Father Wolf waited till his cubs could run a little, and then on the night of the Pack Meeting took them and Mowgli and Mother Wolf to the Council Rock--a hilltop covered with stones and boulders where a hundred wolves could hide. Akela, the great gray Lone Wolf, who led all the Pack by strength and cunning, lay out at full length on his rock, and below him sat forty or more wolves of every size and color, from badger-colored veterans who could handle a buck alone to young black three-year-olds who thought they could. The Lone Wolf had led them for a year now. He had fallen twice into a wolf trap in his youth, and once he had been beaten and left for dead; so he knew the manners and customs of men. There was very little talking at the Rock. The cubs tumbled over each other in the center of the circle where their mothers and fathers sat, and now and again a senior wolf would go quietly up to a cub, look at him carefully, and return to his place on noiseless feet. Sometimes a mother would push her cub far out into the moonlight to be sure that he had not been overlooked. Akela from his rock would cry: “Ye know the Law--ye know the Law. Look well, O Wolves!” And the anxious mothers would take up the call: “Look--look well, O Wolves!”
value.da: Da hvalpene havde lært at løbe lidt, ventede Far Ulv til natten for Flokkens møde. Så tog han dem med, sammen med Mowgli og Mor Ulv, op til Rådsklippen. Det var en bakketop fuld af sten og store blokke, så der kunne gemme sig hundrede ulve. Akela, den store grå Ensomme Ulv, ledede hele Flokken med sin styrke og snildhed. Han lå udstrakt på sin klippe, og under ham sad mindst fyrre ulve i alle størrelser og farver: gamle krigere med grævlingegrå pels, der kunne fælde en buk alene, og unge sorte treårige, der troede, de kunne. Den Ensomme Ulv havde været deres leder i et år. I sin ungdom var han to gange blevet fanget i ulvefælder, og en gang var han blevet slået og efterladt som død. Derfor kendte han menneskers skikke og vaner. Der blev næsten ikke talt ved Klippen. I midten af kredsen af forældre væltede hvalpene rundt oven på hinanden. Af og til gik en ældre ulv stille hen til en hvalp, så nøje på ham og listede lydløst tilbage til sin plads. Nogle gange puffede en mor sin hvalp helt ud i måneskinnet for at være sikker på, at ingen overså ham. Akela råbte fra sin klippe: »I kender Loven — I kender Loven. Se godt efter, I ulve!« Og de urolige mødre gentog: »Se — se godt efter, I ulve!«

value.en: At last--and Mother Wolf’s neck bristles lifted as the time came--Father Wolf pushed “Mowgli the Frog,” as they called him, into the center, where he sat laughing and playing with some pebbles that glistened in the moonlight.
value.da: Til sidst puffede Far Ulv »Mowgli Frøen«, som de kaldte ham, ud i midten — og i det øjeblik rejste Mor Ulvs nakkehår sig. Mowgli sad og lo og legede med nogle småsten, der glimtede i måneskinnet.

value.en: Akela never raised his head from his paws, but went on with the monotonous cry: “Look well!” A muffled roar came up from behind the rocks--the voice of Shere Khan crying: “The cub is mine. Give him to me. What have the Free People to do with a man’s cub?” Akela never even twitched his ears. All he said was: “Look well, O Wolves! What have the Free People to do with the orders of any save the Free People? Look well!”
value.da: Akela løftede ikke hovedet fra poterne, men blev ved med det samme jævne kald: »Se godt efter!« Bag klipperne lød et dæmpet brøl. Det var Shere Khan, der råbte: »Ungen er min. Giv mig ham. Hvad har det Frie Folk med et menneskebarn at gøre?« Akelas ører rørte sig ikke engang. Han sagde bare: »Se godt efter, I ulve! Hvad har det Frie Folk at gøre med at tage imod ordrer fra andre end det Frie Folk selv? Se godt efter!«

value.en: There was a chorus of deep growls, and a young wolf in his fourth year flung back Shere Khan’s question to Akela: “What have the Free People to do with a man’s cub?” Now, the Law of the Jungle lays down that if there is any dispute as to the right of a cub to be accepted by the Pack, he must be spoken for by at least two members of the Pack who are not his father and mother.
value.da: Der steg dybe knurren op overalt. En ung ulv på sit fjerde år kastede Shere Khans spørgsmål tilbage mod Akela: »Hvad har det Frie Folk med et menneskebarn at gøre?« Junglens Lov siger nemlig, at hvis nogen bestrider en hvalps ret til at blive optaget i Flokken, skal mindst to af Flokkens medlemmer tale hans sag, og ingen af dem må være hans far eller mor.

value.en: “Who speaks for this cub?” said Akela. “Among the Free People who speaks?” There was no answer and Mother Wolf got ready for what she knew would be her last fight, if things came to fighting.
value.da: »Hvem vil tale for denne unge?« spurgte Akela. »Hvem af det Frie Folk vil tale?« Ingen svarede. Mor Ulv gjorde sig klar til en kamp, som, vidste hun, ville blive hendes sidste, hvis det kom til kamp.

value.en: Then the only other creature who is allowed at the Pack Council--Baloo, the sleepy brown bear who teaches the wolf cubs the Law of the Jungle: old Baloo, who can come and go where he pleases because he eats only nuts and roots and honey--rose upon his hind quarters and grunted.
value.da: Så rejste det eneste andet væsen, der må deltage i Flokkens Råd, sig på bagbenene og gryntede. Det var Baloo, den søvnige brune bjørn, der lærer ulvehvalpene Junglens Lov. Gamle Baloo kan komme og gå, hvor han vil, fordi han kun spiser nødder, rødder og honning.

value.en: “The man’s cub--the man’s cub?” he said. “I speak for the man’s cub. There is no harm in a man’s cub. I have no gift of words, but I speak the truth. Let him run with the Pack, and be entered with the others. I myself will teach him.”
value.da: »Et menneskebarn — et menneskebarn?« sagde han. »Jeg vil tale for menneskebarnet. Et menneskebarn kan ikke gøre nogen skade. Jeg er ingen stor taler, men det, jeg siger, er sandt. Lad ham løbe med Flokken og blive optaget sammen med de andre. Jeg vil selv lære ham op.«

value.en: “We need yet another,” said Akela. “Baloo has spoken, and he is our teacher for the young cubs. Who speaks besides Baloo?”
value.da: »Vi mangler endnu én stemme,« sagde Akela. »Baloo, som underviser vores unge hvalpe, har talt for ham. Hvem andre vil tale efter Baloo?«

value.en: A black shadow dropped down into the circle. It was Bagheera the Black Panther, inky black all over, but with the panther markings showing up in certain lights like the pattern of watered silk. Everybody knew Bagheera, and nobody cared to cross his path; for he was as cunning as Tabaqui, as bold as the wild buffalo, and as reckless as the wounded elephant. But he had a voice as soft as wild honey dripping from a tree, and a skin softer than down.
value.da: En sort skikkelse sprang ned i kredsen. Det var Bagheera, den Sorte Panter, blæksort fra snude til hale, men i visse lys kunne man ane panterens pletter i pelsen, som mønstret i moiré-silke. Alle kendte ham, og ingen ville stå i vejen for ham. Han var lige så snu som Tabaqui, lige så modig som den vilde bøffel og lige så hensynsløs som en såret elefant. Men hans stemme var blød som vild honning, der drypper fra et træ, og hans pels var blødere end dun.

value.en: “O Akela, and ye the Free People,” he purred, “I have no right in your assembly, but the Law of the Jungle says that if there is a doubt which is not a killing matter in regard to a new cub, the life of that cub may be bought at a price. And the Law does not say who may or may not pay that price. Am I right?”
value.da: »Akela, og I, det Frie Folk,« spandt han, »jeg har ingen ret til at tale ved jeres møde. Men Junglens Lov siger, at når der er strid om en ny unge, og det ikke er en sag om drab, kan ungens liv købes for en pris. Og Loven siger ikke, hvem der må betale den. Har jeg ret?«

value.en: “Good! Good!” said the young wolves, who are always hungry. “Listen to Bagheera. The cub can be bought for a price. It is the Law.”
value.da: »Godt! Godt!« råbte de unge ulve, der altid er sultne. »Hør, hvad Bagheera siger. Ungens liv kan købes for en pris. Det er Loven.«

value.en: “Knowing that I have no right to speak here, I ask your leave.”
value.da: »Da jeg ikke har ret til at tale her, beder jeg jer om lov.«

value.en: “Speak then,” cried twenty voices.
value.da: »Tal så,« råbte tyve stemmer.

value.en: “To kill a naked cub is shame. Besides, he may make better sport for you when he is grown. Baloo has spoken in his behalf. Now to Baloo’s word I will add one bull, and a fat one, newly killed, not half a mile from here, if ye will accept the man’s cub according to the Law. Is it difficult?”
value.da: »At dræbe en forsvarsløs, nøgen unge er en skam. Og når han bliver voksen, kan han måske give jer bedre jagt. Baloo har talt for ham. Til Baloos ord vil jeg lægge en tyr — en fed tyr, nydræbt, mindre end en halv engelsk mil herfra — hvis I vil tage imod menneskebarnet efter Loven. Er det så svært?«

value.en: There was a clamor of scores of voices, saying: “What matter? He will die in the winter rains. He will scorch in the sun. What harm can a naked frog do us? Let him run with the Pack. Where is the bull, Bagheera? Let him be accepted.” And then came Akela’s deep bay, crying: “Look well--look well, O Wolves!”
value.da: Snesevis af stemmer råbte i munden på hinanden: »Hvorfor skulle vi bekymre os? Vinterregnen slår ham ihjel. Solen brænder ham op. Hvordan kan en nøgen frø gøre os noget? Lad ham løbe med Flokken. Hvor har du efterladt tyren, Bagheera? Tag ham ind.« Over larmen steg Akelas dybe kald: »Se godt efter — se godt efter, I ulve!«

value.en: Mowgli was still deeply interested in the pebbles, and he did not notice when the wolves came and looked at him one by one. At last they all went down the hill for the dead bull, and only Akela, Bagheera, Baloo, and Mowgli’s own wolves were left. Shere Khan roared still in the night, for he was very angry that Mowgli had not been handed over to him.
value.da: Mowgli var stadig dybt optaget af stenene og lagde ikke mærke til, da ulvene kom og kiggede på ham én efter én. Til sidst gik de alle ned ad bakken efter den døde tyr, og kun Akela, Bagheera, Baloo og Mowglis egne ulve var tilbage. Shere Khan brølede stadig ude i natten, for han var meget vred over, at Mowgli ikke var blevet udleveret til ham.

value.en: “Ay, roar well,” said Bagheera, under his whiskers, “for the time will come when this naked thing will make thee roar to another tune, or I know nothing of man.”
value.da: »Ja, brøl du bare,« mumlede Bagheera i sine knurhår. »For hvis jeg ellers kender noget til mennesker, kommer der en dag, hvor denne nøgne lille skabning får dig til at brøle om noget helt andet.«

value.en: “It was well done,” said Akela. “Men and their cubs are very wise. He may be a help in time.”
value.da: »Det var godt gjort,« sagde Akela. »Mennesker og deres unger er meget kloge. Han kan blive en hjælp med tiden.«

value.en: “Truly, a help in time of need; for none can hope to lead the Pack forever,” said Bagheera.
value.da: »Sandelig til nytte, når der er brug for hjælp. Ingen kan regne med at være Flokkens leder for evigt,« sagde Bagheera.

value.en: Akela said nothing. He was thinking of the time that comes to every leader of every pack when his strength goes from him and he gets feebler and feebler, till at last he is killed by the wolves and a new leader comes up--to be killed in his turn.
value.da: Akela sagde intet. Han tænkte på den tid, der kommer til enhver leder af enhver flok, hvor styrken forlader ham, og han bliver svagere og svagere, indtil han til sidst bliver dræbt af ulvene, og en ny leder rejser sig — til selv at blive dræbt i sin tur.

value.en: “Take him away,” he said to Father Wolf, “and train him as befits one of the Free People.”
value.da: »Tag ham med,« sagde han til Far Ulv, »og oplær ham, som det sømmer sig for én af det Frie Folk.«

value.en: And that is how Mowgli was entered into the Seeonee Wolf Pack for the price of a bull and on Baloo’s good word.
value.da: Og sådan blev Mowgli medlem af Seeonees Ulveflok, købt med en tyr og på Baloos ord.

value.en: Now you must be content to skip ten or eleven whole years, and only guess at all the wonderful life that Mowgli led among the wolves, because if it were written out it would fill ever so many books. He grew up with the cubs, though they, of course, were grown wolves almost before he was a child. And Father Wolf taught him his business, and the meaning of things in the jungle, till every rustle in the grass, every breath of the warm night air, every note of the owls above his head, every scratch of a bat’s claws as it roosted for a while in a tree, and every splash of every little fish jumping in a pool meant just as much to him as the work of his office means to a business man. When he was not learning he sat out in the sun and slept, and ate and went to sleep again. When he felt dirty or hot he swam in the forest pools; and when he wanted honey (Baloo told him that honey and nuts were just as pleasant to eat as raw meat) he climbed up for it, and that Bagheera showed him how to do. Bagheera would lie out on a branch and call, “Come along, Little Brother,” and at first Mowgli would cling like the sloth, but afterward he would fling himself through the branches almost as boldly as the gray ape. He took his place at the Council Rock, too, when the Pack met, and there he discovered that if he stared hard at any wolf, the wolf would be forced to drop his eyes, and so he used to stare for fun. At other times he would pick the long thorns out of the pads of his friends, for wolves suffer terribly from thorns and burs in their coats. He would go down the hillside into the cultivated lands by night, and look very curiously at the villagers in their huts, but he had a mistrust of men because Bagheera showed him a square box with a drop gate so cunningly hidden in the jungle that he nearly walked into it, and told him that it was a trap. He loved better than anything else to go with Bagheera into the dark warm heart of the forest, to sleep all through the drowsy day, and at night see how Bagheera did his killing. Bagheera killed right and left as he felt hungry, and so did Mowgli--with one exception. As soon as he was old enough to understand things, Bagheera told him that he must never touch cattle because he had been bought into the Pack at the price of a bull’s life. “All the jungle is thine,” said Bagheera, “and thou canst kill everything that thou art strong enough to kill; but for the sake of the bull that bought thee thou must never kill or eat any cattle young or old. That is the Law of the Jungle.” Mowgli obeyed faithfully.
value.da: Nu må du lade ti eller elleve hele år gå og selv forestille dig det vidunderlige liv, Mowgli levede blandt ulvene. At fortælle det hele ville fylde utallige bøger. Han voksede op sammen med hvalpene, selv om de naturligvis var voksne ulve, næsten før han var kommet ud af barndommen. Far Ulv lærte ham alt, hvad han skulle vide, og viste ham, hvad tingene i junglen betød. Snart sagde en raslen i græsset, et pust af varm natteluft, et ugleråb over hovedet, skrabet fra en flagermus' kløer, når den satte sig i et træ for at hvile, eller plasket fra en lille fisk, der sprang i en pøl, lige så meget til ham, som arbejdet på kontoret siger til en forretningsmand. Når han ikke lærte noget, lå han i solen og sov, spiste og faldt i søvn igen. Når han var varm eller snavset, svømmede han i skovens vandhuller. Og når han ville have honning (Baloo havde fortalt ham, at honning og nødder smagte lige så godt som råt kød), klatrede han op efter den, og Bagheera havde vist ham, hvordan man gør. Bagheera lagde sig ud på en gren og kaldte: »Kom så, Lillebror.« Først klamrede Mowgli sig til træet som et dovendyr, men senere kastede han sig fra gren til gren næsten lige så frygtløst som den grå abe. Han havde også sin plads på Rådsklippen, når Flokken mødtes. Dér opdagede han, at hvis han stirrede hårdt på en ulv, måtte ulven slå blikket ned. Så han begyndte at stirre på dem for sjov. Andre gange trak han lange torne ud af sine venners poteballer, for ulve lider meget under torne og burrer i pelsen. Om natten gik han ned ad bakken til de dyrkede marker og kiggede meget nysgerrigt på landsbyboerne i deres hytter, men han stolede ikke på mennesker. Bagheera havde engang vist ham en firkantet kasse med en faldlåge, så snedigt gemt i junglen, at han næsten var trådt ind i den, og havde fortalt ham, at det var en fælde. Mest af alt elskede Mowgli at gå sammen med Bagheera dybt ind i den varme, mørke skov, sove hele den søvnige dag og om natten se Bagheera dræbe. Når Bagheera var sulten, dræbte han, hvad der kom i vejen, og det gjorde Mowgli også — med én undtagelse. Så snart drengen kunne forstå det, fortalte Bagheera ham, at han aldrig måtte røre kvæg, fordi han var blevet købt ind i Flokken med en tyrs liv. »Hele junglen er din,« sagde Bagheera, »og du kan dræbe alt, hvad du er stærk nok til. Men husk tyren, der købte din plads: du må aldrig dræbe eller spise kvæg, hverken ungt eller gammelt. Det er Junglens Lov.« Mowgli holdt trofast den regel.

value.en: And he grew and grew strong as a boy must grow who does not know that he is learning any lessons, and who has nothing in the world to think of except things to eat.
value.da: Han blev større og stærkere, som en dreng nødvendigvis gør, når han aldrig opdager, at han bliver undervist, og ikke har andet i hele verden at bekymre sig om end, hvad han skal spise.

value.en: Mother Wolf told him once or twice that Shere Khan was not a creature to be trusted, and that some day he must kill Shere Khan. But though a young wolf would have remembered that advice every hour, Mowgli forgot it because he was only a boy--though he would have called himself a wolf if he had been able to speak in any human tongue.
value.da: Mor Ulv advarede ham en gang eller to om, at man ikke kunne stole på Shere Khan, og at han en dag ville blive nødt til at dræbe ham. En ung ulv ville have husket den advarsel hver time på dagen. Men Mowgli glemte den, for han var jo bare en dreng — selv om han ville have sagt, at han var en ulv, hvis han havde kunnet et menneskesprog.

value.en: Shere Khan was always crossing his path in the jungle, for as Akela grew older and feebler the lame tiger had come to be great friends with the younger wolves of the Pack, who followed him for scraps, a thing Akela would never have allowed if he had dared to push his authority to the proper bounds. Then Shere Khan would flatter them and wonder that such fine young hunters were content to be led by a dying wolf and a man’s cub. “They tell me,” Shere Khan would say, “that at Council ye dare not look him between the eyes.” And the young wolves would growl and bristle.
value.da: Han stødte hele tiden på Shere Khan i junglen. Efterhånden som Akela blev ældre og svagere, var den halte tiger blevet gode venner med Flokkens yngre ulve. De fulgte efter ham for at få rester. Det ville Akela helt sikkert have forbudt, hvis han havde turdet bruge al sin magt. Shere Khan smigrede dem og undrede sig over, hvordan så fine unge jægere kunne følge en døende ulv og et menneskebarn. »Jeg hører,« plejede han at sige, »at I ikke tør se ham i øjnene til Rådet.« Så knurrede de unge ulve og rejste pelsen.

value.en: Bagheera, who had eyes and ears everywhere, knew something of this, and once or twice he told Mowgli in so many words that Shere Khan would kill him some day. Mowgli would laugh and answer: “I have the Pack and I have thee; and Baloo, though he is so lazy, might strike a blow or two for my sake. Why should I be afraid?”
value.da: Bagheera, der havde øjne og ører overalt, havde hørt noget om det hele. En gang eller to sagde han rent ud til Mowgli, at Shere Khan en dag ville dræbe ham. Mowgli lo bare. »Jeg har Flokken, og jeg har dig,« svarede han. »Selv dovne Baloo kunne vel slå et par slag for min skyld. Hvorfor skulle jeg være bange?«

value.en: It was one very warm day that a new notion came to Bagheera--born of something that he had heard. Perhaps Ikki the Porcupine had told him; but he said to Mowgli when they were deep in the jungle, as the boy lay with his head on Bagheera’s beautiful black skin, “Little Brother, how often have I told thee that Shere Khan is thy enemy?”
value.da: En meget varm dag fik Bagheera en ny tanke, efter noget han havde hørt. Måske var nyheden kommet fra Ikki Pindsvinet. Dybt inde i junglen, mens drengen lå med hovedet på panterens smukke sorte pels, sagde Bagheera: »Lillebror, hvor mange gange har jeg advaret dig om, at Shere Khan er din fjende?«

value.en: “As many times as there are nuts on that palm,” said Mowgli, who, naturally, could not count. “What of it? I am sleepy, Bagheera, and Shere Khan is all long tail and loud talk--like Mao, the Peacock.”
value.da: »Lige så mange gange, som der er nødder på den palme,« sagde Mowgli, der naturligvis aldrig havde lært at tælle. »Hvad så? Jeg er træt, Bagheera. Shere Khan er bare en lang hale og en høj stemme — ligesom Mao, Påfuglen.«

value.en: “But this is no time for sleeping. Baloo knows it; I know it; the Pack know it; and even the foolish, foolish deer know. Tabaqui has told thee too.”
value.da: »Men det er ikke tid til at sove. Det ved Baloo, det ved jeg, det ved Flokken. Selv de dumme, dumme hjorte ved det. Tabaqui har også advaret dig.«

value.en: “Ho! ho!” said Mowgli. “Tabaqui came to me not long ago with some rude talk that I was a naked man’s cub and not fit to dig pig-nuts. But I caught Tabaqui by the tail and swung him twice against a palm-tree to teach him better manners.”
value.da: »Ha! Ha!« sagde Mowgli. »Tabaqui kom til mig for ikke længe siden med noget uforskammet snak om, at jeg var et nøgent menneskebarn og ikke duede til at grave svinerødder op. Men jeg greb Tabaqui i halen og svingede ham to gange mod et palmetræ for at lære ham bedre manerer.«

value.en: “That was foolishness, for though Tabaqui is a mischief-maker, he would have told thee of something that concerned thee closely. Open those eyes, Little Brother. Shere Khan dare not kill thee in the jungle. But remember, Akela is very old, and soon the day comes when he cannot kill his buck, and then he will be leader no more. Many of the wolves that looked thee over when thou wast brought to the Council first are old too, and the young wolves believe, as Shere Khan has taught them, that a man-cub has no place with the Pack. In a little time thou wilt be a man.”
value.da: »Det var dumt gjort. Tabaqui laver ballade, det er sikkert, men han ville have fortalt dig noget, der angår dig meget. Åbn øjnene, Lillebror. Shere Khan tør ikke dræbe dig her i junglen. Men husk, at Akela er blevet meget gammel. Snart kan han ikke fælde sin buk, og så er det slut med hans lederskab. Mange af de ulve, der så på dig, da du første gang blev ført til Rådet, er også gamle nu. De yngre har lært Shere Khans lektie: at et menneskebarn ikke hører til i Flokken. Om ikke længe er du selv en mand.«

value.en: “And what is a man that he should not run with his brothers?” said Mowgli. “I was born in the jungle. I have obeyed the Law of the Jungle, and there is no wolf of ours from whose paws I have not pulled a thorn. Surely they are my brothers!”
value.da: »Hvad er det ved en mand, der gør, at han ikke kan løbe sammen med sine brødre?« spurgte Mowgli. »Junglen er der, hvor jeg er født. Jeg har overholdt Junglens Lov. Der er ikke én ulv hos os, hvis poter jeg ikke har befriet for torne. Selvfølgelig er de mine brødre!«

value.en: Bagheera stretched himself at full length and half shut his eyes. “Little Brother,” said he, “feel under my jaw.”
value.da: Bagheera strakte sig helt ud og lod øjenlågene synke. »Lillebror,« sagde han, »læg din hånd under min kæbe.«

value.en: Mowgli put up his strong brown hand, and just under Bagheera’s silky chin, where the giant rolling muscles were all hid by the glossy hair, he came upon a little bald spot.
value.da: Mowgli rakte sin stærke brune hånd frem. Under Bagheeras bløde, silkeagtige hage, hvor den glatte pels dækkede de store, bevægelige muskler, fandt hans fingre en lille plet uden hår.

value.en: “There is no one in the jungle that knows that I, Bagheera, carry that mark--the mark of the collar; and yet, Little Brother, I was born among men, and it was among men that my mother died--in the cages of the king’s palace at Oodeypore. It was because of this that I paid the price for thee at the Council when thou wast a little naked cub. Yes, I too was born among men. I had never seen the jungle. They fed me behind bars from an iron pan till one night I felt that I was Bagheera--the Panther--and no man’s plaything, and I broke the silly lock with one blow of my paw and came away. And because I had learned the ways of men, I became more terrible in the jungle than Shere Khan. Is it not so?”
value.da: »Ingen i junglen ved, at jeg, Bagheera, bærer det mærke — mærket efter et halsbånd. Men jeg blev født blandt mennesker, Lillebror, og blandt mennesker døde min mor, i burene i kongens palads i Oodeypore. Det var derfor, jeg betalte for dit liv ved Rådet, da du var en lille nøgen unge. Ja, også jeg er født blandt mennesker. Jeg havde aldrig set junglen. Bag tremmer fik jeg mad i en jernskål. Så en nat følte jeg, at jeg var Bagheera — Panteren — og ikke noget menneskes legetøj. Med ét slag af poten smadrede jeg deres latterlige lås og gik min vej. Fordi jeg kendte menneskenes måder, blev jeg mere frygtet i junglen end Shere Khan. Er det ikke sandt?«

value.en: “Yes,” said Mowgli, “all the jungle fear Bagheera--all except Mowgli.”
value.da: »Jo,« sagde Mowgli, »hele junglen frygter Bagheera — alle undtagen Mowgli.«

value: Now you will have to let ten or eleven whole years pass by, and imagine for yourself the wonderful life Mowgli had among the wolves. Telling it all would fill any number of books. He grew up alongside the cubs, although of course they were adult wolves almost before he had reached childhood. Father Wolf taught him everything he needed to know and showed him what things in the jungle meant. Soon a rustle of grass, a breath of warm night air, an owl’s cry overhead, the scraping of a bat’s claws as it settled in a tree for a rest, or the splash of a tiny fish leaping in a pool spoke to him as plainly as the business of an office speaks to the man who works there. Between lessons he lay in the sunshine and slept, ate, and fell asleep again. If he was hot or dirty, he swam in the forest pools. If he wanted honey--Baloo had explained that honey and nuts tasted just as good as raw meat--he climbed to fetch it, using the skills Bagheera taught him. Bagheera would stretch out on a branch and call, “Come on, Little Brother.” At first Mowgli clung to the tree like a sloth; later he hurled himself from branch to branch almost as fearlessly as a gray ape. He also sat at the Council Rock when the Pack gathered. There he found that no wolf could hold his gaze: if he stared hard enough, the wolf had to look down. He took to staring at them for amusement. At other times he pulled long thorns out of his friends’ paw pads, since wolves suffer badly from thorns and from burrs caught in their coats. At night he went down the hill into the farmland and watched the villagers in their huts with great curiosity. Still, he distrusted men. Bagheera had once shown him a square box with a falling gate, hidden so cleverly in the jungle that he almost stepped inside, and explained that it was a trap. What Mowgli loved most was going deep into the warm, dark forest with Bagheera, sleeping through the whole drowsy day, then watching him kill at night. Whenever he grew hungry, Bagheera killed whatever came his way, and Mowgli did the same--with one exception. As soon as the boy could understand, Bagheera told him never to harm cattle, because a bull’s life had paid for his place in the Pack. “The whole jungle belongs to you,” Bagheera said, “and you may kill anything you have the strength to kill. But remember the bull that bought your place: you must never kill cattle or eat them, whether young or old. That is the Law of the Jungle.” Mowgli kept that rule faithfully.

On one very hot day, something Bagheera had heard gave him a new idea. Perhaps the news had come from Ikki the Porcupine. Deep in the jungle, with the boy resting his head on the panther’s lovely black coat, Bagheera said, “Little Brother, how many times have I warned you that Shere Khan is your enemy?”

value.en: “Oh, thou art a man’s cub,” said the Black Panther very tenderly. “And even as I returned to my jungle, so thou must go back to men at last--to the men who are thy brothers--if thou art not killed in the Council.”
value.da: »Åh, du er et menneskebarn,« sagde den Sorte Panter meget kærligt. »Og lige som jeg vendte tilbage til min jungle, sådan må du vende tilbage til menneskene til sidst — til de mennesker, der er dine brødre — hvis du ikke bliver dræbt på Rådet.«

value.en: “But why--but why should any wish to kill me?” said Mowgli.
value.da: »Men hvorfor — men hvorfor skulle nogen ønske at dræbe mig?« sagde Mowgli.

value.en: “Look at me,” said Bagheera. And Mowgli looked at him steadily between the eyes. The big panther turned his head away in half a minute.
value.da: »Se mig ind i øjnene,« sagde Bagheera. Mowgli mødte hans blik uden at blinke. Inden et halvt minut måtte den store panter vende hovedet væk.

value.en: “That is why,” he said, shifting his paw on the leaves. “Not even I can look thee between the eyes, and I was born among men, and I love thee, Little Brother. The others they hate thee because their eyes cannot meet thine; because thou art wise; because thou hast pulled out thorns from their feet--because thou art a man.”
value.da: »Dér har du grunden,« sagde han og flyttede en pote hen over bladene. »Ikke engang jeg kan holde dit blik, selv om jeg er født blandt mennesker og elsker dig, Lillebror. De andre hader dig, fordi de ikke kan møde dine øjne; fordi du er klog; fordi du har trukket torne ud af deres poter — fordi du er et menneske.«

value.en: “I did not know these things,” said Mowgli sullenly, and he frowned under his heavy black eyebrows.
value.da: »Ingen har fortalt mig noget af det her,« sagde Mowgli surt, og hans tykke sorte øjenbryn trak sig sammen i en rynke.

value.en: “What is the Law of the Jungle? Strike first and then give tongue. By thy very carelessness they know that thou art a man. But be wise. It is in my heart that when Akela misses his next kill--and at each hunt it costs him more to pin the buck--the Pack will turn against him and against thee. They will hold a jungle Council at the Rock, and then--and then--I have it!” said Bagheera, leaping up. “Go thou down quickly to the men’s huts in the valley, and take some of the Red Flower which they grow there, so that when the time comes thou mayest have even a stronger friend than I or Baloo or those of the Pack that love thee. Get the Red Flower.”
value.da: »Hvad siger Junglens Lov? Slå til, før du siger en lyd. Netop din ubekymrethed fortæller dem, at du er et menneske. Vær klog nu. Jeg er sikker på, at når Akela næste gang ikke får sit bytte — og for hver jagt bliver det sværere for ham at holde bukken nede — vil Flokken vende sig mod både ham og dig. De vil kalde til jungleråd ved Klippen, og så — og så — jeg ved det!« Bagheera sprang op. »Skynd dig ned til menneskenes hytter i dalen. Hent noget af den Røde Blomst, som de dyrker dér. Når tiden kommer, har du en ven, der er endnu stærkere end mig, Baloo eller de ulve i Flokken, som holder af dig. Hent den Røde Blomst.«

value.en: By Red Flower Bagheera meant fire, only no creature in the jungle will call fire by its proper name. Every beast lives in deadly fear of it, and invents a hundred ways of describing it.
value.da: Den Røde Blomst var Bagheeras navn for ild. Intet væsen i junglen vil sige ildens rigtige navn. De lever alle i dødelig frygt for den og finder på hundrede andre navne at bruge i stedet.

value.en: “The Red Flower?” said Mowgli. “That grows outside their huts in the twilight. I will get some.”
value.da: »Den Røde Blomst?« sagde Mowgli. »Den vokser uden for deres hytter i tusmørket. Jeg vil hente noget.«

value.en: “There speaks the man’s cub,” said Bagheera proudly. “Remember that it grows in little pots. Get one swiftly, and keep it by thee for time of need.”
value.da: »Nu taler et menneskebarn,« sagde Bagheera stolt. »Husk, at den vokser i små krukker. Hent en krukke hurtigt og hav den hos dig, klar til når du får brug for den.«

value.en: “Good!” said Mowgli. “I go. But art thou sure, O my Bagheera”--he slipped his arm around the splendid neck and looked deep into the big eyes--“art thou sure that all this is Shere Khan’s doing?”
value.da: »Godt!« sagde Mowgli. »Jeg går. Men er du sikker, min Bagheera« — han lagde armen om den prægtige hals og søgte i de store øjne — »er du sikker på, at Shere Khan står bag alt dette?«

value.en: “By the Broken Lock that freed me, I am sure, Little Brother.”
value.da: »Ved den Brækkede Lås, der gav mig fri, er jeg sikker, Lillebror.«

value.en: “Then, by the Bull that bought me, I will pay Shere Khan full tale for this, and it may be a little over,” said Mowgli, and he bounded away.
value.da: »Så sværger jeg ved Tyren, der købte mig: Shere Khan skal få fuld betaling for dette, og måske lidt ekstra,« sagde Mowgli og sprang afsted.

value.en: “That is a man. That is all a man,” said Bagheera to himself, lying down again. “Oh, Shere Khan, never was a blacker hunting than that frog-hunt of thine ten years ago!”
value.da: »Der har du et menneske. Et menneske helt igennem,« mumlede Bagheera, mens han lagde sig igen. »Åh, Shere Khan, aldrig bragte nogen jagt mere ulykke end din frøjagt for ti år siden!«

value.en: Mowgli was far and far through the forest, running hard, and his heart was hot in him. He came to the cave as the evening mist rose, and drew breath, and looked down the valley. The cubs were out, but Mother Wolf, at the back of the cave, knew by his breathing that something was troubling her frog.
value.da: Mowgli var nu langt væk og løb gennem skoven med brændende hjerte. Da aftentågen begyndte at stige, nåede han hulen, standsede for at puste og kiggede ned i dalen. Hvalpene var ude. Men Mor Ulv, der lå bagest i hulen, kunne høre på hans åndedræt, at der var noget, der plagede hendes frø.

value.en: “What is it, Son?” she said.
value.da: »Hvad plager dig, min søn?« spurgte hun.

value.en: “Some bat’s chatter of Shere Khan,” he called back. “I hunt among the plowed fields tonight,” and he plunged downward through the bushes, to the stream at the bottom of the valley. There he checked, for he heard the yell of the Pack hunting, heard the bellow of a hunted Sambhur, and the snort as the buck turned at bay. Then there were wicked, bitter howls from the young wolves: “Akela! Akela! Let the Lone Wolf show his strength. Room for the leader of the Pack! Spring, Akela!”
value.da: »Bare noget flagermusesnak om Shere Khan,« råbte han tilbage. »I nat jager jeg nede på de pløjede marker.« Han styrtede gennem buskene mod åen i dalbunden. Dér standsede han brat. Flokkens jagtråb lød, og så brølet fra en sambarhjort, de forfulgte, og en snorken, da bukken vendte sig for at forsvare sig. De unge ulve brød ud i grusomme, hånlige hyl: »Akela! Akela! Lad os se Den Ensomme Ulvs styrke. Plads til Flokkens leder! Spring, Akela!«

value.en: The Lone Wolf must have sprung and missed his hold, for Mowgli heard the snap of his teeth and then a yelp as the Sambhur knocked him over with his forefoot.
value.da: Den Ensomme Ulv må have sprunget og ikke fået fat. Mowgli hørte hans kæber smække i, og derefter et hyl, da sambarhjorten slog ham omkuld med forhoven.

value.en: He did not wait for anything more, but dashed on; and the yells grew fainter behind him as he ran into the croplands where the villagers lived.
value.da: Han ventede ikke på mere, men styrtede afsted; og hylene blev fjernere bag ham, mens han løb ind i de dyrkede marker, hvor landsbyfolkene boede.

value.en: “Bagheera spoke truth,” he panted, as he nestled down in some cattle fodder by the window of a hut. “To-morrow is one day both for Akela and for me.”
value.da: »Bagheera talte sandt,« stønnede han, mens han krøb sammen i en bunke kvægfoder ved vinduet til en hytte. »I morgen er det opgørets dag for både Akela og mig.«

value.en: Then he pressed his face close to the window and watched the fire on the hearth. He saw the husbandman’s wife get up and feed it in the night with black lumps. And when the morning came and the mists were all white and cold, he saw the man’s child pick up a wicker pot plastered inside with earth, fill it with lumps of red-hot charcoal, put it under his blanket, and go out to tend the cows in the byre.
value.da: Han løftede ansigtet op til vinduet for at se ilden brænde på arnen. I løbet af natten så han bondens kone rejse sig og lægge sorte klumper på den. Da morgenen kom med kold, hvid tåge, så han mandens barn tage en flettet krukke, der var beklædt indvendigt med ler. Barnet fyldte den med stykker af glødende trækul, puttede den ind under sit tæppe og gik ud for at passe køerne i stalden.

value.en: “Is that all?” said Mowgli. “If a cub can do it, there is nothing to fear.” So he strode round the corner and met the boy, took the pot from his hand, and disappeared into the mist while the boy howled with fear.
value.da: »Er det alt?« sagde Mowgli. »Hvis en unge kan klare det, er der intet at være bange for.« Han gik frimodigt om hjørnet, stillede sig foran drengen, tog krukken lige ud af hans hånd og forsvandt ind i tågen, mens drengen hylede af skræk.

value.en: “They are very like me,” said Mowgli, blowing into the pot as he had seen the woman do. “This thing will die if I do not give it things to eat”; and he dropped twigs and dried bark on the red stuff. Halfway up the hill he met Bagheera with the morning dew shining like moonstones on his coat.
value.da: »De ligner mig meget,« sagde Mowgli og blæste ind i krukken, som han havde set konen gøre. »Hvis jeg ikke giver den noget at æde, dør den her.« Han lagde tør bark og kviste på de glødende kul. Halvvejs oppe ad bakken mødte han Bagheera, med morgendug, der glimtede som månesten i hans pels.

value.en: “Akela has missed,” said the Panther. “They would have killed him last night, but they needed thee also. They were looking for thee on the hill.”
value.da: »Akela fik ikke sit bytte,« sagde Panteren. »De ville have dræbt ham i nat, men de ville også have fat i dig. De ledte efter dig oppe på bakken.«

value.en: “I was among the plowed lands. I am ready. See!” Mowgli held up the fire-pot.
value.da: »Jeg var ude på de pløjede marker. Jeg er klar. Se!« Mowgli holdt ildkrukken op.

value.en: “Good! Now, I have seen men thrust a dry branch into that stuff, and presently the Red Flower blossomed at the end of it. Art thou not afraid?”
value.da: »Godt! Jeg har set mennesker stikke en tør gren ind i det, og snart blomstrer den Røde Blomst i spidsen af den. Er du ikke bange?«

value.en: “No. Why should I fear? I remember now--if it is not a dream--how, before I was a Wolf, I lay beside the Red Flower, and it was warm and pleasant.”
value.da: »Nej. Hvorfor skulle jeg være bange? Jeg husker nu — hvis det ikke er en drøm — hvordan jeg, før jeg var en Ulv, lå ved siden af den Røde Blomst, og det var varmt og rart.«

value.en: All that day Mowgli sat in the cave tending his fire pot and dipping dry branches into it to see how they looked. He found a branch that satisfied him, and in the evening when Tabaqui came to the cave and told him rudely enough that he was wanted at the Council Rock, he laughed till Tabaqui ran away. Then Mowgli went to the Council, still laughing.
value.da: Mowgli blev hele dagen i hulen og passede sin ildkrukke. Han lagde tørre grene ned i den for at se, hvad der skete, indtil han fandt en, han kunne lide. Den aften kom Tabaqui og fortalte ham meget uforskammet, at han var kaldt til Rådsklippen. Mowgli lo så højt, at Tabaqui løb sin vej. Han lo stadig, da han gik af sted til Rådet.

value.en: Akela the Lone Wolf lay by the side of his rock as a sign that the leadership of the Pack was open, and Shere Khan with his following of scrap-fed wolves walked to and fro openly being flattered. Bagheera lay close to Mowgli, and the fire pot was between Mowgli’s knees. When they were all gathered together, Shere Khan began to speak--a thing he would never have dared to do when Akela was in his prime.
value.da: Akela, Den Ensomme Ulv, lå ved siden af sin klippe som tegn på, at Flokken ikke længere havde nogen leder. Shere Khan gik åbenlyst frem og tilbage med de ulve, han havde fodret med rester, og nød deres smiger. Bagheera lagde sig tæt ved Mowgli, som holdt ildkrukken mellem knæene. Da alle var samlet, begyndte Shere Khan at tale — noget han aldrig ville have turdet, mens Akela var på sit stærkeste.

value.en: “He has no right,” whispered Bagheera. “Say so. He is a dog’s son. He will be frightened.”
value.da: »Han har ingen ret til at tale,« hviskede Bagheera. »Sig det til ham. Den hundesøn bliver bange.«

value.en: Mowgli sprang to his feet. “Free People,” he cried, “does Shere Khan lead the Pack? What has a tiger to do with our leadership?”
value.da: Mowgli sprang op. »Frie Folk,« råbte han, »leder Shere Khan Flokken? Hvad har en tiger med vores lederskab at gøre?«

value.en: “Seeing that the leadership is yet open, and being asked to speak--” Shere Khan began.
value.da: »Da jeg ser, at lederskabet stadig er åbent, og da jeg er blevet bedt om at tale—« begyndte Shere Khan.

value.en: “By whom?” said Mowgli. “Are we all jackals, to fawn on this cattle butcher? The leadership of the Pack is with the Pack alone.”
value.da: »Af hvem?« krævede Mowgli. »Er vi alle blevet sjakaler, der logrer for denne kvægslagter? Det er kun Flokken, der bestemmer, hvem der skal lede Flokken.«

value.en: There were yells of “Silence, thou man’s cub!” “Let him speak. He has kept our Law”; and at last the seniors of the Pack thundered: “Let the Dead Wolf speak.” When a leader of the Pack has missed his kill, he is called the Dead Wolf as long as he lives, which is not long.
value.da: Der lød råb: »Hold mund, dit menneskebarn!« og »Lad ham tale. Han har holdt vores Lov.« Til sidst tordnede de ældre ulve: »Lad Den Døde Ulv tale.« Når en leder af Flokken ikke får sit bytte, kaldes han Den Døde Ulv resten af sit liv — og det bliver ikke langt.

value.en: Akela raised his old head wearily:--
value.da: Træt løftede Akela sit gamle hoved:

value.en: “Free People, and ye too, jackals of Shere Khan, for twelve seasons I have led ye to and from the kill, and in all that time not one has been trapped or maimed. Now I have missed my kill. Ye know how that plot was made. Ye know how ye brought me up to an untried buck to make my weakness known. It was cleverly done. Your right is to kill me here on the Council Rock, now. Therefore, I ask, who comes to make an end of the Lone Wolf? For it is my right, by the Law of the Jungle, that ye come one by one.”
value.da: »Frie Folk — og I også, Shere Khans sjakaler — i tolv sæsoner har jeg ført jer ud på jagt og hjem igen. I alle de år er ikke én af jer blevet fanget i en fælde eller gjort til krøbling. Nu har jeg ikke fået mit bytte. I ved, hvem der planlagde det, og hvordan. I ved, at I sendte mig mod en buk, hvis styrke jeg ikke kendte, for at afsløre min svaghed. Det var en snedig list. I har ret til at dræbe mig her, nu, på Rådsklippen. Derfor spørger jeg: Hvem træder frem og gør en ende på Den Ensomme Ulv? For efter Junglens Lov har jeg ret til, at I kommer én ad gangen.«

value.en: There was a long hush, for no single wolf cared to fight Akela to the death. Then Shere Khan roared: “Bah! What have we to do with this toothless fool? He is doomed to die! It is the man-cub who has lived too long. Free People, he was my meat from the first. Give him to me. I am weary of this man-wolf folly. He has troubled the jungle for ten seasons. Give me the man-cub, or I will hunt here always, and not give you one bone. He is a man, a man’s child, and from the marrow of my bones I hate him!”
value.da: Der var længe stille, for ingen af ulvene ville kæmpe på liv og død mod Akela alene. Til sidst brølede Shere Khan: »Pyt! Hvorfor bekymre os om denne tandløse tåbe? Han skal alligevel dø! Det er menneskebarnet, der har levet for længe. Frie Folk, han var mit bytte fra begyndelsen. Giv ham til mig. Jeg er træt af al den sludder om, at et menneske kan være en ulv. I ti sæsoner har han forstyrret junglen. Udlever menneskebarnet, ellers jager jeg her for evigt og efterlader ikke så meget som ét ben til jer. Han er et menneske, et menneskes barn, og jeg hader ham helt ind i knoglemarven!«

value.en: Then more than half the Pack yelled: “A man! A man! What has a man to do with us? Let him go to his own place.”
value.da: Mere end halvdelen af ulvene råbte tilbage: »Et menneske! Et menneske! Hvad har et menneske med os at gøre? Send ham tilbage, hvor han hører til.«

value.en: “And turn all the people of the villages against us?” clamored Shere Khan. “No, give him to me. He is a man, and none of us can look him between the eyes.”
value.da: »Så han kan vende alle landsbyfolkene imod os?« skreg Shere Khan. »Nej, giv ham til mig. Han er et menneske, og ingen af os kan møde hans blik.«

value.en: Akela lifted his head again and said, “He has eaten our food. He has slept with us. He has driven game for us. He has broken no word of the Law of the Jungle.”
value.da: Akela løftede igen sit hoved og sagde: »Han har spist vores mad. Han har sovet hos os. Han har drevet vildt for os. Han har ikke brudt et eneste ord af Junglens Lov.«

value.en: “Also, I paid for him with a bull when he was accepted. The worth of a bull is little, but Bagheera’s honor is something that he will perhaps fight for,” said Bagheera in his gentlest voice.
value.da: »Desuden betalte jeg for ham med en tyr, da han blev optaget. Værdien af en tyr er ringe, men Bagheeras ære er noget, han måske vil kæmpe for,« sagde Bagheera med sin blideste stemme.

value.en: “A bull paid ten years ago!” the Pack snarled. “What do we care for bones ten years old?”
value.da: »En tyr betalt for ti år siden!« knurrede Flokken. »Hvad bryder vi os om ti år gamle knogler?«

value.en: “Or for a pledge?” said Bagheera, his white teeth bared under his lip. “Well are ye called the Free People!”
value.da: »Eller et løfte?« spurgte Bagheera og trak læben tilbage, så de hvide tænder viste sig. »I fortjener virkelig navnet det Frie Folk!«

value.en: “No man’s cub can run with the people of the jungle,” howled Shere Khan. “Give him to me!”
value.da: »Intet menneskebarn kan løbe med junglens folk,« hylede Shere Khan. »Giv ham til mig!«

value.en: “He is our brother in all but blood,” Akela went on, “and ye would kill him here! In truth, I have lived too long. Some of ye are eaters of cattle, and of others I have heard that, under Shere Khan’s teaching, ye go by dark night and snatch children from the villager’s doorstep. Therefore I know ye to be cowards, and it is to cowards I speak. It is certain that I must die, and my life is of no worth, or I would offer that in the man-cub’s place. But for the sake of the Honor of the Pack,--a little matter that by being without a leader ye have forgotten,--I promise that if ye let the man-cub go to his own place, I will not, when my time comes to die, bare one tooth against ye. I will die without fighting. That will at least save the Pack three lives. More I cannot do; but if ye will, I can save ye the shame that comes of killing a brother against whom there is no fault--a brother spoken for and bought into the Pack according to the Law of the Jungle.”
value.da: »Han er vores bror i alt andet end blod,« fortsatte Akela, »og alligevel vil I dræbe ham her! Jeg har virkelig levet for længe. Nogle af jer æder kvæg.
