Om andre hører jeg, at Shere Khan har lært jer at liste ud i mørke nætter og stjæle børn fra landsbyboernes dørtrin. Derfor ved jeg, at I er kujoner, og det er til kujoner, jeg taler. Min død er sikker. Mit liv er nu intet værd, ellers ville jeg tilbyde det i bytte for menneskebarnets. Men der er Flokkens Ære — den lille ting, I har glemt, siden I mistede jeres leder. For dens skyld lover jeg dette: Lad menneskebarnet vende tilbage til sit eget sted, og når min tid til at dø kommer, vil jeg ikke blotte en eneste tand mod jer. Jeg lader jer dræbe mig uden kamp. Dermed skånes mindst tre liv i Flokken. Det er alt, jeg kan tilbyde. Tag imod det, så kan jeg spare jer for skammen ved at myrde en uskyldig bror — en, der er blevet talt for, og hvis plads i Flokken blev købt efter Junglens Lov.«

value.en: “He is a man--a man--a man!” snarled the Pack. And most of the wolves began to gather round Shere Khan, whose tail was beginning to switch.
value.da: »Et menneske — et menneske — det er det, han er!« snerrede ulvene. De fleste begyndte at samle sig om Shere Khan, hvis hale var begyndt at piske.

value.en: “Now the business is in thy hands,” said Bagheera to Mowgli. “We can do no more except fight.”
value.da: »Nu er det op til dig,« sagde Bagheera til Mowgli. »Der er ikke andet, vi kan gøre for dig end at kæmpe.«

value.en: Mowgli stood upright--the fire pot in his hands. Then he stretched out his arms, and yawned in the face of the Council; but he was furious with rage and sorrow, for, wolflike, the wolves had never told him how they hated him. “Listen you!” he cried. “There is no need for this dog’s jabber. Ye have told me so often tonight that I am a man (and indeed I would have been a wolf with you to my life’s end) that I feel your words are true. So I do not call ye my brothers any more, but sag [dogs], as a man should. What ye will do, and what ye will not do, is not yours to say. That matter is with me; and that we may see the matter more plainly, I, the man, have brought here a little of the Red Flower which ye, dogs, fear.”
value.da: Mowgli rejste sig i sin fulde højde med ildkrukken i hænderne. Han strakte armene ud og gabede lige op i ansigtet på Rådet, selv om raseri og sorg brændte i ham. Ulvene havde nemlig, som ulve gør, aldrig ladet ham mærke, at de hadede ham. »Hør nu efter!« råbte han. »Nu er det slut med at gø som hunde. I har sagt så mange gange i nat, at jeg er et menneske — selv om jeg gerne ville have været ulv hos jer hele mit liv — at jeg føler, I må have ret. Så jeg kalder jer ikke længere mine brødre. Jeg kalder jer sag [hunde], som et menneske bør. Det er ikke op til jer, hvad I vil eller ikke vil gøre. Det bestemmer jeg. For at gøre det helt tydeligt har jeg, mennesket, hentet lidt af den Røde Blomst, som I hunde er bange for.«

value.en: He flung the fire pot on the ground, and some of the red coals lit a tuft of dried moss that flared up, as all the Council drew back in terror before the leaping flames.
value.da: Han kastede ildkrukken på jorden, og nogle af de røde gløder antændte en tot tørret mos, der flammede op, mens hele Rådet trak sig tilbage i rædsel for de springende flammer.

value.en: Mowgli thrust his dead branch into the fire till the twigs lit and crackled, and whirled it above his head among the cowering wolves.
value.da: Mowgli stak sin tørre gren ind i flammerne, til kvistene knitrede og tog ild. Så svingede han den over hovedet, mens han stod blandt de sammenkrøbne ulve.

value.en: “Thou art the master,” said Bagheera in an undertone. “Save Akela from the death. He was ever thy friend.”
value.da: »Du er deres herre nu,« mumlede Bagheera. »Skån Akelas liv. Han har altid stået ved din side som ven.«

value.en: Akela, the grim old wolf who had never asked for mercy in his life, gave one piteous look at Mowgli as the boy stood all naked, his long black hair tossing over his shoulders in the light of the blazing branch that made the shadows jump and quiver.
value.da: Akela, den barske gamle ulv, der aldrig havde bedt om nåde, sendte Mowgli ét bedende blik. Drengen stod nøgen foran ham, med det lange sorte hår flagrende om skuldrene i lyset fra den brændende gren, mens skyggerne sprang og dirrede omkring ham.

value.en: “Good!” said Mowgli, staring round slowly. “I see that ye are dogs. I go from you to my own people--if they be my own people. The jungle is shut to me, and I must forget your talk and your companionship. But I will be more merciful than ye are. Because I was all but your brother in blood, I promise that when I am a man among men I will not betray ye to men as ye have betrayed me.” He kicked the fire with his foot, and the sparks flew up. “There shall be no war between any of us in the Pack. But here is a debt to pay before I go.” He strode forward to where Shere Khan sat blinking stupidly at the flames, and caught him by the tuft on his chin. Bagheera followed in case of accidents. “Up, dog!” Mowgli cried. “Up, when a man speaks, or I will set that coat ablaze!”
value.da: »Godt!« sagde Mowgli og så langsomt rundt på dem. »Nu kan jeg se, at I er hunde. Jeg forlader jer og går til mit eget folk — hvis de virkelig er mit folk. Junglen har lukket sine døre for mig. Jeg må glemme jeres sprog og jeres venskab. Men jeg vil vise mere nåde, end I har vist. Jeg var jeres bror i alt andet end blod, og derfor lover jeg, at når jeg bor som menneske blandt mennesker, vil jeg ikke forråde jer over for dem, som I har forrådt mig.« Han sparkede til ilden, så gnisterne fløj op. »Der skal ikke være krig mellem nogen af os, der hører til Flokken. Men før jeg går, har jeg en gæld at gøre op.« Han gik lige hen til Shere Khan, som sad og blinkede dumt mod ilden, og greb fat i totten under hans hage. Bagheera fulgte efter, klar hvis noget gik galt. »Op, hund!« råbte Mowgli. »Rejs dig, når et menneske taler til dig, ellers sætter jeg ild til din pels!«

value.en: Shere Khan’s ears lay flat back on his head, and he shut his eyes, for the blazing branch was very near.
value.da: Med den brændende gren så tæt på lagde Shere Khan ørerne fladt ind til hovedet og kneb øjnene sammen.

value.en: “This cattle-killer said he would kill me in the Council because he had not killed me when I was a cub. Thus and thus, then, do we beat dogs when we are men. Stir a whisker, Lungri, and I ram the Red Flower down thy gullet!” He beat Shere Khan over the head with the branch, and the tiger whimpered and whined in an agony of fear.
value.da: »Denne kvægslagter sagde, at han ville dræbe mig her på Rådet, fordi han ikke fik dræbt mig, da jeg var en unge. Nå, sådan slår mennesker hunde — sådan her og sådan her. Rør et eneste knurhår, Lungri, og jeg propper den Røde Blomst ned i halsen på dig!« Han slog Shere Khan i hovedet med grenen. I ren pinsel af skræk klynkede og hvinede tigeren.

value.en: “Pah! Singed jungle cat--go now! But remember when next I come to the Council Rock, as a man should come, it will be with Shere Khan’s hide on my head. For the rest, Akela goes free to live as he pleases. Ye will not kill him, because that is not my will. Nor do I think that ye will sit here any longer, lolling out your tongues as though ye were somebodies, instead of dogs whom I drive out--thus! Go!” The fire was burning furiously at the end of the branch, and Mowgli struck right and left round the circle, and the wolves ran howling with the sparks burning their fur. At last there were only Akela, Bagheera, and perhaps ten wolves that had taken Mowgli’s part. Then something began to hurt Mowgli inside him, as he had never been hurt in his life before, and he caught his breath and sobbed, and the tears ran down his face.
value.da: »Pah! Din svedne junglekat — væk med dig! Og husk dette: Næste gang jeg kommer til Rådsklippen, kommer jeg, som et menneske bør, med Shere Khans skind på hovedet. Hvad resten af jer angår, så er Akela fri til at leve, som han vil. I skal ikke dræbe ham, det forbyder jeg. Og jeg tror ikke, I bliver her længere med tungen hængende ud, som om I var vigtige, i stedet for hunde, jeg jager væk — sådan her! Væk!« Enden af grenen brændte vildt. Mowgli slog ud til alle sider rundt om kredsen, og ulvene flygtede hylende med svedet pels efter gnisterne. Til sidst var der kun Akela, Bagheera og måske ti ulve tilbage, der havde holdt med Mowgli. Så begyndte der at gøre ondt inde i ham på en måde, han aldrig havde kendt. Han snappede efter vejret, hulkede, og tårerne løb ned ad kinderne.

value.en: “What is it? What is it?” he said. “I do not wish to leave the jungle, and I do not know what this is. Am I dying, Bagheera?”
value.da: »Hvad er det? Hvad er det?« sagde han. »Jeg ønsker ikke at forlade junglen, og jeg ved ikke, hvad dette er. Er jeg ved at dø, Bagheera?«

value.en: “No, Little Brother. That is only tears such as men use,” said Bagheera. “Now I know thou art a man, and a man’s cub no longer. The jungle is shut indeed to thee henceforward. Let them fall, Mowgli. They are only tears.” So Mowgli sat and cried as though his heart would break; and he had never cried in all his life before.
value.da: »Nej, Lillebror. Det er bare tårer, sådan nogle som mennesker græder,« sagde Bagheera. »Nu ved jeg, at du er et menneske og ikke længere et menneskebarn. Fra nu af er junglen virkelig lukket for dig. Lad dem løbe, Mowgli. Det er kun tårer.« Og Mowgli sad og græd, som om hjertet skulle briste, selv om han aldrig havde grædt i hele sit liv før.

value.en: “Now,” he said, “I will go to men. But first I must say farewell to my mother.” And he went to the cave where she lived with Father Wolf, and he cried on her coat, while the four cubs howled miserably.
value.da: »Nu,« sagde han, »vil jeg gå til menneskene. Men først må jeg sige farvel til min mor.« Og han gik til hulen, hvor hun boede med Far Ulv, og han græd ind i hendes pels, mens de fire hvalpe hylede sørgmodigt.

value.en: “Ye will not forget me?” said Mowgli.
value.da: »I glemmer mig vel ikke?« spurgte Mowgli.

value.en: “Never while we can follow a trail,” said the cubs. “Come to the foot of the hill when thou art a man, and we will talk to thee; and we will come into the croplands to play with thee by night.”
value.da: »Aldrig, så længe vi kan følge et spor,« sagde hvalpene. »Kom til foden af bakken, når du er en mand, og vi vil tale med dig; og vi vil komme ud på de dyrkede marker for at lege med dig om natten.«

value.en: “Come soon!” said Father Wolf. “Oh, wise little frog, come again soon; for we be old, thy mother and I.”
value.da: »Kom snart!« sagde Far Ulv. »Åh, kloge lille frø, kom snart igen; for vi er gamle, din mor og jeg.«

value.en: “Come soon,” said Mother Wolf, “little naked son of mine. For, listen, child of man, I loved thee more than ever I loved my cubs.”
value.da: »Kom snart,« sagde Mor Ulv, »min lille nøgne søn. For hør, menneskebarn, jeg elskede dig mere, end jeg nogensinde elskede mine hvalpe.«

value.en: “I will surely come,” said Mowgli. “And when I come it will be to lay out Shere Khan’s hide upon the Council Rock. Do not forget me! Tell them in the jungle never to forget me!”
value.da: »Jeg lover, at jeg kommer tilbage,« sagde Mowgli. »Og når jeg gør, breder jeg Shere Khans skind ud over Rådsklippen. Glem mig ikke! Sig til alle i junglen, at de aldrig må glemme mig!«

value.en: The dawn was beginning to break when Mowgli went down the hillside alone, to meet those mysterious things that are called men.
value.da: Dagen var ved at gry, da Mowgli gik alene ned ad bakken for at møde de mystiske væsener, der kaldes mennesker.

value.en: Hunting-Song of the Seeonee Pack
value.da: Seeoneeflokkens Jagtsang

value.en:
As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur belled
Once, twice and again!
And a doe leaped up, and a doe leaped up
From the pond in the wood where the wild deer sup.
This I, scouting alone, beheld,
Once, twice and again!
value.da:
Da daggryet brød frem, kaldte sambarhjorten
én, to, og atter en gang!
Og en hind sprang op, og en hind sprang op
fra vandhullet i skoven, hvor de vilde hjorte drikker.
Dette så jeg, da jeg spejdede alene,
én, to, og atter en gang!

value.en:
As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur belled
Once, twice and again!
And a wolf stole back, and a wolf stole back
To carry the word to the waiting pack,
And we sought and we found and we bayed on his track
Once, twice and again!
value.da:
Da daggryet brød frem, brølede sambarhjorten
én, to, og atter en gang!
Og en ulv listede tilbage, og en ulv listede tilbage
for at bringe ordet til den ventende flok,
og vi søgte, og vi fandt, og vi gøede i hans spor
én, to, og atter en gang!

value.en:
As the dawn was breaking the Wolf Pack yelled
Once, twice and again!
Feet in the jungle that leave no mark!
value.da:
Da daggryet brød frem, hylede Ulveflokken
én, to, og atter en gang!
Fødder i junglen, der ikke efterlader spor!

value.en:
Eyes that can see in the dark--the dark!
Tongue--give tongue to it!  Hark!  O hark!
Once, twice and again!
value.da:
Øjne der kan se i mørket — mørket!
Råb — råb ad det! Hør! Åh, hør!
én, to, og atter en gang!

value.en: His spots are the joy of the Leopard: his horns are the Buffalo’s pride. Be clean, for the strength of the hunter is known by the gloss of his hide. If ye find that the Bullock can toss you, or the heavy-browed Sambhur can gore; Ye need not stop work to inform us: we knew it ten seasons before.
value.da: Hans pletter er Leopardens glæde; hans horn er Bøffelens stolthed. Hold dig ren, for en jægers styrke kan ses på pelsens glans. Hvis du opdager, at Tyren kan kaste dig op i luften, eller at den tunge sambarhjort med de tykke bryn kan stange dig, så behøver du ikke afbryde arbejdet for at fortælle os det: vi vidste det allerede for ti årstider siden.

value.en:
Oppress not the cubs of the stranger, but hail them as Sister and Brother,
For though they are little and fubsy, it may be the Bear is their mother.
“There is none like to me!” says the Cub in the pride of his earliest kill;
But the jungle is large and the Cub he is small. Let him think and be still.
_Maxims of Baloo_
value.da:
Plag ikke den fremmedes unger, men hils dem som Søster og Broder,
for selv om de er små og buttede, kan det være, at Bjørnen er deres mor.
»Der findes ingen som mig!« siger Ungen i sin stolthed over sit første drab;
men junglen er stor, og Ungen er lille. Lad ham tænke efter og tie stille.
_Baloos leveregler_

value.en: All that is told here happened some time before Mowgli was turned out of the Seeonee Wolf Pack, or revenged himself on Shere Khan the tiger. It was in the days when Baloo was teaching him the Law of the Jungle. The big, serious, old brown bear was delighted to have so quick a pupil, for the young wolves will only learn as much of the Law of the Jungle as applies to their own pack and tribe, and run away as soon as they can repeat the Hunting Verse--“Feet that make no noise; eyes that can see in the dark; ears that can hear the winds in their lairs, and sharp white teeth, all these things are the marks of our brothers except Tabaqui the Jackal and the Hyaena whom we hate.” But Mowgli, as a man-cub, had to learn a great deal more than this. Sometimes Bagheera the Black Panther would come lounging through the jungle to see how his pet was getting on, and would purr with his head against a tree while Mowgli recited the day’s lesson to Baloo. The boy could climb almost as well as he could swim, and swim almost as well as he could run. So Baloo, the Teacher of the Law, taught him the Wood and Water Laws: how to tell a rotten branch from a sound one; how to speak politely to the wild bees when he came upon a hive of them fifty feet above ground; what to say to Mang the Bat when he disturbed him in the branches at midday; and how to warn the water-snakes in the pools before he splashed down among them. None of the Jungle People like being disturbed, and all are very ready to fly at an intruder. Then, too, Mowgli was taught the Strangers’ Hunting Call, which must be repeated aloud till it is answered, whenever one of the Jungle-People hunts outside his own grounds. It means, translated, “Give me leave to hunt here because I am hungry.” And the answer is, “Hunt then for food, but not for pleasure.”
value.da: Alt det, der fortælles her, skete, før Mowgli blev jaget ud af Seeonee-ulveflokken, og før han tog hævn over tigeren Shere Khan. Dengang lærte Baloo ham stadig Junglens Lov. Den store, alvorlige, gamle brune bjørn var glad for at have en så lærenem elev. De unge ulve lærer nemlig kun den del af Junglens Lov, der handler om deres egen flok og stamme, og de løber deres vej, så snart de kan remse Jagtverset op: »Fødder, der går uden lyd; øjne, der ser i mørke; ører, der kan høre vindene i deres huler; og skarpe hvide tænder — det er kendetegnene på alle vore brødre, undtagen Tabaqui Sjakalen og Hyænen, som vi hader.« Men Mowgli var en menneskeunge og måtte lære langt mere. Nogle gange kom den sorte panter Bagheera slentrende gennem junglen for at se, hvordan hans yndling klarede sig. Han lagde hovedet mod et træ og spandt, mens Mowgli sagde dagens lektie op for Baloo. Drengen kunne nu klatre næsten lige så godt, som han kunne svømme, og svømme næsten lige så godt, som han kunne løbe. Derfor lærte Baloo, Lovens Lærer, ham også Skovens og Vandets Love. Han lærte at kende forskel på rådne grene og stærke, at tale høfligt til de vilde bier, når han fandt en bikube halvtreds fod oppe i et træ, at sige det rigtige til flagermusen Mang, hvis han forstyrrede ham i grenene midt på dagen, og at advare vandslangerne, før han plumpede ned i deres vandhuller. Ingen af Junglens Folk bryder sig om at blive forstyrret, og enhver af dem går straks til angreb mod en ubuden gæst. Mowgli lærte også Fremmedes Jagtråb. Hver gang en af Junglens Folk jager uden for sit eget område, skal han råbe det højt og blive ved, indtil nogen svarer. Oversat betyder det: »Giv mig lov at jage her, for jeg er sulten.« Og svaret er: »Jag da for at få mad, men ikke for sjov.«

value.en: All this will show you how much Mowgli had to learn by heart, and he grew very tired of saying the same thing over a hundred times. But, as Baloo said to Bagheera, one day when Mowgli had been cuffed and run off in a temper, “A man’s cub is a man’s cub, and he must learn all the Law of the Jungle.”
value.da: Alt dette viser, hvor meget Mowgli måtte lære udenad. Han blev dødtræt af at sige det samme over hundrede gange. Men en dag, da Mowgli havde fået en lussing og var løbet væk i raseri, sagde Baloo til Bagheera: »En menneskeunge er en menneskeunge. Han må lære hele Junglens Lov.«

value.en: “But think how small he is,” said the Black Panther, who would have spoiled Mowgli if he had had his own way. “How can his little head carry all thy long talk?”
value.da: »Husk, hvor lille han er,« sagde den sorte panter, som helt sikkert ville have forkælet Mowgli, hvis han havde fået lov. »Hvordan skal det lille hoved kunne rumme alle dine lange taler?«

value.en: “Is there anything in the jungle too little to be killed? No. That is why I teach him these things, and that is why I hit him, very softly, when he forgets.”
value.da: »Er der noget i junglen, der er for lille til at blive dræbt? Nej. Det er derfor, jeg lærer ham alt det her, og det er derfor, jeg giver ham en helt blid lussing, når han glemmer det.«

value.en: “Softly! What dost thou know of softness, old Iron-feet?” Bagheera grunted. “His face is all bruised today by thy--softness. Ugh.”
value.da: »Blidt!« knurrede Bagheera. »Hvad ved du om at være blid, gamle Jernfod? Hans ansigt er fuldt af blå mærker i dag på grund af din — blidhed. Uf.«

value.en: “Better he should be bruised from head to foot by me who love him than that he should come to harm through ignorance,” Baloo answered very earnestly. “I am now teaching him the Master Words of the Jungle that shall protect him with the birds and the Snake People, and all that hunt on four feet, except his own pack. He can now claim protection, if he will only remember the words, from all in the jungle. Is not that worth a little beating?”
value.da: »Det er langt bedre, at jeg giver ham blå mærker fra top til tå, fordi jeg holder af ham, end at han kommer til skade, fordi han ikke ved bedre,« sagde Baloo meget alvorligt. »Jeg lærer ham nu Junglens Mesterord. De skal beskytte ham blandt fuglene, blandt Slangefolket og blandt alle de firbenede jægere uden for hans egen flok. Hvis han bare husker ordene, kan han kræve beskyttelse af alle i junglen. Er det ikke et par slag værd?«

value.en: “Well, look to it then that thou dost not kill the man-cub. He is no tree trunk to sharpen thy blunt claws upon. But what are those Master Words? I am more likely to give help than to ask it”--Bagheera stretched out one paw and admired the steel-blue, ripping-chisel talons at the end of it--“still I should like to know.”
value.da: »Så pas på, at du ikke slår menneskeungen ihjel, mens du lærer ham det. Han er ikke en træstamme, du kan slibe dine sløve kløer på. Men hvad er det for nogle Mesterord? Jeg plejer at hjælpe andre i stedet for at bede om hjælp« — Bagheera strakte en pote frem og beundrede de stålblå kløer, der var skarpe som mejsler og kunne flå ting i stykker — »men jeg vil alligevel gerne høre dem.«

value.en: “I will call Mowgli and he shall say them--if he will. Come, Little Brother!”
value.da: »Jeg kalder på Mowgli, så skal han sige dem — hvis han vil. Kom, Lillebror!«

value.en: “My head is ringing like a bee tree,” said a sullen little voice over their heads, and Mowgli slid down a tree trunk very angry and indignant, adding as he reached the ground: “I come for Bagheera and not for thee, fat old Baloo!”
value.da: »Mit hoved summer som et træ fuldt af bier,« sagde en gnaven lille stemme oven over dem. Mowgli gled ned ad en træstamme, fuld af vrede og forurettelse, og da hans fødder rørte jorden, tilføjede han: »Jeg kommer for Bagheeras skyld, ikke for din, fede gamle Baloo!«

value.en: “That is all one to me,” said Baloo, though he was hurt and grieved. “Tell Bagheera, then, the Master Words of the Jungle that I have taught thee this day.”
value.da: »Det er det samme for mig,« sagde Baloo, selvom han var såret og bedrøvet. »Fortæl da Bagheera Junglens Mesterord, som jeg har lært dig i dag.«

value.en: “Master Words for which people?” said Mowgli, delighted to show off. “The jungle has many tongues. I know them all.”
value.da: »Mesterord for hvilket folk?« spurgte Mowgli, glad for at få lov at vise sig frem. »Junglen har mange sprog, og jeg kender dem alle.«

value.en: “A little thou knowest, but not much. See, O Bagheera, they never thank their teacher. Not one small wolfling has ever come back to thank old Baloo for his teachings. Say the word for the Hunting-People, then--great scholar.”
value.da: »Du kender lidt, og ikke mere end lidt. Se, Bagheera, de takker aldrig dem, der lærer dem noget. Ikke en eneste lille ulv er nogensinde kommet tilbage for at takke gamle Baloo for det, han lærte den. Sig os så Jagtfolkets ord, store lærde.«

value.en: “We be of one blood, ye and I,” said Mowgli, giving the words the Bear accent which all the Hunting People use.
value.da: »Vi er af ét blod, du og jeg,« sagde Mowgli og talte med den bjørneagtige accent, som alle i Jagtfolket har.

value.en: “Good. Now for the birds.”
value.da: »Godt. Nu fuglene.«

value.en: Mowgli repeated, with the Kite’s whistle at the end of the sentence.
value.da: Mowgli gentog det med Glentens fløjt til sidst i sætningen.

value.en: “Now for the Snake-People,” said Bagheera.
value.da: »Nu Slangefolket,« sagde Bagheera.

value.en: The answer was a perfectly indescribable hiss, and Mowgli kicked up his feet behind, clapped his hands together to applaud himself, and jumped on to Bagheera’s back, where he sat sideways, drumming with his heels on the glossy skin and making the worst faces he could think of at Baloo.
value.da: Svaret var en hvæsen, der ikke kan beskrives. Mowgli sparkede bagud, klappede i hænderne for at hylde sin egen optræden og sprang op på Bagheeras ryg. Der sad han sidelæns, trommede med hælene mod den blanke pels og lavede de værste grimasser, han kunne finde på, til Baloo.

value.en: “There--there! That was worth a little bruise,” said the brown bear tenderly. “Some day thou wilt remember me.” Then he turned aside to tell Bagheera how he had begged the Master Words from Hathi the Wild Elephant, who knows all about these things, and how Hathi had taken Mowgli down to a pool to get the Snake Word from a water-snake, because Baloo could not pronounce it, and how Mowgli was now reasonably safe against all accidents in the jungle, because neither snake, bird, nor beast would hurt him.
value.da: »Sådan, sådan! Det var et par blå mærker værd,« sagde den brune bjørn kærligt. »En dag vil du huske mig.« Så vendte han sig mod Bagheera og fortalte, hvordan han havde tigget Mesterordene af den vilde elefant Hathi, der ved alt om den slags. Hathi havde ført Mowgli ned til et vandhul for at lære Slangeordet af en vandslange, fordi Baloo ikke selv kunne sige det. Nu var Mowgli rimeligt godt beskyttet mod uheld i hele junglen, for hverken slange, fugl eller dyr ville gøre ham fortræd.

value.en: “No one then is to be feared,” Baloo wound up, patting his big furry stomach with pride.
value.da: »Så er der ingen tilbage, han skal være bange for,« sluttede Baloo og klappede stolt sin store, lodne mave.

value.en: “Except his own tribe,” said Bagheera, under his breath; and then aloud to Mowgli, “Have a care for my ribs, Little Brother! What is all this dancing up and down?”
value.da: »Undtagen hans egen stamme,« mumlede Bagheera. Så sagde han højt til Mowgli: »Pas på mine ribben, Lillebror! Hvorfor hopper du sådan rundt?«

value.en: Mowgli had been trying to make himself heard by pulling at Bagheera’s shoulder fur and kicking hard. When the two listened to him he was shouting at the top of his voice, “And so I shall have a tribe of my own, and lead them through the branches all day long.”
value.da: Mowgli havde hevet i pelsen på Bagheeras skuldre og sparket hårdt for at få deres opmærksomhed. Da de endelig lyttede, råbte han af fuld hals: »Og så får jeg min helt egen stamme, og jeg vil føre dem gennem trætoppene hele dagen.«

value.en: “What is this new folly, little dreamer of dreams?” said Bagheera.
value.da: »Hvad er det nu for en ny dumhed, du har fundet på, lille drømmer?« spurgte Bagheera.

value.en: “Yes, and throw branches and dirt at old Baloo,” Mowgli went on. “They have promised me this. Ah!”
value.da: »Ja, og kaste grene og snavs på gamle Baloo,« fortsatte Mowgli. »De har lovet mig det. Ah!«

value.en: “Whoof!” Baloo’s big paw scooped Mowgli off Bagheera’s back, and as the boy lay between the big fore-paws he could see the Bear was angry.
value.da: »Whuf!« Med den ene store pote fejede Baloo Mowgli af Bagheeras ryg. Som drengen lå mellem de enorme forpoter, kunne han se, at Bjørnen var vred.

value.en: “Mowgli,” said Baloo, “thou hast been talking with the Bandar-log--the Monkey People.”
value.da: »Mowgli,« sagde Baloo, »du har talt med Bandar-log — Abefolket.«

value.en: Mowgli looked at Bagheera to see if the Panther was angry too, and Bagheera’s eyes were as hard as jade stones.
value.da: Mowgli kiggede på Bagheera for at se, om Panteren også var vred, og Bagheeras øjne var hårde som jadesten.

value.en: “Thou hast been with the Monkey People--the gray apes--the people without a law--the eaters of everything. That is great shame.”
value.da: »Du har været sammen med Abefolket — de grå aber, der lever uden nogen lov og æder alt muligt. Du burde skamme dig gevaldigt.«

value.en: “When Baloo hurt my head,” said Mowgli (he was still on his back), “I went away, and the gray apes came down from the trees and had pity on me. No one else cared.” He snuffled a little.
value.da: »Da Baloo gjorde ondt i mit hoved,« sagde Mowgli, som stadig lå på ryggen, »gik jeg min vej. De grå aber kom ned fra træerne og havde ondt af mig. Ingen andre brød sig om det.« Han snøftede lidt.

value.en: “The pity of the Monkey People!” Baloo snorted. “The stillness of the mountain stream! The cool of the summer sun! And then, man-cub?”
value.da: »Abefolkets medfølelse!« fnyste Baloo. »Så fredfyldt som en bjergbæk! Så kølig som sommersolen! Og hvad så, menneskeunge?«

value.en: “And then, and then, they gave me nuts and pleasant things to eat, and they--they carried me in their arms up to the top of the trees and said I was their blood brother except that I had no tail, and should be their leader some day.”
value.da: »Og så, og så gav de mig nødder og lækre ting at spise, og de — de bar mig i deres arme op til toppen af træerne og sagde, at jeg var deres blodbroder, bortset fra at jeg ikke havde nogen hale, og at jeg en dag skulle være deres leder.«

value.en: “They have no leader,” said Bagheera. “They lie. They have always lied.”
value.da: »De har ingen leder,« sagde Bagheera. »Det, de sagde, er løgn. De har altid løjet.«

value.en: “They were very kind and bade me come again. Why have I never been taken among the Monkey People? They stand on their feet as I do. They do not hit me with their hard paws. They play all day. Let me get up! Bad Baloo, let me up! I will play with them again.”
value.da: »De var meget venlige og bad mig komme igen. Hvorfor er jeg aldrig blevet bragt blandt Abefolket? De står på deres fødder ligesom jeg. De slår mig ikke med deres hårde poter. De leger hele dagen. Lad mig komme op! Slemme Baloo, lad mig op! Jeg vil lege med dem igen.«

value.en: “Listen, man-cub,” said the Bear, and his voice rumbled like thunder on a hot night. “I have taught thee all the Law of the Jungle for all the peoples of the jungle--except the Monkey-Folk who live in the trees. They have no law. They are outcasts. They have no speech of their own, but use the stolen words which they overhear when they listen, and peep, and wait up above in the branches. Their way is not our way. They are without leaders. They have no remembrance. They boast and chatter and pretend that they are a great people about to do great affairs in the jungle, but the falling of a nut turns their minds to laughter and all is forgotten. We of the jungle have no dealings with them. We do not drink where the monkeys drink; we do not go where the monkeys go; we do not hunt where they hunt; we do not die where they die. Hast thou ever heard me speak of the Bandar-log till today?”
value.da: »Hør efter, menneskeunge,« sagde Bjørnen, og hans stemme rumlede som torden på en lummer nat. »Jeg har lært dig hele Junglens Lov for alle junglens folk — undtagen Abefolket oppe i træerne. De har slet ingen lov. De er udstødte. De har intet eget sprog, men stjæler de ord, de opsnapper, når de sidder højt oppe i grenene og lytter og kigger ned. Deres veje er ikke vores veje. De har ingen ledere. De husker ingenting. De praler og pludrer og lader, som om de er et mægtigt folk, der lige er ved at udrette store ting i junglen. Så falder en nød ned, de begynder at le, og så er alt glemt. Vi i junglen vil ikke have noget med dem at gøre. Vi drikker ikke, hvor aberne drikker, og vi går ikke, hvor aberne går. Vi jager ikke, hvor de jager, og vi dør ikke, hvor de dør. Har du før i dag nogensinde hørt mig tale om Bandar-log?«

value.en: “No,” said Mowgli in a whisper, for the forest was very still now Baloo had finished.
value.da: »Nej,« sagde Mowgli hviskende, for skoven var meget stille nu, hvor Baloo havde sluttet.

value.en: “The Jungle-People put them out of their mouths and out of their minds. They are very many, evil, dirty, shameless, and they desire, if they have any fixed desire, to be noticed by the Jungle People. But we do not notice them even when they throw nuts and filth on our heads.”
value.da: »Junglens Folk lader dem ude af mund og sind. De er meget mange, onde, beskidte, skamløse, og de ønsker, hvis de overhovedet har noget fast ønske, at blive bemærket af Junglens Folk. Men vi bemærker dem ikke, selv når de kaster nødder og snavs på vore hoveder.«

value.en: He had hardly spoken when a shower of nuts and twigs spattered down through the branches; and they could hear coughings and howlings and angry jumpings high up in the air among the thin branches.
value.da: Ordene var knap nok sagt, før nødder og kviste raslede ned gennem grenene. Højt oppe i de tynde trætoppe kunne de høre host og hyl og lyden af vrede aber, der sprang rundt.

value.en: “The Monkey-People are forbidden,” said Baloo, “forbidden to the Jungle-People. Remember.”
value.da: »Junglens Folk må ikke have noget med Abefolket at gøre,« sagde Baloo. »Det er forbudt. Husk det.«

value.en: “Forbidden,” said Bagheera, “but I still think Baloo should have warned thee against them.”
value.da: »Forbudt,« sagde Bagheera, »men jeg synes alligevel, Baloo burde have advaret dig mod dem.«

value.en: “I--I? How was I to guess he would play with such dirt. The Monkey People! Faugh!”
value.da: »Jeg — jeg? Hvordan skulle jeg gætte, at han ville lege med sådant skidt. Abefolket! Føj!«

value.en: A fresh shower came down on their heads and the two trotted away, taking Mowgli with them. What Baloo had said about the monkeys was perfectly true. They belonged to the tree-tops, and as beasts very seldom look up, there was no occasion for the monkeys and the Jungle-People to cross each other’s path. But whenever they found a sick wolf, or a wounded tiger, or bear, the monkeys would torment him, and would throw sticks and nuts at any beast for fun and in the hope of being noticed. Then they would howl and shriek senseless songs, and invite the Jungle-People to climb up their trees and fight them, or would start furious battles over nothing among themselves, and leave the dead monkeys where the Jungle-People could see them. They were always just going to have a leader, and laws and customs of their own, but they never did, because their memories would not hold over from day to day, and so they compromised things by making up a saying, “What the Bandar-log think now the jungle will think later,” and that comforted them a great deal. None of the beasts could reach them, but on the other hand none of the beasts would notice them, and that was why they were so pleased when Mowgli came to play with them, and they heard how angry Baloo was.
value.da: Endnu et regnskyl faldt ned over deres hoveder. De to dyr travede af sted med Mowgli imellem sig. Alt, hvad Baloo havde sagt om aberne, var sandt. De boede i trætoppene, og da dyr sjældent ser op, var der normalt ingen grund til, at aberne og Junglens Folk mødtes. Men når aberne fandt en syg ulv eller en såret tiger eller bjørn, plagede de ham. De kastede pinde og nødder efter alle dyr for sjov og i håb om, at nogen ville bemærke dem. De hylede og skreg meningsløse sange, de opfordrede Junglens Folk til at klatre op i deres træer og kæmpe, eller de gik i vilde slagsmål indbyrdes over ingenting og lod de døde ligge, hvor Junglens Folk kunne se dem. De var altid lige ved at vælge en leder og lave egne love og skikke. Det blev aldrig til noget, for de kunne ikke huske deres planer fra den ene dag til den næste. I stedet nøjedes de med et ordsprog, de selv havde fundet på: »Det, Bandar-log tænker i dag, tænker junglen i morgen.« Det trøstede dem meget. Ingen andre dyr kunne nå dem, men ingen andre dyr ville heller bemærke dem. Derfor var de blevet så glade for at lege med Mowgli, og derfor var de så glade for at høre, hvor vred Baloo var.

value.en: They never meant to do any more--the Bandar-log never mean anything at all; but one of them invented what seemed to him a brilliant idea, and he told all the others that Mowgli would be a useful person to keep in the tribe, because he could weave sticks together for protection from the wind; so, if they caught him, they could make him teach them. Of course Mowgli, as a woodcutter’s child, inherited all sorts of instincts, and used to make little huts of fallen branches without thinking how he came to do it. The Monkey-People, watching in the trees, considered his play most wonderful. This time, they said, they were really going to have a leader and become the wisest people in the jungle--so wise that everyone else would notice and envy them. Therefore they followed Baloo and Bagheera and Mowgli through the jungle very quietly till it was time for the midday nap, and Mowgli, who was very much ashamed of himself, slept between the Panther and the Bear, resolving to have no more to do with the Monkey People.
value.da: De havde ikke planlagt mere — Bandar-log planlægger aldrig rigtigt noget. Men en af aberne fik en idé, som forekom ham vidunderlig. Han sagde til de andre, at Mowgli ville være nyttig i stammen, fordi han kunne flette pinde sammen til læ mod vinden. Fangede de ham, kunne de få ham til at lære dem det. Mowgli var en skovhuggers barn og havde naturligvis arvet alle mulige instinkter. Han plejede at bygge små hytter af nedfaldne grene uden at tænke over, hvordan han vidste, hvad han skulle gøre. Abefolket, der så på oppefra, syntes, at hans leg var vidunderlig. Denne gang, sagde de, ville de virkelig få en leder og blive det klogeste folk i junglen — så kloge, at alle andre ville lægge mærke til dem og misunde dem. Stille fulgte de efter Baloo, Bagheera og Mowgli gennem skoven, indtil det blev tid til middagsluren. Mowgli skammede sig dybt og faldt i søvn mellem Bjørnen og Panteren, fast besluttet på aldrig mere at have noget med Abefolket at gøre.

value.en: The next thing he remembered was feeling hands on his legs and arms--hard, strong, little hands--and then a swash of branches in his face, and then he was staring down through the swaying boughs as Baloo woke the jungle with his deep cries and Bagheera bounded up the trunk with every tooth bared. The Bandar-log howled with triumph and scuffled away to the upper branches where Bagheera dared not follow, shouting: “He has noticed us! Bagheera has noticed us. All the Jungle-People admire us for our skill and our cunning.” Then they began their flight; and the flight of the Monkey-People through tree-land is one of the things nobody can describe. They have their regular roads and crossroads, up hills and down hills, all laid out from fifty to seventy or a hundred feet above ground, and by these they can travel even at night if necessary. Two of the strongest monkeys caught Mowgli under the arms and swung off with him through the treetops, twenty feet at a bound. Had they been alone they could have gone twice as fast, but the boy’s weight held them back. Sick and giddy as Mowgli was he could not help enjoying the wild rush, though the glimpses of earth far down below frightened him, and the terrible check and jerk at the end of the swing over nothing but empty air brought his heart between his teeth. His escort would rush him up a tree till he felt the thinnest topmost branches crackle and bend under them, and then with a cough and a whoop would fling themselves into the air outward and downward, and bring up, hanging by their hands or their feet to the lower limbs of the next tree. Sometimes he could see for miles and miles across the still green jungle, as a man on the top of a mast can see for miles across the sea, and then the branches and leaves would lash him across the face, and he and his two guards would be almost down to earth again. So, bounding and crashing and whooping and yelling, the whole tribe of Bandar-log swept along the tree-roads with Mowgli their prisoner.
value.da: Det næste, han vidste, var, at små hænder — hårde, stærke hænder — greb fat om hans arme og ben. Grene strejfede hans ansigt. Så kiggede han ned gennem svajende grene, mens Baloos dybe råb vækkede junglen, og Bagheera for op ad træstammen med alle tænderne blottet. Bandar-log hylede triumferende og klatrede højere op på grene, hvor Bagheera ikke turde følge efter. »Han har lagt mærke til os!« råbte de. »Bagheera har lagt mærke til os. Hele Junglens Folk beundrer vores kløgt og dygtighed.« Så flygtede de. Ingen kan rigtig beskrive, hvordan Abefolket bevæger sig gennem træernes verden. De har deres egne veje og kryds over bakker og dale, alle sammen halvtreds, halvfjerds eller hundrede fod over jorden. De kan følge dem, selv når det er mørkt, hvis det er nødvendigt. To særligt stærke aber greb Mowgli under armene og svingede af sted med ham gennem trætoppene, hvor de tilbagelagde tyve fod i hvert spring. Uden ham kunne de have bevæget sig dobbelt så hurtigt, men hans vægt trak dem ned. Mowgli var svimmel og kvalm, men kunne alligevel ikke lade være med at nyde den vilde fart. Glimtene af jorden langt nede skræmte ham dog, og hvert forfærdeligt ryk, når en svingtur over tom luft blev standset, fik hans hjerte op i halsen. Aberne løb op ad et træ med ham, til han kunne mærke de tynde grene øverst knage og bøje sig under dem. Så kastede de sig med et host og et hvin ud og ned og greb fat i de nederste grene på det næste træ med hænder eller fødder. Nogle gange kunne han se milevidt ud over den stille grønne jungle, ligesom en mand i masten på et skib kan se milevidt ud over havet. Så pískede blade og grene ham i ansigtet, og han og hans to vogtere styrtede næsten ned til jorden igen. Hele Bandar-log-stammen fejede af sted ad vejene i træerne, med Mowgli som fange, og de sprang, brasede, hvinede og råbte.

value.en: For a time he was afraid of being dropped. Then he grew angry but knew better than to struggle, and then he began to think. The first thing was to send back word to Baloo and Bagheera, for, at the pace the monkeys were going, he knew his friends would be left far behind. It was useless to look down, for he could only see the topsides of the branches, so he stared upward and saw, far away in the blue, Rann the Kite balancing and wheeling as he kept watch over the jungle waiting for things to die. Rann saw that the monkeys were carrying something, and dropped a few hundred yards to find out whether their load was good to eat. He whistled with surprise when he saw Mowgli being dragged up to a treetop and heard him give the Kite call for--“We be of one blood, thou and I.” The waves of the branches closed over the boy, but Rann balanced away to the next tree in time to see the little brown face come up again. “Mark my trail!” Mowgli shouted. “Tell Baloo of the Seeonee Pack and Bagheera of the Council Rock.”
value.da: I begyndelsen var han bange for, at de ville tabe ham. Så blev han vred, men havde forstand nok til ikke at kæmpe imod. Til sidst begyndte han at tænke. Han måtte få sendt besked til Baloo og Bagheera, for med den fart ville aberne snart efterlade hans venner langt bagude. Det nyttede ikke at kigge ned, for grenene skjulte alt undtagen deres overside. I stedet kiggede han op. Langt væk på den blå himmel svævede og kredsede glenten Rann og holdt øje med junglen, mens den ventede på, at noget skulle dø. Rann så, at aberne bar på en byrde, og dykkede nogle hundrede meter ned for at se, om det var noget at spise. Han fløjtede forbløffet, da Mowgli blev slæbt op i en trætop, og hørte ham råbe på Glentens sprog: »Vi er af ét blod, du og jeg.« De svajende grene slugte drengen igen, men Rann svævede over til det næste træ og nåede at se det lille brune ansigt dukke op igen. »Følg mit spor!« råbte Mowgli. »Sig til Baloo fra Seeonee-flokken og til Bagheera fra Rådsklippen.«

value.en: “In whose name, Brother?” Rann had never seen Mowgli before, though of course he had heard of him.
value.da: »Hvilket navn skal jeg give dem, Bror?« Rann havde naturligvis hørt om Mowgli, men aldrig set ham før.

value.en: “Mowgli, the Frog. Man-cub they call me! Mark my trail!”
value.da: »Mowgli, Frøen. De kalder mig menneskeunge! Følg mit spor!«

value.en: The last words were shrieked as he was being swung through the air, but Rann nodded and rose up till he looked no bigger than a speck of dust, and there he hung, watching with his telescope eyes the swaying of the treetops as Mowgli’s escort whirled along.
value.da: Han hvinede de sidste ord, mens aberne svingede ham gennem luften. Rann nikkede og steg opad, indtil han ikke så større ud end et støvkorn. Der svævede han og fulgte med sine teleskopskarpe øjne de urolige trætoppe, mens Mowglis fangevogtere fór videre.

value.en: “They never go far,” he said with a chuckle. “They never do what they set out to do. Always pecking at new things are the Bandar-log. This time, if I have any eye-sight, they have pecked down trouble for themselves, for Baloo is no fledgling and Bagheera can, as I know, kill more than goats.”
value.da: »De kommer aldrig særlig langt,« grinede han. »De gør aldrig færdigt, hvad de begynder på. Bandar-log hakker altid i noget nyt. Hvis mine øjne ikke svigter, har de denne gang hakket sig ud i vanskeligheder. Baloo er ingen kylling, og Bagheera kan, det ved jeg, dræbe større ting end geder.«

value.en: So he rocked on his wings, his feet gathered up under him, and waited.
value.da: Han trak fødderne op under sig, balancerede blidt på vingerne og ventede.

value.en: Meantime, Baloo and Bagheera were furious with rage and grief. Bagheera climbed as he had never climbed before, but the thin branches broke beneath his weight, and he slipped down, his claws full of bark.
value.da: I mellemtiden var både Baloo og Bagheera grebet af raseri og sorg. Bagheera klatrede mere vildt, end han nogensinde havde gjort, men de tynde grene knækkede under ham. Han gled ned igen med kløerne fulde af bark.

value.en: “Why didst thou not warn the man-cub?” he roared to poor Baloo, who had set off at a clumsy trot in the hope of overtaking the monkeys. “What was the use of half slaying him with blows if thou didst not warn him?”
value.da: »Hvorfor advarede du ikke menneskeungen?« brølede han til stakkels Baloo, der var begyndt at jokke klodset af sted i håb om at indhente aberne. »Hvad nyttede det at slå ham halvt ihjel, når du aldrig advarede ham?«

value.en: “Haste! O haste! We--we may catch them yet!” Baloo panted.
value.da: »Skynd dig! Åh, skynd dig! Vi — vi kan måske stadig nå dem!« stønnede Baloo.

value.en: “At that speed! It would not tire a wounded cow. Teacher of the Law--cub-beater--a mile of that rolling to and fro would burst thee open. Sit still and think! Make a plan. This is no time for chasing. They may drop him if we follow too close.”
value.da: »Med den fart! Du ville ikke engang kunne udmatte en såret ko. Lovens Lærer — ungeprygler — en engelsk mil af den vraltende gang, og du ville revne. Sæt dig ned og tænk! Læg en plan. Det nytter ikke at jage dem nu. Følger vi for tæt efter, taber de ham måske.«

value.en: “Arrula! Whoo! They may have dropped him already, being tired of carrying him. Who can trust the Bandar-log? Put dead bats on my head! Give me black bones to eat! Roll me into the hives of the wild bees that I may be stung to death, and bury me with the Hyaena, for I am most miserable of bears! Arulala! Wahooa! O Mowgli, Mowgli! Why did I not warn thee against the Monkey-Folk instead of breaking thy head? Now perhaps I may have knocked the day’s lesson out of his mind, and he will be alone in the jungle without the Master Words.”
value.da: »Arrula! Whuu! Måske har de allerede tabt ham, trætte af hans vægt. Hvem kan stole på Bandar-log? Læg døde flagermus på mit hoved! Giv mig sorte knogler at spise! Rul mig ind i vilde biers reder, så de kan stikke mig ihjel, og begrav mig ved siden af Hyænen, for ingen bjørn har nogensinde været mere elendig end jeg! Arulala! Wahooa! Åh, Mowgli, Mowgli! Hvorfor bankede jeg dit hoved i stedet for at advare dig mod Abefolket? Måske har jeg slået dagens lektie helt ud af hans hoved. Måske er han nu helt alene i junglen og kan ikke huske Mesterordene.«

value.en: Baloo clasped his paws over his ears and rolled to and fro moaning.
value.da: Baloo pressede poterne mod ørerne, vuggede fra side til side og stønnede.

value.en: “At least he gave me all the Words correctly a little time ago,” said Bagheera impatiently. “Baloo, thou hast neither memory nor respect. What would the jungle think if I, the Black Panther, curled myself up like Ikki the Porcupine, and howled?”
value.da: »Han sagde i hvert fald alle Ordene rigtigt for mig for lidt siden,« sagde Bagheera utålmodigt. »Baloo, du har hverken hukommelse eller værdighed. Hvad ville junglen sige, hvis jeg, den sorte panter, rullede mig sammen som pindsvinet Ikki og begyndte at hyle?«

value.en: “What do I care what the jungle thinks? He may be dead by now.”
value.da: »Hvad bryder jeg mig om, hvad junglen tænker? Han er måske død nu.«

value.en: “Unless and until they drop him from the branches in sport, or kill him out of idleness, I have no fear for the man-cub. He is wise and well taught, and above all he has the eyes that make the Jungle-People afraid. But (and it is a great evil) he is in the power of the Bandar-log, and they, because they live in trees, have no fear of any of our people.” Bagheera licked one forepaw thoughtfully.
value.da: »Medmindre de smider ham ud af et træ for sjov eller slår ham ihjel af ren kedsomhed, er jeg ikke bange for menneskeungen. Han er klog og godt oplært, og frem for alt har han de øjne, som skræmmer Junglens Folk. Men det forfærdelige er, at Bandar-log har ham i deres vold, og fordi de bor i træerne, er de ikke bange for nogen af os.« Bagheera tænkte over det, mens han slikkede en forpote.

value.en: “Fool that I am! Oh, fat, brown, root-digging fool that I am,” said Baloo, uncoiling himself with a jerk, “it is true what Hathi the Wild Elephant says: `To each his own fear’; and they, the Bandar-log, fear Kaa the Rock Snake. He can climb as well as they can. He steals the young monkeys in the night. The whisper of his name makes their wicked tails cold. Let us go to Kaa.”
value.da: »Sikke en tåbe jeg er! Åh, sikke en fed, brun tåbe, der roder efter rødder,« råbte Baloo og rullede sig pludselig ud. »Den vilde elefant Hathi har ret, når han siger: ›Enhver har sin egen frygt.‹ Bandar-log er bange for Kaa, klippeslangen. Han kan klatre lige så godt som de, og om natten tager han de unge aber. Hvisk bare hans navn, så bliver deres slemme haler kolde. Vi må finde Kaa.«

value.en: “What will he do for us? He is not of our tribe, being footless--and with most evil eyes,” said Bagheera.
value.da: »Hvorfor skulle han hjælpe os? Han har ingen fødder, så han er ikke en af vores slags — og hans øjne er virkelig onde,« sagde Bagheera.

value.en: “He is very old and very cunning. Above all, he is always hungry,” said Baloo hopefully. “Promise him many goats.”
value.da: »Han er meget gammel og meget snu. Frem for alt er han altid sulten,« sagde Baloo håbefuldt. »Lov ham mange geder.«

value.en: “He sleeps for a full month after he has once eaten. He may be asleep now, and even were he awake what if he would rather kill his own goats?” Bagheera, who did not know much about Kaa, was naturally suspicious.
value.da: »Efter et måltid sover han en hel måned. Måske sover han lige nu. Og selv hvis han er vågen, hvad så, hvis han hellere vil fange sine egne geder?« Bagheera vidste ikke meget om Kaa og var naturligvis på vagt over for ham.

value.en: “Then in that case, thou and I together, old hunter, might make him see reason.” Here Baloo rubbed his faded brown shoulder against the Panther, and they went off to look for Kaa the Rock Python.
value.da: »Hvis det kommer til stykket, gamle jæger, kan du og jeg sammen måske få ham til at høre på fornuft.« Baloo gned sin falmede brune skulder mod Panteren, og de to gik af sted for at finde Kaa, klippepytonen.

value.en: They found him stretched out on a warm ledge in the afternoon sun, admiring his beautiful new coat, for he had been in retirement for the last ten days changing his skin, and now he was very splendid--darting his big blunt-nosed head along the ground, and twisting the thirty feet of his body into fantastic knots and curves, and licking his lips as he thought of his dinner to come.
value.da: Den eftermiddag fandt de ham liggende på en varm klippehylde i solen, hvor han beundrede sin smukke nye ham. Han havde været skjult de sidste ti dage for at skifte den gamle, og nu så han pragtfuld ud. Hans store, stumpe hoved fór langs jorden, mens han snoede alle sine tredive fod til fantastiske buer og knuder. Han slikkede sig om munden ved tanken om sit næste måltid.

value.en: “He has not eaten,” said Baloo, with a grunt of relief, as soon as he saw the beautifully mottled brown and yellow jacket. “Be careful, Bagheera! He is always a little blind after he has changed his skin, and very quick to strike.”
value.da: »Hans mave er tom,« gryntede Baloo lettet, da han så det smukke brune og gule marmorerede skind. »Pas på, Bagheera! Han ser altid lidt dårligt lige efter hamskiftet, og han slår meget hurtigt.«

value.en: Kaa was not a poison snake--in fact he rather despised the poison snakes as cowards--but his strength lay in his hug, and when he had once lapped his huge coils round anybody there was no more to be said. “Good hunting!” cried Baloo, sitting up on his haunches. Like all snakes of his breed Kaa was rather deaf, and did not hear the call at first. Then he curled up ready for any accident, his head lowered.
value.da: Kaa havde ikke gift. Han så faktisk ned på giftslanger som kujoner. Hans styrke lå i hans knugende favntag. Når først de vældige slyng lå om en, var der ikke mere at diskutere. »God jagt!« råbte Baloo og satte sig op på bagbenene. Ligesom andre af hans slags var Kaa lidt døv og hørte ikke den første hilsen. Så snoede han sig sammen, sænkede hovedet og gjorde sig klar til hvad som helst.

value.en: “Good hunting for us all,” he answered. “Oho, Baloo, what dost thou do here? Good hunting, Bagheera. One of us at least needs food. Is there any news of game afoot? A doe now, or even a young buck? I am as empty as a dried well.”
value.da: »God jagt til os alle,« svarede han. »Oho, Baloo, hvad bringer dig hertil? God jagt, Bagheera. Mindst én af os er sulten. Har I hørt om noget vildt i nærheden? En hind, måske, eller bare en ung buk? Jeg er tom som en udtørret brønd.«

value.en: “We are hunting,” said Baloo carelessly. He knew that you must not hurry Kaa. He is too big.
value.da: »Vi er ude at jage,« sagde Baloo henkastet. Han vidste, at man ikke skulle presse Kaa. Slangen var alt for stor til det.

value.en: “Give me permission to come with you,” said Kaa. “A blow more or less is nothing to thee, Bagheera or Baloo, but I--I have to wait and wait for days in a wood-path and climb half a night on the mere chance of a young ape. Psshaw! The branches are not what they were when I was young. Rotten twigs and dry boughs are they all.”
value.da: »Lad mig komme med,« sagde Kaa. »Et slag mere eller mindre gør ingen forskel for jer, Bagheera og Baloo. Men jeg — jeg må ligge i dagevis ved en skovsti og så klatre en halv nat for blot at have en chance for at fange en ung abe. Pyt! Grenene er ikke, hvad de var, da jeg var ung. Hver eneste er en rådden kvist eller en tør gren.«

value.en: “Maybe thy great weight has something to do with the matter,” said Baloo.
value.da: »Måske har din store vægt noget med sagen at gøre,« sagde Baloo.

value.en: “I am a fair length--a fair length,” said Kaa with a little pride. “But for all that, it is the fault of this new-grown timber. I came very near to falling on my last hunt--very near indeed--and the noise of my slipping, for my tail was not tight wrapped around the tree, waked the Bandar-log, and they called me most evil names.”
value.da: »Jeg er ret lang — ret lang,« sagde Kaa med et strejf af stolthed. »Alligevel er det dette nyvoksede træs skyld. På min sidste jagt var jeg ved at falde — meget nær, faktisk. Min hale var ikke viklet stramt nok om træet, og da jeg gled, vækkede larmen Bandar-log. De kaldte mig nogle virkelig grimme navne.«

value.en: “Footless, yellow earth-worm,” said Bagheera under his whiskers, as though he were trying to remember something.
value.da: »Fodløs, gul jordorm,« sagde Bagheera under sine knurhår, som om han forsøgte at huske noget.

value.en: “Sssss! Have they ever called me that?” said Kaa.
value.da: »Sssss! Er det det, de har kaldt mig?« spurgte Kaa.

value.en: “Something of that kind it was that they shouted to us last moon, but we never noticed them. They will say anything--even that thou hast lost all thy teeth, and wilt not face anything bigger than a kid, because (they are indeed shameless, these Bandar-log)--because thou art afraid of the he-goat’s horns,” Bagheera went on sweetly.
value.da: »De råbte noget i den retning til os sidste måne, men vi tog os ikke af dem. De siger hvad som helst — selv at du har mistet alle dine tænder, og at du ikke tør gå løs på noget større end et kid, fordi — disse Bandar-log er virkelig skamløse — fordi en gedebuks horn gør dig bange,« fortsatte Bagheera med sin sødeste stemme.

value.en: Now a snake, especially a wary old python like Kaa, very seldom shows that he is angry, but Baloo and Bagheera could see the big swallowing muscles on either side of Kaa’s throat ripple and bulge.
value.da: Slanger lader sjældent deres vrede vise sig, især forsigtige gamle pytoner som Kaa. Alligevel kunne Baloo og Bagheera se de store synkemuskler svulme og bølge langs begge sider af hans hals.

value.en: “The Bandar-log have shifted their grounds,” he said quietly. “When I came up into the sun today I heard them whooping among the tree-tops.”
value.da: »Bandar-log er flyttet et andet sted hen,« sagde han roligt. »Da jeg kom ud for at sole mig i dag, kunne jeg høre dem hyle i trætoppene.«

value.en: “It--it is the Bandar-log that we follow now,” said Baloo, but the words stuck in his throat, for that was the first time in his memory that one of the Jungle-People had owned to being interested in the doings of the monkeys.
value.da: »Det — det er dem, vi følger,« sagde Baloo. Det var næsten ved at kvæle ham at indrømme det. Så langt tilbage, han kunne huske, havde ingen af Junglens Folk nogensinde indrømmet at interessere sig for abernes gøren og laden.

value.en: “Beyond doubt then it is no small thing that takes two such hunters--leaders in their own jungle I am certain--on the trail of the Bandar-log,” Kaa replied courteously, as he swelled with curiosity.
value.da: »Så er det uden tvivl ingen lille sag, der bringer to sådanne jægere — ledere i deres egen jungle, det er jeg sikker på — på sporet af Bandar-log,« svarede Kaa høfligt, mens han svulmede af nysgerrighed.

value.en: “Indeed,” Baloo began, “I am no more than the old and sometimes very foolish Teacher of the Law to the Seeonee wolf-cubs, and Bagheera here--”
value.da: »Ja,« begyndte Baloo, »jeg er bare den gamle og somme tider meget tåbelige Lovens Lærer for ulveungerne i Seeonee. Og hvad Bagheera her angår —«

value.en: “Is Bagheera,” said the Black Panther, and his jaws shut with a snap, for he did not believe in being humble. “The trouble is this, Kaa. Those nut-stealers and pickers of palm leaves have stolen away our man-cub of whom thou hast perhaps heard.”
value.da: »— er Bagheera,« sagde den sorte panter og lukkede kæberne med et smæld. Ydmyghed troede han ikke på. »Sagen er den, Kaa: Disse nøddestjælere og palmebladsplukkere har bortført vores menneskeunge. Måske har du hørt om ham.«

value.en: “I heard some news from Ikki (his quills make him presumptuous) of a man-thing that was entered into a wolf pack, but I did not believe. Ikki is full of stories half heard and very badly told.”
value.da: »Ikki fortalte mig noget — de pigge gør ham alt for dristig — om et menneskevæsen, der var blevet optaget i en ulveflok. Jeg troede ikke på ham. Ikki gentager altid historier, han kun har hørt halvt, og han fortæller dem rigtig dårligt.«

value.en: “But it is true. He is such a man-cub as never was,” said Baloo. “The best and wisest and boldest of man-cubs--my own pupil, who shall make the name of Baloo famous through all the jungles; and besides, I--we--love him, Kaa.”
value.da: »Men det er sandt,« sagde Baloo. »Der har aldrig været en menneskeunge som ham. Han er den bedste, klogeste og modigste af dem alle — min egen elev, som skal gøre Baloos navn berømt i alle junglerne. Og desuden, Kaa, så elsker jeg — vi — ham.«

value.en: “Ts! Ts!” said Kaa, weaving his head to and fro. “I also have known what love is. There are tales I could tell that--”
value.da: »Ts! Ts!« sagde Kaa og vuggede hovedet frem og tilbage. »Også jeg har kendt kærligheden. Jeg kunne fortælle historier, som —«

value.en: “That need a clear night when we are all well fed to praise properly,” said Bagheera quickly. “Our man-cub is in the hands of the Bandar-log now, and we know that of all the Jungle-People they fear Kaa alone.”
value.da: »— som kræver en klar nat og mætte maver, før vi kan værdsætte dem ordentligt,« afbrød Bagheera hurtigt. »Vores menneskeunge er netop nu fange hos Bandar-log. Vi ved, at af alle i Junglens Folk er Kaa den eneste, de frygter.«

value.en: “They fear me alone. They have good reason,” said Kaa. “Chattering, foolish, vain--vain, foolish, and chattering, are the monkeys. But a man-thing in their hands is in no good luck. They grow tired of the nuts they pick, and throw them down. They carry a branch half a day, meaning to do great things with it, and then they snap it in two. That man-thing is not to be envied. They called me also--`yellow fish’ was it not?”
value.da: »De frygter ingen anden. Og det har de god grund til at gøre,« sagde Kaa. »Sikke nogle pludrende, tåbelige, forfængelige væsner aber er — forfængelige, tåbelige, pludrende væsner. Alligevel er det uheldigt, at et menneskevæsen er i deres vold. De samler nødder, bliver trætte af dem og smider dem væk. I en halv dag bærer de på en gren og planlægger vidunderlige ting at bruge den til, og så knækker de den over. Jeg misunder ikke det menneskevæsen dets situation. Og de kaldte også mig — ›gul fisk‹ var det vel?«

value.en: “Worm--worm--earth-worm,” said Bagheera, “as well as other things which I cannot now say for shame.”
value.da: »Orm — orm — jordorm,« rettede Bagheera ham. »Og andre ting, som jeg skammer mig for meget til at gentage.«

value.en: “We must remind them to speak well of their master. Aaa-ssp! We must help their wandering memories. Now, whither went they with the cub?”
value.da: »Vi må minde dem om at tale pænt om deres herre. Aaa-ssp! Vi må hjælpe deres flakkende hukommelse. Nå, hvor gik de hen med ungen?«

value.en: “The jungle alone knows. Toward the sunset, I believe,” said Baloo. “We had thought that thou wouldst know, Kaa.”
value.da: »Det ved kun junglen. Mod solnedgang, tror jeg,« sagde Baloo. »Vi havde tænkt, at du måske vidste det, Kaa.«

value.en: “I? How? I take them when they come in my way, but I do not hunt the Bandar-log, or frogs--or green scum on a water-hole, for that matter.”
value.da: »Jeg? Hvordan? Jeg tager dem, når de kommer i min vej, men jeg jager ikke Bandar-log — eller frøer — eller grønt skum på en vandpyt for den sags skyld.«

value.en: “Up, Up! Up, Up! Hillo! Illo! Illo, look up, Baloo of the Seeonee Wolf Pack!”
value.da: »Op, op! Op, op! Hillo! Illo! Illo, se herop, Baloo af Seeonee-ulveflokken!«

value.en: Baloo looked up to see where the voice came from, and there was Rann the Kite, sweeping down with the sun shining on the upturned flanges of his wings. It was near Rann’s bedtime, but he had ranged all over the jungle looking for the Bear and had missed him in the thick foliage.
value.da: Baloo løftede blikket mod stemmen. Glenten Rann svævede ned, og solen fangede kanterne af hans vinger. Det var næsten hans sengetid, men han havde søgt over hele junglen efter Bjørnen uden at få øje på ham under det tætte løv.

value.en: “What is it?” said Baloo.
value.da: »Hvad er dine nyheder?« spurgte Baloo.

value.en: “I have seen Mowgli among the Bandar-log. He bade me tell you. I watched. The Bandar-log have taken him beyond the river to the monkey city--to the Cold Lairs. They may stay there for a night, or ten nights, or an hour. I have told the bats to watch through the dark time. That is my message. Good hunting, all you below!”
value.da: »Jeg har set Mowgli blandt Bandar-log. Han bad mig fortælle jer det. Jeg holdt udkig. Bandar-log har taget ham over floden til abebyen — til De Kolde Huler. De bliver der måske én nat, eller ti nætter, eller en time. Jeg har bedt flagermusene holde vagt i mørketiden. Det er mit budskab. God jagt, alle I dernede!«

value.en: “Full gorge and a deep sleep to you, Rann,” cried Bagheera. “I will remember thee in my next kill, and put aside the head for thee alone, O best of kites!”
value.da: »Må du få en fyldt mave og dyb søvn, Rann,« råbte Bagheera. »Ved mit næste bytte husker jeg dig og gemmer hovedet til dig alene, du bedste af alle glenter!«

value.en: “It is nothing. It is nothing. The boy held the Master Word. I could have done no less,” and Rann circled up again to his roost.
value.da: »Det var ingenting, slet ingenting. Drengen kendte Mesterordet. Jeg kunne ikke have gjort mindre.« Rann kredsede opad igen mod sin sovepind.

value.en: “He has not forgotten to use his tongue,” said Baloo with a chuckle of pride. “To think of one so young remembering the Master Word for the birds too while he was being pulled across trees!”
value.da: »Han har ikke glemt, hvordan man bruger sin stemme,« sagde Baloo med et stolt grin. »Tænk, at en så ung husker selv fuglenes Mesterord, mens de slæber ham gennem trætoppene!«

value.en: “It was most firmly driven into him,” said Bagheera. “But I am proud of him, and now we must go to the Cold Lairs.”
value.da: »Lektien er i hvert fald blevet banket grundigt ind i ham,« sagde Bagheera. »Men jeg er også stolt af ham. Nu må vi af sted til De Kolde Huler.«

value.en: They all knew where that place was, but few of the Jungle People ever went there, because what they called the Cold Lairs was an old deserted city, lost and buried in the jungle, and beasts seldom use a place that men have once used. The wild boar will, but the hunting tribes do not. Besides, the monkeys lived there as much as they could be said to live anywhere, and no self-respecting animal would come within eyeshot of it except in times of drought, when the half-ruined tanks and reservoirs held a little water.
value.da: Alle tre kendte stedet, men kun få af Junglens Folk kom nogensinde dertil. De Kolde Huler, som de kaldte det, var en gammel, forladt by, skjult og opslugt af skoven. Dyr slår sig sjældent ned, hvor mennesker har boet før dem. Vildsvin gør det, men de jagende dyr holder sig væk fra den slags steder. Desuden boede aberne der, så meget som de overhovedet boede nogen steder. Intet dyr med selvrespekt ville komme inden for synsvidde af byen, undtagen i tørkeperioder, når der var lidt vand tilbage i de halvt ødelagte vandbassiner og cisterner.

value.en: [Illustration: The “Cold Lairs”]
value.da: [Illustration: De »Kolde Huler«]

value.en: “It is half a night’s journey--at full speed,” said Bagheera, and Baloo looked very serious. “I will go as fast as I can,” he said anxiously.
value.da: »Selv i vores hurtigste tempo tager det en halv nat at komme derhen,« sagde Bagheera. Baloo blev alvorlig i ansigtet. »Jeg skal gå så hurtigt, jeg overhovedet kan,« lovede han bekymret.

value.en: “We dare not wait for thee. Follow, Baloo. We must go on the quick-foot--Kaa and I.”
value.da: »Vi tør ikke risikere at vente på dig, Baloo. Følg efter os. Kaa og jeg må af sted i løb.«

value.en: “Feet or no feet, I can keep abreast of all thy four,” said Kaa shortly. Baloo made one effort to hurry, but had to sit down panting, and so they left him to come on later, while Bagheera hurried forward, at the quick panther-canter. Kaa said nothing, but, strive as Bagheera might, the huge Rock-python held level with him. When they came to a hill stream, Bagheera gained, because he bounded across while Kaa swam, his head and two feet of his neck clearing the water, but on level ground Kaa made up the distance.
value.da: »Fødder eller ej, jeg kan følge med alle fire af jeres,« sagde Kaa skarpt. Baloo prøvede at sætte farten op, men måtte snart sætte sig ned og snappe efter vejret. De lod ham komme efter senere, og Bagheera ilede af sted i en panters rappe galop. Kaa sagde ingenting. Uanset hvor hårdt Bagheera anstrengte sig, holdt den enorme klippepyton trit med ham. Ved bjergbækkene kom Bagheera foran, for han sprang over, mens Kaa svømmede med hovedet og to fod af halsen over vandet. Men på flad jord indhentede Kaa ham igen.

value.en: “By the Broken Lock that freed me,” said Bagheera, when twilight had fallen, “thou art no slow goer!”
value.da: »Ved den brudte lås, som satte mig fri,« udbrød Bagheera, da skumringen faldt på, »du ved sandelig, hvordan man kommer af sted!«

value.en: “I am hungry,” said Kaa. “Besides, they called me speckled frog.”
value.da: »Jeg er sulten,« sagde Kaa. »Desuden kaldte de mig en spættet frø.«

value.en: “Worm--earth-worm, and yellow to boot.”
value.da: »Orm — jordorm, og oven i købet gul.«

value.en: “All one. Let us go on,” and Kaa seemed to pour himself along the ground, finding the shortest road with his steady eyes, and keeping to it.
value.da: »Det gør ingen forskel. Lad os komme videre.« Kaa syntes at flyde hen over jorden, og med sit urokkelige blik fandt han den korteste vej og holdt sig til den.

value.en: In the Cold Lairs the Monkey-People were not thinking of Mowgli’s friends at all. They had brought the boy to the Lost City, and were very much pleased with themselves for the time. Mowgli had never seen an Indian city before, and though this was almost a heap of ruins it seemed very wonderful and splendid. Some king had built it long ago on a little hill. You could still trace the stone causeways that led up to the ruined gates where the last splinters of wood hung to the worn, rusted hinges. Trees had grown into and out of the walls; the battlements were tumbled down and decayed, and wild creepers hung out of the windows of the towers on the walls in bushy hanging clumps.
value.da: I De Kolde Huler tænkte Abefolket slet ikke på Mowglis venner. De havde båret drengen ind i Den Tabte By og var i øjeblikket meget tilfredse med sig selv. Mowgli havde aldrig set en indisk by før. Selv om denne næsten kun var ruiner, virkede den forbløffende og pragtfuld på ham. For længe siden havde en konge bygget den på en lille bakke. Man kunne stadig se de stenbelagte veje op til de ødelagte porte, og de sidste rester af træportene hang ved slidte, rustne hængsler. Træer voksede gennem murene, ind og ud af dem. Murtinderne var smuldret og styrtet sammen, og tykke totter af vilde slyngplanter hang ned fra vinduerne i tårnene langs murene.

value.en: A great roofless palace crowned the hill, and the marble of the courtyards and the fountains was split, and stained with red and green, and the very cobblestones in the courtyard where the king’s elephants used to live had been thrust up and apart by grasses and young trees. From the palace you could see the rows and rows of roofless houses that made up the city looking like empty honeycombs filled with blackness; the shapeless block of stone that had been an idol in the square where four roads met; the pits and dimples at street corners where the public wells once stood, and the shattered domes of temples with wild figs sprouting on their sides. The monkeys called the place their city, and pretended to despise the Jungle-People because they lived in the forest. And yet they never knew what the buildings were made for nor how to use them. They would sit in circles on the hall of the king’s council chamber, and scratch for fleas and pretend to be men; or they would run in and out of the roofless houses and collect pieces of plaster and old bricks in a corner, and forget where they had hidden them, and fight and cry in scuffling crowds, and then break off to play up and down the terraces of the king’s garden, where they would shake the rose trees and the oranges in sport to see the fruit and flowers fall. They explored all the passages and dark tunnels in the palace and the hundreds of little dark rooms, but they never remembered what they had seen and what they had not; and so drifted about in ones and twos or crowds telling each other that they were doing as men did. They drank at the tanks and made the water all muddy, and then they fought over it, and then they would all rush together in mobs and shout: “There is no one in the jungle so wise and good and clever and strong and gentle as the Bandar-log.” Then all would begin again till they grew tired of the city and went back to the tree-tops, hoping the Jungle-People would notice them.
value.da: På toppen af bakken lå et stort palads uden tag. Marmoret i gårdene og springvandene var revnet og plettet med rødt og grønt. I den gård, hvor kongens elefanter havde boet, havde græs og små træer skubbet selve brostenene op og fra hinanden. Fra paladset kunne man se ud over række på række af tagløse huse i byen, som tomme bikager fulde af mørke. Der, hvor fire gader mødtes, stod en formløs sten, som engang havde været en afgud. Fordybninger og huller ved gadehjørnerne viste, hvor de offentlige brønde havde ligget, og vilde figentræer voksede ud af siderne på templernes splintrede kupler. Aberne kaldte byen deres egen og lod, som om de foragtede Junglens Folk for at bo i skoven. Alligevel havde de ingen anelse om, hvad bygningerne havde været brugt til, eller hvordan man brugte dem. De sad i kredse i kongens rådssal, kløede sig efter lopper og legede, at de var mennesker. Eller de løb gennem de tagløse huse og stablede stykker af puds og gamle mursten i et hjørne og glemte så, hvor de havde lagt dem. De sloges og skreg i skubbende flokke, men opgav pludselig skænderiet og legede på terrasserne i kongens have, hvor de rystede rosenbuske og appelsintræer for at se blomster og frugt falde ned. De udforskede alle gange og mørke tunneller i paladset og de hundredvis af små, mørke rum. Men de huskede aldrig, hvad de allerede havde set. Så vandrede de rundt alene, to og to eller i flokke og forsikrede hinanden om, at de opførte sig ligesom mennesker. De drak af bassinerne, så vandet blev mudret, og så skændtes de om det. Bagefter styrtede de sammen i store flokke og råbte: »Ingen i junglen er så kloge, så gode, så dygtige, så stærke eller så blide som Bandar-log.« Så begyndte det hele forfra, indtil de blev trætte af byen og vendte tilbage til trætoppene, stadig i håb om, at Junglens Folk ville lægge mærke til dem.

value.en: Mowgli, who had been trained under the Law of the Jungle, did not like or understand this kind of life. The monkeys dragged him into the Cold Lairs late in the afternoon, and instead of going to sleep, as Mowgli would have done after a long journey, they joined hands and danced about and sang their foolish songs. One of the monkeys made a speech and told his companions that Mowgli’s capture marked a new thing in the history of the Bandar-log, for Mowgli was going to show them how to weave sticks and canes together as a protection against rain and cold. Mowgli picked up some creepers and began to work them in and out, and the monkeys tried to imitate; but in a very few minutes they lost interest and began to pull their friends’ tails or jump up and down on all fours, coughing.
value.da: Mowgli var opdraget efter Junglens Lov og hverken forstod eller brød sig om denne måde at leve på. Aberne slæbte ham ind i De Kolde Huler sent på eftermiddagen. I stedet for at sove efter den lange rejse, som han ville have gjort, tog de hinanden i hænderne, dansede rundt og sang deres fjollede sange. En af dem rejste sig for at holde en tale. Han fortalte, at fangsten af Mowgli var et nyt kapitel i Bandar-logs historie: drengen skulle lære dem at flette pinde og rør til læ mod regn og kulde. Mowgli samlede nogle slyngplanter og begyndte at flette dem ind og ud. Aberne prøvede at efterligne ham, men efter få minutter kedede de sig og begyndte at hive i hinandens haler eller at hoste og hoppe rundt på alle fire.

value.en: “I wish to eat,” said Mowgli. “I am a stranger in this part of the jungle. Bring me food, or give me leave to hunt here.”
value.da: »Jeg vil have noget at spise,« sagde Mowgli. »Jeg er en fremmed i denne del af junglen. Bring mig mad, eller giv mig lov at jage her.«

value.en: Twenty or thirty monkeys bounded away to bring him nuts and wild pawpaws. But they fell to fighting on the road, and it was too much trouble to go back with what was left of the fruit. Mowgli was sore and angry as well as hungry, and he roamed through the empty city giving the Strangers’ Hunting Call from time to time, but no one answered him, and Mowgli felt that he had reached a very bad place indeed. “All that Baloo has said about the Bandar-log is true,” he thought to himself. “They have no Law, no Hunting Call, and no leaders--nothing but foolish words and little picking thievish hands. So if I am starved or killed here, it will be all my own fault. But I must try to return to my own jungle. Baloo will surely beat me, but that is better than chasing silly rose leaves with the Bandar-log.”
value.da: Tyve eller tredive aber sprang af sted for at hente nødder og vilde papaja. Men undervejs begyndte de at slås, og det var for besværligt at bære den frugt, der var tilbage, med tilbage. Mowgli var øm, vred og sulten. Han vandrede gennem den forladte by og råbte fra tid til anden Fremmedes Jagtråb, men der kom intet svar. Han begyndte at føle, at han var havnet et rigtig forfærdeligt sted. »Baloo havde ret i alt,« tænkte han. »Bandar-log har ingen Lov, intet Jagtråb og ingen ledere — kun fjollet snak og små hænder, der snupper og stjæler. Hvis jeg sulter ihjel her, har jeg kun mig selv at bebrejde. På en eller anden måde må jeg tilbage til min egen jungle. Baloo vil sikkert tæve mig, men selv det er bedre end at løbe efter fjollede rosenblade sammen med Bandar-log.«

value.en: No sooner had he walked to the city wall than the monkeys pulled him back, telling him that he did not know how happy he was, and pinching him to make him grateful. He set his teeth and said nothing, but went with the shouting monkeys to a terrace above the red sandstone reservoirs that were half-full of rain water. There was a ruined summer-house of white marble in the center of the terrace, built for queens dead a hundred years ago. The domed roof had half fallen in and blocked up the underground passage from the palace by which the queens used to enter. But the walls were made of screens of marble tracery--beautiful milk-white fretwork, set with agates and cornelians and jasper and lapis lazuli, and as the moon came up behind the hill it shone through the open work, casting shadows on the ground like black velvet embroidery. Sore, sleepy, and hungry as he was, Mowgli could not help laughing when the Bandar-log began, twenty at a time, to tell him how great and wise and strong and gentle they were, and how foolish he was to wish to leave them. “We are great. We are free. We are wonderful. We are the most wonderful people in all the jungle! We all say so, and so it must be true,” they shouted. “Now as you are a new listener and can carry our words back to the Jungle-People so that they may notice us in future, we will tell you all about our most excellent selves.” Mowgli made no objection, and the monkeys gathered by hundreds and hundreds on the terrace to listen to their own speakers singing the praises of the Bandar-log, and whenever a speaker stopped for want of breath they would all shout together: “This is true; we all say so.” Mowgli nodded and blinked, and said “Yes” when they asked him a question, and his head spun with the noise. “Tabaqui the Jackal must have bitten all these people,” he said to himself, “and now they have madness. Certainly this is _dewanee_, the madness. Do they never go to sleep? Now there is a cloud coming to cover that moon. If it were only a big enough cloud I might try to run away in the darkness. But I am tired.”
