value.da: »Hvem kalder?« spurgte Shere Khan. En pragtfuld påfugl for skrigende op af kløften med hårde vingeslag.

value.en: “I, Mowgli. Cattle thief, it is time to come to the Council Rock! Down--hurry them down, Akela! Down, Rama, down!”
value.da: »Det er Mowgli, der kalder. Kvægtyv, nu er det tid til at besøge Rådets Klippe! Driv dem ned, Akela, hurtigt! Ned med dig, Rama, ned!«

value.en: The herd paused for an instant at the edge of the slope, but Akela gave tongue in the full hunting-yell, and they pitched over one after the other, just as steamers shoot rapids, the sand and stones spurting up round them. Once started, there was no chance of stopping, and before they were fairly in the bed of the ravine Rama winded Shere Khan and bellowed.
value.da: Et øjeblik tøvede bøflerne ved skråningens kant. Så udstødte Akela sit fulde jagthyl, og de styrtede ud over kanten én efter én, som dampskibe, der skyder ned ad strømfald, og sand og sten sprøjtede omkring dem. Når de først var kommet i gang, kunne de umuligt standse. Før de helt var nået ned på kløftens bund, fik Rama Shere Khans lugt i næsen og brølede.

value.en: “Ha! Ha!” said Mowgli, on his back. “Now thou knowest!” and the torrent of black horns, foaming muzzles, and staring eyes whirled down the ravine just as boulders go down in floodtime; the weaker buffaloes being shouldered out to the sides of the ravine where they tore through the creepers. They knew what the business was before them--the terrible charge of the buffalo herd against which no tiger can hope to stand. Shere Khan heard the thunder of their hoofs, picked himself up, and lumbered down the ravine, looking from side to side for some way of escape, but the walls of the ravine were straight and he had to hold on, heavy with his dinner and his drink, willing to do anything rather than fight. The herd splashed through the pool he had just left, bellowing till the narrow cut rang. Mowgli heard an answering bellow from the foot of the ravine, saw Shere Khan turn (the tiger knew if the worst came to the worst it was better to meet the bulls than the cows with their calves), and then Rama tripped, stumbled, and went on again over something soft, and, with the bulls at his heels, crashed full into the other herd, while the weaker buffaloes were lifted clean off their feet by the shock of the meeting. That charge carried both herds out into the plain, goring and stamping and snorting. Mowgli watched his time, and slipped off Rama’s neck, laying about him right and left with his stick.
value.da: »Ha! Ha!« lo Mowgli fra Ramas ryg. »Nu forstår du det!« En strøm af sorte horn, skummende mule og stirrende øjne fejede ned ad kløften som kampesten i en flod. De svagere dyr blev skubbet ind mod væggene, så de rev slyngplanterne itu. De vidste, hvad der ventede forude: bøffelflokkens frygtelige stormløb, som ingen tiger kan modstå. Shere Khan hørte hovene tordne. Han rejste sig og slingrede ned ad kløften og kiggede til højre og venstre efter en udvej. Men væggene gik lige op. Tung af mad og vand kunne han kun blive ved at løbe og var klar til at prøve alt for at undgå en kamp. Flokken plaskede gennem vandhullet, han lige havde forladt, og brølene rungede i den smalle kløft. Et svarende brøl nåede Mowgli nedefra. Han så Shere Khan vende sig, for tigeren vidste, at hvis han skulle vælge, var tyrene et bedre valg end køer, der forsvarede deres kalve. Rama snublede over noget blødt og stormede videre. Med tyrene lige bag sig brasede han hovedkulds ind i den anden flok. Sammenstødet løftede de svagere bøfler helt fri af jorden. Begge grupper sprang ud på sletten, mens de stangede, trampede og fnøs. Mowgli ventede på sit snit, gled ned fra Ramas nakke og slog omkring sig med sin stok.

value.en: “Quick, Akela! Break them up. Scatter them, or they will be fighting one another. Drive them away, Akela. Hai, Rama! Hai, hai, hai! my children. Softly now, softly! It is all over.”
value.da: »Hurtigt, Akela! Spred dem. Spred dem, ellers vil de slås med hinanden. Driv dem væk, Akela. Hai, Rama! Hai, hai, hai! mine børn. Stille nu, stille! Det hele er forbi.«

value.en: Akela and Gray Brother ran to and fro nipping the buffaloes’ legs, and though the herd wheeled once to charge up the ravine again, Mowgli managed to turn Rama, and the others followed him to the wallows.
value.da: Akela og Grå Bror løb frem og tilbage og snappede bøflernes ben, og selvom flokken én gang drejede for at storme op ad kløften igen, lykkedes det Mowgli at vende Rama, og de andre fulgte ham til mudderbadene.

value.en: Shere Khan needed no more trampling. He was dead, and the kites were coming for him already.
value.da: Det var ikke nødvendigt at trampe på Shere Khan igen. Han lå død, og glenterne var allerede ved at samle sig.

value.en: “Brothers, that was a dog’s death,” said Mowgli, feeling for the knife he always carried in a sheath round his neck now that he lived with men. “But he would never have shown fight. His hide will look well on the Council Rock. We must get to work swiftly.”
value.da: »Det var en hunds død, brødre,« sagde Mowgli og rakte efter den kniv, han nu altid bar i en skede om halsen, ligesom menneskene gør. »Men han ville aldrig have stillet sig og kæmpet. Hans skind vil tage sig godt ud på Rådets Klippe. Vi må skynde os.«

value.en: A boy trained among men would never have dreamed of skinning a ten-foot tiger alone, but Mowgli knew better than anyone else how an animal’s skin is fitted on, and how it can be taken off. But it was hard work, and Mowgli slashed and tore and grunted for an hour, while the wolves lolled out their tongues, or came forward and tugged as he ordered them. Presently a hand fell on his shoulder, and looking up he saw Buldeo with the Tower musket. The children had told the village about the buffalo stampede, and Buldeo went out angrily, only too anxious to correct Mowgli for not taking better care of the herd. The wolves dropped out of sight as soon as they saw the man coming.
value.da: Ingen dreng, der var opdraget blandt mennesker, ville have fundet på at flå en tre meter lang tiger helt alene. Men Mowgli forstod bedre end nogen anden, hvordan et dyrs hud sidder på kroppen, og hvordan man får den af. Alligevel var det svært arbejde. I en time skar og trak og gryntede han, mens ulvene gispede med tungen ude eller trådte til og hev i det, han pegede på. Så rørte en hånd ved hans skulder. Han kiggede op og så Buldeo stå dér med sin Tower-musket. Børnene havde fortalt i landsbyen om bøfler, der var løbet løbsk, og Buldeo var vredt taget af sted, ivrig efter at straffe Mowgli for at have forsømt flokken. Ulvene var forsvundet af syne i det øjeblik, de så manden komme.

value.en: “What is this folly?” said Buldeo angrily. “To think that thou canst skin a tiger! Where did the buffaloes kill him? It is the Lame Tiger too, and there is a hundred rupees on his head. Well, well, we will overlook thy letting the herd run off, and perhaps I will give thee one of the rupees of the reward when I have taken the skin to Khanhiwara.” He fumbled in his waist cloth for flint and steel, and stooped down to singe Shere Khan’s whiskers. Most native hunters always singe a tiger’s whiskers to prevent his ghost from haunting them.
value.da: »Hvad er det for noget sludder?« snerrede Buldeo. »Tænk, at du bilder dig ind, at du kan flå en tiger! Hvor dræbte bøflerne ham? Og det er selveste Den Halte Tiger, med hundrede rupier udlovet for hans hoved. Nå, nå, vi kan se stort på, at du lod flokken løbe væk. Når jeg har bragt skindet til Khanhiwara, giver jeg dig måske én rupie af belønningen.« Han famlede i sit lændeklæde efter flint og stål og bøjede sig derefter ned for at svide Shere Khans knurhår af. De fleste indfødte jægere svider altid knurhårene på en død tiger, så dens spøgelse ikke skal hjemsøge dem.

value.en: “Hum!” said Mowgli, half to himself as he ripped back the skin of a forepaw. “So thou wilt take the hide to Khanhiwara for the reward, and perhaps give me one rupee? Now it is in my mind that I need the skin for my own use. Heh! Old man, take away that fire!”
value.da: »Hm!« mumlede Mowgli, mens han flåede skindet af en forpote. »Så du vil tage skindet med til Khanhiwara, hente belønningen og måske lade mig få én rupie? Det passer sådan set dårligt, for jeg skal bruge skindet til noget af mit eget. Hov! Hold den ild væk, gamle mand!«

value.en: “What talk is this to the chief hunter of the village? Thy luck and the stupidity of thy buffaloes have helped thee to this kill. The tiger has just fed, or he would have gone twenty miles by this time. Thou canst not even skin him properly, little beggar brat, and forsooth I, Buldeo, must be told not to singe his whiskers. Mowgli, I will not give thee one anna of the reward, but only a very big beating. Leave the carcass!”
value.da: »Taler du sådan til landsbyens øverste jæger? Det er kun held og dine bøflers dumhed, der har hjulpet dig til at slå ham ihjel. Han havde lige spist, ellers havde han været tyve engelske mil væk nu. Du kan ikke engang flå ham ordentligt, din lille tiggerunge, og alligevel vover du at sige til mig, Buldeo, at jeg ikke må svide hans knurhår. Du får ingen belønning af mig, Mowgli, ikke en eneste anna, kun en ordentlig omgang tæsk. Gå væk fra kadaveret!«

value.en: “By the Bull that bought me,” said Mowgli, who was trying to get at the shoulder, “must I stay babbling to an old ape all noon? Here, Akela, this man plagues me.”
value.da: »Ved Tyren, som købte mig,« sagde Mowgli, mens han arbejdede sig hen mod skulderen, »skal jeg tilbringe hele middagstiden med at sludre med en gammel abe? Akela, kom her. Den her mand generer mig.«

value.en: Buldeo, who was still stooping over Shere Khan’s head, found himself sprawling on the grass, with a gray wolf standing over him, while Mowgli went on skinning as though he were alone in all India.
value.da: Buldeo, der stadig bøjede sig over Shere Khans hoved, befandt sig pludselig liggende på græsset med en grå ulv stående over sig, mens Mowgli fortsatte med at flå, som var han alene i hele Indien.

value.en: “Ye-es,” he said, between his teeth. “Thou art altogether right, Buldeo. Thou wilt never give me one anna of the reward. There is an old war between this lame tiger and myself--a very old war, and--I have won.”
value.da: »Jo-o,« sagde han mellem tænderne. »Det har du helt ret i, Buldeo. Du kommer aldrig til at give mig så meget som en anna af den belønning. Denne halte tiger og jeg har ført krig i lang tid, en meget lang tid. Og jeg har vundet den.«

value.en: To do Buldeo justice, if he had been ten years younger he would have taken his chance with Akela had he met the wolf in the woods, but a wolf who obeyed the orders of this boy who had private wars with man-eating tigers was not a common animal. It was sorcery, magic of the worst kind, thought Buldeo, and he wondered whether the amulet round his neck would protect him. He lay as still as still, expecting every minute to see Mowgli turn into a tiger too.
value.da: For at være retfærdig over for Buldeo: Ti år tidligere ville han have prøvet sin lykke mod Akela, hvis de var mødtes i skoven. Men det her var ikke en almindelig ulv. Den adlød en dreng, der førte private krige mod menneskeædende tigre. For Buldeo kunne det kun betyde trolddom, den frygteligste slags magi. Han spekulerede på, om amuletten om hans hals ville redde ham. Han lå helt stille og ventede hvert øjeblik på, at Mowgli selv ville forvandle sig til en tiger.

value.en: “Maharaj! Great King,” he said at last in a husky whisper.
value.da: »Maharaj! Store Konge,« sagde han endelig med en hæs hvisken.

value.en: “Yes,” said Mowgli, without turning his head, chuckling a little.
value.da: »Ja?« svarede Mowgli med et lille fnis, uden at gide at se sig om.

value.en: “I am an old man. I did not know that thou wast anything more than a herdsboy. May I rise up and go away, or will thy servant tear me to pieces?”
value.da: »Jeg er en gammel mand. Jeg vidste ikke, at du var andet end en hyrdedreng. Må jeg rejse mig og gå min vej, eller vil din tjener rive mig i stykker?«

value.en: “Go, and peace go with thee. Only, another time do not meddle with my game. Let him go, Akela.”
value.da: »Gå i fred. Men husk næste gang at lade mit bytte være. Akela, lad manden gå.«

value.en: Buldeo hobbled away to the village as fast as he could, looking back over his shoulder in case Mowgli should change into something terrible. When he got to the village he told a tale of magic and enchantment and sorcery that made the priest look very grave.
value.da: Buldeo humpede afsted mod landsbyen, så hurtigt han kunne, og kiggede sig over skulderen i tilfælde af, at Mowgli skulle forvandle sig til noget forfærdeligt. Da han kom til landsbyen, fortalte han en historie om magi og fortryllelse og trolddom, der fik præsten til at se meget alvorlig ud.

value.en: Mowgli went on with his work, but it was nearly twilight before he and the wolves had drawn the great gay skin clear of the body.
value.da: Mowgli fortsatte med sit arbejde, men det var næsten tusmørke, før han og ulvene havde trukket det store farverige skind helt fri af kroppen.

value.en: “Now we must hide this and take the buffaloes home! Help me to herd them, Akela.”
value.da: »Nu må vi skjule det her og få bøflerne hjem! Hjælp mig med at samle dem, Akela.«

value.en: The herd rounded up in the misty twilight, and when they got near the village Mowgli saw lights, and heard the conches and bells in the temple blowing and banging. Half the village seemed to be waiting for him by the gate. “That is because I have killed Shere Khan,” he said to himself. But a shower of stones whistled about his ears, and the villagers shouted: “Sorcerer! Wolf’s brat! Jungle demon! Go away! Get hence quickly or the priest will turn thee into a wolf again. Shoot, Buldeo, shoot!”
value.da: Flokken blev samlet i det dunkle tusmørke, og da de kom nær landsbyen, så Mowgli lys og hørte konkylierne og klokkerne i templet blæse og bimle. Halvdelen af landsbyen syntes at vente på ham ved porten. »Det er, fordi jeg har dræbt Shere Khan,« sagde han til sig selv. Men et regnskyl af sten peb om hans ører, og landsbyboerne råbte: »Troldmand! Ulveunge! Jungledæmon! Gå væk! Forsvind hurtigt, ellers forvandler præsten dig til en ulv igen. Skyd, Buldeo, skyd!«

value.en: The old Tower musket went off with a bang, and a young buffalo bellowed in pain.
value.da: Det gamle Tower-musket gik af med et brag, og en ung bøffel brølede af smerte.

value.en: “More sorcery!” shouted the villagers. “He can turn bullets. Buldeo, that was thy buffalo.”
value.da: »Mere trolddom!« råbte landsbyboerne. »Han kan vende kuglerne. Buldeo, det var din bøffel.«

value.en: “Now what is this?” said Mowgli, bewildered, as the stones flew thicker.
value.da: »Hvad sker der nu?« spurgte Mowgli forvirret, mens endnu flere sten kom flyvende mod ham.

value.en: “They are not unlike the Pack, these brothers of thine,” said Akela, sitting down composedly. “It is in my head that, if bullets mean anything, they would cast thee out.”
value.da: »Dine brødre her minder meget om Flokken,« sagde Akela og satte sig roligt ned. »Hvis jeg ikke har misforstået, hvad kuglerne betyder, tror jeg, de vil jage dig væk.«

value.en: “Wolf! Wolf’s cub! Go away!” shouted the priest, waving a sprig of the sacred tulsi plant.
value.da: »Ulv! Ulveunge! Gå væk!« råbte præsten og svingede en kvist af den hellige tulsi-plante.

value.en: “Again? Last time it was because I was a man. This time it is because I am a wolf. Let us go, Akela.”
value.da: »Igen? Sidste gang var det, fordi jeg var et menneske. Denne gang er det, fordi jeg er en ulv. Lad os gå, Akela.«

value.en: A woman--it was Messua--ran across to the herd, and cried: “Oh, my son, my son! They say thou art a sorcerer who can turn himself into a beast at will. I do not believe, but go away or they will kill thee. Buldeo says thou art a wizard, but I know thou hast avenged Nathoo’s death.”
value.da: En kvinde — det var Messua — løb over til flokken og råbte: »Åh, min søn, min søn! De siger, du er en troldmand, der kan forvandle sig til et dyr efter behag. Jeg tror det ikke, men gå væk, ellers slår de dig ihjel. Buldeo siger, du er en troldkarl, men jeg ved, at du har hævnet Nathoos død.«

value.en: “Come back, Messua!” shouted the crowd. “Come back, or we will stone thee.”
value.da: »Kom tilbage, Messua!« råbte mængden. »Kom tilbage, ellers kaster vi også sten efter dig.«

value.en: Mowgli laughed a little short ugly laugh, for a stone had hit him in the mouth. “Run back, Messua. This is one of the foolish tales they tell under the big tree at dusk. I have at least paid for thy son’s life. Farewell; and run quickly, for I shall send the herd in more swiftly than their brickbats. I am no wizard, Messua. Farewell!”
value.da: En sten ramte Mowgli i munden, og han udstødte en kort, hård latter. »Gå tilbage til dem, Messua. Det her er bare endnu en dum historie som dem, de fortæller under det store træ ved aftenstid. Jeg har i det mindste hævnet din søns død. Farvel. Løb hurtigt, for jeg sender flokken ind hurtigere, end de kan kaste deres knuste mursten. Jeg er ingen troldmand, Messua. Farvel!«

value.en: “Now, once more, Akela,” he cried. “Bring the herd in.”
value.da: »Én gang til, Akela,« råbte han. »Før bøflerne gennem porten.«

value.en: The buffaloes were anxious enough to get to the village. They hardly needed Akela’s yell, but charged through the gate like a whirlwind, scattering the crowd right and left.
value.da: Bøflerne ville ikke andet end at komme hjem. Akela behøvede næsten ikke at kalde, før de brusede gennem porten som en hvirvelvind og skubbede landsbyboerne til begge sider.

value.en: “Keep count!” shouted Mowgli scornfully. “It may be that I have stolen one of them. Keep count, for I will do your herding no more. Fare you well, children of men, and thank Messua that I do not come in with my wolves and hunt you up and down your street.”
value.da: »Tæl efter!« råbte Mowgli hånligt. »Det kan være, jeg har stjålet en af dem. Tæl efter, for jeg vil ikke vogte for jer længere. Lev vel, menneskebørn, og tak Messua for, at jeg ikke kommer ind med mine ulve og jager jer op og ned ad jeres gade.«

value.en: He turned on his heel and walked away with the Lone Wolf, and as he looked up at the stars he felt happy. “No more sleeping in traps for me, Akela. Let us get Shere Khan’s skin and go away. No, we will not hurt the village, for Messua was kind to me.”
value.da: Han vendte sig og gik væk sammen med Den Ensomme Ulv. Han så op på stjernerne og følte sig glad. »Ikke flere nætter i fælder, Akela. Lad os hente Shere Khans skind og tage af sted. Nej, vi gør ikke landsbyen noget. Messua var god mod mig.«

value.en: When the moon rose over the plain, making it look all milky, the horrified villagers saw Mowgli, with two wolves at his heels and a bundle on his head, trotting across at the steady wolf’s trot that eats up the long miles like fire. Then they banged the temple bells and blew the conches louder than ever. And Messua cried, and Buldeo embroidered the story of his adventures in the jungle, till he ended by saying that Akela stood up on his hind legs and talked like a man.
value.da: Da månelyset bredte sig over sletten og gjorde den mælkehvid, så de rædselsslagne landsbyboere Mowgli travende hen over den med en bylt på hovedet og to ulve bag sig. Han bevægede sig i det jævne ulvetrav, der æder engelske mil som ild. Templets klokker ringede og konkylierne lød højere end nogensinde. Messua græd. Buldeo pyntede mere og mere på sit junglefentyr, til han til sidst påstod, at Akela havde rejst sig på bagbenene og talt som et menneske.

value.en: The moon was just going down when Mowgli and the two wolves came to the hill of the Council Rock, and they stopped at Mother Wolf’s cave.
value.da: Da månen begyndte at gå ned, nåede Mowgli og hans to følgesvende bakken under Rådets Klippe. De standsede ved Moderulvens hule.

value.en: “They have cast me out from the Man-Pack, Mother,” shouted Mowgli, “but I come with the hide of Shere Khan to keep my word.”
value.da: »De har jaget mig ud af Menneskeflokken, Mor,« råbte Mowgli, »men jeg kommer med Shere Khans skind for at holde mit ord.«

value.en: Mother Wolf walked stiffly from the cave with the cubs behind her, and her eyes glowed as she saw the skin.
value.da: Moderulven gik stivt ud af hulen med ungerne bag sig, og hendes øjne glødede, da hun så skindet.

value.en: “I told him on that day, when he crammed his head and shoulders into this cave, hunting for thy life, Little Frog--I told him that the hunter would be the hunted. It is well done.”
value.da: »Jeg sagde til ham den dag, da han pressede sit hoved og sine skuldre ind i denne hule på jagt efter dit liv, Lille Frø — jeg sagde, at jægeren skulle blive den jagede. Det er godt gjort.«

value.en: “Little Brother, it is well done,” said a deep voice in the thicket. “We were lonely in the jungle without thee,” and Bagheera came running to Mowgli’s bare feet. They clambered up the Council Rock together, and Mowgli spread the skin out on the flat stone where Akela used to sit, and pegged it down with four slivers of bamboo, and Akela lay down upon it, and called the old call to the Council, “Look--look well, O Wolves,” exactly as he had called when Mowgli was first brought there.
value.da: »Godt gået, Lillebror,« sagde en dyb stemme fra buskene. »Junglen var ensom uden dig.« Bagheera kom løbende hen til Mowglis bare fødder. Sammen klatrede de op på Rådets Klippe. Mowgli lagde skindet over den flade sten, der engang havde været Akelas plads, og fastgjorde det med fire stykker bambus. Akela strakte sig ud på det og udstødte det gamle kald til Rådet: »Se — se godt efter, O Ulve.« Det var det samme kald, som han havde brugt, da Mowgli første gang kom dertil.

value.en: Ever since Akela had been deposed, the Pack had been without a leader, hunting and fighting at their own pleasure. But they answered the call from habit; and some of them were lame from the traps they had fallen into, and some limped from shot wounds, and some were mangy from eating bad food, and many were missing. But they came to the Council Rock, all that were left of them, and saw Shere Khan’s striped hide on the rock, and the huge claws dangling at the end of the empty dangling feet. It was then that Mowgli made up a song that came up into his throat all by itself, and he shouted it aloud, leaping up and down on the rattling skin, and beating time with his heels till he had no more breath left, while Gray Brother and Akela howled between the verses.
value.da: Siden Akela var blevet fjernet, havde Flokken ikke haft nogen leder. Hver ulv jagede og sloges, som han selv ville. Af vane kom de stadig, når kaldet lød. Nogle haltede efter fælder, andre efter skudsår. Nogle havde fået skab af dårlig mad. Mange kom slet ikke. Men alle, der var tilbage, kom til Rådets Klippe. De så Shere Khans stribede skind udbredt over stenen, og de enorme kløer hang ned fra de slappe, tomme poter. En sang steg op i Mowglis hals, helt af sig selv. Han råbte den ud, mens han hoppede på det raslende skind og slog takten med hælene, til han ikke kunne få vejret. Mellem versene hylede Grå Bror og Akela.

value.en: “Look well, O Wolves. Have I kept my word?” said Mowgli. And the wolves bayed “Yes,” and one tattered wolf howled:
value.da: »Se godt efter, O Ulve. Har jeg gjort, som jeg lovede?« spurgte Mowgli. Ulvene hylede deres »Ja«, og en laset ulv råbte:

value.en: “Lead us again, O Akela. Lead us again, O Man-cub, for we be sick of this lawlessness, and we would be the Free People once more.”
value.da: »Led os igen, O Akela. Led os igen, O Menneskeunge, for vi er trætte af denne lovløshed, og vi vil være Det Frie Folk igen.«

value.en: “Nay,” purred Bagheera, “that may not be. When ye are full-fed, the madness may come upon you again. Not for nothing are ye called the Free People. Ye fought for freedom, and it is yours. Eat it, O Wolves.”
value.da: »Nej,« spandt Bagheera, »det kan ikke ske. Når I er fuldfodrede, kan galskaben komme over jer igen. Ikke for ingenting kaldes I Det Frie Folk. I kæmpede for frihed, og den er jeres. Spis den, O Ulve.«

value.en: “Man-Pack and Wolf-Pack have cast me out,” said Mowgli. “Now I will hunt alone in the jungle.”
value.da: »Menneskeflokken og Ulveflokken har jaget mig ud,« sagde Mowgli. »Nu vil jeg jage alene i junglen.«

value.en: “And we will hunt with thee,” said the four cubs.
value.da: »Og vi vil jage med dig,« sagde de fire unger.

value.en: So Mowgli went away and hunted with the four cubs in the jungle from that day on. But he was not always alone, because, years afterward, he became a man and married.
value.da: Så gik Mowgli sin vej og jagede med de fire unger i junglen fra den dag af. Men han var ikke altid alene, for år senere blev han en mand og giftede sig.

value.en: But that is a story for grown-ups.
value.da: Men det er en historie for de voksne.

value.en: Mowgli’s Song
value.da: Mowglis Sang

value.en:
THAT HE SANG AT THE COUNCIL ROCK WHEN HE
DANCED ON SHERE KHAN’S HIDE
value.da:
SOM HAN SANG VED RÅDETS KLIPPE, DA HAN
DANSEDE PÅ SHERE KHANS SKIND

value.original:
The Song of Mowgli—I, Mowgli, am singing. Let the jungle listen to the
things I have done.
Shere Khan said he would kill—would kill! At the gates in the twilight
he would kill Mowgli, the Frog!
He ate and he drank. Drink deep, Shere Khan, for when wilt thou drink
again? Sleep and dream of the kill.
I am alone on the grazing-grounds. Gray Brother, come to me! Come to
me, Lone Wolf, for there is big game afoot!
Bring up the great bull buffaloes, the blue-skinned herd bulls with the
angry eyes. Drive them to and fro as I order.
Sleepest thou still, Shere Khan? Wake, oh, wake! Here come I, and the
bulls are behind.
Rama, the King of the Buffaloes, stamped with his foot. Waters of the
Waingunga, whither went Shere Khan?
He is not Ikki to dig holes, nor Mao, the Peacock, that he should fly.
He is not Mang the Bat, to hang in the branches. Little bamboos that
creak together, tell me where he ran?
_Ow!_ He is there. _Ahoo!_ He is there. Under the feet of Rama lies the
Lame One! Up, Shere Khan!
Up and kill! Here is meat; break the necks of the bulls!
_Hsh!_ He is asleep. We will not wake him, for his strength is very
great. The kites have come down to see it. The black ants have come up
to know it. There is a great assembly in his honor.
_Alala!_ I have no cloth to wrap me. The kites will see that I am
naked. I am ashamed to meet all these people.
Lend me thy coat, Shere Khan. Lend me thy gay striped coat that I may
go to the Council Rock.
By the Bull that bought me I made a promise—a little promise. Only thy
coat is lacking before I keep my word.
With the knife, with the knife that men use, with the knife of the
hunter, I will stoop down for my gift.
Waters of the Waingunga, Shere Khan gives me his coat for the love that
he bears me. Pull, Gray Brother! Pull, Akela! Heavy is the hide of
Shere Khan.
The Man Pack are angry. They throw stones and talk child’s talk. My
mouth is bleeding. Let me run away.
Through the night, through the hot night, run swiftly with me, my
brothers. We will leave the lights of the village and go to the low
moon.
Waters of the Waingunga, the Man-Pack have cast me out. I did them no
harm, but they were afraid of me. Why?
Wolf Pack, ye have cast me out too. The jungle is shut to me and the
village gates are shut. Why?
As Mang flies between the beasts and birds, so fly I between the
village and the jungle. Why?
I dance on the hide of Shere Khan, but my heart is very heavy. My mouth
is cut and wounded with the stones from the village, but my heart is
very light, because I have come back to the jungle. Why?
These two things fight together in me as the snakes fight in the
spring. The water comes out of my eyes; yet I laugh while it falls.
Why?
I am two Mowglis, but the hide of Shere Khan is under my feet.
All the jungle knows that I have killed Shere Khan. Look—look well, O
Wolves!
_Ahae!_ My heart is heavy with the things that I do not understand.
value.da:
Mowglis Sang — Jeg, Mowgli, synger. Lad junglen lytte til de
ting, jeg har gjort.
Shere Khan sagde, han ville dræbe — ville dræbe! Ved portene i tusmørket
ville han dræbe Mowgli, Frøen!
Han åd, og han drak. Drik dybt, Shere Khan, for hvornår skal du drikke
igen? Sov og drøm om byttet.
Jeg er alene på græsgangene. Grå Bror, kom til mig! Kom til
mig, Ensomme Ulv, for der er stort bytte på færde!
Bring de store bøffeltyre, de blåhudede hjordtyre med de
vrede øjne. Driv dem frem og tilbage, som jeg befaler.
Sover du endnu, Shere Khan? Vågn op, åh, vågn op! Her kommer jeg, og
tyrene er bagved.
Rama, Bøflernes Konge, stampede med foden. Waingungas vand,
hvor gik Shere Khan hen?
Han er ikke Ikki, der graver huler, og heller ikke Mao, Påfuglen, så han kan flyve.
Han er ikke Mang, Flagermusen, der hænger i grenene. Små bambusser, der
knirker sammen, fortæl mig, hvor han løb hen?
_Ow!_ Han er der. _Ahoo!_ Han er der. Under Ramas fødder ligger
Den Halte! Op, Shere Khan!
Op og dræb! Her er kød; bræk tyrenes nakker!
_Hys!_ Han sover. Vi vil ikke vække ham, for hans styrke er meget
stor. Glenterne er kommet ned for at se det. De sorte myrer er kommet
op for at få det at vide. Der er en stor forsamling til hans ære.
_Alala!_ Jeg har intet klæde at svøbe mig i. Glenterne vil se, at jeg er
nøgen. Jeg skammer mig over at møde alle disse folk.
Lån mig din pels, Shere Khan. Lån mig din lyse stribede pels, så jeg kan
gå til Rådets Klippe.
Ved Tyren, som købte mig, gav jeg et løfte — et lille løfte. Kun din
pels mangler, før jeg holder mit ord.
Med kniven, med kniven, som mennesker bruger, med jægerens
kniv, vil jeg bøje mig ned efter min gave.
Waingungas vand, Shere Khan giver mig sin pels for den kærlighed,
han bærer til mig. Træk, Grå Bror! Træk, Akela! Tung er Shere
Khans skind.
Menneskeflokken er vred. De kaster sten og taler barnesnak. Min
mund bløder. Lad mig løbe væk.
Gennem natten, gennem den varme nat, løb hurtigt med mig, mine
brødre. Vi vil forlade landsbyens lys og gå til den lave
måne.
Waingungas vand, Menneskeflokken har jaget mig ud. Jeg gjorde dem
ingen skade, men de var bange for mig. Hvorfor?
Ulveflok, I har også jaget mig ud. Junglen er lukket for mig, og
landsbyportene er lukkede. Hvorfor?
Som Mang flyver mellem dyrene og fuglene, sådan flyver jeg mellem
landsbyen og junglen. Hvorfor?
Jeg danser på Shere Khans skind, men mit hjerte er meget tungt. Min mund
er skåret og såret af stenene fra landsbyen, men mit hjerte er
meget let, fordi jeg er kommet tilbage til junglen. Hvorfor?
Disse to ting kæmper i mig som slangerne kæmper i
foråret. Vandet kommer ud af mine øjne; alligevel ler jeg, mens det falder.
Hvorfor?
Jeg er to Mowglier, men Shere Khans skind er under mine fødder.
Hele junglen ved, at jeg har dræbt Shere Khan. Se — se godt, O
Ulve!
_Ahae!_ Mit hjerte er tungt af de ting, jeg ikke forstår.

value.en:
Oh! hush thee, my baby, the night is behind us,
And black are the waters that sparkled so green.
The moon, o’er the combers, looks downward to find us
At rest in the hollows that rustle between.
Where billow meets billow, then soft be thy pillow,
Ah, weary wee flipperling, curl at thy ease!
The storm shall not wake thee, nor shark overtake thee,
Asleep in the arms of the slow-swinging seas!
value.da:
Åh! Hys nu, min lille, natten er bag os,
og sorte er vandene, der før glimtede så grønne.
Månen ser ned over bølgerne og finder os
hvilende i dalene, hvor det suser imellem.
Hvor bølge møder bølge, skal din pude være blød,
åh, trætte lille luffeunge, krøl dig sammen i ro!
Stormen skal ikke vække dig, ingen haj skal nå dig,
mens du sover i de langsomt gyngende bølgers arme!

value.en: Seal Lullaby
value.da: Sælvuggevise

value.en: All these things happened several years ago at a place called Novastoshnah, or North East Point, on the Island of St. Paul, away and away in the Bering Sea. Limmershin, the Winter Wren, told me the tale when he was blown on to the rigging of a steamer going to Japan, and I took him down into my cabin and warmed and fed him for a couple of days till he was fit to fly back to St. Paul’s again. Limmershin is a very quaint little bird, but he knows how to tell the truth.
value.da: Alt dette skete for mange år siden ved Novastoshnah, eller Nordøstpynten, på øen St. Paul, langt ude i Beringhavet. Limmershin, gærdesmutten, fortalte mig historien, efter at vinden havde blæst ham op i takkelagen på en damper på vej til Japan. Jeg tog ham med ned i min kahyt og gav ham varme og mad i to dage, til han kunne flyve tilbage til St. Paul. Limmershin er en mærkelig lille fugl, men han fortæller sandheden.

value.en: Nobody comes to Novastoshnah except on business, and the only people who have regular business there are the seals. They come in the summer months by hundreds and hundreds of thousands out of the cold gray sea. For Novastoshnah Beach has the finest accommodation for seals of any place in all the world.
value.da: Ingen kommer til Novastoshnah, medmindre de har noget at ordne der, og de eneste, der har fast ærinde, er sælerne. Hver sommer kommer mange hundrede tusinder af dem op af det kolde, grå hav. Ingen strand i hele verden har bedre pladser til sæler end Novastoshnah.

value.en: Sea Catch knew that, and every spring would swim from whatever place he happened to be in--would swim like a torpedo-boat straight for Novastoshnah and spend a month fighting with his companions for a good place on the rocks, as close to the sea as possible. Sea Catch was fifteen years old, a huge gray fur seal with almost a mane on his shoulders, and long, wicked dog teeth. When he heaved himself up on his front flippers he stood more than four feet clear of the ground, and his weight, if anyone had been bold enough to weigh him, was nearly seven hundred pounds. He was scarred all over with the marks of savage fights, but he was always ready for just one fight more. He would put his head on one side, as though he were afraid to look his enemy in the face; then he would shoot it out like lightning, and when the big teeth were firmly fixed on the other seal’s neck, the other seal might get away if he could, but Sea Catch would not help him.
value.da: Det vidste Sea Catch godt. Hvert forår svømmede han, uanset hvor han var, lige mod Novastoshnah som en torpedobåd, og så brugte han en måned på at slås med de andre sæler om en god plads på klipperne tæt på vandet. Han var femten år gammel, en kæmpestor grå pelssæl med en slags manke om skuldrene og lange, grumme hjørnetænder. Når han rejste sig på forluffene, stod han over en meter højt, og hvis nogen havde været modig nok til at veje ham, ville de have fundet ud af, at han vejede næsten tre hundrede og tyve kilo. Hele kroppen var arret efter vilde kampe, men han var altid klar til en kamp mere. Han lagde hovedet på skrå, som om han ikke turde møde modstanderens blik, og så skød han det frem som et lyn. Når hans tænder først sad fast i halsen på en anden sæl, kunne den slippe væk, hvis den selv kunne, men Sea Catch ville ikke hjælpe den.

value.en: Yet Sea Catch never chased a beaten seal, for that was against the Rules of the Beach. He only wanted room by the sea for his nursery. But as there were forty or fifty thousand other seals hunting for the same thing each spring, the whistling, bellowing, roaring, and blowing on the beach was something frightful.
value.da: Han forfulgte dog aldrig en besejret sæl, for det var forbudt efter Strandens Regler. Han ville bare have en yngleplads ved vandet. Men fyrre eller halvtreds tusind andre sæler ville det samme hvert forår, og deres fløjten, brøl, hyl og fnys larmede forfærdeligt.

value.en: From a little hill called Hutchinson’s Hill, you could look over three and a half miles of ground covered with fighting seals; and the surf was dotted all over with the heads of seals hurrying to land and begin their share of the fighting. They fought in the breakers, they fought in the sand, and they fought on the smooth-worn basalt rocks of the nurseries, for they were just as stupid and unaccommodating as men. Their wives never came to the island until late in May or early in June, for they did not care to be torn to pieces; and the young two-, three-, and four-year-old seals who had not begun housekeeping went inland about half a mile through the ranks of the fighters and played about on the sand dunes in droves and legions, and rubbed off every single green thing that grew. They were called the holluschickie--the bachelors--and there were perhaps two or three hundred thousand of them at Novastoshnah alone.
value.da: Fra den lille Hutchinsons Bakke kunne man se over tre og en halv engelsk mil jord, der var tæt pakket med kæmpende sæler. I brændingen myldrede sælhoveder, der skyndte sig i land for at være med i kampene. De sloges i de brydende bølger, i sandet og på de glatslidte basaltklipper på ynglepladserne, lige så dumme og stædige som mennesker. Hunnerne kom først sidst i maj eller først i juni, for de havde ingen lyst til at blive flået i stykker. De unge sæler på to, tre og fire år, som endnu ikke havde stiftet familie, gik gennem rækkerne af kæmpere og en halv engelsk mil ind i landet. Der legede de i store flokke og hære på klitterne og gned alt grønt, der voksede, væk. De hed holluschickie — ungkarlene — og alene ved Novastoshnah var der måske to eller tre hundrede tusind af dem.

value.en: Sea Catch had just finished his forty-fifth fight one spring when Matkah, his soft, sleek, gentle-eyed wife, came up out of the sea, and he caught her by the scruff of the neck and dumped her down on his reservation, saying gruffly: “Late as usual. Where have you been?”
value.da: Et forår havde Sea Catch lige afsluttet sin femogfyrretyvende kamp, da hans kone Matkah kom op af havet, blød og glat og med venlige øjne. Han greb hende i nakkeskindet og smed hende ned på sin plads. »Forsinket igen,« brummede han. »Hvor har du været?«

value.en: It was not the fashion for Sea Catch to eat anything during the four months he stayed on the beaches, and so his temper was generally bad. Matkah knew better than to answer back. She looked round and cooed: “How thoughtful of you. You’ve taken the old place again.”
value.da: Sea Catch fulgte sælernes skik og spiste ikke noget som helst i de fire måneder, han var på strandene, og derfor var han som regel i dårligt humør. Matkah vidste bedre end at skændes. Hun så sig omkring og kurrede: »Hvor er du omsorgsfuld. Du har fået vores gamle plads igen.«

value.en: “I should think I had,” said Sea Catch. “Look at me!”
value.da: »Det skulle jeg mene,« sagde Sea Catch. »Se på mig!«

value.en: He was scratched and bleeding in twenty places; one eye was almost out, and his sides were torn to ribbons.
value.da: Han var skrabet og blødende tyve steder; det ene øje var næsten ude, og hans sider var revet i laser.

value.en: “Oh, you men, you men!” Matkah said, fanning herself with her hind flipper. “Why can’t you be sensible and settle your places quietly? You look as though you had been fighting with the Killer Whale.”
value.da: »Åh, I mænd, I mænd!« sukkede Matkah og viftede sig med en bagluffe. »Hvorfor kan I ikke opføre jer fornuftigt og aftale jeres pladser i fred? Du ser ud, som om du har kæmpet mod Spækhuggeren.«

value.en: “I haven’t been doing anything but fight since the middle of May. The beach is disgracefully crowded this season. I’ve met at least a hundred seals from Lukannon Beach, house hunting. Why can’t people stay where they belong?”
value.da: »Jeg har ikke lavet andet end at slås siden midten af maj. Stranden er skammeligt overfyldt i år. Mindst hundrede sæler fra Lukannon-stranden har været her og lede efter et sted at bo. Hvorfor kan folk ikke blive, hvor de hører til?«

value.en: “I’ve often thought we should be much happier if we hauled out at Otter Island instead of this crowded place,” said Matkah.
value.da: »Jeg tænker tit på, at vi ville være gladere, hvis vi gik i land på Otterøen, væk fra al den trængsel,« sagde Matkah.

value.en: “Bah! Only the holluschickie go to Otter Island. If we went there they would say we were afraid. We must preserve appearances, my dear.”
value.da: »Pøh! Otterøen er for holluschickie. Hvis vi tog derhen, ville alle kalde os fejge. Man må bevare facaden, min kære.«

value.en: Sea Catch sunk his head proudly between his fat shoulders and pretended to go to sleep for a few minutes, but all the time he was keeping a sharp lookout for a fight. Now that all the seals and their wives were on the land, you could hear their clamor miles out to sea above the loudest gales. At the lowest counting there were over a million seals on the beach--old seals, mother seals, tiny babies, and holluschickie, fighting, scuffling, bleating, crawling, and playing together--going down to the sea and coming up from it in gangs and regiments, lying over every foot of ground as far as the eye could reach, and skirmishing about in brigades through the fog. It is nearly always foggy at Novastoshnah, except when the sun comes out and makes everything look all pearly and rainbow-colored for a little while.
value.da: Stolt sænkede Sea Catch hovedet mellem de brede skuldre og lod, som om han lagde sig til at sove, men hele tiden holdt han udkig efter en ny kamp. Nu hvor sælerne og deres koner var i land, kunne man høre larmen langt ude på havet, også i de værste storme. Der var mindst en million sæler på stranden: gamle sæler, mødre, helt små unger og holluschickie, og alle sammen sloges, puffede, brægede, kravlede og legede. De gik i flokke og regimenter ned til vandet og op igen. De lå over hver eneste kvadratmeter, så langt øjet rakte, og hele brigader holdt skærmydsler i tågen. Der er næsten altid tåge ved Novastoshnah, bortset fra når solen kommer frem og i et kort øjeblik får alting til at skinne i perlemorsfarver og regnbuefarver.

value.en: Kotick, Matkah’s baby, was born in the middle of that confusion, and he was all head and shoulders, with pale, watery blue eyes, as tiny seals must be, but there was something about his coat that made his mother look at him very closely.
value.da: Midt i al den forvirring blev Matkahs baby, Kotick, født. Som alle små sæler var han mest hoved og skuldre, med blege, vandblå øjne. Men der var noget ved hans pels, som fik hans mor til at se nøje på ham.

value.en: “Sea Catch,” she said, at last, “our baby’s going to be white!”
value.da: »Sea Catch,« sagde hun til sidst, »vores baby bliver hvid!«

value.en: “Empty clam-shells and dry seaweed!” snorted Sea Catch. “There never has been such a thing in the world as a white seal.”
value.da: »Tomme muslingeskaller og tørre tangstrå!« fnyste Sea Catch. »Der har aldrig været en hvid sæl noget sted i verden.«

value.en: “I can’t help that,” said Matkah; “there’s going to be now.” And she sang the low, crooning seal song that all the mother seals sing to their babies:
value.da: »Det er ikke min skyld,« sagde Matkah. »Nu bliver der en.« Og hun begyndte på den bløde, nynnende vuggevise, som alle sælmødre synger for deres unger:

value.en:
You mustn’t swim till you’re six weeks old,
Or your head will be sunk by your heels;
And summer gales and Killer Whales
Are bad for baby seals.
value.da:
Du må ikke svømme, før du er seks uger gammel,
ellers vil dit hoved synke under dine hæle;
og sommerstorme og spækhuggere
er slemme for små sælunger.

value.en:
Are bad for baby seals, dear rat,
As bad as bad can be;
But splash and grow strong,
And you can’t be wrong.
Child of the Open Sea!
value.da:
Slemme for små sælunger, kære skat,
så slemme som det kan blive;
men plask og bliv stærk,
og du kan ikke fejle.
Barn af det åbne hav!

value.en: Of course the little fellow did not understand the words at first. He paddled and scrambled about by his mother’s side, and learned to scuffle out of the way when his father was fighting with another seal, and the two rolled and roared up and down the slippery rocks. Matkah used to go to sea to get things to eat, and the baby was fed only once in two days, but then he ate all he could and throve upon it.
value.da: Til at begynde med forstod ungen naturligvis ingenting af det. Han padlede og tumlede rundt ved siden af sin mor og lærte at skynde sig af vejen, når hans far kæmpede mod en anden sæl, og de to rullede brølende hen over de glatte klipper. Matkah tog ud på havet for at finde mad, så Kotick fik kun mad hver anden dag. Men når det endelig var spisetid, åd han, så meget hans lille mave kunne rumme, og af de måltider blev han stærk.

value.en: The first thing he did was to crawl inland, and there he met tens of thousands of babies of his own age, and they played together like puppies, went to sleep on the clean sand, and played again. The old people in the nurseries took no notice of them, and the holluschickie kept to their own grounds, and the babies had a beautiful playtime.
value.da: Hans første udflugt var en kravletur ind i landet. Der fandt han titusinder af unger på sin egen alder, som tumlede rundt som hvalpe, sov på det rene sand og begyndte at lege igen. De voksne på ynglepladserne tog ingen notits af dem, holluschickie holdt sig på deres egne områder, og ungerne havde det vidunderligt.

value.en: When Matkah came back from her deep-sea fishing she would go straight to their playground and call as a sheep calls for a lamb, and wait until she heard Kotick bleat. Then she would take the straightest of straight lines in his direction, striking out with her fore flippers and knocking the youngsters head over heels right and left. There were always a few hundred mothers hunting for their children through the playgrounds, and the babies were kept lively. But, as Matkah told Kotick, “So long as you don’t lie in muddy water and get mange, or rub the hard sand into a cut or scratch, and so long as you never go swimming when there is a heavy sea, nothing will hurt you here.”
value.da: Når Matkah kom tilbage fra dybhavsfiskeriet, gik hun direkte til legepladsen. Hun kaldte, som et får, der leder efter sit lam, og ventede på, at Kotick brægede tilbage. Så gik hun lige hen imod ham, svingede forluffene og fik ungerne til at vælte til begge sider. Der var altid et par hundrede andre mødre, som ledte efter deres unger på legepladserne, så de små sæler havde nok at se til og blev ved med at være i bevægelse. Matkah sagde til Kotick: »Du må ikke ligge i mudret vand og få skab, du må ikke gnide groft sand ind i et sår eller en rift, og du må aldrig svømme, når der er uroligt hav. Hvis du holder dig til det, kan intet her gøre dig noget.«

value.en: Little seals can no more swim than little children, but they are unhappy till they learn. The first time that Kotick went down to the sea a wave carried him out beyond his depth, and his big head sank and his little hind flippers flew up exactly as his mother had told him in the song, and if the next wave had not thrown him back again he would have drowned.
value.da: Små sæler kan lige så lidt svømme som små børn, men de er ulykkelige, indtil de lærer det. Første gang Kotick gik ned i vandet, bar en bølge ham ud, hvor han ikke kunne bunde. Hans tunge hoved sank, og de små baglufferne fløj i vejret, præcis som sangen havde advaret om. Hvis den næste bølge ikke havde kastet ham tilbage, var han druknet.

value.en: After that, he learned to lie in a beach pool and let the wash of the waves just cover him and lift him up while he paddled, but he always kept his eye open for big waves that might hurt. He was two weeks learning to use his flippers; and all that while he floundered in and out of the water, and coughed and grunted and crawled up the beach and took catnaps on the sand, and went back again, until at last he found that he truly belonged to the water.
value.da: Derefter øvede han sig i en lav strandpøl, hvor han lod vandet dække og løfte sig, mens han padlede, og hele tiden holdt han udkig efter store bølger, der kunne være farlige. I to hele uger arbejdede han på at lære at bruge luffene, og for hvert forsøg forstod han lidt mere af, hvad de var til. Han plumpede ind og ud af vandet, hostede, gryntede, kravlede op på stranden og tog en høneblund i sandet og gik så ud igen. Til sidst opdagede han, at vandet virkelig var hans hjem.

value.en: Then you can imagine the times that he had with his companions, ducking under the rollers; or coming in on top of a comber and landing with a swash and a splutter as the big wave went whirling far up the beach; or standing up on his tail and scratching his head as the old people did; or playing “I’m the King of the Castle” on slippery, weedy rocks that just stuck out of the wash. Now and then he would see a thin fin, like a big shark’s fin, drifting along close to shore, and he knew that that was the Killer Whale, the Grampus, who eats young seals when he can get them; and Kotick would head for the beach like an arrow, and the fin would jig off slowly, as if it were looking for nothing at all.
value.da: Forestil dig, hvor sjovt han og vennerne havde det: de dykkede under de store bølger, red på en brydende bølge ind mod land med et plask og en prusten, mens den skyllede højt op ad stranden, stod på halen og kløede sig i hovedet som de voksne, eller legede »Jeg er konge på borgen« på glatte, tangdækkede klipper, der lige netop stak op over bølgeskyllet. Nu og da drev en tynd finne, som en stor hajs, forbi tæt på land. Kotick vidste, at den tilhørte Spækhuggeren, Grampusen, som fanger unge sæler, når han kan. Så skød han som en pil ind mod stranden, og finnen drev langsomt væk, som om ejeren slet ikke ledte efter noget.

value.en: Late in October the seals began to leave St. Paul’s for the deep sea, by families and tribes, and there was no more fighting over the nurseries, and the holluschickie played anywhere they liked. “Next year,” said Matkah to Kotick, “you will be a holluschickie; but this year you must learn how to catch fish.”
value.da: Sidst i oktober begyndte familier og stammer at forlade St. Paul og tage ud på det dybe, åbne hav. Der blev ikke længere kæmpet om ynglepladserne, og holluschickie legede, hvor de ville. »Næste år bliver du en holluschickie,« sagde Matkah til Kotick. »I år skal du lære at fange fisk.«

value.en: They set out together across the Pacific, and Matkah showed Kotick how to sleep on his back with his flippers tucked down by his side and his little nose just out of the water. No cradle is so comfortable as the long, rocking swell of the Pacific. When Kotick felt his skin tingle all over, Matkah told him he was learning the “feel of the water,” and that tingly, prickly feelings meant bad weather coming, and he must swim hard and get away.
value.da: Sammen svømmede de tværs over Stillehavet. Matkah lærte ham at sove flydende på ryggen med luffene trukket ind til siden og kun den lille snude over vandet. Ingen vugge gynger mere behageligt end Stillehavets lange dønninger. Da Koticks hud begyndte at prikke over det hele, forklarede hun, at han var ved at få »fornemmelsen for vandet«. Den snurren varslede dårligt vejr på vej, og så skulle han svømme hårdt for at slippe væk.

value.en: “In a little time,” she said, “you’ll know where to swim to, but just now we’ll follow Sea Pig, the Porpoise, for he is very wise.” A school of porpoises were ducking and tearing through the water, and little Kotick followed them as fast as he could. “How do you know where to go to?” he panted. The leader of the school rolled his white eye and ducked under. “My tail tingles, youngster,” he said. “That means there’s a gale behind me. Come along! When you’re south of the Sticky Water [he meant the Equator] and your tail tingles, that means there’s a gale in front of you and you must head north. Come along! The water feels bad here.”
value.da: »Snart ved du selv, hvilken vej du skal svømme,« sagde hun. »Lige nu følger vi Sea Pig, marsvinet, for han er klog.« En hel stime marsvin dykkede og skød af sted gennem bølgerne foran dem, og lille Kotick fulgte efter, så hurtigt han kunne svømme. »Hvordan ved I, hvor I skal hen?« gispede han. Lederen rullede med det hvide øje og dykkede. »Min hale prikker, knægt. Der er en storm bag mig. Kom nu! Syd for Det Klistrede Vand [han mente Ækvator] betyder en prikkende hale, at stormen er foran en, så man skal vende nordpå. Kom nu! Vandet føles forkert her.«

value.en: This was one of very many things that Kotick learned, and he was always learning. Matkah taught him to follow the cod and the halibut along the under-sea banks and wrench the rockling out of his hole among the weeds; how to skirt the wrecks lying a hundred fathoms below water and dart like a rifle bullet in at one porthole and out at another as the fishes ran; how to dance on the top of the waves when the lightning was racing all over the sky, and wave his flipper politely to the stumpy-tailed Albatross and the Man-of-war Hawk as they went down the wind; how to jump three or four feet clear of the water like a dolphin, flippers close to the side and tail curved; to leave the flying fish alone because they are all bony; to take the shoulder-piece out of a cod at full speed ten fathoms deep, and never to stop and look at a boat or a ship, but particularly a row-boat. At the end of six months what Kotick did not know about deep-sea fishing was not worth the knowing. And all that time he never set flipper on dry ground.
value.da: Det var kun én af de mange ting, Kotick lærte, for han opdagede hele tiden noget nyt, og der var altid en ny lektie. Matkah viste ham, hvordan man følger torsk og helleflynder langs undersøiske banker og trækker havkvabber ud af deres tangfyldte huller. Hun viste ham, hvordan man svinger rundt om vrag, der ligger hundrede favne nede, og farer som en riffelkugle ind gennem det ene koøje og ud gennem det andet efter flygtende fisk. Hun viste ham, hvordan man danser på bølgerne under en himmel fuld af lyn og høfligt vinker med en luffe til den korthalede albatros og fregatfuglen, når de glider forbi på vinden. Han lærte at springe som en delfin en meter op af havet med luffene tæt ind til kroppen og halen bøjet, at holde sig fra de benrige flyvefisk, at bide en torsk i skulderen i fuld fart ti favne nede og aldrig at blive hængende i nærheden af en båd eller et skib, og allermindst en robåd. Efter et halvt år var der næsten ikke noget om dybhavsfiskeri, han ikke vidste. Hele den tid rørte han aldrig land.

value.en: One day, however, as he was lying half asleep in the warm water somewhere off the Island of Juan Fernandez, he felt faint and lazy all over, just as human people do when the spring is in their legs, and he remembered the good firm beaches of Novastoshnah seven thousand miles away, the games his companions played, the smell of the seaweed, the seal roar, and the fighting. That very minute he turned north, swimming steadily, and as he went on he met scores of his mates, all bound for the same place, and they said: “Greeting, Kotick! This year we are all holluschickie, and we can dance the Fire-dance in the breakers off Lukannon and play on the new grass. But where did you get that coat?”
value.da: En dag lå han halvt i søvn i det varme vand ud for øen Juan Fernández og følte sig sløj og rastløs, lidt som mennesker, når foråret rører sig i benene. Han huskede Novastoshnahs faste strande syv tusind engelske mil væk, vennernes lege, lugten af tang, de brølende sæler og kampene. I samme øjeblik vendte han snuden mod nord og begyndte at svømme støt hjemad. Mens han svømmede, dukkede flere og flere kammerater op, snesevis af dem, alle på vej samme vej. »Hej, Kotick!« råbte de. »I år er vi alle holluschickie. Vi kan danse Ilddansen i brændingen ved Lukannon og lege i det friske græs. Hvor har du fået den pels fra?«

value.en: Kotick’s fur was almost pure white now, and though he felt very proud of it, he only said, “Swim quickly! My bones are aching for the land.” And so they all came to the beaches where they had been born, and heard the old seals, their fathers, fighting in the rolling mist.
value.da: Koticks pels var nu næsten helt hvid, og han var meget stolt af den. Men han svarede kun: »Skynd jer! Hver en knogle i mig længes efter land.« Sammen nåede de det sted, hvor de var født, og hørte deres fædre, de gamle sæler, slås i den drivende tåge.

value.en: That night Kotick danced the Fire-dance with the yearling seals. The sea is full of fire on summer nights all the way down from Novastoshnah to Lukannon, and each seal leaves a wake like burning oil behind him and a flaming flash when he jumps, and the waves break in great phosphorescent streaks and swirls. Then they went inland to the holluschickie grounds and rolled up and down in the new wild wheat and told stories of what they had done while they had been at sea. They talked about the Pacific as boys would talk about a wood that they had been nutting in, and if anyone had understood them he could have gone away and made such a chart of that ocean as never was. The three- and four-year-old holluschickie romped down from Hutchinson’s Hill crying: “Out of the way, youngsters! The sea is deep and you don’t know all that’s in it yet. Wait till you’ve rounded the Horn. Hi, you yearling, where did you get that white coat?”
value.da: Den nat var Kotick med i de etåriges Ilddans. På sommernætter lyser havet hele vejen mellem Novastoshnah og Lukannon. Hver sæl efterlader et spor, der ligner brændende olie, og blinker som en flamme, når den hopper, og bølgerne brydes i lysende striber og spiraler. Bagefter rullede de rundt i den friske vilde hvede på holluschickie-områderne inde i landet og fortalte hinanden om deres rejser. De talte om det enorme Stillehav, som om det var en skov, hvor en flok drenge havde været sammen for at samle nødder. Hvis nogen havde forstået dem, kunne han have tegnet et enestående søkort over havet. De tre- og fireårige holluschickie tumlede ned ad Hutchinsons Bakke og råbte: »Plads, småfolk! Havet er dybt, og I har ikke opdaget alt, hvad der er i det. Vent, til I har rundet Kap Horn. Hej, du etårige, hvor har du fået den hvide pels fra?«

value: One day, half asleep in warm water off Juan Fernandez Island, Kotick felt weak and restless, rather as humans do when spring stirs in their legs. He remembered Novastoshnah’s firm beaches seven thousand miles away, his friends’ games, seaweed smells, roaring seals, and battles. At that very moment he turned his nose northward and began swimming steadily toward home. As he continued on his way, more and more of his companions came into sight. Dozens of companions joined him, heading the same way. “Greetings, Kotick!” they called. “We’re all holluschickie this year. We can dance the Fire-dance in Lukannon’s surf and play on the fresh grass. Where did you find that coat?”

value.en: “I didn’t get it,” said Kotick. “It grew.” And just as he was going to roll the speaker over, a couple of black-haired men with flat red faces came from behind a sand dune, and Kotick, who had never seen a man before, coughed and lowered his head. The holluschickie just bundled off a few yards and sat staring stupidly. The men were no less than Kerick Booterin, the chief of the seal-hunters on the island, and Patalamon, his son. They came from the little village not half a mile from the sea nurseries, and they were deciding what seals they would drive up to the killing pens--for the seals were driven just like sheep--to be turned into seal-skin jackets later on.
value.da: »Jeg har ikke fundet den,« svarede Kotick. »Den er vokset.« Han var lige ved at vælte taleren, da to mænd dukkede op bag en klit, sorthårede og med flade, røde ansigter. Kotick havde aldrig set et menneske før. Han hostede og sænkede hovedet. De andre holluschickie rykkede nogle meter væk og stirrede dumt. Det var Kerick Booterin, høvding for øens sæljægere, og hans søn Patalamon. De boede i den lille landsby mindre end en halv engelsk mil fra ynglepladserne. Nu udvalgte de sæler, som de kunne drive som får hen til slagtefoldene, hvor rejsen mod at blive til sælskindsjakker begyndte.

value.en: “Ho!” said Patalamon. “Look! There’s a white seal!”
value.da: »Ho!« sagde Patalamon. »Se! Der er en hvid sæl!«

value.en: Kerick Booterin turned nearly white under his oil and smoke, for he was an Aleut, and Aleuts are not clean people. Then he began to mutter a prayer. “Don’t touch him, Patalamon. There has never been a white seal since--since I was born. Perhaps it is old Zaharrof’s ghost. He was lost last year in the big gale.”
value.da: Under sit lag af røg og olie blev Kerick Booterin næsten bleg. Han var aleut, og aleuter er ikke renlige folk. Han mumlede en bøn og sagde: »Lad ham være, Patalamon. Der har ikke været en hvid sæl siden — siden jeg blev født. Måske er det gamle Zaharrofs spøgelse. Den store storm tog ham sidste år.«

value.en: “I’m not going near him,” said Patalamon. “He’s unlucky. Do you really think he is old Zaharrof come back? I owe him for some gulls’ eggs.”
value.da: »Jeg går ikke nær ham,« sagde Patalamon. »Han bringer ulykke. Tror du virkelig, det er gamle Zaharrof, der er kommet tilbage? Jeg skylder ham for nogle mågeæg.«

value.en: “Don’t look at him,” said Kerick. “Head off that drove of four-year-olds. The men ought to skin two hundred to-day, but it’s the beginning of the season and they are new to the work. A hundred will do. Quick!”
value.da: »Stirr ikke på ham,« sagde Kerick. »Skil de fireårige fra. Mændene burde flå to hundrede i dag, men sæsonen er lige begyndt, og de er ikke vant til arbejdet endnu. Hundrede er nok. Skynd dig!«

value.en: Patalamon rattled a pair of seal’s shoulder bones in front of a herd of holluschickie and they stopped dead, puffing and blowing. Then he stepped near and the seals began to move, and Kerick headed them inland, and they never tried to get back to their companions. Hundreds and hundreds of thousands of seals watched them being driven, but they went on playing just the same. Kotick was the only one who asked questions, and none of his companions could tell him anything, except that the men always drove seals in that way for six weeks or two months of every year.
value.da: Patalamon raslede med to skulderblade af sæl foran en flok holluschickie, og de standsede, pustende og prustende. Når han kom nærmere, gik de videre, og Kerick styrede dem ind i landet, og ingen af dem prøvede at komme tilbage til vennerne. Hundredtusinder så dem blive drevet bort, men legede videre. Kotick var den eneste, der ville vide, hvad der foregik, og han begyndte at spørge alle sine kammerater. Ingen kunne forklare, hvor sælerne skulle hen, eller hvad mændene ville gøre. De vidste kun, at mændene gjorde det i seks uger eller to måneder hvert år.

value.en: “I am going to follow,” he said, and his eyes nearly popped out of his head as he shuffled along in the wake of the herd.
value.da: »Jeg går med,« sagde han, og hans øjne sprang næsten ud af hovedet på ham, mens han traskede afsted i kølvandet på flokken.

value.en: “The white seal is coming after us,” cried Patalamon. “That’s the first time a seal has ever come to the killing-grounds alone.”
value.da: »Den hvide sæl kommer efter os,« råbte Patalamon. »Det er første gang, en sæl nogensinde er kommet alene til slagtepladsen.«

value.en: “Hsh! Don’t look behind you,” said Kerick. “It is Zaharrof’s ghost! I must speak to the priest about this.”
value.da: »Hys! Vend dig ikke om,« advarede Kerick. »Det er Zaharrofs spøgelse! Det må jeg tale med præsten om.«

value.en: The distance to the killing-grounds was only half a mile, but it took an hour to cover, because if the seals went too fast Kerick knew that they would get heated and then their fur would come off in patches when they were skinned. So they went on very slowly, past Sea Lion’s Neck, past Webster House, till they came to the Salt House just beyond the sight of the seals on the beach. Kotick followed, panting and wondering. He thought that he was at the world’s end, but the roar of the seal nurseries behind him sounded as loud as the roar of a train in a tunnel. Then Kerick sat down on the moss and pulled out a heavy pewter watch and let the drove cool off for thirty minutes, and Kotick could hear the fog-dew dripping off the brim of his cap. Then ten or twelve men, each with an iron-bound club three or four feet long, came up, and Kerick pointed out one or two of the drove that were bitten by their companions or too hot, and the men kicked those aside with their heavy boots made of the skin of a walrus’s throat, and then Kerick said, “Let go!” and then the men clubbed the seals on the head as fast as they could.
value.da: Slagtepladserne lå kun en halv engelsk mil væk, men det tog en time at komme derhen. Kerick vidste, at hvis man jagede sælerne for hurtigt, blev de overophedede, og så faldt pelsen af i totter, når de blev flået. Så de gik meget langsomt, forbi Søløvehalsen og Webster House, til de nåede Salthuset, lige uden for syne af strandsælerne. Forpustet og forvirret fulgte Kotick med. Han følte, at han var nået til verdens ende, selvom ynglepladsen i det fjerne brølede som et tog i en tunnel. Kerick satte sig på mosset, tog et tungt tinur frem og gav sælerne tredive minutter til at køle af. Mens mændene ventede, og sælerne kølede af, kunne Kotick høre de små tågedråber falde en efter en fra kanten af Kericks kasket. Ti eller tolv mænd kom med jernbeslåede køller på omkring en meter. Kerick udpegede nogle få sæler, der var for varme eller bidt af de andre, og mændene sparkede dem til side med deres tunge støvler af skind fra hvalrossers hals. Da Kerick havde udpeget de uegnede dyr og set dem sparket ud af flokken, gav han endelig ordren. »Slip dem løs!« råbte han, og så slog mændene de andre i hovedet så hurtigt, de kunne.

value.en: Ten minutes later little Kotick did not recognize his friends any more, for their skins were ripped off from the nose to the hind flippers, whipped off and thrown down on the ground in a pile. That was enough for Kotick. He turned and galloped (a seal can gallop very swiftly for a short time) back to the sea; his little new mustache bristling with horror. At Sea Lion’s Neck, where the great sea lions sit on the edge of the surf, he flung himself flipper-overhead into the cool water and rocked there, gasping miserably. “What’s here?” said a sea lion gruffly, for as a rule the sea lions keep themselves to themselves.
value.da: Ti minutter senere kunne Kotick ikke længere genkende sine venner. Skindene var skåret op fra snuden til baglufferne, revet af og lagt i en bunke på jorden. Mere kunne han ikke holde ud. Han vendte om og galopperede mod havet — sæler kan galoppere forbløffende hurtigt over korte stykker — og hans lille, nye knurhår stod stift af rædsel. Ved Søløvehalsen, hvor store søløver sidder ved brændingen, dykkede han hovedkulds ned i det kølige vand og lå og vuggede, gispende af elendighed. »Hvad sker der?« brummede en søløve; søløver blander sig ellers sjældent i andres sager.

value.en: “Scoochnie! Ochen scoochnie!” (“I’m lonesome, very lonesome!”) said Kotick. “They’re killing all the holluschickie on all the beaches!”
value.da: »Scoochnie! Ochen scoochnie!« (»Jeg er ensom, meget ensom!«) sagde Kotick. »De slår alle holluschickie ihjel på alle strandene!«

value.en: The Sea Lion turned his head inshore. “Nonsense!” he said. “Your friends are making as much noise as ever. You must have seen old Kerick polishing off a drove. He’s done that for thirty years.”
value.da: Søløven vendte hovedet mod land. »Sludder!« sagde han. »Dine venner laver lige så meget larm som altid. Du må have set gamle Kerick rydde op i en flok. Det har han gjort i tredive år.«

value.en: “It’s horrible,” said Kotick, backing water as a wave went over him, and steadying himself with a screw stroke of his flippers that brought him all standing within three inches of a jagged edge of rock.
value.da: »Det er forfærdeligt,« sagde Kotick og padlede baglæns under en bølge. Med et drej af lufferne holdt han sig i ro og stod lodret højst syv centimeter fra en takket klippekant.

value.en: “Well done for a yearling!” said the Sea Lion, who could appreciate good swimming. “I suppose it is rather awful from your way of looking at it, but if you seals will come here year after year, of course the men get to know of it, and unless you can find an island where no men ever come you will always be driven.”
value.da: »Godt svømmet af en etårig!« sagde søløven, som holdt af god svømning. »Set fra dit synspunkt er det vist ubehageligt. Men I sæler kommer tilbage hvert eneste år, så selvfølgelig finder mændene ud af det. Medmindre I finder en ø, hvor mænd aldrig kommer, bliver I altid drevet af dem.«

value.en: “Isn’t there any such island?” began Kotick.
value.da: »Findes der ikke sådan en ø?« spurgte Kotick.

value.en: “I’ve followed the poltoos [the halibut] for twenty years, and I can’t say I’ve found it yet. But look here--you seem to have a fondness for talking to your betters--suppose you go to Walrus Islet and talk to Sea Vitch. He may know something. Don’t flounce off like that. It’s a six-mile swim, and if I were you I should haul out and take a nap first, little one.”
value.da: »Jeg har jaget poltoos [helleflynder] i tyve år uden at finde en sådan ø. Men du ser ud til at nyde at tale med dem, der er ældre og bedre end dig. Hvorfor ikke tage hen til Hvalrosholmen og spørge Sea Vitch? Han ved det måske. Du skal ikke stikke af sådan. Der er seks engelske mil over. Hvis jeg var dig, lille, ville jeg gå i land og sove først.«

value.en: Kotick thought that that was good advice, so he swam round to his own beach, hauled out, and slept for half an hour, twitching all over, as seals will. Then he headed straight for Walrus Islet, a little low sheet of rocky island almost due northeast from Novastoshnah, all ledges and rock and gulls’ nests, where the walrus herded by themselves.
value.da: Kotick tog imod det fornuftige råd. Han svømmede til sin egen strand og sov i en halv time på land, og hans krop trak sig i spjæt, som sæler gør. Så satte han kursen lige mod Hvalrosholmen, en lav klippeø næsten lige nordøst for Novastoshnah, fuld af klippehylder og mågereder. Hvalrosserne boede dér for sig selv.

value.en: He landed close to old Sea Vitch--the big, ugly, bloated, pimpled, fat-necked, long-tusked walrus of the North Pacific, who has no manners except when he is asleep--as he was then, with his hind flippers half in and half out of the surf.
value.da: Han gik i land ved siden af gamle Sea Vitch, som sov med baglufferne delvis i brændingen. Denne enorme hvalros fra det nordlige Stillehav var grim, oppustet, fuld af bumser, tykhalset og langtandet og havde ingen manerer undtagen når han sov.

value.en: “Wake up!” barked Kotick, for the gulls were making a great noise.
value.da: »Vågn op!« råbte Kotick over mågernes skrig.

value.p32: This was only one of the many things Kotick learned, for he was continually discovering something new and there was always another lesson to learn. Matkah showed him how to track cod and halibut along underwater banks and haul rockling from their weedy holes; how to sweep around wrecks a hundred fathoms down, shooting through one porthole and out another like a rifle bullet after fleeing fish; how to dance on waves beneath a lightning-filled sky, politely waving a flipper to the short-tailed Albatross and Man-of-war Hawk as they rode the wind. He learned dolphin-like leaps three or four feet clear of the sea, flippers tucked and tail curved; to avoid bony flying fish; to bite a cod’s shoulder at full speed ten fathoms down; and never to linger near a boat or ship, especially a rowing boat. After six months, anything he didn’t know about deep-sea fishing scarcely mattered. Throughout those months he never once touched land.
value.p45: The killing-grounds lay just half a mile away, but getting there took an hour. Kerick knew that rushing overheated seals, making their fur fall out in patches during skinning. Slowly they passed Sea Lion’s Neck and Webster House, reaching the Salt House beyond the beach seals’ view. Panting and puzzled, Kotick followed. He felt he had reached the world’s end, though the distant nursery roared like a train inside a tunnel. Kerick sat on the moss, produced a heavy pewter watch, and allowed thirty minutes for the seals to cool. While the men waited and the seals cooled, Kotick could hear the tiny drops of moisture gathered from the fog falling one after another from the brim of Kerick’s cap. Ten or twelve men arrived carrying iron-bound clubs three or four feet long. Kerick indicated a few seals that were overheated or bitten. Wearing heavy boots of walrus-throat skin, the men kicked those aside. After pointing out these unsuitable animals and seeing them kicked clear of the drove, Kerick finally gave the order. “Let go!” he shouted, and they clubbed the others’ heads as fast as possible.

value.en: “Hah! Ho! Hmph! What’s that?” said Sea Vitch, and he struck the next walrus a blow with his tusks and waked him up, and the next struck the next, and so on till they were all awake and staring in every direction but the right one.
value.da: »Hah! Ho! Hmf! Hvad er det?« sagde Sea Vitch, og han gav den næste hvalros et slag med sine stødtænder og vækkede ham, og den næste slog den næste, og så videre, indtil de alle var vågne og stirrede i alle retninger undtagen den rigtige.

value.en: “Hi! It’s me,” said Kotick, bobbing in the surf and looking like a little white slug.
value.da: »Hallo! Herovre,« råbte Kotick, mens han duvede som en lille hvid snegl i bølgerne.

value.en: “Well! May I be--skinned!” said Sea Vitch, and they all looked at Kotick as you can fancy a club full of drowsy old gentlemen would look at a little boy. Kotick did not care to hear any more about skinning just then; he had seen enough of it. So he called out: “Isn’t there any place for seals to go where men don’t ever come?”
value.da: »Nå! Så må jeg blive — flået!« sagde Sea Vitch. Alle hvalrosserne så på Kotick, som en klub af søvnige gamle herrer, der bliver konfronteret med en lille dreng. Lige i det øjeblik havde Kotick ingen lyst til at høre mere om flåning; han havde allerede set mere af det, end han kunne holde ud. Han råbte: »Findes der et sted, hvor sæler kan bo, og hvor mænd aldrig kommer?«

value.en: “Go and find out,” said Sea Vitch, shutting his eyes. “Run away. We’re busy here.”
value.da: »Tag af sted og find ud af det,« sagde Sea Vitch og lukkede øjnene. »Forsvind. Vi har travlt her.«

value.en: Kotick made his dolphin-jump in the air and shouted as loud as he could: “Clam-eater! Clam-eater!” He knew that Sea Vitch never caught a fish in his life but always rooted for clams and seaweed; though he pretended to be a very terrible person. Naturally the Chickies and the Gooverooskies and the Epatkas--the Burgomaster Gulls and the Kittiwakes and the Puffins, who are always looking for a chance to be rude, took up the cry, and--so Limmershin told me--for nearly five minutes you could not have heard a gun fired on Walrus Islet. All the population was yelling and screaming “Clam-eater! Stareek [old man]!” while Sea Vitch rolled from side to side grunting and coughing.
value.da: Kotick sprang som en delfin og råbte så højt, han kunne: »Muslingeæder! Muslingeæder!« Han vidste, at Sea Vitch, trods al sin vilde optræden, aldrig havde fanget en fisk, men kun rodede rundt efter muslinger og tang. Chickies, Gooverooskies og Epatkaer — borgmestermåger, ride og lunder — lader aldrig en chance for uforskammethed gå fra sig. De tog alle ivrigt råbet op og skreg det tilbage mod hvalrossen, og hver fugl prøvede at overdøve de andre. Limmershin fortalte mig, at et skud ikke ville have kunnet høres på Hvalrosholmen i næsten fem minutter. Alle skreg: »Muslingeæder! Stareek [gamle mand]!« Sea Vitch rullede frem og tilbage og hostede og gryntede.

value.en: “Now will you tell?” said Kotick, all out of breath.
value.da: »Vil du nu fortælle det?« sagde Kotick helt forpustet.

value.en: “Go and ask Sea Cow,” said Sea Vitch. “If he is living still, he’ll be able to tell you.”
value.da: »Gå hen og spørg Sea Cow,« sagde Sea Vitch. »Hvis han stadig lever, vil han kunne fortælle dig det.«

value.en: “How shall I know Sea Cow when I meet him?” said Kotick, sheering off.
value.da: »Hvordan kan jeg kende Sea Cow, når jeg møder ham?« spurgte Kotick og begyndte at svømme væk.

value.en: “He’s the only thing in the sea uglier than Sea Vitch,” screamed a Burgomaster gull, wheeling under Sea Vitch’s nose. “Uglier, and with worse manners! Stareek!”
value.da: »Han er den eneste ting i havet, der er grimmere end Sea Vitch,« skreg en borgmestermåge, mens den drejede under Sea Vitchs næse. »Grimmere, og med værre manerer! Stareek!«

value.en: Kotick swam back to Novastoshnah, leaving the gulls to scream. There he found that no one sympathized with him in his little attempt to discover a quiet place for the seals. They told him that men had always driven the holluschickie--it was part of the day’s work--and that if he did not like to see ugly things he should not have gone to the killing grounds. But none of the other seals had seen the killing, and that made the difference between him and his friends. Besides, Kotick was a white seal.
value.da: Kotick svømmede tilbage til Novastoshnah og lod mågerne skrige. Der var ingen, der bakkede op om hans søgen efter et fredeligt hjem for sælerne. Mænd havde altid drevet holluschickie, sagde de; det hørte til hverdagen. Hvis han ikke kunne lide forfærdelige syn, skulle han ikke have gået med til slagtepladserne. Men hans venner havde aldrig set drabene. Ingen af de andre sæler havde selv set deres venner blive dræbt. Den viden, som han alene havde, gjorde hele forskellen mellem Kotick og kammeraterne, der ikke ville forstå ham. Desuden var Kotick en hvid sæl.

value.en: “What you must do,” said old Sea Catch, after he had heard his son’s adventures, “is to grow up and be a big seal like your father, and have a nursery on the beach, and then they will leave you alone. In another five years you ought to be able to fight for yourself.” Even gentle Matkah, his mother, said: “You will never be able to stop the killing. Go and play in the sea, Kotick.” And Kotick went off and danced the Fire-dance with a very heavy little heart.
value.da: »Bliv en stor sæl som din far og få din egen yngleplads her,« sagde Sea Catch, efter at han havde hørt om hans oplevelser. »Så lader de dig være i fred. Om fem år burde du kunne kæmpe dine egne kampe.« Selv blide Matkah sagde: »Du kan ikke stoppe drabene. Gå ud og leg i vandet, Kotick.« Så Kotick svømmede ud i havet og var med i Ilddansen sammen med de andre, men mens han dansede, var hans lille hjerte frygtelig tungt.

value.en: That autumn he left the beach as soon as he could, and set off alone because of a notion in his bullet-head. He was going to find Sea Cow, if there was such a person in the sea, and he was going to find a quiet island with good firm beaches for seals to live on, where men could not get at them. So he explored and explored by himself from the North to the South Pacific, swimming as much as three hundred miles in a day and a night. He met with more adventures than can be told, and narrowly escaped being caught by the Basking Shark, and the Spotted Shark, and the Hammerhead, and he met all the untrustworthy ruffians that loaf up and down the seas, and the heavy polite fish, and the scarlet spotted scallops that are moored in one place for hundreds of years, and grow very proud of it; but he never met Sea Cow, and he never found an island that he could fancy.
value.da: Det efterår tog han af sted så tidligt som muligt, alene, med en idé i sit runde hoved. Han ville finde Sea Cow, hvis sådan et væsen fandtes, og en fredelig ø med faste strande uden for menneskers rækkevidde.
