Han søgte hele Stillehavet igennem fra nord til syd og svømmede nogle gange tre hundrede engelske mil på et døgn. Han udforskede og udforskede helt alene, fra det nordlige Stillehav og helt ned til de sydlige farvande. Der skete flere ting på de rejser, end der er plads til at fortælle her. Brugden, den plettede haj og hammerhajen var lige ved at få fat i ham. Han mødte de upålidelige slyngler, der strejfer rundt i havene, tunge, høflige fisk og skarlagenplettede kammuslinger, som har siddet fast samme sted i hundredvis af år og er umådelig stolte af det. Men på alle disse rejser mødte han aldrig Sea Cow og fandt aldrig en ø, som han kunne forestille sig som det hjem, han ønskede sig til sælerne.

value.en: If the beach was good and hard, with a slope behind it for seals to play on, there was always the smoke of a whaler on the horizon, boiling down blubber, and Kotick knew what that meant. Or else he could see that seals had once visited the island and been killed off, and Kotick knew that where men had come once they would come again.
value.da: Hver gang han fandt faste strande med skråninger til leg, var horisonten markeret af røgen fra en hvalfanger, hvor mænd kogte spæk. Kotick vidste præcis, hvad røgen betød, og forstod, hvorfor sådan en strand ikke kunne blive et tilflugtssted for sæler. Andre steder var der tegn på, at der havde boet sæler, som var blevet slagtet. Han vidste, at mænd, der én gang havde været der, ville komme igen.

value.en: He picked up with an old stumpy-tailed albatross, who told him that Kerguelen Island was the very place for peace and quiet, and when Kotick went down there he was all but smashed to pieces against some wicked black cliffs in a heavy sleet-storm with lightning and thunder. Yet as he pulled out against the gale he could see that even there had once been a seal nursery. And it was so in all the other islands that he visited.
value.da: En gammel korthalet albatros anbefalede Kerguelen som et fredens fristed. Kotick tog derhen, men var nær ved at smadre sig mod grumme sorte klipper i et sludvejr fuldt af torden og lyn. Mens han kæmpede sig tilbage mod stormen, så han, at selv dette sted engang havde haft sælynglepladser. Det samme nedslående syn mødte han på alle de andre øer, han besøgte: ingen af dem var det uberørte hjem, han ledte efter.

value.en: Limmershin gave a long list of them, for he said that Kotick spent five seasons exploring, with a four months’ rest each year at Novastoshnah, when the holluschickie used to make fun of him and his imaginary islands. He went to the Gallapagos, a horrid dry place on the Equator, where he was nearly baked to death; he went to the Georgia Islands, the Orkneys, Emerald Island, Little Nightingale Island, Gough’s Island, Bouvet’s Island, the Crossets, and even to a little speck of an island south of the Cape of Good Hope. But everywhere the People of the Sea told him the same things. Seals had come to those islands once upon a time, but men had killed them all off. Even when he swam thousands of miles out of the Pacific and got to a place called Cape Corrientes (that was when he was coming back from Gough’s Island), he found a few hundred mangy seals on a rock and they told him that men came there too.
value.da: Limmershin nævnte mange øer. Kotick ledte i fem sæsoner, sagde han, og hvilede hvert år fire måneder ved Novastoshnah, mens holluschickie gjorde nar af hans indbildte tilflugtssteder. På Galápagos, et frygteligt tørt sted ved Ækvator, blev han næsten stegt levende. Han besøgte Georgia-øerne, Orkneyøerne, Smaragdøen, Lille Nattergaleø, Goughøen, Bouvetøen, Crozetøerne og endda en lille ø syd for Kap det Gode Håb. På hvert af disse steder talte han med Havets Folk, og overalt fik han det samme nedslående svar: Sæler var engang kommet dertil, men mænd havde dræbt dem alle. På vej hjem fra Goughøen svømmede han tusinder af engelske mil ud over Stillehavet til Kap Corrientes. Selv dér trængtes nogle hundrede skabede sæler på en klippe og fortalte ham, at mænd kom forbi.

value.en: That nearly broke his heart, and he headed round the Horn back to his own beaches; and on his way north he hauled out on an island full of green trees, where he found an old, old seal who was dying, and Kotick caught fish for him and told him all his sorrows. “Now,” said Kotick, “I am going back to Novastoshnah, and if I am driven to the killing-pens with the holluschickie I shall not care.”
value.da: Næsten knust i hjertet svømmede han rundt om Kap Horn og satte kursen mod hjemmet. På vej nordpå gik han i land på en ø dækket af grønne træer. Dér fandt han en meget, meget gammel sæl, som var ved at dø. Kotick fangede fisk til ham og fortalte ham alt, hvad der havde gjort hans rejser så sørgelige. »Jeg tager tilbage til Novastoshnah,« sagde han. »Hvis de driver mig til slagtefoldene sammen med holluschickie, er jeg ligeglad.«

value.en: The old seal said, “Try once more. I am the last of the Lost Rookery of Masafuera, and in the days when men killed us by the hundred thousand there was a story on the beaches that some day a white seal would come out of the North and lead the seal people to a quiet place. I am old, and I shall never live to see that day, but others will. Try once more.”
value.da: Den gamle sæl sagde: »Prøv én gang til. Jeg er den sidste af den Tabte Yngleplads på Masafuera, og dengang mænd dræbte os i hundredtusindvis, var der en historie på strandene om, at en dag ville en hvid sæl komme fra nord og føre sælfolket til et fredeligt sted. Jeg er gammel og kommer aldrig til at leve at se den dag, men andre vil. Prøv én gang til.«

value.en: And Kotick curled up his mustache (it was a beauty) and said, “I am the only white seal that has ever been born on the beaches, and I am the only seal, black or white, who ever thought of looking for new islands.”
value.da: Og Kotick krøllede sine knurhår op (de var en pragt) og sagde: »Jeg er den eneste hvide sæl, der nogensinde er født på strandene, og jeg er den eneste sæl, sort eller hvid, der nogensinde har tænkt på at lede efter nye øer.«

value.en: This cheered him immensely; and when he came back to Novastoshnah that summer, Matkah, his mother, begged him to marry and settle down, for he was no longer a holluschick but a full-grown sea-catch, with a curly white mane on his shoulders, as heavy, as big, and as fierce as his father. “Give me another season,” he said. “Remember, Mother, it is always the seventh wave that goes farthest up the beach.”
value.da: Tanken gav ham stort mod. Da han den sommer kom tilbage til Novastoshnah, bad Matkah ham om at gifte sig og slå sig ned. Han var ikke længere en ungkarl, men en fuldvoksen hansæl med krøllet hvid manke, lige så tung, stor og vild som sin far. »Giv mig endnu en sæson,« svarede han. »Husk, mor: den syvende bølge når altid længst op ad stranden.«

value.en: Curiously enough, there was another seal who thought that she would put off marrying till the next year, and Kotick danced the Fire-dance with her all down Lukannon Beach the night before he set off on his last exploration. This time he went westward, because he had fallen on the trail of a great shoal of halibut, and he needed at least one hundred pounds of fish a day to keep him in good condition. He chased them till he was tired, and then he curled himself up and went to sleep on the hollows of the ground swell that sets in to Copper Island. He knew the coast perfectly well, so about midnight, when he felt himself gently bumped on a weed-bed, he said, “Hm, tide’s running strong tonight,” and turning over under water opened his eyes slowly and stretched. Then he jumped like a cat, for he saw huge things nosing about in the shoal water and browsing on the heavy fringes of the weeds.
value.da: Det skete, at en anden sæl også besluttede at vente et år med at gifte sig. Aftenen før sin sidste rejse dansede Kotick Ilddansen ved siden af hende langs Lukannon-stranden. Denne gang satte han kursen mod vest efter en kæmpestime helleflynder. For at holde sig i form skulle han bruge mindst 45 kilo fisk om dagen. Han jagtede fiskene, til han var træt, og krøllede sig så sammen for at sove. Den lange dønning, der rullede mod Kobberøen, bar ham med sig i sine dale, mens han hvilede. Han kendte denne kyst godt. Omkring midnat mærkede han et blidt stød mod noget tang og mumlede: »Hm, stærk strøm i nat.« Han rullede rundt under vandet, åbnede langsomt øjnene og strakte sig. Så sprang han som en kat: enorme væsener nosede rundt i det lave vand og græssede på tykke frynser af tang.

value: Limmershin listed many islands. Kotick searched for five seasons, he said, resting four months yearly at Novastoshnah while the holluschickie mocked his imaginary refuges. At the Gallapagos, a dreadful dry place on the Equator, he nearly roasted alive. He visited the Georgia Islands, the Orkneys, Emerald Island, Little Nightingale Island, Gough’s Island, Bouvet’s Island, the Crossets, and even a tiny island south of the Cape of Good Hope. At every one of these places he spoke with the People of the Sea, and everywhere they gave him the same discouraging answer: seals had once come, but men killed them all. Returning from Gough’s Island, he swam thousands of miles beyond the Pacific to Cape Corrientes. Even there, a few hundred mangy seals crowded a rock and told him men visited.

value.en: “By the Great Combers of Magellan!” he said, beneath his mustache. “Who in the Deep Sea are these people?”
value.da: »Ved Magellans Store Brændinger!« mumlede han ind i knurhårene. »Hvem i det Dybe Hav er de her skabninger?«

value.en: They were like no walrus, sea lion, seal, bear, whale, shark, fish, squid, or scallop that Kotick had ever seen before. They were between twenty and thirty feet long, and they had no hind flippers, but a shovel-like tail that looked as if it had been whittled out of wet leather. Their heads were the most foolish-looking things you ever saw, and they balanced on the ends of their tails in deep water when they weren’t grazing, bowing solemnly to each other and waving their front flippers as a fat man waves his arm.
value.da: De lignede ingen hvalros, søløve, sæl, bjørn, hval, haj, fisk, blæksprutte eller kammusling, han kendte. De var seks til ni meter lange og havde ingen baglufser. Deres skovlformede haler så ud, som om de var skåret ud af vådt læder. Deres hoveder var det mest fjollede, man nogensinde kunne håbe at se i havet. Når de ikke græssede, balancerede de på halerne i dybere vand, bukkede højtideligt og viftede med forluffene, som tykke mænd vifter med armene.

value.en: “Ahem!” said Kotick. “Good sport, gentlemen?” The big things answered by bowing and waving their flippers like the Frog Footman. When they began feeding again Kotick saw that their upper lip was split into two pieces that they could twitch apart about a foot and bring together again with a whole bushel of seaweed between the splits. They tucked the stuff into their mouths and chumped solemnly.
value.da: »Hm!« sagde Kotick. »God fangst, mine herrer?« De bukkede og viftede som Frølakajen. Da de gik i gang med at æde igen, så han, at deres overlæber var delt i to halvdele, som kunne åbnes omkring tredive centimeter fra hinanden og så lukkes om en hel skæppe tang. De stoppede de store bundter tang i munden og tyggede videre, lige så højtideligt, som om det at æde var en meget alvorlig sag.

value.en: “Messy style of feeding, that,” said Kotick. They bowed again, and Kotick began to lose his temper. “Very good,” he said. “If you do happen to have an extra joint in your front flipper you needn’t show off so. I see you bow gracefully, but I should like to know your names.” The split lips moved and twitched; and the glassy green eyes stared, but they did not speak.
value.da: »En rodet måde at spise på,« sagde Kotick. De bukkede mere, og hans tålmodighed blev sat på prøve. »Nå, godt. Et ekstra led i forluffene er ikke nogen grund til at brase sig. Jeg indrømmer, at I bukker elegant, men hvad hedder I?« Deres delte læber trak sig, de glasagtige grønne øjne stirrede, og der kom ikke noget svar.

value.en: “Well!” said Kotick. “You’re the only people I’ve ever met uglier than Sea Vitch--and with worse manners.”
value.da: »Nå!« sagde Kotick. »I er de eneste folk, jeg nogensinde har mødt, der er grimmere end Sea Vitch — og med værre manerer.«

value.en: Then he remembered in a flash what the Burgomaster gull had screamed to him when he was a little yearling at Walrus Islet, and he tumbled backward in the water, for he knew that he had found Sea Cow at last.
value.da: Pludselig huskede han, hvad borgmestermågen havde skreget, dengang han var etårig ved Hvalrosholmen. Han tumlede overrasket baglæns i vandet, for han forstod, at han endelig havde fundet Sea Cow.

value.en: The sea cows went on schlooping and grazing and chumping in the weed, and Kotick asked them questions in every language that he had picked up in his travels; and the Sea People talk nearly as many languages as human beings. But the sea cows did not answer because Sea Cow cannot talk. He has only six bones in his neck where he ought to have seven, and they say under the sea that that prevents him from speaking even to his companions. But, as you know, he has an extra joint in his foreflipper, and by waving it up and down and about he makes what answers to a sort of clumsy telegraphic code.
value.da: Søkøerne blev ved med at slubre og tygge tang, mens Kotick prøvede alle de sprog, han havde lært på sine rejser. Han havde samlet mange sprog op, for Havets Folk har næsten lige så mange måder at tale på som mennesker. Men Sea Cow kan ikke tale. Hans hals har seks knogler i stedet for syv, og under havet siger man, at det gør ham ude af stand til at tale, selv med sine kammerater. Men som du ved, har hans forluffe et ekstra led. Ved at vifte med den op, ned og rundt giver han besked på en klodset slags telegrafkode.

value.en: By daylight Kotick’s mane was standing on end and his temper was gone where the dead crabs go. Then the Sea Cow began to travel northward very slowly, stopping to hold absurd bowing councils from time to time, and Kotick followed them, saying to himself, “People who are such idiots as these are would have been killed long ago if they hadn’t found out some safe island. And what is good enough for the Sea Cow is good enough for the Sea Catch. All the same, I wish they’d hurry.”
value.da: Ved daggry stod Koticks manke ret op, og hans tålmodighed var gået dér, hvor døde krabber går hen. Søkøerne svømmede langsomt mod nord og stoppede af og til for at holde latterlige bukkemøder. Kotick fulgte tålmodigt efter, i hvert fald udadtil, og mens han så på de højtidelige buk, sagde han til sig selv: »Sådan nogle idioter var blevet dræbt for længe siden, hvis de ikke kendte en sikker ø. Et sted, der er godt nok til Sea Cow, er godt nok til Sea Catch. Men jeg ville ønske, de ville skynde sig.«

value.en: It was weary work for Kotick. The herd never went more than forty or fifty miles a day, and stopped to feed at night, and kept close to the shore all the time; while Kotick swam round them, and over them, and under them, but he could not hurry them up one-half mile. As they went farther north they held a bowing council every few hours, and Kotick nearly bit off his mustache with impatience till he saw that they were following up a warm current of water, and then he respected them more.
value.da: Det var udmattende at følge dem. De kom kun fyrre eller halvtreds engelske mil om dagen, holdt sig tæt ind til kysten og stoppede om natten for at æde. Kotick svømmede rundt om dem, over dem og under dem, men fik dem ikke til at gå en halv engelsk mil hurtigere. Længere mod nord holdt de bukkemøder med få timers mellemrum. Han var lige ved at bide sit knurhår over af frustration, indtil han opdagede, at de fulgte en varm strøm. Da han forstod det, fik han en del mere respekt for dem.

value.en: One night they sank through the shiny water--sank like stones--and for the first time since he had known them began to swim quickly. Kotick followed, and the pace astonished him, for he never dreamed that Sea Cow was anything of a swimmer. They headed for a cliff by the shore--a cliff that ran down into deep water, and plunged into a dark hole at the foot of it, twenty fathoms under the sea. It was a long, long swim, and Kotick badly wanted fresh air before he was out of the dark tunnel they led him through.
value.da: En nat sank de som sten gennem det glimtende vand og begyndte for første gang at svømme hurtigt. Kotick fulgte efter, forbløffet: han havde aldrig forestillet sig, at Sea Cow kunne svømme godt. De nærmede sig en klint ved kysten, der stupte ned i dybt vand, og svømmede ind i et mørkt hul tyve favne under overfladen. De førte ham gennem en mørk undersøisk tunnel, og det var, som om svømmeturen tog meget, meget lang tid. Før han kom ud af mørket, trængte Kotick desperat til at trække vejret igen.

value.en: “My wig!” he said, when he rose, gasping and puffing, into open water at the farther end. “It was a long dive, but it was worth it.”
value.da: »Min paryk!« sagde han, da han steg op gispende og pustende i åbent vand i den anden ende. »Det var et langt dyk, men det var det værd.«

value.en: The sea cows had separated and were browsing lazily along the edges of the finest beaches that Kotick had ever seen. There were long stretches of smooth-worn rock running for miles, exactly fitted to make seal-nurseries, and there were play-grounds of hard sand sloping inland behind them, and there were rollers for seals to dance in, and long grass to roll in, and sand dunes to climb up and down, and, best of all, Kotick knew by the feel of the water, which never deceives a true sea catch, that no men had ever come there.
value.da: Søkøerne havde spredt sig for at græsse dovent ved siden af de fineste strande, han nogensinde havde set. Glat klippe strakte sig i mange engelske mil, perfekt til sælynglepladser. Bagved lå faste, sandede legepladser, der skrånede ind i landet. Der var store rullende bølger, hvor sæler kunne danse, lange stræk med græs, hvor de kunne rulle rundt, og sandklitter at kravle op og ned ad. Og bedst af alt: vandets fornemmelse, som aldrig snyder en ægte hansæl, fortalte Kotick, at intet menneske nogensinde havde været her.

value.en: The first thing he did was to assure himself that the fishing was good, and then he swam along the beaches and counted up the delightful low sandy islands half hidden in the beautiful rolling fog. Away to the northward, out to sea, ran a line of bars and shoals and rocks that would never let a ship come within six miles of the beach, and between the islands and the mainland was a stretch of deep water that ran up to the perpendicular cliffs, and somewhere below the cliffs was the mouth of the tunnel.
value.da: Før han gjorde andet, sikrede han sig, at fiskeriet var godt i disse farvande, og at der ville være masser af mad til sælerne. Så svømmede han langs kysterne og talte dejlige lave sandøer, der var halvt skjult af smuk, drivende tåge. Mod nord ville en kæde af sandbanker, grunde og klipper holde skibe mindst seks engelske mil fra strandene. Mellem fastlandet og øerne gik dybt vand helt ind til de lodrette klipper. Et sted under dem lå tunnelens indgang.

value.en: “It’s Novastoshnah over again, but ten times better,” said Kotick. “Sea Cow must be wiser than I thought. Men can’t come down the cliffs, even if there were any men; and the shoals to seaward would knock a ship to splinters. If any place in the sea is safe, this is it.”
value.da: »Endnu et Novastoshnah, bare ti gange bedre,« sagde Kotick. »Sea Cow er klogere, end jeg troede. Selv hvis mænd boede her, kunne de ikke komme ned ad de klipper. Grundene ud for kysten ville smadre deres skibe. Hvis noget sted i havet er sikkert, er det her.«

value.en: He began to think of the seal he had left behind him, but though he was in a hurry to go back to Novastoshnah, he thoroughly explored the new country, so that he would be able to answer all questions.
value.da: Han begyndte at tænke på den sæl, han havde efterladt, og selvom han havde travlt med at komme tilbage til Novastoshnah, udforskede han grundigt det nye land, så han ville være i stand til at besvare alle spørgsmål.

value.en: Then he dived and made sure of the mouth of the tunnel, and raced through to the southward. No one but a sea cow or a seal would have dreamed of there being such a place, and when he looked back at the cliffs even Kotick could hardly believe that he had been under them.
value.da: Så dykkede han og forvissede sig om tunnelens munding, og fór gennem den mod syd. Ingen anden end en søko eller en sæl ville have drømt om, at der var sådan et sted, og da han så tilbage på klipperne, kunne selv Kotick næsten ikke tro, at han havde været under dem.

value.en: He was six days going home, though he was not swimming slowly; and when he hauled out just above Sea Lion’s Neck the first person he met was the seal who had been waiting for him, and she saw by the look in his eyes that he had found his island at last.
value.da: Trods sin fart tog det ham seks dage at komme hjem. Han gik i land oven for Søløvehalsen og mødte straks sælen, der havde ventet på ham. Hun så ham i øjnene og vidste med det samme, uden at vente på hans historie, at han havde fundet den ø, han havde ledt efter.

value.en: But the holluschickie and Sea Catch, his father, and all the other seals laughed at him when he told them what he had discovered, and a young seal about his own age said, “This is all very well, Kotick, but you can’t come from no one knows where and order us off like this. Remember we’ve been fighting for our nurseries, and that’s a thing you never did. You preferred prowling about in the sea.”
value.da: Men hans far Sea Catch, holluschickie og alle de andre sæler lo ad ham, da han fortalte dem om alt, hvad han havde opdaget. En ung hansæl på omtrent hans egen alder indvendte: »Det er alt sammen meget fint, Kotick, men du kan ikke komme farende fra Gud ved hvor og kommandere os væk. Vi har kæmpet for vores ynglepladser, og det har du aldrig gidet. Du foretrak at strejfe rundt i havet.«

value.en: The other seals laughed at this, and the young seal began twisting his head from side to side. He had just married that year, and was making a great fuss about it.
value.da: De andre lo, og den unge hansæl drejede hovedet fra side til side. Han var nygift det år og regnede det for en overordentlig vigtig bedrift.

value.en: “I’ve no nursery to fight for,” said Kotick. “I only want to show you all a place where you will be safe. What’s the use of fighting?”
value.da: »Jeg har ingen yngleplads, der er værd at slås om,« svarede Kotick. »Jeg vil vise alle et sted, hvor man kan leve i sikkerhed. Hvorfor skulle det kræve en kamp?«

value: “I have no nursery worth fighting over,” Kotick replied. “I want to show everyone a safe place to live. Why should that require a fight?”

value.en: “Oh, if you’re trying to back out, of course I’ve no more to say,” said the young seal with an ugly chuckle.
value.da: »Åh, hvis du leder efter en undskyldning for at trække dig, har jeg ikke mere at sige,« fnisede den unge sæl ondskabsfuldt.

value.en: “Will you come with me if I win?” said Kotick. And a green light came into his eye, for he was very angry at having to fight at all.
value.da: »Hvis jeg slår dig, kommer du så med?« spurgte Kotick. Der blinkede grønt i hans øjne; det gjorde ham rasende at blive tvunget til at slås.

value.en: “Very good,” said the young seal carelessly. “If you win, I’ll come.”
value.da: »Udmærket,« sagde den unge sæl skødesløst. »Hvis du vinder, kommer jeg med.«

value.en: He had no time to change his mind, for Kotick’s head was out and his teeth sunk in the blubber of the young seal’s neck. Then he threw himself back on his haunches and hauled his enemy down the beach, shook him, and knocked him over. Then Kotick roared to the seals: “I’ve done my best for you these five seasons past. I’ve found you the island where you’ll be safe, but unless your heads are dragged off your silly necks you won’t believe. I’m going to teach you now. Look out for yourselves!”
value.da: Før den unge nåede at skifte mening, skød Kotick frem og borede tænderne ind i spækket om hans hals. Han stemte fra på bagkroppen, slæbte ham ned ad stranden, rystede ham og væltede ham. Så brølede han til de andre: »Jeg har arbejdet for jer i fem sæsoner. Jeg har fundet en ø, hvor I vil være i sikkerhed. Men medmindre nogen river hovederne af jeres tåbelige halse, tror I ikke på det. Nu skal jeg lære jer det. Pas på!«

value.en: Limmershin told me that never in his life--and Limmershin sees ten thousand big seals fighting every year--never in all his little life did he see anything like Kotick’s charge into the nurseries. He flung himself at the biggest sea catch he could find, caught him by the throat, choked him and bumped him and banged him till he grunted for mercy, and then threw him aside and attacked the next. You see, Kotick had never fasted for four months as the big seals did every year, and his deep-sea swimming trips kept him in perfect condition, and, best of all, he had never fought before. His curly white mane stood up with rage, and his eyes flamed, and his big dog teeth glistened, and he was splendid to look at. Old Sea Catch, his father, saw him tearing past, hauling the grizzled old seals about as though they had been halibut, and upsetting the young bachelors in all directions; and Sea Catch gave a roar and shouted: “He may be a fool, but he is the best fighter on the beaches! Don’t tackle your father, my son! He’s with you!”
value.da: Limmershin ser hvert år ti tusind store sæler kæmpe. Men aldrig i sit lille liv, fortalte han mig, havde han set noget som det angreb, Kotick gik til, da han kastede sig lige ind i de overfyldte ynglepladser. Kotick kastede sig over den største hansæl, han kunne finde, greb ham om struben, kvalte, slog og bankede ham, til han bad om nåde, og smed ham så til side og angreb den næste. Kotick havde aldrig fastet i fire måneder hvert år som de store sæler. Rejserne over havet holdt ham i topform, og, bedst af alt, havde han aldrig kæmpet før. Hans hvide krøller stod stift af raseri, øjnene flammede, og de lange tænder blinkede: et storslået syn. Sea Catch så sin søn slæbe rundt på gråsprængte gamle sæler som helleflyndere og sprede unge ungkarle til alle sider. Han brølede: »Han er måske en tåbe, men ingen sæl kæmper bedre! Skån din far, søn! Jeg er på din side!«

value.en: Kotick roared in answer, and old Sea Catch waddled in with his mustache on end, blowing like a locomotive, while Matkah and the seal that was going to marry Kotick cowered down and admired their men-folk. It was a gorgeous fight, for the two fought as long as there was a seal that dared lift up his head, and when there were none they paraded grandly up and down the beach side by side, bellowing.
value.da: Kotick brølede igen. Sea Catch vraltede ind i kampen med strittende knurhår og pustede som et lokomotiv. Matkah og sælen, der skulle blive Koticks kone, dukkede sig sammen og beundrede deres mandfolk. Det var en pragtfuld kamp at se på, for begge kæmpede deres allerbedste. Far og søn blev ved, til ingen sæl turde løfte hovedet. Så marcherede de side om side langs stranden og brølede storslået.

value.en: At night, just as the Northern Lights were winking and flashing through the fog, Kotick climbed a bare rock and looked down on the scattered nurseries and the torn and bleeding seals. “Now,” he said, “I’ve taught you your lesson.”
value.da: Den nat, mens nordlyset flimrede gennem tågen, kravlede Kotick op på en bar klippe. Under ham lå de spredte ynglepladser og de blødende, forslåede sæler. »Nu,« erklærede han, »har I fået jeres lektie.«

value.en: “My wig!” said old Sea Catch, boosting himself up stiffly, for he was fearfully mauled. “The Killer Whale himself could not have cut them up worse. Son, I’m proud of you, and what’s more, I’ll come with you to your island--if there is such a place.”
value.da: »Min paryk!« sagde gamle Sea Catch og hjalp sig stivt op, for han var frygteligt forslået. »Spækhuggeren selv kunne ikke have skåret dem værre i stykker. Søn, jeg er stolt af dig, og hvad mere er, jeg kommer med dig til din ø — hvis der er sådan et sted.«

value.en: “Hear you, fat pigs of the sea. Who comes with me to the Sea Cow’s tunnel? Answer, or I shall teach you again,” roared Kotick.
value.da: »Hør mig, fede havsvin. Hvem kommer med mig til Sea Cows tunnel? Svar, ellers lærer jeg jer det igen,« brølede Kotick.

value.en: There was a murmur like the ripple of the tide all up and down the beaches. “We will come,” said thousands of tired voices. “We will follow Kotick, the White Seal.”
value.da: Der var en mumlen som tidevandets krusning op og ned ad strandene. »Vi kommer,« sagde tusinder af trætte stemmer. »Vi følger Kotick, Den Hvide Sæl.«

value.en: Then Kotick dropped his head between his shoulders and shut his eyes proudly. He was not a white seal any more, but red from head to tail. All the same he would have scorned to look at or touch one of his wounds.
value.da: Så lod Kotick hovedet falde mellem skuldrene og lukkede stolt øjnene. Han var ikke længere en hvid sæl, men rød fra hoved til hale. Alligevel ville han have foragtet at se på eller røre ved noget af sine sår.

value.en: A week later he and his army (nearly ten thousand holluschickie and old seals) went away north to the Sea Cow’s tunnel, Kotick leading them, and the seals that stayed at Novastoshnah called them idiots. But next spring, when they all met off the fishing banks of the Pacific, Kotick’s seals told such tales of the new beaches beyond Sea Cow’s tunnel that more and more seals left Novastoshnah. Of course it was not all done at once, for the seals are not very clever, and they need a long time to turn things over in their minds, but year after year more seals went away from Novastoshnah, and Lukannon, and the other nurseries, to the quiet, sheltered beaches where Kotick sits all the summer through, getting bigger and fatter and stronger each year, while the holluschickie play around him, in that sea where no man comes.
value.da: En uge senere førte han sin hær nordpå: næsten ti tusind holluschickie og ældre sæler på vej til Sea Cows tunnel. De, der blev tilbage ved Novastoshnah, kaldte dem tåber. Men da de mødtes igen ved Stillehavets fiskebanker næste forår, beskrev de rejsende deres nye strande så vidunderligt, at flere og flere forlod Novastoshnah. Det skete selvfølgelig ikke i løbet af én sæson eller på én gang, for det var langsomt arbejde at ændre vanerne hos så mange sæler. Sæler er ikke særlig kloge og tænker langsomt. Men år efter år forlod flere Novastoshnah, Lukannon og de andre ynglepladser for de fredelige, beskyttede strande. Dér tilbringer Kotick hver sommer og bliver større, federe og stærkere for hvert år, mens holluschickie leger rundt om ham i hav, som mænd aldrig har rørt.

value.en: Lukannon
value.da: Lukannon

value.en: This is the great deep-sea song that all the St. Paul seals sing when they are heading back to their beaches in the summer. It is a sort of very sad seal National Anthem.
value.da: Det er den store havsang, som alle sælerne på St. Paul synger, når de vender tilbage til deres sommerstrande. Den er en slags nationalsang for sælerne, og en meget sørgelig en.

value.en: I met my mates in the morning (and, oh, but I am old!) Where roaring on the ledges the summer ground-swell rolled; I heard them lift the chorus that drowned the breakers’ song— The Beaches of Lukannon—two million voices strong.
value.da: Jeg mødte mine fæller om morgenen (og åh, hvor er jeg gammel!), hvor sommerens dønning rullede brølende ind over klippehylderne; jeg hørte dem synge med i koret, der overdøvede brændingens sang — Lukannons Strande — to millioner stemmer stærkt.

value.en:
_The song of pleasant stations beside the salt lagoons,
The song of blowing squadrons that shuffled down the dunes,
The song of midnight dances that churned the sea to flame—
The Beaches of Lukannon—before the sealers came!_
value.da:
_Sangen om hyggelige hjem ved saltlagunerne,
sangen om de prustende eskadroner, der slæbte sig ned ad klitterne,
sangen om midnatsdansene, der pidskede havet til flammer —
Lukannons Strande — før sæljægerne kom!_

value.en: I met my mates in the morning (I’ll never meet them more!); They came and went in legions that darkened all the shore. And o’er the foam-flecked offing as far as voice could reach We hailed the landing-parties and we sang them up the beach.
value.da: Jeg mødte mine fæller om morgenen (jeg møder dem aldrig mere!); de kom og gik i legioner, så de mørklagde hele kysten. Og over det skumplettede vand, så langt stemmen kunne række, hilste vi landgangsholdene og sang dem op ad stranden.

value.en:
_The Beaches of Lukannon—the winter wheat so tall—
The dripping, crinkled lichens, and the sea-fog drenching all!
The platforms of our playground, all shining smooth and worn!
The Beaches of Lukannon—the home where we were born!_
value.da:
_Lukannons Strande — den høje vinterhvede —
de dryppende, rynkede laver og havtågen, der gennemvæder alt!
Vores legepladsers platforme, skinnende glatte og slidte!
Lukannons Strande — det hjem, hvor vi blev født!_

value.en: I met my mates in the morning, a broken, scattered band. Men shoot us in the water and club us on the land; Men drive us to the Salt House like silly sheep and tame, And still we sing Lukannon—before the sealers came.
value.da: Jeg mødte mine fæller om morgenen, en knust, spredt flok. Mænd skyder os i vandet og klubber os på landet; mænd driver os til Salthuset som dumme, tamme får, og alligevel synger vi om Lukannon — før sæljægerne kom.

value.en:
_Wheel down, wheel down to southward; oh, Gooverooska, go!
And tell the Deep-Sea Viceroys the story of our woe;
Ere, empty as the shark’s egg the tempest flings ashore,
The Beaches of Lukannon shall know their sons no more!_
value.da:
_Drej ned, drej ned mod syd; åh, Gooverooska, drag af sted!
Og fortæl Dybhavets vicekonger historien om vores sorg;
Før, tomme som hajens æg, som stormen kaster i land,
skal Lukannons Strande ikke længere kende deres sønner!_

value.en:
At the hole where he went in
Red-Eye called to Wrinkle-Skin.
Hear what little Red-Eye saith:
“Nag, come up and dance with death!”
value.da:
Ved hullet, hvor han gik ind,
råbte Rødøje på Rynkehud.
Hør, hvad lille Rødøje siger:
»Nag, kom op og dans med døden!«

value.en:
Eye to eye and head to head,
(_Keep the measure, Nag._)
This shall end when one is dead;
(_At thy pleasure, Nag._)
Turn for turn and twist for twist—
(_Run and hide thee, Nag._)
Hah! The hooded Death has missed!
(_Woe betide thee, Nag!_)
value.da:
Øje mod øje og hoved mod hoved,
(_Hold takten, Nag._)
Dette skal ende, når én er død;
(_Som du behager, Nag._)
Drej for drej og vrid for vrid —
(_Løb og skjul dig, Nag._)
Hah! Den hættede Død ramte ved siden af!
(_Ve dig, Nag!_)

value.en: This is the story of the great war that Rikki-tikki-tavi fought single-handed, through the bath-rooms of the big bungalow in Segowlee cantonment. Darzee, the Tailorbird, helped him, and Chuchundra, the muskrat, who never comes out into the middle of the floor, but always creeps round by the wall, gave him advice, but Rikki-tikki did the real fighting.
value.da: Her er historien om den store krig, som Rikki-tikki-tavi næsten helt alene udkæmpede gennem badeværelserne i en stor bungalow i garnisonsbyen Segowlee. Darzee, skrædderfuglen, hjalp ham, og moskusrotten Chuchundra kom med gode råd. Chuchundra lister altid langs væggen og tør aldrig gå ud midt på gulvet. Men selve kampen måtte Rikki-tikki klare.

value.en: He was a mongoose, rather like a little cat in his fur and his tail, but quite like a weasel in his head and his habits. His eyes and the end of his restless nose were pink. He could scratch himself anywhere he pleased with any leg, front or back, that he chose to use. He could fluff up his tail till it looked like a bottle brush, and his war cry as he scuttled through the long grass was: “Rikk-tikk-tikki-tikki-tchk!”
value.da: Han var en mangust, med pels og hale lidt som en lille kats, men med en væsels hoved og vaner. Hans øjne var lyserøde, og det samme var spidsen af hans næse, som aldrig holdt stille. Han kunne klø sig, hvor han ville, med hvilket som helst af sine fire ben. Han kunne pjuske halen ud som en flaskebørste, og når han fór gennem det høje græs, lød hans krigsråb: »Rikk-tikk-tikki-tikki-tchk!«

value.en: One day, a high summer flood washed him out of the burrow where he lived with his father and mother, and carried him, kicking and clucking, down a roadside ditch. He found a little wisp of grass floating there, and clung to it till he lost his senses. When he revived, he was lying in the hot sun on the middle of a garden path, very draggled indeed, and a small boy was saying, “Here’s a dead mongoose. Let’s have a funeral.”
value.da: En sommerflod skyllede ham ud af hulen, hvor han boede sammen med sin far og mor, og bar ham sparkende og klukkende ned ad en vejgrøft. Han fik fat i en lille tot flydende græs og klamrede sig til den, til han besvimede. Da han vågnede, lå han våd og forpjusket i den varme sol midt på en havegang, og en lille dreng sagde: »Her er en død mangust. Lad os holde begravelse.«

value.en: “No,” said his mother, “let’s take him in and dry him. Perhaps he isn’t really dead.”
value.da: »Nej,« sagde hans mor, »lad os tage ham med ind og tørre ham. Måske er han ikke rigtig død.«

value.en: They took him into the house, and a big man picked him up between his finger and thumb and said he was not dead but half choked. So they wrapped him in cotton wool, and warmed him over a little fire, and he opened his eyes and sneezed.
value.da: De tog ham med ind i huset, og en stor mand løftede ham op mellem finger og tommel og sagde, at han ikke var død, men halvt kvalt. Så svøbte de ham i vat og varmede ham over en lille ild, og han åbnede øjnene og nyste.

value.en: “Now,” said the big man (he was an Englishman who had just moved into the bungalow), “don’t frighten him, and we’ll see what he’ll do.”
value.da: »Nu,« sagde den store mand (han var en englænder, der lige var flyttet ind i bungalowen), »skræm ham ikke, så ser vi, hvad han vil gøre.«

value.en: It is the hardest thing in the world to frighten a mongoose, because he is eaten up from nose to tail with curiosity. The motto of all the mongoose family is “Run and find out,” and Rikki-tikki was a true mongoose. He looked at the cotton wool, decided that it was not good to eat, ran all round the table, sat up and put his fur in order, scratched himself, and jumped on the small boy’s shoulder.
value.da: Det er næsten umuligt at skræmme en mangust, for han er fuld af nysgerrighed fra snude til hale. »Løb og find ud af det« er hele mangustfamiliens motto, og Rikki-tikki var en ægte mangust. Han kiggede nøje på vattet og besluttede, at det bestemt ikke var noget, man kunne spise. Så løb han rundt om bordet, satte sig op og redte sin pels, kløede sig og sprang op på drengens skulder.

value.en: “Don’t be frightened, Teddy,” said his father. “That’s his way of making friends.”
value.da: »Vær ikke bange, Teddy,« sagde hans far. »Det er hans måde at få venner på.«

value.en: “Ouch! He’s tickling under my chin,” said Teddy.
value.da: »Av! Han kilder mig under hagen,« sagde Teddy.

value.en: Rikki-tikki looked down between the boy’s collar and neck, snuffed at his ear, and climbed down to the floor, where he sat rubbing his nose.
value.da: Rikki-tikki kiggede ind mellem drengens krave og hals, snusede til hans øre og klatrede ned på gulvet, hvor han blev siddende og gned sig på næsen.

value.en: “Good gracious,” said Teddy’s mother, “and that’s a wild creature! I suppose he’s so tame because we’ve been kind to him.”
value.da: »Du milde,« sagde Teddys mor, »et vildt dyr, der opfører sig sådan! Han er vist blevet tam, fordi vi har været venlige mod ham.«

value.en: “All mongooses are like that,” said her husband. “If Teddy doesn’t pick him up by the tail, or try to put him in a cage, he’ll run in and out of the house all day long. Let’s give him something to eat.”
value.da: »Alle mangoster er sådan,« sagde hendes mand. »Hvis Teddy ikke tager fat i halen på ham eller spærrer ham inde i et bur, vil han løbe ind og ud af huset hele dagen. Vi skal give ham noget at spise.«

value.en: They gave him a little piece of raw meat. Rikki-tikki liked it immensely, and when it was finished he went out into the veranda and sat in the sunshine and fluffed up his fur to make it dry to the roots. Then he felt better.
value.da: De gav ham et lille stykke råt kød. Det smagte Rikki-tikki fremragende, og bagefter gik han ud på verandaen, satte sig i solskinnet og pjuskede pelsen op, så den kunne tørre helt ind til rødderne. Så havde han det bedre.

value.en: “There are more things to find out about in this house,” he said to himself, “than all my family could find out in all their lives. I shall certainly stay and find out.”
value.da: »Der er flere ting at undersøge i dette hus,« tænkte han, »end hele min familie ville nå at opdage i hele deres liv. Jeg bliver her og finder ud af det hele.«

value.en: He spent all that day roaming over the house. He nearly drowned himself in the bath-tubs, put his nose into the ink on a writing table, and burned it on the end of the big man’s cigar, for he climbed up in the big man’s lap to see how writing was done. At nightfall he ran into Teddy’s nursery to watch how kerosene lamps were lighted, and when Teddy went to bed Rikki-tikki climbed up too. But he was a restless companion, because he had to get up and attend to every noise all through the night, and find out what made it. Teddy’s mother and father came in, the last thing, to look at their boy, and Rikki-tikki was awake on the pillow. “I don’t like that,” said Teddy’s mother. “He may bite the child.” “He’ll do no such thing,” said the father. “Teddy’s safer with that little beast than if he had a bloodhound to watch him. If a snake came into the nursery now--”
value.da: Hele dagen strejfede han rundt og undersøgte huset. Han var lige ved at drukne i badekarrene, stak næsen ned i blækket på skrivebordet og brændte den på den store mands cigar, da han var klatret op på hans skød for at se, hvordan man skrev. Ved aftenstid løb han ind på Teddys børneværelse for at se, hvordan man tændte petroleumslamperne. Da Teddy gik i seng, krøb Rikki-tikki op til ham. Han var en urolig sengekammerat, for hver eneste lyd fik ham op for at finde ud af, hvad der lavede den. Teddys mor og far kiggede ind til drengen en sidste gang, og Rikki-tikki lå vågen på puden. »Det kan jeg ikke lide,« sagde Teddys mor. »Han kan komme til at bide barnet.« »Slet ikke,« sagde faren. »Teddy er tryggere ved det lille dyr, end hvis vi havde en blodhund til at passe på ham. Hvis en slange nu kom ind på børneværelset —«

value.en: But Teddy’s mother wouldn’t think of anything so awful.
value.da: Men Teddys mor ville slet ikke tænke på noget så skrækkeligt.

value.en: Early in the morning Rikki-tikki came to early breakfast in the veranda riding on Teddy’s shoulder, and they gave him banana and some boiled egg. He sat on all their laps one after the other, because every well-brought-up mongoose always hopes to be a house mongoose some day and have rooms to run about in; and Rikki-tikki’s mother (she used to live in the general’s house at Segowlee) had carefully told Rikki what to do if ever he came across white men.
value.da: Tidligt næste morgen red han på Teddys skulder ud til morgenmad på verandaen, hvor han fik banan og kogt æg. Han sad på alles skød efter tur. Enhver velopdragen mangust håber en dag at blive husmangust med værelser at løbe rundt i. Rikki-tikkis mor, der havde boet i generalens hus i Segowlee, havde omhyggeligt lært ham, hvordan han skulle opføre sig, hvis han mødte hvide mænd.

value.en: Then Rikki-tikki went out into the garden to see what was to be seen. It was a large garden, only half cultivated, with bushes, as big as summer-houses, of Marshal Niel roses, lime and orange trees, clumps of bamboos, and thickets of high grass. Rikki-tikki licked his lips. “This is a splendid hunting-ground,” he said, and his tail grew bottle-brushy at the thought of it, and he scuttled up and down the garden, snuffing here and there till he heard very sorrowful voices in a thorn-bush.
value.da: Bagefter udforskede han haven. Den var stor, men kun halvdelen var dyrket. Der var Marshal Niel-rosenbuske, store som lysthuse, lime- og appelsintræer, klumper af bambus og krat af højt græs. Rikki-tikki slikkede sig om munden. »Sikke et dejligt jagtområde,« sagde han, og halen svulmede op som en flaskebørste. Han fór rundt og snusede overalt, indtil han hørte sørgmodige stemmer fra en tornebusk.

value.en: It was Darzee, the Tailorbird, and his wife. They had made a beautiful nest by pulling two big leaves together and stitching them up the edges with fibers, and had filled the hollow with cotton and downy fluff. The nest swayed to and fro, as they sat on the rim and cried.
value.da: Det var Darzee, Skrædderfuglen, og hans kone. De havde lavet en smuk rede ved at trække to store blade sammen og sy dem sammen langs kanterne med fibre, og havde fyldt fordybningen med bomuld og dunfnug. Reden svajede frem og tilbage, mens de sad på kanten og græd.

value.en: “What is the matter?” asked Rikki-tikki.
value.da: »Hvad er der i vejen?« spurgte Rikki-tikki.

value.en: “We are very miserable,” said Darzee. “One of our babies fell out of the nest yesterday and Nag ate him.”
value.da: »Vi er rædsomt kede af det,« sagde Darzee. »I går faldt en af vores unger ud af reden, og Nag slugte ham.«

value.en: “H’m!” said Rikki-tikki, “that is very sad--but I am a stranger here. Who is Nag?”
value.da: »Hm!« sagde Rikki-tikki. »Det er meget trist. Men jeg er lige kommet hertil. Hvem er den Nag?«

value.en: Darzee and his wife only cowered down in the nest without answering, for from the thick grass at the foot of the bush there came a low hiss--a horrid cold sound that made Rikki-tikki jump back two clear feet. Then inch by inch out of the grass rose up the head and spread hood of Nag, the big black cobra, and he was five feet long from tongue to tail. When he had lifted one-third of himself clear of the ground, he stayed balancing to and fro exactly as a dandelion tuft balances in the wind, and he looked at Rikki-tikki with the wicked snake’s eyes that never change their expression, whatever the snake may be thinking of.
value.da: Ingen af fuglene svarede. De krøb sammen i reden, for nede fra det tykke græs steg en lav hvæsen, en frygtelig kold lyd, der fik Rikki-tikki til at springe to fod baglæns. Så kom hovedet af Nag langsomt op af græsset, tomme for tomme, med den brede hætte allerede spilet helt ud. Den store sorte kobra var fem fod lang fra tunge til hale. Han løftede en tredjedel af sig selv op fra jorden og svajede som en mælkebøtte i vinden. Han stirrede på Rikki-tikki med slangens onde øjne, hvis udtryk aldrig ændrer sig, uanset hvad der foregår bagved.

value.en: “Who is Nag?” said he. “I am Nag. The great God Brahm put his mark upon all our people, when the first cobra spread his hood to keep the sun off Brahm as he slept. Look, and be afraid!”
value.da: »Hvem er Nag?« gentog han. »Jeg er Nag. Den mægtige gud Brahma mærkede hele vores folk, dengang den første kobra skyggede for den sovende gud med sin hætte, så solen ikke ramte ham. Se på mig, og frygt!«

value.en: He spread out his hood more than ever, and Rikki-tikki saw the spectacle-mark on the back of it that looks exactly like the eye part of a hook-and-eye fastening. He was afraid for the minute, but it is impossible for a mongoose to stay frightened for any length of time, and though Rikki-tikki had never met a live cobra before, his mother had fed him on dead ones, and he knew that all a grown mongoose’s business in life was to fight and eat snakes. Nag knew that too and, at the bottom of his cold heart, he was afraid.
value.da: Han spilede hætten endnu mere ud, og Rikki-tikki så brillemærket bagpå, som ligner nøjagtigt malle-delen af en hægte og malle. Et øjeblik blev han bange. Men en mangust kan ikke være bange længe. Han havde aldrig mødt en levende kobra, men hans mor havde givet ham døde at spise, og han vidste, at en voksen mangusts livsopgave var at slås med slanger og æde dem. Det vidste kobraen Nag også godt, og dybt inde i hans kolde hjerte var han bange.

value.en: “Well,” said Rikki-tikki, and his tail began to fluff up again, “marks or no marks, do you think it is right for you to eat fledglings out of a nest?”
value.da: »Nå,« sagde Rikki-tikki, og halen pjuskede op igen, »mærke eller ej, synes du, det er i orden at stjæle unger fra reden og æde dem?«

value.en: Nag was thinking to himself, and watching the least little movement in the grass behind Rikki-tikki. He knew that mongooses in the garden meant death sooner or later for him and his family, but he wanted to get Rikki-tikki off his guard. So he dropped his head a little, and put it on one side.
value.da: Nag overvejede sit svar, mens han holdt øje med den mindste bevægelse i græsset bag Rikki-tikki. Han vidste, at mangoster i haven før eller siden ville betyde døden for hans familie. Men lige nu skulle han have Rikki-tikki til at slække på opmærksomheden. Så han sænkede hovedet lidt og vippede det til siden.

value.en: “Let us talk,” he said. “You eat eggs. Why should not I eat birds?”
value.da: »Lad os tale sammen,« sagde han. »Du spiser æg. Hvorfor skulle jeg ikke spise fugle?«

value.en: “Behind you! Look behind you!” sang Darzee.
value.da: »Bag dig! Pas på bagfra!« råbte Darzee.

value.en: Rikki-tikki knew better than to waste time in staring. He jumped up in the air as high as he could go, and just under him whizzed by the head of Nagaina, Nag’s wicked wife. She had crept up behind him as he was talking, to make an end of him. He heard her savage hiss as the stroke missed. He came down almost across her back, and if he had been an old mongoose he would have known that then was the time to break her back with one bite; but he was afraid of the terrible lashing return stroke of the cobra. He bit, indeed, but did not bite long enough, and he jumped clear of the whisking tail, leaving Nagaina torn and angry.
value.da: Rikki-tikki spildte ikke tid på at kigge sig tilbage. Han sprang så højt, han kunne, og lige under ham susede hovedet af Nagaina forbi. Hun var Nags onde kone og havde listet sig ind på ham, mens han talte, for at dræbe ham. Han hørte hendes rasende hvæsen, da hun ramte ved siden af. Da han kom ned igen, landede han næsten på tværs af hendes ryg. En erfaren mangust ville straks have brækket den med ét bid. Men Rikki-tikki var stadig ung, og han var bange for det frygtelige slag, som kobraen kunne give, når hun piskede tilbage mod ham. Han bed, men slap for tidligt og sprang væk fra den piskende hale. Nagaina var såret og rasende.

value.en: “Wicked, wicked Darzee!” said Nag, lashing up as high as he could reach toward the nest in the thorn-bush. But Darzee had built it out of reach of snakes, and it only swayed to and fro.
value.da: »Onde, onde Darzee!« råbte Nag og huggede opad mod reden i tornebusken, så højt han kunne. Men Darzee havde bygget den uden for slangers rækkevidde, så den bare svingede frem og tilbage.

value.en: Rikki-tikki felt his eyes growing red and hot (when a mongoose’s eyes grow red, he is angry), and he sat back on his tail and hind legs like a little kangaroo, and looked all round him, and chattered with rage. But Nag and Nagaina had disappeared into the grass. When a snake misses its stroke, it never says anything or gives any sign of what it means to do next. Rikki-tikki did not care to follow them, for he did not feel sure that he could manage two snakes at once. So he trotted off to the gravel path near the house, and sat down to think. It was a serious matter for him.
value.da: Rikki-tikkis øjne blev røde af hede (røde øjne betyder, at en mangust er vred). Han satte sig op på bagbenene og halen som en lille kænguru, kiggede sig omkring og fnyste af raseri. Men begge kobraer var forsvundet ind i græsset. En slange, der har misset, siger aldrig noget og giver aldrig tegn på, hvad den vil gøre næste gang. Rikki-tikki havde ingen lyst til at følge efter dem ind i det græs, for han var ikke sikker på, at han kunne klare to slanger, der angreb ham på én gang. Så han travede hen til grusstien ved huset og satte sig for at tænke over det alvorlige problem.

value.en: If you read the old books of natural history, you will find they say that when the mongoose fights the snake and happens to get bitten, he runs off and eats some herb that cures him. That is not true. The victory is only a matter of quickness of eye and quickness of foot--snake’s blow against mongoose’s jump--and as no eye can follow the motion of a snake’s head when it strikes, this makes things much more wonderful than any magic herb. Rikki-tikki knew he was a young mongoose, and it made him all the more pleased to think that he had managed to escape a blow from behind. It gave him confidence in himself, and when Teddy came running down the path, Rikki-tikki was ready to be petted.
value.da: Gamle bøger om naturen påstår, at en mangust, der bliver bidt i kamp, løber hen og finder en urt, som helbreder ham. Det passer slet ikke, uanset hvor ofte de gamle bøger gentager det. Sejren kommer af skarpe øjne og hurtige fødder: mangustens spring mod slangens hug. Intet menneskeøje kan følge hovedet på en slange, der hugger, og det gør bedriften mere vidunderlig end nogen magisk plante. Rikki-tikki vidste, at han var ung, og han var ekstra glad for at have undgået et angreb bagfra. Mens han tænkte over det, fik han mere og mere tillid til sig selv og til, at han kunne gøre det, en mangust skal. Da Teddy kom løbende ned ad stien, var han helt klar til at blive kælet for.

value.en: But just as Teddy was stooping, something wriggled a little in the dust, and a tiny voice said: “Be careful. I am Death!” It was Karait, the dusty brown snakeling that lies for choice on the dusty earth; and his bite is as dangerous as the cobra’s. But he is so small that nobody thinks of him, and so he does the more harm to people.
value.da: Netop som Teddy bøjede sig ned, rørte der sig noget i støvet. »Pas på. Jeg er Døden!« advarede en lillebitte stemme. Det var Karait, den lille støvbrune slange, der helst ligger på støvet jord. Hans bid er lige så dødeligt som en kobras. Fordi han er så lille, er der ingen, der lægger mærke til ham, og derfor gør han skade på endnu flere mennesker.

value.en: Rikki-tikki’s eyes grew red again, and he danced up to Karait with the peculiar rocking, swaying motion that he had inherited from his family. It looks very funny, but it is so perfectly balanced a gait that you can fly off from it at any angle you please, and in dealing with snakes this is an advantage. If Rikki-tikki had only known, he was doing a much more dangerous thing than fighting Nag, for Karait is so small, and can turn so quickly, that unless Rikki bit him close to the back of the head, he would get the return stroke in his eye or his lip. But Rikki did not know. His eyes were all red, and he rocked back and forth, looking for a good place to hold. Karait struck out. Rikki jumped sideways and tried to run in, but the wicked little dusty gray head lashed within a fraction of his shoulder, and he had to jump over the body, and the head followed his heels close.
value.da: Rikki-tikkis øjne blev røde igen. Han nærmede sig Karait i den vuggende, svajende dans, som han havde arvet fra sin familie. Den ser morsom ud, men den holder en mangust perfekt i balance, så han kan springe til alle sider, og det er en stor fordel mod slanger. Uden at vide det var han i større fare end ved kampen med Nag. Karait var så lille, at han kunne vende sig lynhurtigt, og hvis Rikki ikke tog fat lige bag hovedet, kunne slangen bide ham tilbage i læben eller øjet. Men Rikki-tikki vidste ikke, hvor meget farligere det var. Han havde ingen erfaring, der kunne fortælle ham, hvad det ville sige at kæmpe mod en så lille og hurtig slange. Med røde øjne vuggede han og ledte efter et sted at bide fast. Karait huggede ud. Rikki sprang til siden og forsøgte at fare ind, men det onde lille grå hoved piskede forbi knap en hårsbredde fra hans skulder. Han sprang hen over slangens krop, og hovedet fulgte tæt efter hans hæle.

value.en: Teddy shouted to the house: “Oh, look here! Our mongoose is killing a snake.” And Rikki-tikki heard a scream from Teddy’s mother. His father ran out with a stick, but by the time he came up, Karait had lunged out once too far, and Rikki-tikki had sprung, jumped on the snake’s back, dropped his head far between his forelegs, bitten as high up the back as he could get hold, and rolled away. That bite paralyzed Karait, and Rikki-tikki was just going to eat him up from the tail, after the custom of his family at dinner, when he remembered that a full meal makes a slow mongoose, and if he wanted all his strength and quickness ready, he must keep himself thin.
value.da: »Se her!« råbte Teddy mod huset. »Vores mangust dræber en slange.« Hans mor skreg. Teddys far kom løbende ud med en stok, men da var Karait allerede kommet én gang for langt frem. Rikki-tikki sprang op på hans ryg, stak hovedet ind mellem forbenene, bed så højt oppe på rygraden, som han kunne, og rullede væk. Bidet gjorde Karait helt lammet. Rikki var lige ved at spise ham og begynde ved halen, som hans familie plejede at gøre til middag, da han huskede, at en mæt mave gør en mangust langsom. Hvis han ville have al sin fart og styrke, måtte han holde sig slank.

value.en: He went away for a dust bath under the castor-oil bushes, while Teddy’s father beat the dead Karait. “What is the use of that?” thought Rikki-tikki. “I have settled it all;” and then Teddy’s mother picked him up from the dust and hugged him, crying that he had saved Teddy from death, and Teddy’s father said that he was a providence, and Teddy looked on with big scared eyes. Rikki-tikki was rather amused at all the fuss, which, of course, he did not understand. Teddy’s mother might just as well have petted Teddy for playing in the dust. Rikki was thoroughly enjoying himself.
value.da: Han gik hen for at tage et støvbad under ricinusbuskene, mens Teddys far slog løs på den døde slange. »Hvad skal det nytte?« tænkte Rikki-tikki. »Jeg har jo allerede klaret det hele.« Teddys mor tog ham op af støvet og krammede ham og græd over, at han havde reddet hendes søns liv. Teddys far sagde, at han var sendt af forsynet, og Teddy stirrede med store, forskrækkede øjne. Rikki morede sig over postyret, uden at forstå det. Hun kunne lige så godt have rost Teddy for at lege i støvet. For Rikki var der ingen tvivl: han morede sig kongeligt.

value.en: That night at dinner, walking to and fro among the wine-glasses on the table, he might have stuffed himself three times over with nice things. But he remembered Nag and Nagaina, and though it was very pleasant to be patted and petted by Teddy’s mother, and to sit on Teddy’s shoulder, his eyes would get red from time to time, and he would go off into his long war cry of “Rikk-tikk-tikki-tikki-tchk!”
value.da: Ved middagen gik han rundt mellem vinglassene på bordet. Han kunne have spist sig mæt tre gange i lækker mad. Men han tænkte på de to kobraer. Selv om han nød at blive klappet og kælet for af Teddys mor og sidde på Teddys skulder, blev hans øjne fra tid til anden røde, og så brød hans lange krigsråb ud: »Rikk-tikk-tikki-tikki-tchk!«

value.en: Teddy carried him off to bed, and insisted on Rikki-tikki sleeping under his chin. Rikki-tikki was too well bred to bite or scratch, but as soon as Teddy was asleep he went off for his nightly walk round the house, and in the dark he ran up against Chuchundra, the muskrat, creeping around by the wall. Chuchundra is a broken-hearted little beast. He whimpers and cheeps all the night, trying to make up his mind to run into the middle of the room. But he never gets there.
value.da: Teddy tog ham med i seng og insisterede på, at han skulle sove under hans hage. Rikki-tikki var for høflig til at bide eller kradse, så han ventede, til drengen sov, og begyndte så sin natlige runde. I mørket mødte han moskusrotten Chuchundra, som listede langs væggen. Chuchundra er et stakkels lille dyr, der klynker og piber hele natten for at samle mod til at krydse rummet. Men han når aldrig ud til midten.

value.en: “Don’t kill me,” said Chuchundra, almost weeping. “Rikki-tikki, don’t kill me!”
value.da: »Dræb mig ikke,« sagde Chuchundra næsten grædende. »Rikki-tikki, dræb mig ikke!«

value.en: “Do you think a snake-killer kills muskrats?” said Rikki-tikki scornfully.
value.da: »Tror du, en slangedræber gider dræbe moskusrotter?« sagde Rikki-tikki foragtende.

value.en: “Those who kill snakes get killed by snakes,” said Chuchundra, more sorrowfully than ever. “And how am I to be sure that Nag won’t mistake me for you some dark night?”
value.da: »De, der dræber slanger, bliver dræbt af slanger,« sagde Chuchundra mere sørgmodigt end nogensinde. »Og hvordan kan jeg være sikker på, at Nag ikke forveksler mig med dig en mørk nat?«

value.en: “There’s not the least danger,” said Rikki-tikki. “But Nag is in the garden, and I know you don’t go there.”
value.da: »Det er der ingen fare for,« sagde Rikki-tikki. »Og Nag holder til i haven, og dér kommer du jo aldrig.«

value.en: “My cousin Chua, the rat, told me--” said Chuchundra, and then he stopped.
value.da: »Min fætter Chua, rotten, fortalte mig —« sagde Chuchundra, og så standsede han.

value.en: “Told you what?”
value.da: »Fortalte dig hvad?«

value.en: “H’sh! Nag is everywhere, Rikki-tikki. You should have talked to Chua in the garden.”
value.da: »Hys! Nag er overalt, Rikki-tikki. Du skulle have talt med Chua i haven.«

value.en: “I didn’t--so you must tell me. Quick, Chuchundra, or I’ll bite you!”
value.da: »Det gjorde jeg ikke — så du må fortælle mig det. Hurtigt, Chuchundra, ellers bider jeg dig!«

value.en: Chuchundra sat down and cried till the tears rolled off his whiskers. “I am a very poor man,” he sobbed. “I never had spirit enough to run out into the middle of the room. H’sh! I mustn’t tell you anything. Can’t you hear, Rikki-tikki?”
value.da: Chuchundra blev siddende og græd, til tårerne dryppede fra hans knurhår. »Jeg er sådan et ynkeligt lille dyr,« hulkede han. »Jeg har aldrig haft mod nok til at løbe ud midt på gulvet. Hys! Jeg må ikke sige noget. Kan du ikke høre det, Rikki-tikki?«

value.en: Rikki-tikki listened. The house was as still as still, but he thought he could just catch the faintest scratch-scratch in the world--a noise as faint as that of a wasp walking on a window-pane--the dry scratch of a snake’s scales on brick-work.
value.da: Rikki-tikki lyttede. Huset var helt stille, men han syntes alligevel, han kunne høre den allersvageste lille kradsen, knapt højere end en hvepsefod på en vinduesrude. Det var den tørre skrabelyd af slangeskæl mod mursten.

value.en: “That’s Nag or Nagaina,” he said to himself, “and he is crawling into the bath-room sluice. You’re right, Chuchundra; I should have talked to Chua.”
value.da: »Det er Nag eller Nagaina,« tænkte han. »Den kommer ind gennem badeværelsets afløb. Chuchundra havde ret: jeg skulle have talt med Chua.«

value.en: He stole off to Teddy’s bath-room, but there was nothing there, and then to Teddy’s mother’s bathroom. At the bottom of the smooth plaster wall there was a brick pulled out to make a sluice for the bath water, and as Rikki-tikki stole in by the masonry curb where the bath is put, he heard Nag and Nagaina whispering together outside in the moonlight.
value.da: Han listede ind på Teddys badeværelse, men det var tomt, og så ind på hans mors. I bunden af den glatte pudsede væg manglede der en mursten, og hullet var afløb for badevandet. Rikki-tikki listede forbi den opmurede kant rundt om badet og hørte Nag og Nagaina hviske udenfor i måneskinnet.

value.en: “When the house is emptied of people,” said Nagaina to her husband, “he will have to go away, and then the garden will be our own again. Go in quietly, and remember that the big man who killed Karait is the first one to bite. Then come out and tell me, and we will hunt for Rikki-tikki together.”
value.da: »Når huset er tomt for mennesker,« sagde Nagaina til sin mand, »må han flytte. Så bliver haven vores igen. Gå stille ind. Bid den store mand først, ham der dræbte Karait. Kom så ud og fortæl mig det, og så jager vi Rikki-tikki sammen.«

value.en: “But are you sure that there is anything to be gained by killing the people?” said Nag.
value.da: »Er du sikker på, at det virkelig hjælper os at dræbe menneskene?« spurgte Nag.

value.en: “Everything. When there were no people in the bungalow, did we have any mongoose in the garden? So long as the bungalow is empty, we are king and queen of the garden; and remember that as soon as our eggs in the melon bed hatch (as they may tomorrow), our children will need room and quiet.”
value.da: »Det løser alt. Før menneskene flyttede ind i bungalowen, boede der så nogen mangust i vores have? Når huset er tomt, er vi konge og dronning her. Og husk, at vores æg i melonbedet måske klækkes allerede i morgen. Vores børn får brug for fred og plads.«

value.en: “I had not thought of that,” said Nag. “I will go, but there is no need that we should hunt for Rikki-tikki afterward. I will kill the big man and his wife, and the child if I can, and come away quietly. Then the bungalow will be empty, and Rikki-tikki will go.”
value.da: »Det havde jeg ikke tænkt på,« sagde Nag. »Jeg går. Men bagefter behøver vi ikke jage Rikki-tikki. Jeg dræber manden, hans kone og, hvis jeg kan, deres barn, og så går jeg stille min vej. Når bungalowen er tom, må Rikki-tikki jo tage et andet sted hen.«

value.en: Rikki-tikki tingled all over with rage and hatred at this, and then Nag’s head came through the sluice, and his five feet of cold body followed it. Angry as he was, Rikki-tikki was very frightened as he saw the size of the big cobra. Nag coiled himself up, raised his head, and looked into the bathroom in the dark, and Rikki could see his eyes glitter.
value.da: Rikki-tikki rystede af had og raseri. Nags hoved gled ind gennem afløbet, og efter det kom fem fod kold krop. Trods sin vrede blev mangusten bange for kobraens størrelse. Nag rullede sig sammen, løftede hovedet og så sig om i det mørke badeværelse. Hans øjne glimtede, så Rikki kunne se dem.

value.en: “Now, if I kill him here, Nagaina will know; and if I fight him on the open floor, the odds are in his favor. What am I to do?” said Rikki-tikki-tavi.
value.da: »Hvis jeg dræber ham her, får Nagaina det at vide,« tænkte Rikki-tikki-tavi. »Og hvis jeg angriber ham på det åbne gulv, har han fordelen. Hvad skal jeg gøre?«

value.en: Nag waved to and fro, and then Rikki-tikki heard him drinking from the biggest water-jar that was used to fill the bath. “That is good,” said the snake. “Now, when Karait was killed, the big man had a stick. He may have that stick still, but when he comes in to bathe in the morning he will not have a stick. I shall wait here till he comes. Nagaina--do you hear me?--I shall wait here in the cool till daytime.”
value.da: Nag svajede og drak så af den største krukke, som man brugte til at fylde badet. Rikki-tikki hørte ham sige: »Det er godt. Manden havde en stok, da han dræbte Karait. Måske har han den stadig. Men når han skal bade i morgen tidlig, har han den ikke med. Jeg venter på ham. Nagaina, kan du høre mig? Jeg bliver her på det kølige sted til dagslys.«

value.en: There was no answer from outside, so Rikki-tikki knew Nagaina had gone away. Nag coiled himself down, coil by coil, round the bulge at the bottom of the water jar, and Rikki-tikki stayed still as death. After an hour he began to move, muscle by muscle, toward the jar. Nag was asleep, and Rikki-tikki looked at his big back, wondering which would be the best place for a good hold. “If I don’t break his back at the first jump,” said Rikki, “he can still fight. And if he fights--O Rikki!” He looked at the thickness of the neck below the hood, but that was too much for him; and a bite near the tail would only make Nag savage.
value.da: Der kom intet svar, så Rikki-tikki vidste, at Nagaina var gået. Nag lagde sig til rette i ringe, ring for ring, rundt om den buede bund af vandkrukken. Mangusten sad helt stille. En time senere begyndte han at liste hen mod ham, én muskel ad gangen. Nag sov. Rikki så på hans brede ryg og overvejede, hvor han skulle tage fat. »Hvis ikke det første spring brækker hans rygrad, kan han slå tilbage. Og hvis han gør det — åh, Rikki!« Han så på den tykke hals lige under hætten, men den var alt for tyk til, at han kunne få tænderne ordentligt rundt om den. Og et bid nær halen ville bare gøre kobraen rasende.

value.en: “It must be the head”’ he said at last; “the head above the hood. And, when I am once there, I must not let go.”
value.da: »Det må blive hovedet,« besluttede han til sidst, »stedet oven for hætten. Når jeg først har fat dér, må jeg aldrig give slip.«

value.en: Then he jumped. The head was lying a little clear of the water jar, under the curve of it; and, as his teeth met, Rikki braced his back against the bulge of the red earthenware to hold down the head. This gave him just one second’s purchase, and he made the most of it. Then he was battered to and fro as a rat is shaken by a dog--to and fro on the floor, up and down, and around in great circles, but his eyes were red and he held on as the body cart-whipped over the floor, upsetting the tin dipper and the soap dish and the flesh brush, and banged against the tin side of the bath. As he held he closed his jaws tighter and tighter, for he made sure he would be banged to death, and, for the honor of his family, he preferred to be found with his teeth locked. He was dizzy, aching, and felt shaken to pieces when something went off like a thunderclap just behind him. A hot wind knocked him senseless and red fire singed his fur. The big man had been wakened by the noise, and had fired both barrels of a shotgun into Nag just behind the hood.
value.da: Han sprang. Nags hoved lå lidt væk fra krukken, under dens runding. Da hans tænder lukkede sig, pressede Rikki ryggen mod den røde lerkrukkes bule for at holde hovedet nede. Det gav ham et helt sekunds støtte, og det udnyttede han fuldt ud. Så begyndte kobraen at slå ham frem og tilbage, ligesom en hund ryster en rotte, den har fanget: hen over gulvet, op og ned, rundt i store cirkler. Med røde øjne klamrede han sig fast, mens kroppen piskede som en svøbe, væltede blikøsen, sæbeskålen og gnidebørsten og knaldede mod blikbadekarret. Han regnede med at blive slået ihjel og bed kæberne sammen for sin families ære: de skulle finde ham med tænderne stadig låst fast. Svimmel og øm og rystet i stykker hørte han et tordenskrald bag sig. En brændende varme slog ham bevidstløs, og rød ild svedede hans pels. Manden var blevet vækket af larmen og havde skudt begge løb af et haglgevær ind i Nag lige under hætten.

value.en: Rikki-tikki held on with his eyes shut, for now he was quite sure he was dead. But the head did not move, and the big man picked him up and said, “It’s the mongoose again, Alice. The little chap has saved our lives now.”
value.da: Rikki-tikki holdt stadig fast med lukkede øjne, nu helt sikker på, at han selv var død. Men hovedet holdt op med at bevæge sig. Manden løftede mangusten op. »Det er ham igen, Alice. Den lille fyr har reddet vores liv denne gang.«

value.en: Then Teddy’s mother came in with a very white face, and saw what was left of Nag, and Rikki-tikki dragged himself to Teddy’s bedroom and spent half the rest of the night shaking himself tenderly to find out whether he really was broken into forty pieces, as he fancied.
value.da: Teddys mor kom ind med et hvidt ansigt og så, hvad der var tilbage af Nag. Rikki-tikki slæbte sig ind på drengens værelse. I halvdelen af resten af natten rystede han sig forsigtigt for at se, om han virkelig var gået i fyrre stykker, som det føltes.

value.en: When morning came he was very stiff, but well pleased with his doings. “Now I have Nagaina to settle with, and she will be worse than five Nags, and there’s no knowing when the eggs she spoke of will hatch. Goodness! I must go and see Darzee,” he said.
value.da: Da det blev morgen, var han stiv i hele kroppen, men meget tilfreds med, hvad han havde udrettet i løbet af natten. »Nu er det Nagainas tur. Hun bliver værre end fem Nager, og de æg kan klække når som helst. Du milde! Jeg må tale med Darzee.«

value.en: Without waiting for breakfast, Rikki-tikki ran to the thornbush where Darzee was singing a song of triumph at the top of his voice. The news of Nag’s death was all over the garden, for the sweeper had thrown the body on the rubbish-heap.
value.da: Uden engang at vente på morgenmaden løb han hen til tornebusken. Darzee sang sejrssang af fuld hals. Alle i haven vidste, at Nag var død: rengøringsmanden havde smidt hans krop på skraldebunken.

value.en: “Oh, you stupid tuft of feathers!” said Rikki-tikki angrily. “Is this the time to sing?”
value.da: »Din dumme fjertot!« snerrede Rikki-tikki. »Er det nu, man skal synge?«

value.en: “Nag is dead--is dead--is dead!” sang Darzee. “The valiant Rikki-tikki caught him by the head and held fast. The big man brought the bang-stick, and Nag fell in two pieces! He will never eat my babies again.”
value.da: »Nag er død — er død — er død!« sang Darzee. »Den modige Rikki-tikki greb ham i hovedet og ville ikke give slip. Manden hentede knaldstokken, og Nag knækkede i to! Han skal aldrig mere sluge en af mine unger.«

value.en: “All that’s true enough. But where’s Nagaina?” said Rikki-tikki, looking carefully round him.
value.da: »Det passer. Men hvor er Nagaina?« spurgte Rikki-tikki og kiggede forsigtigt rundt omkring sig.

value.en: “Nagaina came to the bathroom sluice and called for Nag,” Darzee went on, “and Nag came out on the end of a stick--the sweeper picked him up on the end of a stick and threw him upon the rubbish heap. Let us sing about the great, the red-eyed Rikki-tikki!” And Darzee filled his throat and sang.
value.da: »Nagaina kaldte på Nag ved badeværelsets afløb,« fortsatte Darzee, »og han kom ud på en stok. Rengøringsmanden løftede ham op på enden af den og smed ham på skraldebunken. Lad os prise den mægtige, rødøjede Rikki-tikki!« Darzee tog en indånding og sang videre.

value.en: “If I could get up to your nest, I’d roll your babies out!” said Rikki-tikki. “You don’t know when to do the right thing at the right time. You’re safe enough in your nest there, but it’s war for me down here. Stop singing a minute, Darzee.”
value.da: »Hvis jeg kunne nå op til den rede, ville jeg vippe dine unger ud!« råbte Rikki-tikki. »Du ved aldrig, hvornår man skal gøre det, der skal gøres. Du er i sikkerhed deroppe, men hernede fører jeg krig. Hold op med at synge et øjeblik, Darzee.«

value.en: “For the great, the beautiful Rikki-tikki’s sake I will stop,” said Darzee. “What is it, O Killer of the terrible Nag?”
value.da: »For den vidunderlige, storslåede Rikki-tikkis skyld vil jeg tie stille,« sagde Darzee. »Hvad har du brug for, du som dræbte den frygtelige Nag?«

value.en: “Where is Nagaina, for the third time?”
value.da: »Hvor er Nagaina blevet af? Det er tredje gang, jeg spørger.«

value.en: “On the rubbish heap by the stables, mourning for Nag. Great is Rikki-tikki with the white teeth.”
value.da: »Hun er ved staldene og sørger over Nag på skraldebunken. Mægtig er Rikki-tikki med de hvide tænder.«

value.en: “Bother my white teeth! Have you ever heard where she keeps her eggs?”
value.da: »Glem mine hvide tænder! Ved du, hvor hun har gemt sine æg?«

value.en: “In the melon bed, on the end nearest the wall, where the sun strikes nearly all day. She hid them there weeks ago.”
value.da: »I melonbedet ved muren, hvor solen skinner næsten hele dagen. Hun lagde dem der for flere uger siden.«

value.en: “And you never thought it worth while to tell me? The end nearest the wall, you said?”
value.da: »Og det syntes du ikke var værd at nævne? Enden nærmest muren, sagde du?«

value.en: “Rikki-tikki, you are not going to eat her eggs?”
value.da: »Rikki-tikki, du vil da ikke spise hendes æg?«

value.en: “Not eat exactly; no. Darzee, if you have a grain of sense you will fly off to the stables and pretend that your wing is broken, and let Nagaina chase you away to this bush. I must get to the melon-bed, and if I went there now she’d see me.”
value.da: »Ikke ligefrem spise dem, nej. Hvis du har nogen fornuft, Darzee, flyver du ned til staldene, lader som om din vinge er brækket og lokker Nagaina efter dig hen mod denne busk. Jeg skal ind til melonbedet. Hvis jeg går derhen nu, ser hun mig.«

value.en: Darzee was a feather-brained little fellow who could never hold more than one idea at a time in his head. And just because he knew that Nagaina’s children were born in eggs like his own, he didn’t think at first that it was fair to kill them. But his wife was a sensible bird, and she knew that cobra’s eggs meant young cobras later on. So she flew off from the nest, and left Darzee to keep the babies warm, and continue his song about the death of Nag. Darzee was very like a man in some ways.
value.da: Darzee var spredt i hovedet og kunne ikke holde to tanker på én gang. Fordi Nagainas unger kom ud af æg ligesom hans egne, syntes han først, det var uretfærdigt at dræbe dem. Hans kone var mere fornuftig: kobraæg ville snart blive til små kobraer. Hun fløj selv fra reden og lod Darzee blive tilbage for at holde deres unger varme og digte videre på sin sang om Nags død, mens hun tog sig af det arbejde, der skulle gøres. På nogle måder lignede Darzee et menneske.

value.en: She fluttered in front of Nagaina by the rubbish heap and cried out, “Oh, my wing is broken! The boy in the house threw a stone at me and broke it.” Then she fluttered more desperately than ever.
value.da: Hun baskede foran Nagaina ved skraldebunken. »Åh, min vinge er brækket!« råbte hun. »Drengen kastede en sten og brækkede den.« Så baskede hun endnu mere fortvivlet end før.

value.en: Nagaina lifted up her head and hissed, “You warned Rikki-tikki when I would have killed him. Indeed and truly, you’ve chosen a bad place to be lame in.” And she moved toward Darzee’s wife, slipping along over the dust.
value.da: Nagaina løftede hovedet og hvæsede: »Du advarede Rikki-tikki, lige da jeg ville dræbe ham. Du har sandelig valgt et uheldigt sted at blive lam.« Hun gled hen over støvet mod fuglen.

value.en: “The boy broke it with a stone!” shrieked Darzee’s wife.
value.da: »Drengen brækkede den med en sten!« skreg Darzees kone.

value.en: “Well! It may be some consolation to you when you’re dead to know that I shall settle accounts with the boy. My husband lies on the rubbish heap this morning, but before night the boy in the house will lie very still. What is the use of running away? I am sure to catch you. Little fool, look at me!”
value.da: »Nå! Måske er det en trøst for dig, når du er død, at jeg skal gøre op med den dreng. Min mand ligger på skraldebunken i dag tidlig. Inden i aften ligger barnet derinde i huset også helt stille. Hvorfor løbe væk? Jeg fanger dig alligevel. Se på mig, din lille tåbe!«

value.en: Darzee’s wife knew better than to do that, for a bird who looks at a snake’s eyes gets so frightened that she cannot move. Darzee’s wife fluttered on, piping sorrowfully, and never leaving the ground, and Nagaina quickened her pace.
