value.da: Darzees kone vidste, at hun ikke måtte lystre. En fugl, der møder en slanges blik, bliver for bange til at røre sig. Hun baskede videre uden at lette fra jorden og pibede ynkeligt, mens Nagaina nærmede sig hurtigere.

value.en: Rikki-tikki heard them going up the path from the stables, and he raced for the end of the melon patch near the wall. There, in the warm litter above the melons, very cunningly hidden, he found twenty-five eggs, about the size of a bantam’s eggs, but with whitish skin instead of shell.
value.da: Rikki-tikki hørte dem komme forbi på stien fra staldene og løb hen til melonbedet ved muren. Dér lå femogtyve æg, snildt skjult i varmt affald oven på melonerne, hvert på størrelse med et dværghønseæg og med bleg, læderagtig hud i stedet for skal.

value.en: “I was not a day too soon,” he said, for he could see the baby cobras curled up inside the skin, and he knew that the minute they were hatched they could each kill a man or a mongoose. He bit off the tops of the eggs as fast as he could, taking care to crush the young cobras, and turned over the litter from time to time to see whether he had missed any. At last there were only three eggs left, and Rikki-tikki began to chuckle to himself, when he heard Darzee’s wife screaming:
value.da: »Det var på høje tid,« sagde han. Gennem den blege hud kunne han se de små kobraer ligge sammenkrøllede indeni, og han vidste, at så snart de klækkede, kunne hver af dem dræbe et menneske eller en mangust. Så hurtigt han kunne, bed han toppen af hvert æg og sørgede for at knuse den lille slange indeni. Af og til vendte han det løse affald rundt for at se, om der lå flere æg skjult. Til sidst var der kun tre tilbage. Han begyndte at fnise for sig selv, men så hørte han Darzees kone skrige:

value.en: “Rikki-tikki, I led Nagaina toward the house, and she has gone into the veranda, and--oh, come quickly--she means killing!”
value.da: »Rikki-tikki, jeg har ført Nagaina hen mod huset. Hun er på verandaen nu — åh, skynd dig — hun vil dræbe!«

value.en: Rikki-tikki smashed two eggs, and tumbled backward down the melon-bed with the third egg in his mouth, and scuttled to the veranda as hard as he could put foot to the ground. Teddy and his mother and father were there at early breakfast, but Rikki-tikki saw that they were not eating anything. They sat stone-still, and their faces were white. Nagaina was coiled up on the matting by Teddy’s chair, within easy striking distance of Teddy’s bare leg, and she was swaying to and fro, singing a song of triumph.
value.da: Han knuste to æg, tog det tredje i munden, tumlede baglæns ud af melonbedet og spurtede hen til verandaen. Teddy og hans forældre sad ved den tidlige morgenmad uden at røre maden. Alle tre sad stille som sten, og deres ansigter var helt hvide af skræk. Ved siden af Teddys stol lå Nagaina sammenrullet på måtten, lige inden for rækkevidde af hans bare ben. Hun svajede og sang om sin sejr.

value.en: “Son of the big man that killed Nag,” she hissed, “stay still. I am not ready yet. Wait a little. Keep very still, all you three! If you move I strike, and if you do not move I strike. Oh, foolish people, who killed my Nag!”
value.da: »Søn af manden, der dræbte Nag,« hvæsede hun, »bliv stille. Ikke endnu, jeg er ikke klar. Vent. Ingen af jer tre må røre sig! Rører I jer, hugger jeg. Bliver I stille, hugger jeg. Åh, tåbelige mennesker, der myrdede min Nag!«

value.en: Teddy’s eyes were fixed on his father, and all his father could do was to whisper, “Sit still, Teddy. You mustn’t move. Teddy, keep still.”
value.da: Teddy stirrede på sin far, som kun kunne hviske: »Sid stille, Teddy. Du må ikke røre dig. Teddy, du skal være helt stille.«

value.en: Then Rikki-tikki came up and cried, “Turn round, Nagaina. Turn and fight!”
value.da: Så kom Rikki-tikki op og råbte: »Vend dig om, Nagaina. Vend dig og kæmp!«

value.en: “All in good time,” said she, without moving her eyes. “I will settle my account with you presently. Look at your friends, Rikki-tikki. They are still and white. They are afraid. They dare not move, and if you come a step nearer I strike.”
value.da: »Om lidt,« svarede hun uden at flytte blikket. »Din tur kommer. Se på dine venner: blege, stivnede, rædselsslagne. De tør ikke røre sig. Et skridt nærmere fra dig, Rikki-tikki, og jeg hugger.«

value.en: “Look at your eggs,” said Rikki-tikki, “in the melon bed near the wall. Go and look, Nagaina!”
value.da: »Se på dine æg,« sagde Rikki-tikki, »i melonbedet nær muren. Gå og se, Nagaina!«

value.en: The big snake turned half around, and saw the egg on the veranda. “Ah-h! Give it to me,” she said.
value.da: Kobraen vendte sig halvt om og så ægget på verandaen. »Ah-h! Giv mig det,« krævede hun.

value.en: Rikki-tikki put his paws one on each side of the egg, and his eyes were blood-red. “What price for a snake’s egg? For a young cobra? For a young king cobra? For the last--the very last of the brood? The ants are eating all the others down by the melon bed.”
value.da: Rikki-tikki satte en pote på hver side af ægget og stirrede med blodrøde øjne. »Hvad vil du give for et slangeæg? En lille kobra? En ung kongekobra? Det sidste, det allersidste af dit kuld? Myrerne æder alle de andre nede ved melonerne.«

value.en: Nagaina spun clear round, forgetting everything for the sake of the one egg. Rikki-tikki saw Teddy’s father shoot out a big hand, catch Teddy by the shoulder, and drag him across the little table with the tea-cups, safe and out of reach of Nagaina.
value.da: Nagaina vendte sig helt om mod ham og glemte alt andet end sit sidste æg. Teddys far rakte sin store hånd ud, greb drengen i skulderen og slæbte ham hen over det lille bord med tekopperne, i sikkerhed uden for kobraens rækkevidde.

value.en: “Tricked! Tricked! Tricked! Rikk-tck-tck!” chuckled Rikki-tikki. “The boy is safe, and it was I--I--I that caught Nag by the hood last night in the bathroom.” Then he began to jump up and down, all four feet together, his head close to the floor. “He threw me to and fro, but he could not shake me off. He was dead before the big man blew him in two. I did it! Rikki-tikki-tck-tck! Come then, Nagaina. Come and fight with me. You shall not be a widow long.”
value.da: »Snydt! Snydt! Snydt! Rikk-tck-tck!« fnisede Rikki-tikki. »Drengen er i sikkerhed. Og i nat på badeværelset var det mig — mig — mig, der greb fat i Nags hætte.« Han hoppede op og ned på alle fire ben med hovedet tæt ved gulvet. »Han kastede mig rundt overalt, men kunne ikke få mig til at give slip. Før manden skød ham i to stykker, var han allerede død. Jeg dræbte ham! Rikki-tikki-tck-tck! Kom så, Nagaina. Kæmp mod mig. Du bliver ikke længe enke.«

value.en: Nagaina saw that she had lost her chance of killing Teddy, and the egg lay between Rikki-tikki’s paws. “Give me the egg, Rikki-tikki. Give me the last of my eggs, and I will go away and never come back,” she said, lowering her hood.
value.da: Nagaina så, at hun havde mistet chancen for at dræbe Teddy, og ægget lå mellem Rikki-tikkis poter. »Giv mig ægget, Rikki-tikki. Giv mig det sidste af mine æg, og jeg går min vej og kommer aldrig tilbage,« sagde hun og sænkede sin hætte.

value.en: “Yes, you will go away, and you will never come back. For you will go to the rubbish heap with Nag. Fight, widow! The big man has gone for his gun! Fight!”
value.da: »Ja, du går din vej, og du kommer aldrig tilbage. For du går til affaldsbunken med Nag. Slås, enke! Den store mand er gået efter sit gevær! Slås!«

value.en: Rikki-tikki was bounding all round Nagaina, keeping just out of reach of her stroke, his little eyes like hot coals. Nagaina gathered herself together and flung out at him. Rikki-tikki jumped up and backward. Again and again and again she struck, and each time her head came with a whack on the matting of the veranda and she gathered herself together like a watch spring. Then Rikki-tikki danced in a circle to get behind her, and Nagaina spun round to keep her head to his head, so that the rustle of her tail on the matting sounded like dry leaves blown along by the wind.
value.da: Rikki-tikki sprang rundt om hende med øjne, der brændte som gløder, og holdt sig lige uden for hugafstand. Nagaina trak hele sin lange krop sammen, samlede kræfter til slaget og slog så hovedet lige ud mod ham. Han sprang baglæns og opad. Igen og igen huggede hun og slog hver gang hovedet mod måtten på verandaen, før hun trak sig sammen som en urfjeder. Så dansede Rikki-tikki i en hel cirkel for at komme om bag hende, og hun vendte sig for hele tiden at have ham foran sig. Hendes hale raslede hen over måtten som tørre blade i vinden.

value.en: He had forgotten the egg. It still lay on the veranda, and Nagaina came nearer and nearer to it, till at last, while Rikki-tikki was drawing breath, she caught it in her mouth, turned to the veranda steps, and flew like an arrow down the path, with Rikki-tikki behind her. When the cobra runs for her life, she goes like a whip-lash flicked across a horse’s neck.
value.da: Han havde helt glemt ægget, der lå lige ved. Nagaina krøb hen mod det, og mens han trak vejret, snappede hun det i munden. Hun vendte sig mod trappen og skød ned ad stien med Rikki-tikki efter sig. En kobra, der flygter for livet, bevæger sig som et piskesmæld over en hests hals.

value.en: Rikki-tikki knew that he must catch her, or all the trouble would begin again. She headed straight for the long grass by the thorn-bush, and as he was running Rikki-tikki heard Darzee still singing his foolish little song of triumph. But Darzee’s wife was wiser. She flew off her nest as Nagaina came along, and flapped her wings about Nagaina’s head. If Darzee had helped they might have turned her, but Nagaina only lowered her hood and went on. Still, the instant’s delay brought Rikki-tikki up to her, and as she plunged into the rat-hole where she and Nag used to live, his little white teeth were clenched on her tail, and he went down with her--and very few mongooses, however wise and old they may be, care to follow a cobra into its hole. It was dark in the hole; and Rikki-tikki never knew when it might open out and give Nagaina room to turn and strike at him. He held on savagely, and stuck out his feet to act as brakes on the dark slope of the hot, moist earth.
value.da: Rikki-tikki vidste, at han måtte fange hende, ellers ville ulykkerne begynde forfra. Hun satte kursen mod det høje græs ved tornebusken, hvor Darzee stadig sang sin dumme sejrssang. Hans klogere kone forlod reden og slog med vingerne om hovedet på Nagaina. Med Darzees hjælp havde de måske kunnet få hende til at dreje af, men alene fik hun bare kobraen til at sænke hætten og fortsætte. Den korte forsinkelse gjorde, at Rikki nåede hende. Lige som Nagaina styrtede ind i rottehullet, som hun og Nag havde delt, greb hans små hvide tænder om hendes hale. Han fulgte efter hende ned. Der er ikke mange mangoster, hvor erfarne de end er, som frivilligt følger en kobra ned under jorden. I mørket kunne han ikke vide, hvor gangen blev bred nok til, at hun kunne vende sig og hugge. Han holdt hårdt fast og spredte fødderne som bremser mod den varme, fugtige jord på skråningen nedad.

value.en: Then the grass by the mouth of the hole stopped waving, and Darzee said, “It is all over with Rikki-tikki! We must sing his death song. Valiant Rikki-tikki is dead! For Nagaina will surely kill him underground.”
value.da: Så holdt græsset ved hullets munding op med at bølge, og Darzee sagde: »Det er forbi med Rikki-tikki! Vi må synge hans dødssang. Den modige Rikki-tikki er død! For Nagaina vil sikkert dræbe ham under jorden.«

value.en: So he sang a very mournful song that he made up on the spur of the minute, and just as he got to the most touching part, the grass quivered again, and Rikki-tikki, covered with dirt, dragged himself out of the hole leg by leg, licking his whiskers. Darzee stopped with a little shout. Rikki-tikki shook some of the dust out of his fur and sneezed. “It is all over,” he said. “The widow will never come out again.” And the red ants that live between the grass stems heard him, and began to troop down one after another to see if he had spoken the truth.
value.da: Straks digtede han en sørgelig sang. Lige da han nåede det mest rørende sted, rørte græsset sig igen. Beskidt og med tungen over knurhårene trak Rikki-tikki sig ud, ben for ben. Darzee holdt op midt i sangen og udstødte et lille forskrækket udråb. Rikki rystede støvet af pelsen og nyste. »Det er overstået,« sagde han. »Enken kommer aldrig op igen.« De røde myrer, der bor mellem græsstråene, hørte ham og marcherede én efter én ned i hullet for at tjekke, om det passede.

value.en: Rikki-tikki curled himself up in the grass and slept where he was--slept and slept till it was late in the afternoon, for he had done a hard day’s work.
value.da: Rikki-tikki rullede sig sammen lige dér i græsset og sov. Efter en så hård dags arbejde sov han og sov til sent på eftermiddagen.

value.en: “Now,” he said, when he awoke, “I will go back to the house. Tell the Coppersmith, Darzee, and he will tell the garden that Nagaina is dead.”
value.da: »Nu,« sagde han, da han vågnede, »går jeg tilbage til huset. Sig det til Kobbersmeden, Darzee, så fortæller han haven, at Nagaina er død.«

value.en: The Coppersmith is a bird who makes a noise exactly like the beating of a little hammer on a copper pot; and the reason he is always making it is because he is the town crier to every Indian garden, and tells all the news to everybody who cares to listen. As Rikki-tikki went up the path, he heard his “attention” notes like a tiny dinner gong, and then the steady “Ding-dong-tock! Nag is dead--dong! Nagaina is dead! Ding-dong-tock!” That set all the birds in the garden singing, and the frogs croaking, for Nag and Nagaina used to eat frogs as well as little birds.
value.da: Kobbersmedens kald lyder præcis som en lille hammer, der slår på en kobbergryde. Han bliver ved med det, fordi han er byråber i de indiske haver og fortæller de nyeste nyheder til alle skabninger i haven, som gider stoppe op og lytte. Mens Rikki gik hjemad, hørte han først opmærksomhedssignalet, som lød som en lille middagsgong, og derefter de jævne kald: »Ding-dong-tock! Nag er død — dong! Nagaina er død! Ding-dong-tock!« Fuglene begyndte at synge overalt, og frøerne kvækkede også. Kobraerne havde nemlig spist frøer og små fugle.

value.en: When Rikki got to the house, Teddy and Teddy’s mother (she looked very white still, for she had been fainting) and Teddy’s father came out and almost cried over him; and that night he ate all that was given him till he could eat no more, and went to bed on Teddy’s shoulder, where Teddy’s mother saw him when she came to look late at night.
value.da: Teddy og begge hans forældre mødte ham udenfor og var tæt på at græde. Hans mor var stadig bleg efter sine besvimelser. Den aften spiste Rikki alt, hvad han fik, til han ikke kunne sluge mere. Så gik han i seng på Teddys skulder, og hans mor så ham dér, da hun kiggede ind sent om natten.

value.en: “He saved our lives and Teddy’s life,” she said to her husband. “Just think, he saved all our lives.”
value.da: »Han reddede vores liv og Teddys liv,« sagde hun til sin mand. »Tænk dog, han reddede alle vores liv.«

value.en: Rikki-tikki woke up with a jump, for the mongooses are light sleepers.
value.da: Rikki-tikki for op ved lyden af deres stemmer, for mangoster sover let.

value.en: “Oh, it’s you,” said he. “What are you bothering for? All the cobras are dead. And if they weren’t, I’m here.”
value.da: »Åh, det er jer,« sagde han. »Hvorfor al den ståhej? Alle kobraerne er døde. Og selv hvis én ikke var, er jeg jo her.«

value.en: Rikki-tikki had a right to be proud of himself. But he did not grow too proud, and he kept that garden as a mongoose should keep it, with tooth and jump and spring and bite, till never a cobra dared show its head inside the walls.
value.da: Han havde fortjent sin stolthed, men blev aldrig for stolt. Han passede den have, som en mangust skal, med spring, bid og tænder, til ikke en eneste kobra turde løfte hovedet inden for murene.

value.en: Darzee’s Chant
value.da: Darzees Sang

value.en: (Sung in honor of Rikki-tikki-tavi)
value.da: (Sunget til ære for Rikki-tikki-tavi)

value.en:
Singer and tailor am I--
Doubled the joys that I know--
Proud of my lilt to the sky,
Proud of the house that I sew--
Over and under, so weave I my music--so weave I the house that I
sew.
value.da:
Sanger og skrædder er jeg —
dobbelt er glæden, jeg har —
stolt af min sang mod himlen,
stolt af det hus, jeg syr —
Over og under væver jeg min musik og væver det hus, jeg
syr.

value.en:
Sing to your fledglings again,
Mother, oh lift up your head!
Evil that plagued us is slain,
Death in the garden lies dead.
Terror that hid in the roses is impotent--flung on the dung-hill
and dead!
value.da:
Syng for dine unger igen,
Mor, åh, løft dit hoved!
Det onde, der plagede os, er dræbt,
Døden ligger død i haven.
Rædslen, der gemte sig i roserne, er magtesløs — smidt på møddingen
og død!

value.en:
Who has delivered us, who?
Tell me his nest and his name.
Rikki, the valiant, the true,
Tikki, with eyeballs of flame,
Rikk-tikki-tikki, the ivory-fanged, the hunter with eyeballs of
flame!
value.da:
Hvem har befriet os, hvem?
Fortæl mig hans rede og hans navn.
Rikki, den modige, den sande,
Tikki, med øjne af flamme,
Rikk-tikki-tikki, med tænder af elfenben, jægeren med øjne af
flamme!

value.en:
Give him the Thanks of the Birds,
Bowing with tail feathers spread!
Praise him with nightingale words--
Nay, I will praise him instead.
Hear!  I will sing you the praise of the bottle-tailed Rikki, with
eyeballs of red!
value.da:
Giv ham Fuglenes Tak,
bukkende med spredte halefjer!
Pris ham med nattergaleord —
nej, jeg vil prise ham i stedet.
Hør! Jeg vil synge om den flaskebørstehalede Rikki, med
røde øjne som ild!

value.en: (_Here Rikki-tikki interrupted, and the rest of the song is lost._)
value.da: (_Her afbrød Rikki-tikki, og resten af sangen er gået tabt._)

value.en:
I will remember what I was, I am sick of rope and chain--
I will remember my old strength and all my forest affairs.
I will not sell my back to man for a bundle of sugar-cane:
I will go out to my own kind, and the wood-folk in their lairs.
value.da:
Jeg vil huske, hvad jeg var, jeg er led og ked af reb og lænke —
jeg vil huske min gamle styrke og hele mit liv i skoven.
Jeg vil ikke sælge min ryg til mennesket for et bundt sukkerrør:
jeg vil tilbage til min egen art, til skovfolket i deres huler.

value.en:
I will go out until the day, until the morning break--
Out to the wind’s untainted kiss, the water’s clean caress;
I will forget my ankle-ring and snap my picket stake.
I will revisit my lost loves, and playmates masterless!
value.da:
Jeg vil ud, indtil dagen, indtil morgenen bryder frem —
ud til vindens uplettede kys, vandets rene kærtegn;
jeg vil glemme min ankelring og knække min pløkpæl.
Jeg vil besøge mine tabte kærligheder og legekammerater uden mester!

value.en: Kala Nag, which means Black Snake, had served the Indian Government in every way that an elephant could serve it for forty-seven years, and as he was fully twenty years old when he was caught, that makes him nearly seventy--a ripe age for an elephant. He remembered pushing, with a big leather pad on his forehead, at a gun stuck in deep mud, and that was before the Afghan War of 1842, and he had not then come to his full strength.
value.da: Kala Nag betyder Sort Slange. I syvogfyrre år havde han tjent den indiske regering i alle de opgaver, en elefant kan klare. Han var allerede tyve år gammel, da han blev fanget, så nu var han næsten halvfjerds — en fin alder for en elefant. Han huskede, at han engang havde skubbet en kanon op af dybt mudder med en tyk lædermadras til at beskytte panden. Det var før krigen i Afghanistan i 1842, dengang han endnu ikke var fuldvoksen.

value.en: His mother Radha Pyari,--Radha the darling,--who had been caught in the same drive with Kala Nag, told him, before his little milk tusks had dropped out, that elephants who were afraid always got hurt. Kala Nag knew that that advice was good, for the first time that he saw a shell burst he backed, screaming, into a stand of piled rifles, and the bayonets pricked him in all his softest places. So, before he was twenty-five, he gave up being afraid, and so he was the best-loved and the best-looked-after elephant in the service of the Government of India. He had carried tents, twelve hundred pounds’ weight of tents, on the march in Upper India. He had been hoisted into a ship at the end of a steam crane and taken for days across the water, and made to carry a mortar on his back in a strange and rocky country very far from India, and had seen the Emperor Theodore lying dead in Magdala, and had come back again in the steamer entitled, so the soldiers said, to the Abyssinian War medal. He had seen his fellow elephants die of cold and epilepsy and starvation and sunstroke up at a place called Ali Musjid, ten years later; and afterward he had been sent down thousands of miles south to haul and pile big balks of teak in the timberyards at Moulmein. There he had half killed an insubordinate young elephant who was shirking his fair share of work.
value.da: Hans mor, Radha Pyari — Radha den elskede — var blevet fanget i samme drev. Før hans mælketænder var faldet ud, fortalte hun ham, at bange elefanter altid kommer til skade. Det viste sig at passe: Første gang en granat sprang tæt ved ham, bakkede han skrigende ind i en stak geværer, og bajonetterne stak ham de allermest ømme steder. Før han blev femogtyve, var han holdt op med at være bange. Ingen elefant i den indiske regerings tjeneste var mere elsket eller bedre passet. Han havde båret tolv hundrede pund telte på march gennem Øvre Indien. Engang var han blevet hejst om bord på et skib med en dampkran og sejlet i dagevis over havet, langt væk fra Indien. I et fjernt, klippefuldt land havde han båret en mørser og set kejser Theodore ligge død i Magdala. Bagefter var han kommet tilbage med dampskibet. Soldaterne sagde, at han havde fortjent den abessinske krigsmedalje for sit arbejde dér. Ti år senere, ved Ali Musjid, havde han set andre elefanter dø af kulde, epilepsi, sult og solstik. Siden var han blevet sendt tusindvis af engelske mil mod syd, til tømmerpladserne i Moulmein, for at slæbe og stable store teaktræsbjælker. Dér havde han næsten dræbt en genstridig ung elefant, som nægtede at tage sin del af arbejdet.

value.en: After that he was taken off timber-hauling, and employed, with a few score other elephants who were trained to the business, in helping to catch wild elephants among the Garo hills. Elephants are very strictly preserved by the Indian Government. There is one whole department which does nothing else but hunt them, and catch them, and break them in, and send them up and down the country as they are needed for work.
value.da: Derefter blev han taget af tømmerarbejdet og sendt af sted med flere dusin trænede elefanter for at hjælpe med at fange vilde elefanter i Garo-bjergene. Den indiske regering passer strengt på elefanterne. Der er en hel afdeling i staten, som kun beskæftiger sig med dem. Dens eneste opgave er at opspore dem, fange dem, tæmme dem til tjeneste og sende dem rundt i landet, hvorhen der er brug for dem til arbejde.

value.en: Kala Nag stood ten fair feet at the shoulders, and his tusks had been cut off short at five feet, and bound round the ends, to prevent them splitting, with bands of copper; but he could do more with those stumps than any untrained elephant could do with the real sharpened ones. When, after weeks and weeks of cautious driving of scattered elephants across the hills, the forty or fifty wild monsters were driven into the last stockade, and the big drop gate, made of tree trunks lashed together, jarred down behind them, Kala Nag, at the word of command, would go into that flaring, trumpeting pandemonium (generally at night, when the flicker of the torches made it difficult to judge distances), and, picking out the biggest and wildest tusker of the mob, would hammer him and hustle him into quiet while the men on the backs of the other elephants roped and tied the smaller ones.
value.da: Kala Nag var hele ti fod høj ved skuldrene. Hans stødtænder var skåret ned til fem fod og havde kobberbånd om enderne, så de ikke kunne flække. Alligevel kunne han udrette mere med de stubbe end en utrænet elefant med spidse, ægte stødtænder. Efter uger med forsigtigt at drive spredte vilde elefanter gennem bjergene kom fyrre eller halvtreds store dyr ind i den sidste indhegning. Bag dem faldt en tung port af sammensurrede træstammer. På kommando gik Kala Nag ind i det flammende, trompeterende kaos — som regel om natten, når flakkende fakler gjorde det svært at se, hvor langt der var til tingene. Af hele flokken udvalgte han den største og mest uregerlige tyr. Så hamrede han løs på ham og puffede ham rundt, til den vilde elefant var rolig nok til at blive styret. Imens bandt mændene på de andre elefanter de mindre fangede dyr med reb.

value.en: There was nothing in the way of fighting that Kala Nag, the old wise Black Snake, did not know, for he had stood up more than once in his time to the charge of the wounded tiger, and, curling up his soft trunk to be out of harm’s way, had knocked the springing brute sideways in mid-air with a quick sickle cut of his head, that he had invented all by himself; had knocked him over, and kneeled upon him with his huge knees till the life went out with a gasp and a howl, and there was only a fluffy striped thing on the ground for Kala Nag to pull by the tail.
value.da: Den gamle, kloge Sorte Slange kendte alle kampens kneb. Mere end én gang havde han mødt en såret tigers angreb. Han krøllede sin sårbare snabel sikkert til side og mødte den springende tiger med et hurtigt, buet sving af hovedet, et slag, han selv havde opfundet. Det slog dyret sidelæns ud af luften. Så knælede Kala Nag på det med sine vældige knæ, til et gisp og et hyl gjorde ende på dets liv. Tilbage på jorden lå kun en blød, stribet bunke, som elefanten kunne trække af sted i halen.

value.en: “Yes,” said Big Toomai, his driver, the son of Black Toomai who had taken him to Abyssinia, and grandson of Toomai of the Elephants who had seen him caught, “there is nothing that the Black Snake fears except me. He has seen three generations of us feed him and groom him, and he will live to see four.”
value.da: »Sorte Slange er ikke bange for nogen undtagen mig,« sagde Store Toomai, hans mahout. Hans far, Sorte Toomai, havde taget Kala Nag med til Abessinien, og hans bedstefar, Toomai af elefanterne, havde set ham blive fanget. »Tre slægtled i vores familie har fodret og plejet ham. Han vil leve længe nok til at se et fjerde.«

value.en: “He is afraid of me also,” said Little Toomai, standing up to his full height of four feet, with only one rag upon him. He was ten years old, the eldest son of Big Toomai, and, according to custom, he would take his father’s place on Kala Nag’s neck when he grew up, and would handle the heavy iron ankus, the elephant goad, that had been worn smooth by his father, and his grandfather, and his great-grandfather.
value.da: »Han er også bange for mig,« sagde Lille Toomai og rejste sig til sin fulde højde på fire fod, kun iført en enkelt klud. Han var ti år gammel, ældste søn af Store Toomai. Efter skik skulle han en dag sidde på Kala Nags nakke i sin fars sted. Han skulle føre den tunge jernankus, krogen, man styrer en elefant med, som var slidt glat af hans far, hans bedstefar og hans oldefar.

value.en: He knew what he was talking of; for he had been born under Kala Nag’s shadow, had played with the end of his trunk before he could walk, had taken him down to water as soon as he could walk, and Kala Nag would no more have dreamed of disobeying his shrill little orders than he would have dreamed of killing him on that day when Big Toomai carried the little brown baby under Kala Nag’s tusks, and told him to salute his master that was to be.
value.da: Han vidste, hvad han sagde. Han var født i Kala Nags skygge, havde leget med spidsen af hans snabel, før han lærte at gå, og havde ført ham ned til vandet, så snart han kunne. Kala Nag ville aldrig drømme om at trodse de skingre kommandoer. Det var heller aldrig faldet ham ind at gøre det lille brune barn noget, dengang Store Toomai bar ham ind under stødtænderne og befalede elefanten at hilse sin kommende herre.

value.en: “Yes,” said Little Toomai, “he is afraid of me,” and he took long strides up to Kala Nag, called him a fat old pig, and made him lift up his feet one after the other.
value.da: »Ja,« sagde Lille Toomai, »han er bange for mig.« Og han tog lange skridt hen til Kala Nag, kaldte ham en fed gammel gris og fik ham til at løfte fødderne én efter én.

value.en: “Wah!” said Little Toomai, “thou art a big elephant,” and he wagged his fluffy head, quoting his father. “The Government may pay for elephants, but they belong to us mahouts. When thou art old, Kala Nag, there will come some rich rajah, and he will buy thee from the Government, on account of thy size and thy manners, and then thou wilt have nothing to do but to carry gold earrings in thy ears, and a gold howdah on thy back, and a red cloth covered with gold on thy sides, and walk at the head of the processions of the King. Then I shall sit on thy neck, O Kala Nag, with a silver ankus, and men will run before us with golden sticks, crying, `Room for the King’s elephant!’ That will be good, Kala Nag, but not so good as this hunting in the jungles.”
value.da: »Vah! Sikke en stor elefant du er,« sagde drengen og rystede sit pjuskede hoved. Han gentog bare sin fars ord. »Regeringen betaler, men elefanterne tilhører os mahouter. Når du bliver gammel, Kala Nag, vil en rig rajah købe dig for din størrelse og dine gode manerer. Så har du ikke andet at lave end at gå forrest i kongens optog. Du får guldringe i ørerne, en gylden howdah (rytterens sæde) på ryggen og et rødt klæde med guld langs siderne. Jeg skal sidde på din nakke, Kala Nag, med en sølvankus. Mænd med gyldne stave løber foran og råber: ›Plads til kongens elefant!‹ Det bliver fint — men ikke så fint som at jage gennem disse jungler.«

value.en: “Umph!” said Big Toomai. “Thou art a boy, and as wild as a buffalo-calf. This running up and down among the hills is not the best Government service. I am getting old, and I do not love wild elephants. Give me brick elephant lines, one stall to each elephant, and big stumps to tie them to safely, and flat, broad roads to exercise upon, instead of this come-and-go camping. Aha, the Cawnpore barracks were good. There was a bazaar close by, and only three hours’ work a day.”
value.da: »Umph!« sagde Store Toomai. »Du er en dreng og lige så vild som en bøffelkalv. At løbe rundt i disse bjerge er ikke regeringens fineste tjeneste. Jeg bliver gammel, og jeg bryder mig ikke om vilde elefanter. Giv mig elefantstalde af mursten, en bås til hver elefant, kraftige pæle at binde dem til og brede, flade veje at motionere dem på, i stedet for al den evige flytten rundt med lejren. Ah, kasernerne i Cawnpore var dejlige. En basar lige i nærheden og kun tre timers arbejde om dagen.«

value.en: Little Toomai remembered the Cawnpore elephant-lines and said nothing. He very much preferred the camp life, and hated those broad, flat roads, with the daily grubbing for grass in the forage reserve, and the long hours when there was nothing to do except to watch Kala Nag fidgeting in his pickets.
value.da: Lille Toomai tænkte på Cawnpore og sagde ingenting. Livet i lejren passede ham langt bedre. Han hadede de brede, flade veje, den daglige græsslåning på foderengen og de lange, tomme timer, hvor han bare kunne se Kala Nag trippe urolig ved sine pæle, uden at der var andet at lave.

value.en: What Little Toomai liked was to scramble up bridle paths that only an elephant could take; the dip into the valley below; the glimpses of the wild elephants browsing miles away; the rush of the frightened pig and peacock under Kala Nag’s feet; the blinding warm rains, when all the hills and valleys smoked; the beautiful misty mornings when nobody knew where they would camp that night; the steady, cautious drive of the wild elephants, and the mad rush and blaze and hullabaloo of the last night’s drive, when the elephants poured into the stockade like boulders in a landslide, found that they could not get out, and flung themselves at the heavy posts only to be driven back by yells and flaring torches and volleys of blank cartridge.
value.da: Han elskede at kravle ad stier, som kun elefanter kunne gå, at styrte ned i dale og få glimt af vilde flokke, der græssede milevis væk. Han elskede grisene og påfuglene, der fór væk fra Kala Nags fødder, den varme, blændende regn, der fik dale og bjerge til at dampe, og de dejlige tågede morgener, hvor ingen vidste, hvor natten ville finde lejren. Han elskede det langsomme, forsigtige arbejde med at drive de vilde elefanter og den sidste nats vilde jagt, flammer og postyr. Da væltede elefanterne ind i indhegningen som stenblokke i et jordskred, opdagede, at de var fanget, og kastede sig mod de kraftige pæle, men veg tilbage for råbende mænd, flammende fakler og salver af løsskud.

value.en: Even a little boy could be of use there, and Toomai was as useful as three boys. He would get his torch and wave it, and yell with the best. But the really good time came when the driving out began, and the Keddah--that is, the stockade--looked like a picture of the end of the world, and men had to make signs to one another, because they could not hear themselves speak. Then Little Toomai would climb up to the top of one of the quivering stockade posts, his sun-bleached brown hair flying loose all over his shoulders, and he looking like a goblin in the torch-light. And as soon as there was a lull you could hear his high-pitched yells of encouragement to Kala Nag, above the trumpeting and crashing, and snapping of ropes, and groans of the tethered elephants. “Mael, mael, Kala Nag! (Go on, go on, Black Snake!) Dant do! (Give him the tusk!) Somalo! Somalo! (Careful, careful!) Maro! Mar! (Hit him, hit him!) Mind the post! Arre! Arre! Hai! Yai! Kya-a-ah!” he would shout, and the big fight between Kala Nag and the wild elephant would sway to and fro across the Keddah, and the old elephant catchers would wipe the sweat out of their eyes, and find time to nod to Little Toomai wriggling with joy on the top of the posts.
value.da: Selv en lille dreng kunne gøre gavn, og Toomai udrettede arbejde for tre. Han svingede sin fakkel og råbte lige så højt som nogen. Det bedste kom, da de drev fangerne ud. Keddahen — indhegningen — lignede verdens ende. Mændene måtte vinke og give hinanden tegn, for hvor højt de end råbte, kunne de ikke høre deres egne stemmer i den vældige larm. Toomai klatrede op på en skælvende pæl med sit solblegede brune hår flagrende over skuldrene og lignede en trold i fakkelskæret. Hver gang larmen stilnede af et øjeblik, kunne man høre Lille Toomais skingre stemme opmuntre Kala Nag. Hans råb steg op over alle trompeterne og braget, over lyden af sprængte reb og stønnen fra elefanter, der kæmpede mod deres bindinger. »Mael, mael, Kala Nag! (Fremad, fremad, Sorte Slange!) Dant do! (Giv ham din stødtand!) Somalo! Somalo! (Forsigtigt, forsigtigt!) Maro! Mar! (Slå ham, slå ham!) Pas på pælen! Arre! Arre! Hai! Yai! Kya-a-ah!« Mens Kala Nag og hans vilde modstander kæmpede sig hen over indhegningen, fandt de gamle, svedende elefantfangere stadig tid til at nikke til drengen, der vred sig af glæde oven over dem.

value.en: He did more than wriggle. One night he slid down from the post and slipped in between the elephants and threw up the loose end of a rope, which had dropped, to a driver who was trying to get a purchase on the leg of a kicking young calf (calves always give more trouble than full-grown animals). Kala Nag saw him, caught him in his trunk, and handed him up to Big Toomai, who slapped him then and there, and put him back on the post.
value.da: Han gjorde mere end at vride sig. En nat gled han ned i indhegningen mellem elefanterne, tog en ende af et reb, der var faldet, og kastede den op til en mahout, der forsøgte at binde benet på en sparkende ung elefant. Kalve giver altid mere besvær end voksne dyr. Kala Nag fik øje på ham, løftede ham med snablen og rakte ham op til Store Toomai. Hans far gav ham straks en lussing og satte ham tilbage på pælen.

value.en: Next morning he gave him a scolding and said, “Are not good brick elephant lines and a little tent carrying enough, that thou must needs go elephant catching on thy own account, little worthless? Now those foolish hunters, whose pay is less than my pay, have spoken to Petersen Sahib of the matter.” Little Toomai was frightened. He did not know much of white men, but Petersen Sahib was the greatest white man in the world to him. He was the head of all the Keddah operations--the man who caught all the elephants for the Government of India, and who knew more about the ways of elephants than any living man.
value.da: Næste morgen skældte hans far ham ud. »Er pæne stalde af mursten og det at bære telte ikke nok? Skal du ud at fange elefanter på egen hånd, din lille værdiløse stakkel? Disse dumme jægere, der får mindre i løn end jeg, har fortalt det til Petersen Sahib.« Lille Toomai blev bange ved tanken. Han vidste ikke ret meget om hvide mænd og deres måder, men for ham var Petersen Sahib den største hvide mand i hele verden. Han ledede alt keddah-arbejdet, fangede elefanter for den indiske regering og forstod dem bedre end nogen anden levende.

value.en: “What--what will happen?” said Little Toomai.
value.da: »Hvad — hvad vil der ske med mig?« spurgte Lille Toomai.

value.en: “Happen! The worst that can happen. Petersen Sahib is a madman. Else why should he go hunting these wild devils? He may even require thee to be an elephant catcher, to sleep anywhere in these fever-filled jungles, and at last to be trampled to death in the Keddah. It is well that this nonsense ends safely. Next week the catching is over, and we of the plains are sent back to our stations. Then we will march on smooth roads, and forget all this hunting. But, son, I am angry that thou shouldst meddle in the business that belongs to these dirty Assamese jungle folk. Kala Nag will obey none but me, so I must go with him into the Keddah, but he is only a fighting elephant, and he does not help to rope them. So I sit at my ease, as befits a mahout,--not a mere hunter,--a mahout, I say, and a man who gets a pension at the end of his service. Is the family of Toomai of the Elephants to be trodden underfoot in the dirt of a Keddah? Bad one! Wicked one! Worthless son! Go and wash Kala Nag and attend to his ears, and see that there are no thorns in his feet. Or else Petersen Sahib will surely catch thee and make thee a wild hunter--a follower of elephant’s foot tracks, a jungle bear. Bah! Shame! Go!”
value.da: »Hvad der vil ske! Det værst tænkelige. Petersen Sahib er gal — hvorfor skulle han ellers jage vilde djævle? Han gør dig måske til elefantfanger, så du må sove hvor som helst i skove fulde af feber, til du bliver trampet ihjel i en keddah. Heldigvis ender dette tåbelige arbejde uden ulykker. Næste uge er fangsten slut, og vi fra sletterne vender tilbage til vores stationer. Så får vi jævne veje igen og ingen jagt mere. Men, min dreng, jeg er vred på dig, fordi du blander dig i noget, der ikke kommer dig ved, noget, der er arbejde for disse beskidte assamesere fra junglen. Kala Nag adlyder kun mig, så jeg må ind i indhegningen. Men han er en kampelefant og ikke en elefant til at binde dyr med reb. Jeg sidder behageligt, som en mahout skal — en mahout, ikke en almindelig jæger, en mand, der har ret til pension, når hans tjeneste er forbi. Skal en mand af slægten Toomai af elefanterne trampes ned i keddahens snavs? Din slemme dreng! Din onde dreng! Din værdiløse søn! Gå og vask Kala Nag, rens hans ører og se efter torne i hans fødder. Ellers tager Petersen Sahib dig helt sikkert og gør dig til en vild jæger, der følger elefantspor som en bjørn i junglen. Bah! Skam dig! Gå!«

value.en: Little Toomai went off without saying a word, but he told Kala Nag all his grievances while he was examining his feet. “No matter,” said Little Toomai, turning up the fringe of Kala Nag’s huge right ear. “They have said my name to Petersen Sahib, and perhaps--and perhaps--and perhaps--who knows? Hai! That is a big thorn that I have pulled out!”
value.da: Lille Toomai gik tavst væk, men mens han undersøgte Kala Nags fødder, fortalte han ham alle sine klager. Han løftede kanten af elefantens store højre øre og sagde: »Det gør ikke noget. De har nævnt mit navn for Petersen Sahib, og måske — måske — måske — hvem ved? Hai! Sikke en kæmpetorn, jeg har trukket ud!«

value.en: The next few days were spent in getting the elephants together, in walking the newly caught wild elephants up and down between a couple of tame ones to prevent them giving too much trouble on the downward march to the plains, and in taking stock of the blankets and ropes and things that had been worn out or lost in the forest.
value.da: I nogle dage samlede de elefanterne og førte hver nyfanget elefant mellem to tamme dyr for at gøre den klar til turen ned til sletterne. De gjorde også status over alle tæpperne, alle rebene og det øvrige udstyr, som var slidt op eller gået tabt i ugerne i skoven.

value.en: Petersen Sahib came in on his clever she-elephant Pudmini; he had been paying off other camps among the hills, for the season was coming to an end, and there was a native clerk sitting at a table under a tree, to pay the drivers their wages. As each man was paid he went back to his elephant, and joined the line that stood ready to start. The catchers, and hunters, and beaters, the men of the regular Keddah, who stayed in the jungle year in and year out, sat on the backs of the elephants that belonged to Petersen Sahib’s permanent force, or leaned against the trees with their guns across their arms, and made fun of the drivers who were going away, and laughed when the newly caught elephants broke the line and ran about.
value.da: Petersen Sahib kom ridende på sin kloge hunelefant Pudmini. Sæsonen var ved at slutte, og han havde udbetalt løn i de andre bjerglejre. Under et træ sad en lokal skriver ved et bord og delte mahouternes løn ud. Når en mand havde fået sin løn, gik han tilbage til sin elefant og stillede sig i rækken, der var ved at drage af sted. De faste keddah-folk — fangere, jægere og drivere, som boede i junglen hele året — sad på Petersen Sahibs egne elefanter eller lænede sig op ad træerne med geværer over armene. De gjorde nar af mahouterne, der skulle af sted til sletterne. Og hver gang en af de nyfangede elefanter brød ud af den ventende række og begyndte at løbe rundt, lo junglefolkene af det postyr, det skabte.

value.en: Big Toomai went up to the clerk with Little Toomai behind him, and Machua Appa, the head tracker, said in an undertone to a friend of his, “There goes one piece of good elephant stuff at least. ’Tis a pity to send that young jungle-cock to molt in the plains.”
value.da: Store Toomai gik hen til skriveren med sin lille søn bag sig. Machua Appa, hovedsporeren, mumlede til en ven: »Der er da i det mindste én, der kan blive en god elefantmand. Det er synd at sende den unge junglehane ned på sletterne for at fælde fjer.«

value.en: Now Petersen Sahib had ears all over him, as a man must have who listens to the most silent of all living things--the wild elephant. He turned where he was lying all along on Pudmini’s back and said, “What is that? I did not know of a man among the plains-drivers who had wit enough to rope even a dead elephant.”
value.da: Petersen Sahib virkede, som om han havde ører over hele kroppen. Den, der lytter efter den vilde elefant, det stilleste af alle levende væsner, må kunne høre hver en lille lyd omkring sig. Han lå udstrakt på Pudminis ryg og vendte sig om. »Hvad var det? Jeg vidste ikke, at nogen mahout fra sletterne havde forstand nok til at binde selv en død elefant.«

value.en: “This is not a man, but a boy. He went into the Keddah at the last drive, and threw Barmao there the rope, when we were trying to get that young calf with the blotch on his shoulder away from his mother.”
value.da: »Ikke en mand, men en dreng. Under det sidste drev gik han ind i keddahen og kastede rebet til Barmao, dengang vi forsøgte at trække den unge kalv med pletten på skulderen væk fra dens mor.«

value.en: Machua Appa pointed at Little Toomai, and Petersen Sahib looked, and Little Toomai bowed to the earth.
value.da: Machua Appa pegede på Lille Toomai, og Petersen Sahib kiggede, og Lille Toomai bøjede sig til jorden.

value.en: “He throw a rope? He is smaller than a picket-pin. Little one, what is thy name?” said Petersen Sahib.
value.da: »Han kastede et reb? Han er mindre end en pløkpæl. Lille ven, hvad hedder du?« sagde Petersen Sahib.

value.en: Little Toomai was too frightened to speak, but Kala Nag was behind him, and Toomai made a sign with his hand, and the elephant caught him up in his trunk and held him level with Pudmini’s forehead, in front of the great Petersen Sahib. Then Little Toomai covered his face with his hands, for he was only a child, and except where elephants were concerned, he was just as bashful as a child could be.
value.da: Lille Toomai var for bange til at svare og pegede bagud på Kala Nag. Elefanten løftede ham med snablen og holdt ham i højde med Pudminis pande, lige foran den store Petersen Sahib. Drengen skjulte ansigtet i hænderne. Han var jo kun et barn, og når der ikke var elefanter i nærheden, var han lige så genert som et hvilket som helst andet barn.

value.en: “Oho!” said Petersen Sahib, smiling underneath his mustache, “and why didst thou teach thy elephant that trick? Was it to help thee steal green corn from the roofs of the houses when the ears are put out to dry?”
value.da: »Oho!« sagde Petersen Sahib og smilede under sit overskæg. »Og hvorfor har du lært din elefant det trick? Var det for at hjælpe dig med at stjæle grøn majs fra hustagene, når aksene lægges ud til tørring?«

value: Too frightened to answer, Little Toomai gestured to Kala Nag behind him. The elephant lifted him in his trunk, holding him level with Pudmini’s forehead before the great Petersen Sahib. The boy hid his face in his hands. After all, he was only a child, and away from elephants he was as shy as any child could be.

value.en: “Not green corn, Protector of the Poor,--melons,” said Little Toomai, and all the men sitting about broke into a roar of laughter. Most of them had taught their elephants that trick when they were boys. Little Toomai was hanging eight feet up in the air, and he wished very much that he were eight feet underground.
value.da: »Ikke grøn majs, De Fattiges Beskytter — meloner,« sagde Lille Toomai, og alle mændene, der sad omkring, brød ud i et brøl af latter. De fleste af dem havde lært deres elefanter det trick, da de var drenge. Lille Toomai hang otte fod oppe i luften, og han ønskede meget gerne, at han var otte fod under jorden.

value.en: “He is Toomai, my son, Sahib,” said Big Toomai, scowling. “He is a very bad boy, and he will end in a jail, Sahib.”
value.da: »Han er Toomai, min søn, Sahib,« sagde Store Toomai med rynket pande. »Han er en meget slem dreng, og han ender i et fængsel, Sahib.«

value.en: “Of that I have my doubts,” said Petersen Sahib. “A boy who can face a full Keddah at his age does not end in jails. See, little one, here are four annas to spend in sweetmeats because thou hast a little head under that great thatch of hair. In time thou mayest become a hunter too.” Big Toomai scowled more than ever. “Remember, though, that Keddahs are not good for children to play in,” Petersen Sahib went on.
value.da: »Det tvivler jeg på,« sagde Petersen Sahib. »Et barn på hans alder, der tør gå ind i en keddah fuld af elefanter, ender ikke i fængsel. Hør, lille ven: her er fire annas (små indiske mønter) til slik. Der er noget værd i det hoved under den store hårmanke. Måske bliver du selv jæger en dag.« Store Toomai rynkede panden endnu mere. »Men husk,« tilføjede Petersen Sahib, »at keddaher ikke er legeplads for børn.«

value.en: “Must I never go there, Sahib?” asked Little Toomai with a big gasp.
value.da: »Må jeg aldrig gå derhen, Sahib?« spurgte Lille Toomai med et stort gisp.

value.en: “Yes.” Petersen Sahib smiled again. “When thou hast seen the elephants dance. That is the proper time. Come to me when thou hast seen the elephants dance, and then I will let thee go into all the Keddahs.”
value.da: »Jo,« sagde Petersen Sahib med endnu et smil, »når du har set elefanterne danse. Det er det rette tidspunkt. Kom og fortæl mig, når du har set deres dans, så giver jeg dig adgang til alle keddaher.«

value.en: There was another roar of laughter, for that is an old joke among elephant-catchers, and it means just never. There are great cleared flat places hidden away in the forests that are called elephants’ ball-rooms, but even these are only found by accident, and no man has ever seen the elephants dance. When a driver boasts of his skill and bravery the other drivers say, “And when didst thou see the elephants dance?”
value.da: Der lød endnu et brøl af latter, for det er en gammel vits blandt elefantfangere, og det betyder simpelthen aldrig. Der er store ryddede flade steder skjult inde i skovene, som kaldes elefanternes balsale, men selv disse findes kun ved tilfælde, og ingen har nogensinde set elefanterne danse. Når en mahout praler af sin færdighed og tapperhed, siger de andre mahouter: »Og hvornår så du elefanterne danse?«

value.en: Kala Nag put Little Toomai down, and he bowed to the earth again and went away with his father, and gave the silver four-anna piece to his mother, who was nursing his baby brother, and they all were put up on Kala Nag’s back, and the line of grunting, squealing elephants rolled down the hill path to the plains. It was a very lively march on account of the new elephants, who gave trouble at every ford, and needed coaxing or beating every other minute.
value.da: Kala Nag satte drengen ned, og han bøjede sig igen til jorden og fulgte sin far. Sølvmønten på fire annas gav han til sin mor, mens hun ammede hans lillebror. Så klatrede alle op på Kala Nag. Den hvinende, gryntende række drog ned mod sletterne. De nyfangede elefanter gjorde turen livlig; de voldte besvær ved hvert vadested og skulle hele tiden enten overtales eller have tæsk.

value.en: Big Toomai prodded Kala Nag spitefully, for he was very angry, but Little Toomai was too happy to speak. Petersen Sahib had noticed him, and given him money, so he felt as a private soldier would feel if he had been called out of the ranks and praised by his commander-in-chief.
value.da: Store Toomai var stadig rasende og stak ondskabsfuldt til Kala Nag. Hans lille søn var alt for glad til at sige noget som helst. Petersen Sahib havde lagt mærke til ham og belønnet ham. Han følte sig som en helt almindelig soldat, der bliver kaldt ud af rækkerne for at blive rost af sin øverstkommanderende.

value.en: “What did Petersen Sahib mean by the elephant dance?” he said, at last, softly to his mother.
value.da: »Hvad mente Petersen Sahib med elefantdansen?« sagde han endelig sagte til sin mor.

value.en: Big Toomai heard him and grunted. “That thou shouldst never be one of these hill buffaloes of trackers. That was what he meant. Oh, you in front, what is blocking the way?”
value.da: Hans far hørte det og gryntede. »Han mente, at du aldrig må blive en af de sporere fra bjergene, der er lige så vilde som bøfler. Det er det hele. Hej, dér foran — hvad spærrer vejen?«

value.en: An Assamese driver, two or three elephants ahead, turned round angrily, crying: “Bring up Kala Nag, and knock this youngster of mine into good behavior. Why should Petersen Sahib have chosen me to go down with you donkeys of the rice fields? Lay your beast alongside, Toomai, and let him prod with his tusks. By all the Gods of the Hills, these new elephants are possessed, or else they can smell their companions in the jungle.” Kala Nag hit the new elephant in the ribs and knocked the wind out of him, as Big Toomai said, “We have swept the hills of wild elephants at the last catch. It is only your carelessness in driving. Must I keep order along the whole line?”
value.da: En assamesisk mahout, to eller tre elefanter foran dem, vendte sig vredt om. »Kom herop med Kala Nag og lær min unge elefant at opføre sig. Hvorfor skulle Petersen Sahib sende mig ned sammen med jer, æsler fra rismarkerne? Kør dit dyr hen ved siden af, Toomai, og lad ham bruge sine stødtænder. Ved alle bjergenes guder, disse fangede dyr er besatte — eller også kan de lugte deres venner i junglen.« Kala Nag stødte den unge elefant i ribbenene, så den tabte vejret. Store Toomai sagde: »Vores sidste drev har ryddet disse bjerge for vilde elefanter. Det er din sjuskede styring, der er problemet. Skal jeg holde orden på hele rækken?«

value.en: “Hear him!” said the other driver. “We have swept the hills! Ho! Ho! You are very wise, you plains people. Anyone but a mud-head who never saw the jungle would know that they know that the drives are ended for the season. Therefore all the wild elephants to-night will--but why should I waste wisdom on a river-turtle?”
value.da: »Hør ham!« hånede mahouten. »Vi har ryddet bjergene! Ho! Ho! Sikke nogle kloge folk fra sletten. Alle andre end et mudderhoved, der aldrig har set en jungle, ville vide, at elefanterne ved, at årets drev er slut. I nat vil alle de vilde elefanter — men hvorfor spilde forstand på en flodskildpadde?«

value.en: “What will they do?” Little Toomai called out.
value.da: »Hvad vil de gøre i nat?« råbte Lille Toomai frem til ham.

value.en: “Ohe, little one. Art thou there? Well, I will tell thee, for thou hast a cool head. They will dance, and it behooves thy father, who has swept all the hills of all the elephants, to double-chain his pickets to-night.”
value.da: »Ohe, lille ven, er du der? Så skal jeg fortælle dig det, for du har et fornuftigt hoved. De vil danse. Din far, som har ryddet alle bjergene for alle elefanter, skulle hellere lænke sine dyr dobbelt i nat.«

value.en: “What talk is this?” said Big Toomai. “For forty years, father and son, we have tended elephants, and we have never heard such moonshine about dances.”
value.da: »Hvad er det for noget sludder?« sagde Store Toomai. »Far og søn har vi passet elefanter i fyrre år, og vi har aldrig hørt sådan noget sludder om dans.«

value.en: “Yes; but a plainsman who lives in a hut knows only the four walls of his hut. Well, leave thy elephants unshackled tonight and see what comes. As for their dancing, I have seen the place where--Bapree-bap! How many windings has the Dihang River? Here is another ford, and we must swim the calves. Stop still, you behind there.”
value.da: »Selvfølgelig. En mand fra sletten kender kun de fire vægge i sin hytte. Lad dine elefanter gå løse i nat og se, hvad der sker. Hvad dansen angår, har jeg set stedet, hvor — Bapree-bap! Hvor mange gange slår Dihang-floden egentlig et sving? Endnu et vadested, og her må kalvene svømme. Stands dér, I bagved!«

value.en: And in this way, talking and wrangling and splashing through the rivers, they made their first march to a sort of receiving camp for the new elephants. But they lost their tempers long before they got there.
value.da: Og på den måde, talende og skændende og plaskende gennem floderne, gjorde de deres første march til en slags modtagelejr for de nye elefanter. Men de mistede tålmodigheden længe før, de nåede frem.

value.en: Then the elephants were chained by their hind legs to their big stumps of pickets, and extra ropes were fitted to the new elephants, and the fodder was piled before them, and the hill drivers went back to Petersen Sahib through the afternoon light, telling the plains drivers to be extra careful that night, and laughing when the plains drivers asked the reason.
value.da: De lænkede elefanternes bagben til tunge pæle, lagde ekstra reb om de nye dyr og stablede foder op foran dem. I eftermiddagslyset vendte bjergmahouterne tilbage til Petersen Sahib. De bad sletternes mahouter være særligt på vagt den nat, og de lo, hver gang nogen spurgte hvorfor.

value.en: Little Toomai attended to Kala Nag’s supper, and as evening fell, wandered through the camp, unspeakably happy, in search of a tom-tom. When an Indian child’s heart is full, he does not run about and make a noise in an irregular fashion. He sits down to a sort of revel all by himself. And Little Toomai had been spoken to by Petersen Sahib! If he had not found what he wanted, I believe he would have been ill. But the sweetmeat seller in the camp lent him a little tom-tom--a drum beaten with the flat of the hand--and he sat down, cross-legged, before Kala Nag as the stars began to come out, the tom-tom in his lap, and he thumped and he thumped and he thumped, and the more he thought of the great honor that had been done to him, the more he thumped, all alone among the elephant fodder. There was no tune and no words, but the thumping made him happy.
value.da: Lille Toomai gav Kala Nag hans aftensmad. Da aftenen nærmede sig, gennemsøgte han lejren, fyldt til randen af lykke, efter en tomtom. Et indisk barn, hvis hjerte er fuldt, løber ikke rundt og råber på må og få; det sætter sig og holder en fest helt for sig selv. Og Petersen Sahib havde talt til Lille Toomai! Jeg tror, han var blevet syg, hvis han ikke havde fundet sin tromme. Slikhandleren lånte ham en lille tomtom, som man spiller på med flad hånd. Da stjernerne kom frem, satte han sig med korslagte ben foran Kala Nag med trommen i skødet. Han trommede og trommede og trommede. Jo mere han mindede sig selv om den store ære, jo hårdere slog han, helt alene blandt elefantfoder. Der var ingen melodi i det og ingen ord til trommeslagene. Han blev bare ved med at tromme, for selve trommeriet gjorde ham glad.

value.en: The new elephants strained at their ropes, and squealed and trumpeted from time to time, and he could hear his mother in the camp hut putting his small brother to sleep with an old, old song about the great God Shiv, who once told all the animals what they should eat. It is a very soothing lullaby, and the first verse says:
value.da: De nye elefanter trak i deres reb og hvinede eller trompeterede nu og da. Fra hytten hørte han sin mor dysse hans lillebror i søvn med en uendelig gammel sang om den store gud Shiv, som tildelte alle dyr deres føde. Det er en meget beroligende vuggevise. Første vers lyder:

value.en:
Shiv, who poured the harvest and made the winds to blow,
Sitting at the doorways of a day of long ago,
Gave to each his portion, food and toil and fate,
From the King upon the _guddee_ to the Beggar at the gate.
All things made he--Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo!  Mahadeo!  He made all--
Thorn for the camel, fodder for the kine,
And mother’s heart for sleepy head, O little son of mine!
value.da:
Shiv, som øste høsten ud og lod vindene blæse,
sad ved dørene en dag for længe siden,
og gav enhver sin del, føde og arbejde og skæbne,
fra kongen på sin _guddee_ til tiggeren ved porten.
Alt skabte han — Shiva Bevareren.
Mahadeo! Mahadeo! Han skabte alt —
torn til kamelen, foder til kvæget,
og moders hjerte til søvnigt hoved, o min lille dreng!

value.en: Little Toomai came in with a joyous tunk-a-tunk at the end of each verse, till he felt sleepy and stretched himself on the fodder at Kala Nag’s side. At last the elephants began to lie down one after another as is their custom, till only Kala Nag at the right of the line was left standing up; and he rocked slowly from side to side, his ears put forward to listen to the night wind as it blew very slowly across the hills. The air was full of all the night noises that, taken together, make one big silence--the click of one bamboo stem against the other, the rustle of something alive in the undergrowth, the scratch and squawk of a half-waked bird (birds are awake in the night much more often than we imagine), and the fall of water ever so far away. Little Toomai slept for some time, and when he waked it was brilliant moonlight, and Kala Nag was still standing up with his ears cocked. Little Toomai turned, rustling in the fodder, and watched the curve of his big back against half the stars in heaven, and while he watched he heard, so far away that it sounded no more than a pinhole of noise pricked through the stillness, the “hoot-toot” of a wild elephant.
value.da: Ved slutningen af hvert vers føjede Lille Toomai et muntert tunk-a-tunk til, til han blev så søvnig, at han strakte sig ud på foderet ved siden af Kala Nag. Efterhånden lagde elefanterne sig ned som sædvanlig. Til sidst stod kun Kala Nag tilbage, oprejst yderst til højre i rækken. Han vuggede langsomt med ørerne fremad og lyttede til den svage nattevind over bjergene. Natteluften var fuld af alle de små lyde, som, når man hører dem sammen, virker som én vældig stilhed over hele skoven: bambusstammer, der klikker mod hinanden, et dyr, der rasler i underskoven, kradsen og skrigen fra en halvt vågen fugl — fugle vågner om natten langt oftere, end vi tror — og vand, der falder langt væk. Toomai sov et stykke tid. Da han vågnede i skarpt måneskin, stod Kala Nag stadig og lyttede. Lille Toomai vendte sig, så det tørre foder raslede under ham, og lå og så på kurven af Kala Nags store ryg mod himlen. Den dækkede halvdelen af stjernerne, når drengen så op på den. Så, uendelig langt væk og som et nålestik gennem stilheden, lød en vild elefants »tut-tut«.

value.en: All the elephants in the lines jumped up as if they had been shot, and their grunts at last waked the sleeping mahouts, and they came out and drove in the picket pegs with big mallets, and tightened this rope and knotted that till all was quiet. One new elephant had nearly grubbed up his picket, and Big Toomai took off Kala Nag’s leg chain and shackled that elephant fore-foot to hind-foot, but slipped a loop of grass string round Kala Nag’s leg, and told him to remember that he was tied fast. He knew that he and his father and his grandfather had done the very same thing hundreds of times before. Kala Nag did not answer to the order by gurgling, as he usually did. He stood still, looking out across the moonlight, his head a little raised and his ears spread like fans, up to the great folds of the Garo hills.
value.da: Alle elefanterne sprang op, som var de blevet skudt. Deres grynt vækkede til sidst mahouterne, som bankede pæle dybere ned med tunge køller, strammede reb, knyttede knuderne om og fik ro igen. En af de fangede elefanter havde næsten revet sin pæl op. Store Toomai tog Kala Nags lænke af og spændte den elefants forfod fast til dens bagfod. I stedet for jernlænken lagde han en løs løkke af græssnor om Kala Nags ben og sagde til den gamle elefant, at han skulle huske, at han var bundet godt fast og ikke måtte gå væk. Både han selv, hans far og hans bedstefar havde gjort det hundredvis af gange. Normalt svarede Kala Nag med en gurglen, men ikke nu. Han stod og så ud over de store folder af Garo-bjergene i måneskin med hovedet en smule løftet og ørerne bredt udspilet.

value.en: “Tend to him if he grows restless in the night,” said Big Toomai to Little Toomai, and he went into the hut and slept. Little Toomai was just going to sleep, too, when he heard the coir string snap with a little “tang,” and Kala Nag rolled out of his pickets as slowly and as silently as a cloud rolls out of the mouth of a valley. Little Toomai pattered after him, barefooted, down the road in the moonlight, calling under his breath, “Kala Nag! Kala Nag! Take me with you, O Kala Nag!” The elephant turned, without a sound, took three strides back to the boy in the moonlight, put down his trunk, swung him up to his neck, and almost before Little Toomai had settled his knees, slipped into the forest.
value.da: »Pas på ham, hvis han bliver urolig,« sagde Store Toomai til sin søn, før han gik i seng igen. Lille Toomai var lige ved at falde i søvn, da han hørte en lille »tang« ved siden af sig: kokossnoren var sprunget. Kala Nag forlod sine pæle lige så langsomt og lydløst som en sky, der forlader en dal. Drengen trippede barfodet efter ham ned ad den måneoplyste vej og hviskede: »Kala Nag! Kala Nag! Tag mig med, Kala Nag!« Lydløst vendte elefanten sig, gik tre skridt tilbage, sænkede snablen og svingede barnet op på sin nakke. Næsten før Toomai havde fået knæene på plads, var de forsvundet ind i skoven.

value.en: There was one blast of furious trumpeting from the lines, and then the silence shut down on everything, and Kala Nag began to move. Sometimes a tuft of high grass washed along his sides as a wave washes along the sides of a ship, and sometimes a cluster of wild-pepper vines would scrape along his back, or a bamboo would creak where his shoulder touched it. But between those times he moved absolutely without any sound, drifting through the thick Garo forest as though it had been smoke. He was going uphill, but though Little Toomai watched the stars in the rifts of the trees, he could not tell in what direction.
value.da: Der lød ét vildt trompetstød fra de lænkede elefanter, så lukkede stilheden sig bag dem. Kala Nag gik videre. Nu og da strejfede højt græs hans sider som bølger mod et skib. Vilde peberranker skrabede hen over hans ryg, eller bambus knirkede mod hans skulder. Men mellem de små lyde kom der ikke en lyd fra den store elefant. Han gled gennem de tætte træer og krat i Garo-skoven så let og lydløst, som var hele skoven kun røg. De gik opad. Selv om Toomai så stjerner gennem hullerne i grenene, kunne han ikke se, hvilken retning de gik.

value.en: Then Kala Nag reached the crest of the ascent and stopped for a minute, and Little Toomai could see the tops of the trees lying all speckled and furry under the moonlight for miles and miles, and the blue-white mist over the river in the hollow. Toomai leaned forward and looked, and he felt that the forest was awake below him--awake and alive and crowded. A big brown fruit-eating bat brushed past his ear; a porcupine’s quills rattled in the thicket; and in the darkness between the tree stems he heard a hog-bear digging hard in the moist warm earth, and snuffing as it digged.
value.da: Oppe på toppen standsede Kala Nag. Trætoppe i måneskin strakte sig milevidt, plettede og lodne at se på, og blåhvid tåge lå over floden dernede. Lille Toomai lænede sig frem over elefantens nakke og kiggede nøje ned i dalen. Han havde en fornemmelse af, at hele skoven under ham var vågen — vågen, levende og fuld af dyr, der bevægede sig rundt. En stor brun frugtflagermus strøg forbi hans øre. Et hulepindsvins pigge raslede i buskene i nærheden. Mellem de mørke stammer gravede en svinebjørn ivrigt i den varme, fugtige jord og snøftede under arbejdet.

value.en: Then the branches closed over his head again, and Kala Nag began to go down into the valley--not quietly this time, but as a runaway gun goes down a steep bank--in one rush. The huge limbs moved as steadily as pistons, eight feet to each stride, and the wrinkled skin of the elbow points rustled. The undergrowth on either side of him ripped with a noise like torn canvas, and the saplings that he heaved away right and left with his shoulders sprang back again and banged him on the flank, and great trails of creepers, all matted together, hung from his tusks as he threw his head from side to side and plowed out his pathway. Then Little Toomai laid himself down close to the great neck lest a swinging bough should sweep him to the ground, and he wished that he were back in the lines again.
value.da: Grenene lukkede sig over dem, og Kala Nag gik ned i dalen. Denne gang listede han ikke: han fór af sted som en løbsk kanon ned ad en stejl skrænt. De enorme ben arbejdede jævnt som stempler og tog otte fod i hvert skridt; den rynkede hud ved albuerne raslede. Underskoven revnede til begge sider som lærred. Unge træer, som hans skuldre skubbede til side, smækkede tilbage mod hans flanker. Sammenfiltrede slyngplanter hang fra hans stødtænder, mens hans svingende hoved pløjede en vej. Lille Toomai lagde sig så fladt, han kunne, tæt ind til elefantens store nakke. Han var bange for, at en af de grene, der svingede tilbage over deres vej, ville feje ham af og kaste ham til jorden. Han ønskede af hele sit hjerte, at han var tilbage blandt de lænkede elefanter.

value.en: The grass began to get squashy, and Kala Nag’s feet sucked and squelched as he put them down, and the night mist at the bottom of the valley chilled Little Toomai. There was a splash and a trample, and the rush of running water, and Kala Nag strode through the bed of a river, feeling his way at each step. Above the noise of the water, as it swirled round the elephant’s legs, Little Toomai could hear more splashing and some trumpeting both upstream and down--great grunts and angry snortings, and all the mist about him seemed to be full of rolling, wavy shadows.
value.da: Græsset blev vådt, og hvert tungt skridt sugede og sjaskede. Dalens tåge kølede drengen. Plasken og trampen bar dem ud i strømmende vand, og Kala Nag krydsede flodlejet og mærkede sig frem ved hvert skridt. Over lyden af vandet, der hvirvlede om elefantens ben, kunne Lille Toomai høre endnu mere plasken. Både opstrøms og nedstrøms lød trompeten, store dybe grynt og vrede prusten fra andre dyr, der krydsede floden. Rundt om ham syntes tågen fuld af ustadige, bevægelige skygger.

value.en: “Ai!” he said, half aloud, his teeth chattering. “The elephant-folk are out tonight. It is the dance, then!”
value.da: »Ai!« mumlede han med klaprende tænder. »Elefantfolket er ude i nat. Så må det her være deres dans!«

value.en: Kala Nag swashed out of the water, blew his trunk clear, and began another climb. But this time he was not alone, and he had not to make his path. That was made already, six feet wide, in front of him, where the bent jungle-grass was trying to recover itself and stand up. Many elephants must have gone that way only a few minutes before. Little Toomai looked back, and behind him a great wild tusker with his little pig’s eyes glowing like hot coals was just lifting himself out of the misty river. Then the trees closed up again, and they went on and up, with trumpetings and crashings, and the sound of breaking branches on every side of them.
value.da: Kala Nag kom plaskende op af floden, blæste vand ud af snablen og begyndte at stige igen. Nu var der andre med ham, og han behøvede ikke at bane en ny sti. Foran dem strakte sig allerede en seks fod bred åbning, hvor det nedtrampede junglegræs stadig kæmpede for at rejse sig. Drengen kunne se, at mange elefanter måtte have fulgt netop den sti kun få minutter, før Kala Nag nåede den. Da Toomai så tilbage, så han en vældig vild tyr rejse sig op af den tågede flod, mens dens små grisøjne glødede som kul. Så skjulte træerne den igen. De fortsatte opad, omgivet af trompetstød, brag og knækkende grene på alle sider.

value.en: At last Kala Nag stood still between two tree-trunks at the very top of the hill. They were part of a circle of trees that grew round an irregular space of some three or four acres, and in all that space, as Little Toomai could see, the ground had been trampled down as hard as a brick floor. Some trees grew in the center of the clearing, but their bark was rubbed away, and the white wood beneath showed all shiny and polished in the patches of moonlight. There were creepers hanging from the upper branches, and the bells of the flowers of the creepers, great waxy white things like convolvuluses, hung down fast asleep. But within the limits of the clearing there was not a single blade of green--nothing but the trampled earth.
value.da: På toppen af bakken standsede Kala Nag mellem to stammer i en ring af træer, der omgav en ujævn lysning på tre eller fire acre (et par fodboldbaner). Overalt derinde var jorden trampet så hård som et gulv af mursten. Et par træer stod midt i lysningen med barken gnedet af, så det hvide træ lyste blankt og poleret i pletterne af måneskin. Slyngplanter hang ned fra de øverste grene. Deres store, voksagtige hvide klokker, der lignede snerleblomster, hang og sov. Men uanset hvor drengen så hen inden for lysningens grænser, søgte han forgæves efter noget grønt, der voksede på jorden. Der var ikke så meget som ét græsstrå tilbage. Under træerne var der intet andet end den hårde jord, som elefanterne havde trampet.

value.en: The moonlight showed it all iron gray, except where some elephants stood upon it, and their shadows were inky black. Little Toomai looked, holding his breath, with his eyes starting out of his head, and as he looked, more and more and more elephants swung out into the open from between the tree trunks. Little Toomai could only count up to ten, and he counted again and again on his fingers till he lost count of the tens, and his head began to swim. Outside the clearing he could hear them crashing in the undergrowth as they worked their way up the hillside, but as soon as they were within the circle of the tree trunks they moved like ghosts.
value.da: Måneskinnet gjorde jorden jerngrå, og skyggerne under de stående elefanter var sorte som blæk. Lille Toomai holdt vejret og stirrede så hårdt, at øjnene næsten stod ud af hovedet. Mens han kiggede, svingede flere elefanter, og flere, og endnu flere ud i det åbne mellem træstammerne. Han kunne kun tælle til ti. Igen og igen talte han på fingrene, til han mistede tællingen af tiere, og hovedet svimlede. Udenfor brasede elefanter gennem underskoven, mens de klatrede op ad bjergsiden. Men i det øjeblik de kom ind i træernes ring, blev deres bevægelser spøgelsesagtigt lydløse.

value.en: There were white-tusked wild males, with fallen leaves and nuts and twigs lying in the wrinkles of their necks and the folds of their ears; fat, slow-footed she-elephants, with restless, little pinky black calves only three or four feet high running under their stomachs; young elephants with their tusks just beginning to show, and very proud of them; lanky, scraggy old-maid elephants, with their hollow anxious faces, and trunks like rough bark; savage old bull elephants, scarred from shoulder to flank with great weals and cuts of bygone fights, and the caked dirt of their solitary mud baths dropping from their shoulders; and there was one with a broken tusk and the marks of the full-stroke, the terrible drawing scrape, of a tiger’s claws on his side.
value.da: De vilde hanner havde lange hvide stødtænder og faldne blade, nødder og kviste i halsens rynker og ørernes folder. Tykke hunner gik langsomt, mens rastløse, lyserødsorte kalve på tre eller fire fod løb under deres maver. Unge dyr viste stolt deres nye stødtænder frem. Der var ranglede, magre gamle jomfruer med hule, bekymrede ansigter og snabler så ru som bark, og vilde gamle tyre, ar fra skulder til flanke efter gamle kampe, med tørret mudder fra ensomme bade, der smuldrede af deres skuldre. En havde en brækket stødtand og det lange, forfærdelige mærke efter en tigers fulde kløerslag ned ad siden.

value.en: They were standing head to head, or walking to and fro across the ground in couples, or rocking and swaying all by themselves--scores and scores of elephants.
value.da: De stod hoved mod hoved, eller gik frem og tilbage hen over jorden i par, eller vuggede og svajede helt for sig selv — snese og snese af elefanter.

value.en: Toomai knew that so long as he lay still on Kala Nag’s neck nothing would happen to him, for even in the rush and scramble of a Keddah drive a wild elephant does not reach up with his trunk and drag a man off the neck of a tame elephant. And these elephants were not thinking of men that night. Once they started and put their ears forward when they heard the chinking of a leg iron in the forest, but it was Pudmini, Petersen Sahib’s pet elephant, her chain snapped short off, grunting, snuffling up the hillside. She must have broken her pickets and come straight from Petersen Sahib’s camp; and Little Toomai saw another elephant, one that he did not know, with deep rope galls on his back and breast. He, too, must have run away from some camp in the hills about.
value.da: Toomai vidste, at han var i sikkerhed, så længe han lå stille på Kala Nag. Selv i en vild keddah-jagt rækker vilde elefanter ikke op og trækker ryttere ned fra tamme elefanters nakke. Den nat tænkte de slet ikke på mennesker. Én gang fór de alle sammen op og stillede ørerne frem, da de hørte jern klirre i skoven. Men det var Petersen Sahibs yndlingselefant Pudmini, der gryntende og snusende kom op ad bakken med en kæde, der var sprængt over. Hun måtte være sluppet løs fra sine pæle og være kommet direkte fra hans lejr. Lille Toomai så også en anden elefant, som han slet ikke kendte. Dybe rebsår prægede dens ryg og bryst. Den måtte også være undsluppet fra en lejr i bjergene omkring.

value.en: At last there was no sound of any more elephants moving in the forest, and Kala Nag rolled out from his station between the trees and went into the middle of the crowd, clucking and gurgling, and all the elephants began to talk in their own tongue, and to move about.
value.da: Til sidst kunne man ikke høre flere elefanter komme gennem skoven. Kala Nag forlod sin plads mellem træerne og gik ind i mængden, klukkende og gurglende. Rundt om ham begyndte hele forsamlingen at bevæge sig og tale på sit eget sprog.

value.en: Still lying down, Little Toomai looked down upon scores and scores of broad backs, and wagging ears, and tossing trunks, and little rolling eyes. He heard the click of tusks as they crossed other tusks by accident, and the dry rustle of trunks twined together, and the chafing of enormous sides and shoulders in the crowd, and the incessant flick and hissh of the great tails. Then a cloud came over the moon, and he sat in black darkness. But the quiet, steady hustling and pushing and gurgling went on just the same. He knew that there were elephants all round Kala Nag, and that there was no chance of backing him out of the assembly; so he set his teeth and shivered. In a Keddah at least there was torchlight and shouting, but here he was all alone in the dark, and once a trunk came up and touched him on the knee.
value.da: Toomai lå fladt ned og så ud over snesevis af brede rygge, baskende ører, slyngende snabler og rullende små øjne. Stødtænder klikkede, når de tilfældigt krydsede hinanden; sammenslyngede snabler raslede tørt. Enorme skuldre og sider gned mod hinanden, og store haler piskede og hvislede uafbrudt. En sky dækkede månen, og han blev efterladt i sort mørke. Alligevel fortsatte den stille, jævne skubben og puffen på nøjagtig samme måde som før. Elefanterne blev ved med at bakse og gurgle til hinanden rundt om ham, selv om han nu ikke kunne se dem. Elefanter omgav Kala Nag; det var umuligt at bakke ud. Drengen bed tænderne sammen og rystede. I en keddah var der i det mindste råbende mænd og fakkelskær. Her lå han alene i mørket. Én gang kom en snabel op og rørte ved hans knæ.

value.en: Then an elephant trumpeted, and they all took it up for five or ten terrible seconds. The dew from the trees above spattered down like rain on the unseen backs, and a dull booming noise began, not very loud at first, and Little Toomai could not tell what it was. But it grew and grew, and Kala Nag lifted up one forefoot and then the other, and brought them down on the ground--one-two, one-two, as steadily as trip-hammers. The elephants were stamping all together now, and it sounded like a war drum beaten at the mouth of a cave.
