39 EN “That depends,” said the troop-horse. “Generally I have to go in among a lot of yelling, hairy men with knives--long shiny knives, worse than the farrier’s knives--and I have to take care that Dick’s boot is just touching the next man’s boot without crushing it. I can see Dick’s lance to the right of my right eye, and I know I’m safe. I shouldn’t care to be the man or horse that stood up to Dick and me when we’re in a hurry.”
DA »Det varierer,« svarede hesten. »Som regel skal jeg lige ind i en flok skrigende, behårede mænd med lange, glinsende knive, værre end hovsmedens. Dicks støvle skal netop røre naboens uden at knuse den. Jeg ser hans lanse ved mit højre øje og ved, at jeg er sikker. Jeg ville ikke ønske at være manden eller hesten, der spærrer vejen for os, når vi har travlt.«

40 EN “Don’t the knives hurt?” said the young mule.
DA »Kan de knive gøre dig ondt?« spurgte det unge muldyr.

41 EN “Well, I got one cut across the chest once, but that wasn’t Dick’s fault--”
DA »Engang fik jeg et snit på tværs af brystet, men det var ikke Dicks skyld —«

42 EN “A lot I should have cared whose fault it was, if it hurt!” said the young mule.
DA »Jeg ville være ligeglad med, hvis skyld det var, hvis det gjorde ondt!« sagde det unge muldyr.

43 EN “You must,” said the troop horse. “If you don’t trust your man, you may as well run away at once. That’s what some of our horses do, and I don’t blame them. As I was saying, it wasn’t Dick’s fault. The man was lying on the ground, and I stretched myself not to tread on him, and he slashed up at me. Next time I have to go over a man lying down I shall step on him--hard.”
DA »Det er man nødt til,« svarede hesten. »Hvis man ikke stoler på sin rytter, kan man lige så godt stikke af med det samme. Det gør nogle heste, og jeg bebrejder dem ikke. Som sagt var det ikke Dicks skyld. En mand lå på jorden, og jeg strakte mig for ikke at træde på ham, og så huggede han opad. Næste gang jeg går hen over en faldet mand, træder jeg lige ned på ham.«

44 EN “H’m!” said Billy. “It sounds very foolish. Knives are dirty things at any time. The proper thing to do is to climb up a mountain with a well-balanced saddle, hang on by all four feet and your ears too, and creep and crawl and wriggle along, till you come out hundreds of feet above anyone else on a ledge where there’s just room enough for your hoofs. Then you stand still and keep quiet--never ask a man to hold your head, young un--keep quiet while the guns are being put together, and then you watch the little poppy shells drop down into the tree-tops ever so far below.”
DA »Hm!« sagde Billy. »Det lyder tåbeligt. Knive er ubehagelige, uanset hvornår. Rigtig kamp er at klatre op ad et bjerg med en velafbalanceret sadel og hænge fast med alle fire fødder og ørerne også. Man kryber, kravler og vrider sig, til man er flere hundrede fod over alle andre, på en hylde, der knap er bred nok til hovene. Så skal man stå helt stille — og bed ikke nogen om at holde dit hoved, unge — mens mændene samler kanonerne. Bagefter kan man se de små smældende granater falde ned mellem trætoppene langt, langt nedenfor.«

45 EN “Don’t you ever trip?” said the troop-horse.
DA »Snubler I aldrig deroppe?« spurgte hesten.

46 EN “They say that when a mule trips you can split a hen’s ear,” said Billy. “Now and again perhaps a badly packed saddle will upset a mule, but it’s very seldom. I wish I could show you our business. It’s beautiful. Why, it took me three years to find out what the men were driving at. The science of the thing is never to show up against the sky line, because, if you do, you may get fired at. Remember that, young un. Always keep hidden as much as possible, even if you have to go a mile out of your way. I lead the battery when it comes to that sort of climbing.”
DA »Man siger, at når et muldyr snubler, kan man flække et hønseøre,« svarede Billy. »En dårligt afbalanceret last kan nogle gange vælte et muldyr, men det er sjældent. Jeg ville ønske, du kunne se vores arbejde. Det er smukt. Det tog mig hele tre år at finde ud af, hvad mændene egentlig ville have, jeg skulle gøre, og forstå, hvad de prøvede at opnå. Det vigtigste trick er aldrig at tegne sig mod horisonten, for så bliver man skudt på. Husk det, unge. Hold dig skjult, selv om det betyder en omvej på en engelsk mil. Når batteriet skal klatre sådan, er det mig, der fører hele flokken op ad bjerget.«

47 EN “Fired at without the chance of running into the people who are firing!” said the troop-horse, thinking hard. “I couldn’t stand that. I should want to charge--with Dick.”
DA »Man bliver skudt på uden at kunne storme ind på dem, der skyder!« sagde hesten og tænkte meget grundigt over det. »Umuligt for mig. Jeg ville storme af sted sammen med Dick.«

48 EN “Oh, no, you wouldn’t. You know that as soon as the guns are in position they’ll do all the charging. That’s scientific and neat. But knives--pah!”
DA »Nej, det ville du ikke. Så snart kanonerne er i stilling, klarer de selv stormløbet. Det er ordentligt og videnskabeligt. Men knive — pah!«

49 EN The baggage-camel had been bobbing his head to and fro for some time past, anxious to get a word in edgewise. Then I heard him say, as he cleared his throat, nervously:
DA Bagagekamelen havde vippet sit hoved frem og tilbage et stykke tid, ivrig efter at få et ord indført. Så hørte jeg ham sige, mens han nervøst rømmede sig:

50 EN “I--I--I have fought a little, but not in that climbing way or that running way.”
DA »Jeg — jeg — jeg har set lidt kamp, men der var hverken klatring eller løb.«

51 EN “No. Now you mention it,” said Billy, “you don’t look as though you were made for climbing or running--much. Well, how was it, old Hay-bales?”
DA »Nej, nu du nævner det,« sagde Billy, »ser du ikke ud, som om du er skabt til meget klatring eller løb. Fortæl, gamle Høbylte, hvordan klarede du det?«

52 EN “The proper way,” said the camel. “We all sat down--”
DA »På den rette måde,« sagde kamelen. »Vi satte os alle ned —«

53 EN “Oh, my crupper and breastplate!” said the troop-horse under his breath. “Sat down!”
DA »Min halerem og min brystrem!« mumlede hesten. »De satte sig ned!«

54 EN “We sat down--a hundred of us,” the camel went on, “in a big square, and the men piled our packs and saddles, outside the square, and they fired over our backs, the men did, on all sides of the square.”
DA »Hundrede af os satte os i en stor firkant,« fortsatte kamelen. »Mændene stablede vores pakker og sadler uden for den. Så skød de hen over vores rygge fra alle fire sider.«

55 EN “What sort of men? Any men that came along?” said the troop-horse. “They teach us in riding school to lie down and let our masters fire across us, but Dick Cunliffe is the only man I’d trust to do that. It tickles my girths, and, besides, I can’t see with my head on the ground.”
DA »Hvilke mænd? Hvem som helst, der kom forbi?« spurgte hesten. »På rideskolen lærer de os at lægge os ned, så vores ryttere kan skyde hen over os. Men det er kun Dick Cunliffe, jeg ville stole nok på til at gøre det. Det kilder under bugremmene, og desuden kan jeg ikke se noget med hovedet nede.«

56 EN “What does it matter who fires across you?” said the camel. “There are plenty of men and plenty of other camels close by, and a great many clouds of smoke. I am not frightened then. I sit still and wait.”
DA »Hvorfor skulle det gøre noget, hvem der skyder?« spurgte kamelen. »Jeg har mange mænd og kameler omkring mig og store skyer af røg. Så er jeg ikke bange. Jeg sidder og venter helt roligt.«

57 EN “And yet,” said Billy, “you dream bad dreams and upset the camp at night. Well, well! Before I’d lie down, not to speak of sitting down, and let a man fire across me, my heels and his head would have something to say to each other. Did you ever hear anything so awful as that?”
DA »Og alligevel har du dårlige drømme og ødelægger alles lejr midt om natten,« bemærkede Billy. »Nå, nå! Før jeg ville lægge mig — slet ikke sætte mig — for at en mand kunne skyde hen over mig, ville mine hæle tage en samtale med hans hoved. Har du nogensinde hørt noget mere forfærdeligt?«

58 EN There was a long silence, and then one of the gun bullocks lifted up his big head and said, “This is very foolish indeed. There is only one way of fighting.”
DA Efter en lang tavshed løftede en af studene sit store hoved. »Det er alt sammen meget tåbeligt,« sagde han. »Der er kun én måde at kæmpe på.«

59 EN “Oh, go on,” said Billy. “Please don’t mind me. I suppose you fellows fight standing on your tails?”
DA »Sig frem,« svarede Billy. »Lad mig ikke stoppe jer. Jeg går ud fra, at I herrer kæmper stående på halen?«

60 EN “Only one way,” said the two together. (They must have been twins.) “This is that way. To put all twenty yoke of us to the big gun as soon as Two Tails trumpets.” (“Two Tails” is camp slang for the elephant.)
DA »Kun én måde,« sagde de i kor — de måtte være tvillinger. »I det øjeblik To Haler trompeterer, bliver alle tyve åg af os spændt for den tunge kanon.« To Haler er lejrens kælenavn for en elefant.

61 EN “What does Two Tails trumpet for?” said the young mule.
DA »Hvorfor trompeterer To Haler?« sagde det unge muldyr.

62 EN “To show that he is not going any nearer to the smoke on the other side. Two Tails is a great coward. Then we tug the big gun all together--Heya--Hullah! Heeyah! Hullah! We do not climb like cats nor run like calves. We go across the level plain, twenty yoke of us, till we are unyoked again, and we graze while the big guns talk across the plain to some town with mud walls, and pieces of the wall fall out, and the dust goes up as though many cattle were coming home.”
DA »For at fortælle, at han ikke vil gå tættere på røgen over for os. To Haler er en stor kujon. Så trækker vi kanonen sammen — Heya — Hullah! Heeyah! Hullah! Vi behøver ikke klatre rundt som katte, og vi løber heller ikke rundt som unge kalve. Alle tyve par går over den flade slette, indtil vi bliver spændt fra. Vi græsser, mens kanonerne taler henover sletten til en by med lermure. Stykker falder af murene og rejser støv som en flok kvæg, der kommer hjem.«

63 EN “Oh! And you choose that time for grazing?” said the young mule.
DA »Åh! Og det tidspunkt vælger I til at græsse?« sagde det unge muldyr.

64 EN “That time or any other. Eating is always good. We eat till we are yoked up again and tug the gun back to where Two Tails is waiting for it. Sometimes there are big guns in the city that speak back, and some of us are killed, and then there is all the more grazing for those that are left. This is Fate. None the less, Two Tails is a great coward. That is the proper way to fight. We are brothers from Hapur. Our father was a sacred bull of Shiva. We have spoken.”
DA »Da eller når som helst. Mad er altid velkommen. Vi spiser, indtil vi bliver spændt for igen, og så trækker vi kanonen tilbage til To Haler, der venter. Nogle gange svarer kanonerne inde i byen og dræber nogle af os. Så er der mere græs til dem, der er tilbage. Det er skæbnen. Alligevel er To Haler en kujon. Vores måde er den rette måde at kæmpe på. Vi er brødre fra Hapur, sønner af Shivas hellige tyr. Vi har sagt, hvad vi ville sige.«

65 EN “Well, I’ve certainly learned something tonight,” said the troop-horse. “Do you gentlemen of the screw-gun battery feel inclined to eat when you are being fired at with big guns, and Two Tails is behind you?”
DA »Nå, i aften har jeg lært noget,« bemærkede hesten. »I herrer fra skruekanon-batteriet — har I lyst til at spise under kraftig artilleriild, mens To Haler venter bag jer?«

66 EN “About as much as we feel inclined to sit down and let men sprawl all over us, or run into people with knives. I never heard such stuff. A mountain ledge, a well-balanced load, a driver you can trust to let you pick your own way, and I’m your mule. But--the other things--no!” said Billy, with a stamp of his foot.
DA »Lige så meget som at lægge os ned, så mænd kan vælte sig hen over os, eller at storme ind på knive,« sagde Billy og stampede. »Sikke noget vrøvl. Giv mig en bjergafsats, en velafbalanceret last og en fører, der stoler på, at jeg selv vælger, hvor jeg sætter fødderne, så er jeg dit muldyr. Men ingen af de andre ting!«

67 EN “Of course,” said the troop horse, “everyone is not made in the same way, and I can quite see that your family, on your father’s side, would fail to understand a great many things.”
DA »Selvfølgelig,« svarede hesten, »er ikke alle skabt på nøjagtig samme måde. Jeg forestiller mig, at din familie på din fars side ville have svært ved at forstå en hel del ting.«

68 EN “Never you mind my family on my father’s side,” said Billy angrily, for every mule hates to be reminded that his father was a donkey. “My father was a Southern gentleman, and he could pull down and bite and kick into rags every horse he came across. Remember that, you big brown Brumby!”
DA »Lad min fars familie være ude af det,« snerrede Billy. Muldyr hader at blive mindet om, at deres fædre var æsler. »Min far var en gentleman fra Syden. Han kunne trække enhver hest, han mødte, ned, bide den og sparke den i laser. Husk det, din store brune Brumby!«

69 EN Brumby means wild horse without any breeding. Imagine the feelings of Sunol if a car-horse called her a “skate,” and you can imagine how the Australian horse felt. I saw the white of his eye glitter in the dark.
DA En Brumby er en vild hest uden stamtavle. Forestil dig, hvor rasende Sunol, en berømt væddeløbshest, ville blive, hvis en vognhest kaldte hende en »krikke« — så forstår du, hvad australieren følte. Det hvide i hans øjne glimtede i mørket.

70 EN “See here, you son of an imported Malaga jackass,” he said between his teeth, “I’d have you know that I’m related on my mother’s side to Carbine, winner of the Melbourne Cup, and where I come from we aren’t accustomed to being ridden over roughshod by any parrot-mouthed, pig-headed mule in a pop-gun pea-shooter battery. Are you ready?”
DA »Hør her, din søn af et importeret æsel fra Malaga,« sagde han gennem sammenbidte tænder. »På min mors side er jeg i familie med Carbine, vinderen af Melbourne Cup. Hvor jeg kommer fra, lader vi os ikke trampe ned af et stædigt muldyr med papegøjemund fra et legetøjsbatteri med ærteskydere. Er du klar?«

71 EN “On your hind legs!” squealed Billy. They both reared up facing each other, and I was expecting a furious fight, when a gurgly, rumbly voice, called out of the darkness to the right--“Children, what are you fighting about there? Be quiet.”
DA »Op på bagbenene!« hvinede Billy. De stejlede begge og stod over for hinanden. Jeg ventede en vild kamp, men så lød der en dyb, boblende rumlen fra mørket til højre: »Børn, hvorfor slås I? Vær nu stille.«

72 EN Both beasts dropped down with a snort of disgust, for neither horse nor mule can bear to listen to an elephant’s voice.
DA Begge dyr faldt ned med et fnys af afsky, for hverken hest eller muldyr kan udholde at lytte til en elefants stemme.

73 EN “It’s Two Tails!” said the troop-horse. “I can’t stand him. A tail at each end isn’t fair!”
DA »Det er To Haler!« sagde hesten. »Jeg kan ikke fordrage ham. En hale i hver ende er ikke fair!«

74 EN “My feelings exactly,” said Billy, crowding into the troop-horse for company. “We’re very alike in some things.”
DA »Præcis min mening,« sagde Billy og trykkede sig op ad hesten for at få trøst. »På nogle punkter ligner vi hinanden meget.«

75 EN “I suppose we’ve inherited them from our mothers,” said the troop horse. “It’s not worth quarreling about. Hi! Two Tails, are you tied up?”
DA »Måske gennem vores mødre,« sagde hesten. »Det er næppe værd at skændes om. Hej! To Haler, har de bundet dig?«

76 EN “Yes,” said Two Tails, with a laugh all up his trunk. “I’m picketed for the night. I’ve heard what you fellows have been saying. But don’t be afraid. I’m not coming over.”
DA »Ja,« lød det med en latter, der løb hele vejen gennem snabelen. »Jeg er bundet fast for natten. Jeg hørte, hvad I sagde. Men vær ikke bange. Jeg kommer ikke nærmere.«

77 EN The bullocks and the camel said, half aloud, “Afraid of Two Tails--what nonsense!” And the bullocks went on, “We are sorry that you heard, but it is true. Two Tails, why are you afraid of the guns when they fire?”
DA »Bange for To Haler — sikke noget vrøvl!« mumlede kamelen og studene. Studene tilføjede: »Beklager, at du hørte det, men vi sagde sandheden. To Haler, hvorfor er du så bange for kanonerne, når de begynder at skyde?«

78 EN “Well,” said Two Tails, rubbing one hind leg against the other, exactly like a little boy saying a poem, “I don’t quite know whether you’d understand.”
DA »Tja,« svarede han og gned bagbenene mod hinanden som et barn, der siger et digt op, »jeg er ikke sikker på, at I kan forstå det.«

79 EN “We don’t, but we have to pull the guns,” said the bullocks.
DA »Det gør vi ikke, men vi skal trække kanonerne,« sagde studene.

80 EN “I know it, and I know you are a good deal braver than you think you are. But it’s different with me. My battery captain called me a Pachydermatous Anachronism the other day.”
DA »Det ved jeg, og jeg ved, at I er en del modigere, end I tror. Men det er anderledes med mig. Min batterikaptajn kaldte mig en Pakydermatisk Anakronisme forleden dag.«

81 EN “That’s another way of fighting, I suppose?” said Billy, who was recovering his spirits.
DA »Det er vel endnu en måde at kæmpe på?« sagde Billy, der var ved at komme i bedre humør.

82 EN “You don’t know what that means, of course, but I do. It means betwixt and between, and that is just where I am. I can see inside my head what will happen when a shell bursts, and you bullocks can’t.”
DA »I ved selvfølgelig ikke, hvad det betyder, men det gør jeg. Det betyder midt imellem, og det er præcis, hvor jeg er. Jeg kan se inde i mit hoved, hvad der vil ske, når en granat sprænger, og det kan I stude ikke.«

83 EN “I can,” said the troop-horse. “At least a little bit. I try not to think about it.”
DA »Det kan jeg,« sagde hesten. »I hvert fald en lille smule. Jeg prøver at lade være med at tænke på det.«

84 EN “I can see more than you, and I do think about it. I know there’s a great deal of me to take care of, and I know that nobody knows how to cure me when I’m sick. All they can do is to stop my driver’s pay till I get well, and I can’t trust my driver.”
DA »Jeg ser mere end I, og jeg bliver ved med at tænke på det. Der er en hel masse krop for mig at passe på. Ingen ved, hvordan man helbreder mig, hvis jeg bliver syg. De holder bare min førers løn tilbage, til jeg er rask igen, og jeg stoler ikke på ham.«

85 EN “Ah!” said the troop horse. “That explains it. I can trust Dick.”
DA »Ah!« sagde hesten. »Det forklarer det hele. Jeg ved, at jeg kan stole på Dick.«

86 EN “You could put a whole regiment of Dicks on my back without making me feel any better. I know just enough to be uncomfortable, and not enough to go on in spite of it.”
DA »Du kunne sætte et helt regiment af Dicks på min ryg, uden at det ville få mig til at føle mig bedre tilpas. Jeg ved nok til at være utilpas og ikke nok til at fortsætte trods det.«

87 EN “We do not understand,” said the bullocks.
DA »Vi forstår ikke,« sagde studene.

88 EN “I know you don’t. I’m not talking to you. You don’t know what blood is.”
DA »Selvfølgelig kan I ikke det. Jeg talte ikke til jer. I ved ikke engang, hvad blod er.«

89 EN “We do,” said the bullocks. “It is red stuff that soaks into the ground and smells.”
DA »Det gør vi,« svarede de. »Det er noget rødt, der lugter og siver ned i jorden.«

90 EN The troop-horse gave a kick and a bound and a snort.
DA Tropshesten gav et spark og et hop og et fnys.

91 EN “Don’t talk of it,” he said. “I can smell it now, just thinking of it. It makes me want to run--when I haven’t Dick on my back.”
DA »Tal ikke om det,« sagde han. »Bare ved at tænke på det kan jeg lugte det igen. Jeg får lyst til at stikke af — medmindre Dick rider på mig.«

92 EN “But it is not here,” said the camel and the bullocks. “Why are you so stupid?”
DA »Men der er ingen her,« indvendte kamelen og studene. »Hvorfor opfører du dig så tåbeligt?«

93 EN “It’s vile stuff,” said Billy. “I don’t want to run, but I don’t want to talk about it.”
DA »Frygteligt noget,« var Billy enig. »Det får mig ikke til at løbe, men jeg vil bestemt ikke tale om det.«

94 EN “There you are!” said Two Tails, waving his tail to explain.
DA »Dér har du det!« sagde To Haler og viftede med halen for at forklare.

95 EN “Surely. Yes, we have been here all night,” said the bullocks.
DA »Sandelig. Ja, vi har været her hele natten,« sagde studene.

96 EN Two Tails stamped his foot till the iron ring on it jingled. “Oh, I’m not talking to you. You can’t see inside your heads.”
DA To Haler stampede og fik jernringen om anklen til at klirre. »Åh, jeg taler ikke til jer. I kan ikke se billeder inde i hovedet.«

97 EN “No. We see out of our four eyes,” said the bullocks. “We see straight in front of us.”
DA »Nej, vi ser ud af vores fire øjne,« svarede de. »Og vi ser lige frem.«

98 EN “If I could do that and nothing else, you wouldn’t be needed to pull the big guns at all. If I was like my captain--he can see things inside his head before the firing begins, and he shakes all over, but he knows too much to run away--if I was like him I could pull the guns. But if I were as wise as all that I should never be here. I should be a king in the forest, as I used to be, sleeping half the day and bathing when I liked. I haven’t had a good bath for a month.”
DA »Hvis jeg kunne gøre det og intet andet, ville I slet ikke være nødvendige til at trække de store kanoner. Hvis jeg var som min kaptajn — han kan se ting inde i sit hoved, før skyderiet begynder, og han ryster over hele kroppen, men han ved for meget til at løbe væk — hvis jeg var som ham, kunne jeg trække kanonerne. Men hvis jeg var så klog, ville jeg aldrig være her. Jeg ville være konge i skoven, som jeg plejede, sovende halvdelen af dagen og badende, når jeg ville. Jeg har ikke fået et ordentligt bad i en måned.«

99 EN “That’s all very fine,” said Billy. “But giving a thing a long name doesn’t make it any better.”
DA »Det er alt sammen meget godt,« sagde Billy. »Men at give en ting et langt navn gør den ikke bedre.«

100 EN “H’sh!” said the troop horse. “I think I understand what Two Tails means.”
DA »Tys!« sagde hesten. »Jeg tror, jeg forstår, hvad To Haler mener.«

101 EN “You’ll understand better in a minute,” said Two Tails angrily. “Now you just explain to me why you don’t like this!”
DA »Du vil forstå bedre om et øjeblik,« sagde To Haler vredt. »Forklar mig nu, hvorfor I ikke kan lide dette!«

102 EN He began trumpeting furiously at the top of his trumpet.
DA Han begyndte at trompetere rasende af fuld kraft.

103 EN “Stop that!” said Billy and the troop horse together, and I could hear them stamp and shiver. An elephant’s trumpeting is always nasty, especially on a dark night.
DA »Stop det!« sagde Billy og hesten sammen, og jeg kunne høre dem stampe og ryste. Det er altid ubehageligt at høre en elefant trompetere, særlig i en mørk nat.

104 EN “I shan’t stop,” said Two Tails. “Won’t you explain that, please? Hhrrmph! Rrrt! Rrrmph! Rrrhha!” Then he stopped suddenly, and I heard a little whimper in the dark, and knew that Vixen had found me at last. She knew as well as I did that if there is one thing in the world the elephant is more afraid of than another it is a little barking dog. So she stopped to bully Two Tails in his pickets, and yapped round his big feet. Two Tails shuffled and squeaked. “Go away, little dog!” he said. “Don’t snuff at my ankles, or I’ll kick at you. Good little dog--nice little doggie, then! Go home, you yelping little beast! Oh, why doesn’t someone take her away? She’ll bite me in a minute.”
DA »Jeg stopper ikke,« sagde To Haler. »Forklar mig, hvorfor I reagerer sådan. Hhrrmph! Rrrt! Rrrmph! Rrrhha!« Pludselig tav han. Et lille klynk fortalte mig, at Vixen endelig havde fundet mig. Hun vidste lige så godt som jeg, at elefanter frygter små gøende hunde mere end næsten noget andet. Så hun stoppede hos ham ved hans pløkke for at drille ham og løb og gøede rundt om de store fødder, der var meget større end hele hende. Den store elefant sjokkede med fødderne og begyndte at hvine ynkeligt, mens han prøvede at komme væk fra hende, selv om han var bundet til pløkkene. »Væk, lille hund! Snus ikke til mine ankler, ellers sparker jeg. Godt, godt — søde lille vovse! Gå hjem, dit støjende lille bæst! Hvorfor tager ingen hende væk? Hun bider mig lige om lidt.«

105 EN “Seems to me,” said Billy to the troop horse, “that our friend Two Tails is afraid of most things. Now, if I had a full meal for every dog I’ve kicked across the parade-ground I should be as fat as Two Tails nearly.”
DA »Det ser ud til, at vores ven er bange for næsten alt,« sagde Billy til hesten. »Hvis jeg fik et måltid for hver hund, jeg har sparket hen over paradepladsen, ville jeg være næsten lige så fed som To Haler.«

106 EN I whistled, and Vixen ran up to me, muddy all over, and licked my nose, and told me a long tale about hunting for me all through the camp. I never let her know that I understood beast talk, or she would have taken all sorts of liberties. So I buttoned her into the breast of my overcoat, and Two Tails shuffled and stamped and growled to himself.
DA Jeg fløjtede, og Vixen løb hen til mig, mudret over det hele, og slikkede min næse og fortalte mig en lang historie om at jage efter mig gennem hele lejren. Jeg lod hende aldrig vide, at jeg forstod dyresprog, ellers ville hun have taget sig alle mulige friheder. Så knappede jeg hende ind ved brystet på min frakke, og To Haler sjokkede og stampede og brummede ved sig selv.

107 EN “Extraordinary! Most extraordinary!” he said. “It runs in our family. Now, where has that nasty little beast gone to?”
DA »Mærkeligt! Helt usædvanligt!« mumlede han. »Det går i arv i vores familie. Hvor blev det grimme lille dyr af?«

108 EN I heard him feeling about with his trunk.
DA Jeg hørte ham føle rundt med snablen.

109 EN “We all seem to be affected in various ways,” he went on, blowing his nose. “Now, you gentlemen were alarmed, I believe, when I trumpeted.”
DA »Vi er åbenbart alle sårbare over for forskellige ting,« fortsatte han og pustede i snablen. »I herrer virkede bange, da jeg trompeterede.«

110 EN “Not alarmed, exactly,” said the troop-horse, “but it made me feel as though I had hornets where my saddle ought to be. Don’t begin again.”
DA »Ikke ligefrem bange,« rettede hesten ham. »Mere som om jeg havde gedehamse, hvor sadlen sidder. Gør det ikke igen.«

111 EN “I’m frightened of a little dog, and the camel here is frightened by bad dreams in the night.”
DA »Jeg er bange for en lille hund, og kamelen her er bange for slemme drømme om natten.«

112 EN “It is very lucky for us that we haven’t all got to fight in the same way,” said the troop-horse.
DA »Det er meget heldigt for os, at vi ikke alle skal kæmpe på samme måde,« sagde hesten.

113 EN “What I want to know,” said the young mule, who had been quiet for a long time--“what I want to know is, why we have to fight at all.”
DA »Det, jeg vil vide,« sagde det unge muldyr, der havde været stille i lang tid — »det, jeg vil vide, er, hvorfor vi overhovedet skal kæmpe.«

114 EN “Because we’re told to,” said the troop-horse, with a snort of contempt.
DA »Fordi vi får besked på det,« sagde hesten med et hånligt fnys.

115 EN “Orders,” said Billy the mule, and his teeth snapped.
DA »Ordrer,« sagde Billy og klaprede med tænderne.

116 EN “Hukm hai!” (It is an order!), said the camel with a gurgle, and Two Tails and the bullocks repeated, “Hukm hai!”
DA »Hukm hai!« (Det er en ordre!), sagde kamelen med en gurgle, og To Haler og studene gentog: »Hukm hai!«

117 EN “Yes, but who gives the orders?” said the recruit-mule.
DA »Ja, men hvem giver ordrerne?« sagde rekrut-muldyret.

118 EN “The man who walks at your head--Or sits on your back--Or holds the nose rope--Or twists your tail,” said Billy and the troop-horse and the camel and the bullocks one after the other.
DA »Manden, der går ved dit hoved — eller sidder på din ryg — eller holder næserebet — eller drejer din hale,« sagde Billy og hesten og kamelen og studene én efter én.

119 EN “But who gives them the orders?”
DA »Men hvem giver dem ordrerne?«

120 EN “Now you want to know too much, young un,” said Billy, “and that is one way of getting kicked. All you have to do is to obey the man at your head and ask no questions.”
DA »Nu spørger du for meget, unge,« svarede Billy. »Den slags spørgsmål giver spark. Du skal bare adlyde manden ved dit hoved, som giver dig dine ordrer, og ikke stille ham spørgsmål.«

121 EN “He’s quite right,” said Two Tails. “I can’t always obey, because I’m betwixt and between. But Billy’s right. Obey the man next to you who gives the order, or you’ll stop all the battery, besides getting a thrashing.”
DA »Rigtigt,« var To Haler enig. »Jeg kan ikke altid adlyde, for jeg sidder fast midt imellem. Men Billy har ret: adlyd den, der står ved siden af dig og giver ordrer. Ellers stopper du hele batteriet og får tæsk oven i købet.«

122 EN The gun-bullocks got up to go. “Morning is coming,” they said. “We will go back to our lines. It is true that we only see out of our eyes, and we are not very clever. But still, we are the only people to-night who have not been afraid. Good-night, you brave people.”
DA Studene rejste sig. »Det bliver snart dag. Vi går tilbage til vores rækker. Vi ser kun gennem øjnene og er ikke særlig kloge. Men alligevel er vi de eneste af alle jer, der har talt her i nat, som aldrig har været bange for noget. Godnat, modige folk.«

123 EN Nobody answered, and the troop-horse said, to change the conversation, “Where’s that little dog? A dog means a man somewhere about.”
DA Ingen svarede, og hesten sagde, for at skifte emne: »Hvor er den lille hund? En hund betyder en mand et sted i nærheden.«

124 EN “Here I am,” yapped Vixen, “under the gun tail with my man. You big, blundering beast of a camel you, you upset our tent. My man’s very angry.”
DA »Her er jeg,« gøede Vixen. »Under kanonens bagende sammen med min mand. Din store, klodsede kamel, du væltede vores telt. Han er meget vred på dig.«

125 EN “Phew!” said the bullocks. “He must be white!”
DA »Hold da op!« sagde studene. »Han må være en hvid mand!«

126 EN “Of course he is,” said Vixen. “Do you suppose I’m looked after by a black bullock-driver?”
DA »Naturligvis er han det,« sagde Vixen. »Tror I, jeg passes af en sort studedriver?«

127 EN “Huah! Ouach! Ugh!” said the bullocks. “Let us get away quickly.”
DA »Huah! Ouach! Ugh!« sagde studene. »Lad os hurtigt komme væk.«

128 EN They plunged forward in the mud, and managed somehow to run their yoke on the pole of an ammunition wagon, where it jammed.
DA De væltede frem gennem mudderet og fik på en eller anden måde åget hægtet fast i stangen på en ammunitionsvogn, hvor det blev siddende helt fast.

129 EN “Now you have done it,” said Billy calmly. “Don’t struggle. You’re hung up till daylight. What on earth’s the matter?”
DA »Flot,« sagde Billy roligt. »Lad være med at kæmpe imod. I sidder fast, til det bliver lyst. Hvad er der egentlig galt med jer?«

130 EN The bullocks went off into the long hissing snorts that Indian cattle give, and pushed and crowded and slued and stamped and slipped and nearly fell down in the mud, grunting savagely.
DA Lange, hvæsende fnys brød ud af studene — den lyd, indisk kvæg laver. De skubbede, trængte, vred sig, stampede og gled og var nær ved at falde i mudderet, mens de gryntede vredt.

131 EN “You’ll break your necks in a minute,” said the troop-horse. “What’s the matter with white men? I live with ’em.”
DA »I brækker halsen om et øjeblik,« sagde hesten. »Hvad er der i vejen med hvide mænd? Jeg bor sammen med dem.«

132 EN “They--eat--us! Pull!” said the near bullock. The yoke snapped with a twang, and they lumbered off together.
DA »De — spiser — os! Træk!« sagde den nærmeste stud. Åget knækkede med et brag, og de ravede af sted sammen.

133 EN I never knew before what made Indian cattle so scared of Englishmen. We eat beef--a thing that no cattle-driver touches--and of course the cattle do not like it.
DA Jeg havde aldrig vidst før, hvad der gjorde indisk kvæg så bange for englændere. Vi spiser oksekød — en ting, som ingen kvægdriver rører ved — og selvfølgelig kan kvæget ikke lide det.

134 EN “May I be flogged with my own pad-chains! Who’d have thought of two big lumps like those losing their heads?” said Billy.
DA »Må jeg blive pisket med mine egne sadelkæder! Hvem skulle have tænkt, at to store klodser som dem ville miste fatningen?« sagde Billy.

135 EN “Never mind. I’m going to look at this man. Most of the white men, I know, have things in their pockets,” said the troop-horse.
DA »Glem dem. Jeg vil undersøge denne mand,« sagde hesten. »De fleste hvide mænd har noget spændende i lommerne.«

136 EN “I’ll leave you, then. I can’t say I’m over-fond of ’em myself. Besides, white men who haven’t a place to sleep in are more than likely to be thieves, and I’ve a good deal of Government property on my back. Come along, young un, and we’ll go back to our lines. Good-night, Australia! See you on parade to-morrow, I suppose. Good-night, old Hay-bale!--try to control your feelings, won’t you? Good-night, Two Tails! If you pass us on the ground tomorrow, don’t trumpet. It spoils our formation.”
DA »Så går jeg. Jeg er heller ikke særligt glad for dem. Desuden er en hvid mand uden seng nok en tyv, og jeg har masser af statens ejendom på ryggen. Kom, unge, tilbage til vores rækker. Godnat, Australien! Vi ses nok til morgendagens parade. Godnat, gamle Høbylte! — hold dine følelser i ave, ikke? Godnat, To Haler! Hvis du går forbi os i morgen, så lad være med at trompetere. Det ødelægger vores formation.«

137 EN Billy the Mule stumped off with the swaggering limp of an old campaigner, as the troop-horse’s head came nuzzling into my breast, and I gave him biscuits, while Vixen, who is a most conceited little dog, told him fibs about the scores of horses that she and I kept.
DA Muldyret Billy humpede af sted med en gammel feltsoldats svajende, let halte gang. Hesten snusede mod mit bryst, og jeg gav ham kiks. Imens fandt Vixen, der er en frygtelig indbildsk lille hund, på historier om de snesevis af heste, som hun og jeg ejede.

138 EN “I’m coming to the parade to-morrow in my dog-cart,” she said. “Where will you be?”
DA »I morgen kommer jeg til paraden i min lette, åbne vogn,« meddelte hun. »Hvor finder jeg dig?«

139 EN “On the left hand of the second squadron. I set the time for all my troop, little lady,” he said politely. “Now I must go back to Dick. My tail’s all muddy, and he’ll have two hours’ hard work dressing me for parade.”
DA »Yderst til venstre i anden eskadron. Jeg bestemmer farten for min trop, lille frøken,« svarede han høfligt. »Nu må jeg finde Dick. Min hale er mudret, og det koster ham to timers hårdt arbejde at gøre mig klar til paraden.«

140 EN The big parade of all the thirty thousand men was held that afternoon, and Vixen and I had a good place close to the Viceroy and the Amir of Afghanistan, with high, big black hat of astrakhan wool and the great diamond star in the center. The first part of the review was all sunshine, and the regiments went by in wave upon wave of legs all moving together, and guns all in a line, till our eyes grew dizzy. Then the cavalry came up, to the beautiful cavalry canter of “Bonnie Dundee,” and Vixen cocked her ear where she sat on the dog-cart. The second squadron of the Lancers shot by, and there was the troop-horse, with his tail like spun silk, his head pulled into his breast, one ear forward and one back, setting the time for all his squadron, his legs going as smoothly as waltz music. Then the big guns came by, and I saw Two Tails and two other elephants harnessed in line to a forty-pounder siege gun, while twenty yoke of oxen walked behind. The seventh pair had a new yoke, and they looked rather stiff and tired. Last came the screw guns, and Billy the mule carried himself as though he commanded all the troops, and his harness was oiled and polished till it winked. I gave a cheer all by myself for Billy the mule, but he never looked right or left.
DA Samme eftermiddag var alle de tredive tusind mænd på parade. Vixen og jeg havde fremragende pladser tæt på vicekongen og Afghanistans emir, hvis høje sorte astrakanhue bar en stor diamantstjerne. Under den første del af mønstringen skinnede solen klart, og vi kunne se tropperne tydeligt fra vores gode plads. Regiment efter regiment gik forbi med benene i takt og kanonerne på perfekt række, til vi blev svimle af at se på det. Så kom kavaleriet i smuk galop til »Bonnie Dundee«. Vixen spidsede øret fra vognen. Lancers' anden eskadron fejede forbi. Dér var vores hest med hale som spundet silke, hovedet trukket ind mod brystet, det ene øre frem og det andet tilbage. Benene bevægede sig som valsemusik og satte takten for hele eskadronen. Efter kavaleriet begyndte de store, tunge kanoner at komme forbi vores plads. To Haler og to andre elefanter trak en belejringskanon på fyrre pund i række, og tyve åg okser gik bagved. Det syvende par havde fået et nyt åg og så stive og trætte ud. Til sidst kom skruekanonerne. Billy bar sig, som om han kommanderede hele hæren, og hans olierede og polerede seletøj glimtede. Helt alene råbte jeg hurra for muldyret Billy, da han gik forbi os. Men han vendte aldrig hovedet, så hverken til højre eller venstre og fortsatte med sit batteri.

141 EN The rain began to fall again, and for a while it was too misty to see what the troops were doing. They had made a big half circle across the plain, and were spreading out into a line. That line grew and grew and grew till it was three-quarters of a mile long from wing to wing--one solid wall of men, horses, and guns. Then it came on straight toward the Viceroy and the Amir, and as it got nearer the ground began to shake, like the deck of a steamer when the engines are going fast.
DA Regnen vendte tilbage og skjulte et øjeblik tropperne i dis. De havde stillet sig i en bred halvcirkel hen over sletten og var ved at åbne sig til en række. Mens vi så på, strakte rækken sig længere og længere hen over sletten. Den blev ved med at vokse, til der var tre fjerdedele engelsk mil fra den ene fløj til den anden: en ubrudt mur af mænd, heste og kanoner. Den rykkede lige frem mod vicekongen og emiren. Da den kom nærmere, rystede jorden som dækket på en damper med maskinerne i fuld fart.

142 EN Unless you have been there you cannot imagine what a frightening effect this steady come-down of troops has on the spectators, even when they know it is only a review. I looked at the Amir. Up till then he had not shown the shadow of a sign of astonishment or anything else. But now his eyes began to get bigger and bigger, and he picked up the reins on his horse’s neck and looked behind him. For a minute it seemed as though he were going to draw his sword and slash his way out through the English men and women in the carriages at the back. Then the advance stopped dead, the ground stood still, the whole line saluted, and thirty bands began to play all together. That was the end of the review, and the regiments went off to their camps in the rain, and an infantry band struck up with--
DA Medmindre man har oplevet det, kan man ikke forestille sig, hvor skræmmende den jævne fremrykning ser ud, selv når man ved, at det kun er en parade. Jeg så på emiren. Indtil da havde han ikke vist det mindste tegn på overraskelse eller nogen anden følelse, hvor nøje jeg end iagttog hans ansigt. Nu blev hans øjne store. Han tog tøjlerne op fra hestens hals og så sig tilbage. Et øjeblik troede jeg, at han ville trække sit sværd og hugge sig vej gennem de engelske damer og herrer i vognene bagved. Så standsede hele den fremrykkende række pludselig på stedet. Den kom ikke et skridt nærmere, og bevægelsen, der havde virket så truende, var forbi. Jorden holdt op med at ryste, hele rækken hilste, og tredive musikkorps spillede på én gang. Mønstringen var slut. Regimenterne vendte tilbage til lejren gennem regnen, mens et infanterimusikkorps begyndte at spille:

143 EN The animals went in two by two,
Hurrah!
The animals went in two by two,
The elephant and the battery mul’,
and they all got into the Ark
For to get out of the rain!
DA Dyrene gik ind to og to,
Hurra!
Dyrene gik ind to og to,
elefanten og batteri-muldyret,
og de kom alle ind i Arken
for at slippe væk fra regnen!

144 EN Then I heard an old grizzled, long-haired Central Asian chief, who had come down with the Amir, asking questions of a native officer.
DA Så hørte jeg en ældre, gråhåret og langhåret høvding fra Centralasien, som fulgte med emiren, udspørge en indfødt officer.

145 EN “Now,” said he, “in what manner was this wonderful thing done?”
DA »Fortæl mig,« spurgte han, »hvordan blev denne forbløffende ting gjort?«

146 EN And the officer answered, “An order was given, and they obeyed.”
DA Og officeren svarede: »En ordre blev givet, og de adlød.«

147 EN “But are the beasts as wise as the men?” said the chief.
DA »Men er dyrene lige så kloge som mændene?« sagde høvdingen.

148 EN “They obey, as the men do. Mule, horse, elephant, or bullock, he obeys his driver, and the driver his sergeant, and the sergeant his lieutenant, and the lieutenant his captain, and the captain his major, and the major his colonel, and the colonel his brigadier commanding three regiments, and the brigadier the general, who obeys the Viceroy, who is the servant of the Empress. Thus it is done.”
DA »De adlyder, ligesom mændene gør. Muldyr, hest, elefant, stud — hver følger sin fører. Føreren følger sin sergent, sergenten sin løjtnant, løjtnanten sin kaptajn, kaptajnen sin major, majoren sin oberst. Obersten adlyder sin brigadegeneral, der kommanderer tre regimenter, brigadegeneralen adlyder generalen, generalen adlyder vicekongen, og vicekongen tjener kejserinden. Sådan gøres det.«

149 EN “Would it were so in Afghanistan!” said the chief, “for there we obey only our own wills.”
DA »Gid Afghanistan var sådan!« udbrød høvdingen. »Hjemme følger vi kun vores egne ønsker.«

150 EN “And for that reason,” said the native officer, twirling his mustache, “your Amir whom you do not obey must come here and take orders from our Viceroy.”
DA »Og derfor,« sagde officeren og snoede sit overskæg, »må den emir, som I nægter at adlyde, komme hertil og få sine ordrer fra vores vicekonge.«

151 EN Parade Song of the Camp Animals
DA Paradesang for lejrens dyr

152 EN ELEPHANTS OF THE GUN TEAMS
DA KANONHOLDENES ELEFANTER

153 EN We lent to Alexander the strength of Hercules,
The wisdom of our foreheads, the cunning of our knees;
We bowed our necks to service: they ne’er were loosed again,--
Make way there--way for the ten-foot teams
Of the Forty-Pounder train!
DA Vi lånte Alexander Herkules' styrke,
vores panders visdom, vores knæs list;
vi bøjede nakken i tjenesten og blev aldrig fri igen —
gør plads — plads for tifodsholdene
fra Fyrrepunds-toget!

154 EN GUN BULLOCKS
DA KANONSTUDE

155 EN Those heroes in their harnesses avoid a cannon-ball,
And what they know of powder upsets them one and all;
Then we come into action and tug the guns again--
Make way there--way for the twenty yoke
Of the Forty-Pounder train!
DA De helte i seletøj undgår en kanonkugle,
og hvad de ved om krudt, ryster dem alle som én;
så går vi i aktion og trækker kanonerne igen —
gør plads — plads for de tyve åg
fra Fyrrepunds-toget!

156 EN CAVALRY HORSES
DA KAVALERIHESTE

157 EN By the brand on my shoulder, the finest of tunes
Is played by the Lancers, Hussars, and Dragoons,
And it’s sweeter than “Stables” or “Water” to me--
The Cavalry Canter of “Bonnie Dundee”!
DA Ved brændemærket på min skulder: den fineste melodi
spilles af lancers, husarer og dragoner,
og den er sødere for mig end »Stalde« eller »Vand« —
kavalerigaloppen »Bonnie Dundee«!

158 EN Then feed us and break us and handle and groom,
And give us good riders and plenty of room,
And launch us in column of squadron and see
The way of the war-horse to “Bonnie Dundee”!
DA Så fodr os og træn os og pas os og strigl,
og giv os gode ryttere og masser af plads,
og send os afsted i eskadronskolonner og se
krigshestens vej til »Bonnie Dundee«!

159 EN SCREW-GUN MULES
DA SKRUEKANON-MULDYR

160 EN As me and my companions were scrambling up a hill,
The path was lost in rolling stones, but we went forward still;
For we can wriggle and climb, my lads, and turn up everywhere,
Oh, it’s our delight on a mountain height, with a leg or two to
spare!
DA Mens jeg og mine kammerater klatrede op ad en bakke,
forsvandt stien i rullende sten, men vi gik stadig fremad;
for vi kan vride os og klatre, drenge, og dukke op overalt,
åh, det er vores fryd på en bjergtop, med et ben eller to
til overs!

161 EN Good luck to every sergeant, then, that lets us pick our road;
Bad luck to all the driver-men that cannot pack a load:
For we can wriggle and climb, my lads, and turn up everywhere,
Oh, it’s our delight on a mountain height, with a leg or two to
spare!
DA Held og lykke til hver sergent, der lader os vælge vejen;
uheld til alle førere, der ikke kan pakke en last:
for vi kan vride os og klatre, drenge, og dukke op overalt,
åh, det er vores fryd på en bjergtop, med et ben eller to
til overs!

162 EN COMMISSARIAT CAMELS
DA FORSYNINGSKAMELER

163 EN We haven’t a camelty tune of our own
To help us trollop along,
But every neck is a hair trombone
(_Rtt-ta-ta-ta!_ is a hair trombone!)
And this our marching-song:
_Can’t!  Don’t!  Sha’n’t!  Won’t!_
Pass it along the line!
Somebody’s pack has slid from his back,
Wish it were only mine!
Somebody’s load has tipped off in the road--
Cheer for a halt and a row!
_Urrr!  Yarrh!  Grr!  Arrh!_
Somebody’s catching it now!
DA Vi har ikke nogen kamelsang af vores egen
til at hjælpe os med at traske afsted,
men hver hals er en hårtrombone
(_Rtt-ta-ta-ta!_ er en hårtrombone!)
og det er vores marchsang:
_Kan ikke! Gør ikke! Vil ikke! Skal ikke!_
Send det videre i rækken!
Nogens pakke er gledet af hans ryg,
bare det var min!
Nogens last er væltet på vejen —
hurra for et stop og et postyr!
_Urrr! Yarrh! Grr! Arrh!_
Nogen får det nu!

164 EN ALL THE BEASTS TOGETHER
DA ALLE DYR SAMMEN

165 EN Children of the Camp are we,
Serving each in his degree;
Children of the yoke and goad,
Pack and harness, pad and load.
See our line across the plain,
Like a heel-rope bent again,
Reaching, writhing, rolling far,
Sweeping all away to war!
While the men that walk beside,
Dusty, silent, heavy-eyed,
Cannot tell why we or they
March and suffer day by day.
_Children of the Camp are we,
Serving each in his degree;
Children of the yoke and goad,
Pack and harness, pad and load!_
DA Vi er lejrens børn,
hver tjener på sin plads;
åget og pigstavens børn,
pakke og seletøj, sadelpude og last.
Se vores række hen over sletten,
som et hælreb, der bøjes igen,
strækkende, vridende, rullende langt,
og fejende alt af sted til krig!
Mens mændene, der går ved siden af,
støvede, tavse, tunge i øjnene,
ikke kan sige, hvorfor vi eller de
marcherer og lider dag efter dag.
_Vi er lejrens børn,
hver tjener på sin plads;
åget og pigstavens børn,
pakke og seletøj, sadelpude og last!_

That afternoon all thirty thousand men paraded. Vixen and I had excellent places near the Viceroy and Afghanistan’s Amir, whose tall black astrakhan hat bore a great diamond star. During the first part of the review the sun shone brightly, and we could see the troops passing clearly from the excellent place where we sat. Regiment after regiment passed, legs moving together, guns perfectly aligned, until we grew dizzy watching. Then cavalry cantered beautifully to “Bonnie Dundee.” Vixen pricked an ear from the dog-cart. The Lancers’ second squadron swept by. There was our horse, tail like spun silk, head tucked toward his chest, one ear forward, one back. His legs moved like waltz music, setting his squadron’s rhythm. After the cavalry, the great heavy guns began to come past our place in the parade. Two Tails and two fellow elephants pulled a forty-pounder siege gun in line, with twenty yoke of oxen behind. Pair number seven wore a new yoke and looked stiff and tired. Last came the screw-guns. Billy carried himself as if commanding the entire army, his oiled and polished harness sparkling. All by myself I gave a cheer for Billy the mule as he passed us. But he never turned his head, never looked to the right or to the left, and went on with his battery.

en.title: The Jungle Book
en.author: Rudyard Kipling
en.openingText: It was seven o'clock of a very warm evening in the Seeonee hills when Father Wolf woke up from his day's rest, scratched himself, yawned, and spread out his paws one after the other to get rid of the sleepy feeling in their tips. Mother Wolf lay with her big gray nose dropped across her four tumbling, squealing cubs, and the moon shone into the mouth of the cave where they all lived. Then from the thicket came a sound that even Father Wolf knew — the drag and scramble and hiss of a big snake — and Tabaqui the Dish-licker, more than anyone else in the jungle, is able to make even a tiger unhappy.
en.about:
The Jungle Book is seven stories set in the jungles of India, each governed by a single law. The most famous three follow Mowgli, a human child raised from infancy by wolves, taught to hunt and speak by Baloo the bear and Bagheera the black panther, and eventually forced to choose between the wolf pack that is his family and the human village that is his origin. The other stories are complete in themselves: Rikki-Tikki-Tavi the mongoose versus a pair of cobras, the White Seal who leads his people to safety, and Kotick the seal's solo migration across the Pacific. Every story is about an individual learning the rules of the world they were born into — and whether those rules can hold when a creature doesn't fit the category the rules were written for.

Kipling published the stories in magazines in 1893 and collected them in 1894. The jungle world runs on the Law — a set of rules older than memory, governing every creature's behavior, enforced by the strong and respected by the wise. Mowgli's peculiar position is that he is the only creature who does not fully belong anywhere: too human for the jungle, too feral for the village, too intelligent for either. The stories that follow him from infancy to young manhood are about that displacement — and about what happens to creatures who know the Law perfectly but are not quite the thing the Law was designed for.

angleCards.title: The Law and the outlaw.
angleCards.text: The jungle runs on Law. Mowgli knows it better than anyone. And yet he is the one creature the Law cannot quite contain. What does it mean to master a set of rules you were never born into?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the question of what happens when a creature knows the Law perfectly but doesn't belong to the world that wrote it.

angleCards.title: Belonging and exile.
angleCards.text: Mowgli is refused by the wolves, feared by the village, and accepted by neither. His story is not about finding home — it is about learning to move without one. That is a harder lesson than survival.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Mowgli's displacement — the cost of belonging to two worlds and being fully claimed by neither.

angleCards.title: Power and loyalty.
angleCards.text: Shere Khan the tiger wants Mowgli dead from the beginning. Baloo and Bagheera protect him. The question the book keeps asking is who you owe your loyalty to when the ones who raised you and the ones who made you are different creatures.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track the loyalties — who protects Mowgli, who threatens him, and what he owes each of them in return.

angleCards.title: Each creature in its place.
angleCards.text: The non-Mowgli stories — the mongoose, the seal, the elephant — each follow a single creature discovering what it means to be exactly what it is. Kipling's argument is that knowing your nature is the beginning of mastery.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the standalone stories as arguments about nature and self-knowledge — each animal a case study in what it means to be fully what you are.

cast.name: Mowgli
cast.description: A human child who crawled into a wolf's den as an infant after Shere Khan killed his parents. Raised by Father Wolf and Mother Wolf, taught the Law by Baloo and strategy by Bagheera. He is stronger than any human child of his age, can speak every jungle tongue, and is the only creature who can stare a snake into stillness — because he is human, and humans have that gift. His problem is that the gift marks him as different from both worlds he inhabits, and the jungle and the village eventually force him to choose.

cast.name: Baloo
cast.description: The old brown bear, sleepy and enormous, who teaches the wolf cubs the Law of the Jungle. He takes a particular interest in Mowgli and spends years drumming the Master Words — the passwords of the jungle — into him. He is affectionate in the way of a creature that has watched many generations of cubs grow up and knows which ones will last. His claws are slow, but his knowledge is total, and he is the one Mowgli disobeys at the greatest cost to himself.

cast.name: Bagheera
cast.description: The black panther who bought Mowgli's life from the wolf pack with a freshly killed bull the night Mowgli was accepted. He was born in captivity in the King's palace at Oodeypore and has never forgotten what a cage is. He is the most intelligent adult in Mowgli's world — the one who tells Mowgli unpleasant truths, warns him about Shere Khan, and eventually shepherds him toward the human village. He loves Mowgli with the particular tenderness of a creature who knows what it is to not belong.

cast.name: Shere Khan
cast.description: The tiger who tried to kill Mowgli as an infant and has wanted him dead for fifteen years. He is lame from birth — the cattle villages he hunts have named the deformity — and the lameness makes him angry in the way of a creature who blames others for what he cannot change about himself. He is the tiger who hunts men because hunting men is easier than hunting deer, and he is the thing the jungle's other creatures fear most because he has no restraint. His quarrel with Mowgli is not personal at first; it becomes personal.

cast.name: Rikki-Tikki-Tavi
cast.description: A young mongoose washed out of his burrow by a flood and adopted by a British family in their garden bungalow. He is curious in the way all mongooses are curious — the motto of the family is 'run and find out' — and curiosity combined with a mongoose's reflexes makes him a lethal opponent. His opponents are Nag and Nagaina, the two king cobras who regard the garden as theirs by right. The story is a complete unit: a creature discovering what it is made for and proving it.

cast.name: Akela
cast.description: The leader of the Seeonee pack, old and dignified, who presided over the night Mowgli was accepted. He is one of those rare leaders whose authority rests entirely on demonstrated ability — he has led every hunt for years without a miss — and when he finally misses a kill, the pack is waiting for it. His fate and Mowgli's are tied from the beginning, and his loyalty to Mowgli is the loyalty of a leader who recognized something worth protecting when it was still small.

whyItMatters.title: A Foundational Myth of Belonging
whyItMatters.body: Mowgli's story is the founding version of a problem that every subsequent coming-of-age narrative has borrowed from: what happens to a person who grows up between worlds and is claimed by neither. The Tarzan stories, The Martian Chronicles, The Gruffalo — every narrative about a creature who must learn the rules of a community it wasn't born into is working in territory Kipling mapped. The specific genius of Kipling's version is that Mowgli never quite resolves the problem. He masters both worlds and belongs fully to neither. The ending is not a homecoming; it is an acknowledgment that some creatures have to keep moving. That is a harder and more honest conclusion than most of the versions that followed it.

whyItMatters.title: The Law as the Hidden Argument
whyItMatters.body: The Law of the Jungle is not decoration. It is the book's actual subject. Kipling's jungle runs on a set of rules older than memory — when to hunt, when to step aside, how a stronger creature treats a weaker one, what you owe the pack that raised you. The animal fables are the teaching mechanism; the Law is the philosophy. Every story tests the Law against an edge case: what happens when the creature who knows the rules best doesn't fit the category the rules were written for? What happens when a mongoose owns a garden that belongs to cobras by prior claim? The book is a sustained argument that order is valuable, that rules exist for reasons, and that the exceptions are the places where you discover what the reasons actually were. That argument has not dated.

whyItMatters.title: Kipling's Verse and the Voice of the Wild
whyItMatters.body: Each story opens with an epigraph in verse — the Night-Song in the Jungle, Mowgli's Song, the Law of the Jungle itself — and the verse register and the prose register are doing different things throughout the book. The prose is precise, sensory, and occasionally comic. The verse is ceremonial, older in feeling, closer to incantation than to narrative. Reading Kipling for the prose alone misses half the book. The verse carries the emotional claims — what the jungle is, what the Law demands, what it costs to be cast out of it — and the prose shows the cost in action. The combination is unusual in English children's literature and unique in the tradition the book founded.

responses.theme: The Law of the Jungle — what it actually is
responses.response:
The Law of the Jungle is the most misunderstood element of The Jungle Book. In popular use, "law of the jungle" means chaos — the strong doing whatever they want to the weak. In Kipling's book, it means the opposite. The Law is an ancient, intricate code governing every creature's behavior: when a wolf may hunt alone and when it must join the pack, how a stronger animal must treat a weaker one that submits, what rights a mother has over her cubs, what kills are forbidden and why. It is closer to a constitution than to anarchy.

Kipling's jungle is not savage in the sense of lawless. It is savage in the sense of serious. The consequences for breaking the Law are real — exile, death, social destruction — and the Law is enforced not by a single ruler but by collective memory and the pressure of the pack. Akela, the head wolf, does not make the Law; he embodies it. When he misses a hunt, he loses his authority not because someone overthrows him but because the Law specifies what authority requires.

Mowgli's position is illuminating precisely because he knows the Law better than most of the animals who were born into it. Baloo teaches it to him as a language student learns grammar — systematically, until the rules are internalized. The Master Words that open every creature's submission are part of the Law. The Law says no animal may kill a Man-cub in front of another. The Law says the river is neutral territory. The Law has provisions for every contingency.

And yet Mowgli doesn't quite fit inside it. He is human, which means he can make fire — the Red Flower — and fire is power the Law was not written to account for. When he drives the pack with fire at the end of "Mowgli's Brothers," he is using something outside the Law's categories. The Law cannot stop him. It also cannot contain him. That gap — between perfect knowledge of a system and genuine membership in it — is what the book keeps examining.

The question the Law raises is one every institution eventually faces: what do you do with the person who knows your rules better than your founding members, but was not there at the founding? The jungle's answer is to exile Mowgli. Whether that answer is right is what the book leaves for the reader to decide.

responses.theme: Kipling's India — the colonial context and what to do with it
responses.response:
Rudyard Kipling was born in Bombay in 1865, the son of a British colonial official. He spent his early childhood in India before being sent to England for schooling, and he spent his formative adult years back in India as a journalist. The Jungle Book was written in Vermont in 1892-93, from memory and imagination, by a man who knew India deeply and was also, unmistakably, a product of the British Empire.

The colonial question is real and cannot be avoided. Kipling's jungle is partly a vision of India that serves an imperial imagination: a landscape ordered by law and hierarchy, where strong and wise creatures maintain structures that lesser ones depend on, where the human village is backward and the creatures who know better stay clear of it. The contempt Mowgli eventually feels for the Bandar-log — the monkeys, who have no Law and no memory and no discipline — is the contempt of the organized for the chaotic. It is also the contempt a colonial administrator might feel for a society he considered ungoverned.

And yet Mowgli himself is not quite an imperial figure. He is a human child raised by animals — which inverts the usual hierarchy — and his power over both worlds depends not on force but on knowledge and cunning. The fire he wields at the end of the first story is dangerous precisely because it is not a civilized weapon; it is a jungle weapon in human hands. The book does not straightforwardly celebrate British civilization over Indian wilderness; it celebrates the Law, which both jungle and village fall short of.

The most honest approach to Kipling in 2026 is to read him knowing what he was, to recognize the period assumptions built into the text, and to take seriously what the stories are actually arguing — which is often stranger and less comfortable than colonial triumphalism. The Jungle Book was controversial in Kipling's own time for presenting animals as more dignified than humans. That argument has not entirely dated. The book is worth reading with both eyes open: for what it accomplishes and for what it cannot see.

Three of the seven stories in The Jungle Book have nothing to do with Mowgli. Rikki-Tikki-Tavi follows a young mongoose in a British family's garden in India. The White Seal follows Kotick, a white Pacific fur seal, on a decade-long search for a safe beach where his people can live without being slaughtered for their fur. Toomai of the Elephants follows a ten-year-old boy who witnesses the elephants' secret dance. These three stories feel different in register from the Mowgli cycle — shorter, more fable-like, each complete in one sitting.

The case for reading them is that they are the clearest statements of the book's deepest argument, which the Mowgli stories approach more obliquely. Each of the non-Mowgli stories follows a single creature discovering exactly what it is made for. Rikki-Tikki-Tavi is a mongoose: his nature is to kill snakes, and the story is about that nature being tested and proven. Kotick is a white seal with an unusual conscience: he cannot accept the slaughter as normal, searches for years for the alternative, and finds it. Toomai is a boy who loves elephants more than anything else, and his reward is to see what no human has seen.

Kipling's argument across all seven stories is consistent: the creatures who know their nature and act from it are the ones who survive and matter. The Bandar-log are pitiful because they have no nature — no consistent character, no law they hold to, no memory. Shere Khan is dangerous not because he is powerful but because his power has no principle behind it; he hunts men out of laziness and blames the resulting deformity on others. Baloo is formidable because he has been exactly what he is for so long that he has become very good at it.

The non-Mowgli stories are the book's argument in its simplest form. They are easier to read quickly; they are harder to misread. Kipling is not recommending determinism or fatalism. He is recommending the kind of self-knowledge that comes from taking seriously what you are actually drawn to, rather than what you think you should be. That is the argument. The mongoose knows. Does Mowgli?

preReadingChat.fallback: The Jungle Book is seven stories about creatures learning what they are and what they owe the world that made them. Mowgli is the most famous case — a human child raised by wolves, claimed by neither jungle nor village — but the whole book is an argument about the Law: the ancient set of rules governing every creature's behavior, and what happens at the edges where the rules don't quite fit. Ask me about anything from the Law to the colonial context to why the mongoose story is worth as much as the Mowgli stories.
